[[The World Factbook]] reports the total as 643,801 km2 (248,573 sq mi).{{Cite web |title=Field Listing :: Area |url=https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2147.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140131115000/https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2147.html |archive-date=31 January 2014 |access-date=1 November 2015 |website=The World Factbook |publisher=CIA}} {{PD-notice}} | today = | official_website = {{URL|www.gouvernement.fr}} }} '''France''' ({{Audio-IPA|en-us-France.ogg|/ˈfræns/}} or {{IPA|/ˈfrɑːns/}}; {{IPA-fr|fʁɑ̃s}}), officially the '''French Republic''' ({{lang-fr|link=no|République française}}, {{IPA-fr|ʁepyblik fʁɑ̃sɛz}}), is a country in [[Western Europe]]. It also includes various departments and territories of France overseas. Mainland France extends from the [[Mediterranean Sea]] to the [[English Channel]] and the [[North Sea]], and from the [[Rhine]] to the Atlantic Ocean. It is sometimes referred to as ''L’Hexagone'' ("The [[Hexagon]]") because of the shape of its territory. France is a [[unitary state|unitary]] [[semi-presidential]] republic. The [[head of state]] is the President, who is also a politician. The Prime Minister is secondary to the President. [[Metropolitan France]] is bordered (clockwise from the North) by [[Belgium]], [[Luxembourg]], [[Germany]], [[Switzerland]], [[Italy]], [[Monaco]], [[Andorra]], and Spain. The overseas departments and collectives of France share land borders with Brazil and [[Suriname]] (bordering [[French Guiana]]), and the [[Netherlands Antilles]] (bordering [[Collectivity of Saint Martin|Saint Martin]]). France is linked to the United Kingdom by the [[Channel Tunnel]], which passes under the English Channel. France is the largest country in the [[European Union]] and the second largest in Europe. It has been a major global power for centuries. During the 17th and 18th centuries, France colonized much of North America. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, France built one of the largest colonial empires of the time. This included large parts of [[North Africa|North]], [[West Africa|West]] and Central Africa, Southeast Asia, and many [[Pacific Islands]]. France is a [[developed country]] and has a large economy.[https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/fields/2195.html Field listing - GDP (official exchange rate)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081004071135/https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook//fields/2195.html |date=4 October 2008 }}, CIA World Factbook: List of countries by nominal GDP figures. It is the most visited country in the world, with 82 million foreign visitors every year.{{cite web|publisher=Direction du Tourisme (French government's tourism agency)|url=http://www.tourisme.gouv.fr/fr/z2/stat/tis/att00018288/TIS_EVE2007_2008-5.pdf|title=Le tourisme international en France en 2007|accessdate=5 June 2008|archive-date=24 June 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080624195206/http://www.tourisme.gouv.fr/fr/z2/stat/tis/att00018288/TIS_EVE2007_2008-5.pdf|url-status=dead}} {{in lang|fr}} France was one of the first members of the [[European Union]], and has the largest land area of all members. It is also a founding member of the United Nations, and a member of the [[Organisation internationale de la Francophonie|Francophonie]], the [[G8]], [[NATO]], and the [[Latin Union]]. It is one of the five permanent members of the [[United Nations Security Council]]. France has the largest number of [[nuclear weapon]]s with active warheads, and the largest number of [[nuclear power]] plants, in the European Union. France's official language is [[French language|French]], which is also official in 29 other countries. == Geography and climate == France is in Western Europe.{{cite web|url=http://www.essex.ac.uk/armedcon/world/europe/western_europe/default.html|title=Western Europe|accessdate=2 August 2010|archive-date=12 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160912161954/http://www.essex.ac.uk/armedcon/world/europe/western_europe/default.html|url-status=live}} France shares its borders with [[Belgium]], [[Luxembourg]], Germany, [[Switzerland]], Italy, [[Monaco]], [[Andorra]], and Spain.{{cite web|url=http://www.kwintessential.co.uk/articles/article/France/Geography-of-France/540|title=French Geography|accessdate=2 August 2010|archive-date=31 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110831213549/http://www.kwintessential.co.uk/articles/article/france/Geography-of-France/540|url-status=live}} France has two mountain ranges near its borders: the [[Alps]] in the east and the [[Pyrenees]] in the south. France has a [[Mediterranean climate]]. The climate of southern France is similar to that of [[Greece]]. There are many rivers in France, including the [[Seine]] and the [[Loire River|Loire]].{{cite web|url=http://www.francethisway.com/tourism/french-rivers.php|title=French Rivers|accessdate=2 August 2010|archive-date=27 June 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100627160207/http://www.francethisway.com/tourism/french-rivers.php|url-status=live}} In the north and the west of France, there are low hills and river valleys. In France there are many different [[climate]]s.{{cite web|url=http://www.worldtravelguide.net/country/92/climate/Europe/France.html|title=Climates of France|author=World Travel Guide|accessdate=2 August 2010|archive-date=5 August 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100805103456/http://www.worldtravelguide.net/country/92/climate/Europe/France.html|url-status=live}} The [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] has a major effect on the weather in the north and west. This means the temperature is about the same most of the year. It is in the marine west coast climate region. In the east, winters are cold and the weather is good. Summers are hot and stormy. In the south, winters are cool and [[rain|wet]]. Summers are hot and dry.{{cite web|url=http://www.francetourism.com/practicalinfo/general.htm|publisher=French Tourist Office|accessdate=30 September 2009|title=Practical Information on France – General|archive-date=5 August 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090805195645/http://www.francetourism.com/practicalinfo/general.htm|url-status=dead}} The north has a temperate climate similar to that of the United Kingdom and other Northern European countries. France has the second-largest [[exclusive economic zone]] (EEZ) in the world.{{cite web|url=http://www.developpementdurable.com/economie/2010/07/A2769/mediterranee-la-france-prend-le-controle-en-creant-une-zone-economique-exclusive.html|title=EEZ of France|accessdate=1 August 2010|archive-date=30 April 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110430124908/http://www.developpementdurable.com/economie/2010/07/A2769/mediterranee-la-france-prend-le-controle-en-creant-une-zone-economique-exclusive.html|url-status=live}} {{in lang|fr}} It covers 11,035,000 km2 (4,260,637 sq mi). Only the United States has a larger one. == History == === Name === The name "France" comes from the [[Latin]] word Francia, which means "land of the [[Franks]]".{{cite web|url=http://www.thesunchronicle.com/articles/2008/04/20/features/3057797.txt|title=Origin of Francia|work=The Sun Chronicle|date=20 April 2008 |accessdate=3 August 2010}} === Roman Gaul === The borders of modern France are about the same as those of ancient [[Gaul]] in which [[Celt]]ic Gauls inhabited. [[Julius Caesar]] conquered Gaul for [[Roman Republic|Rome]] in the 1st century BC.{{cite web|url=http://www.discoverfrance.net/France/History/Roman_Empire.shtml|title=Caesar Conquered Gaul|work=discoverfrance.net|author=Discover France|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=12 June 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612002809/http://discoverfrance.net/France/History/Roman_Empire.shtml|url-status=live}} Eventually, the Gauls adopted the Romans' language,[[Latin]], from which [[French]] evolved, and culture. [[History of Christianity|Christianity]] first appeared in the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD and became firmly established by the 4th and 5th centuries. [[File:Map France 1477-fr.svg|thumb|left|France in 1477. Red line: limit of the Kingdom of France; light blue: the royal domain]] === Franks === In the 4th century AD, the [[Germanic peoples|Germanic tribes]], principally the Franks, invaded the Gauls, when the name ''Francie'' appeared. The modern name "France" comes from the name of the [[Capetian dynasty|Capetian]] Kings of France around Paris. The Franks were the first tribe of Europe after the fall of the Roman Empire to convert to the [[pope]]'s Christianity, rather than [[Arianism]]. The French called themselves "the most Christian Kingdom of France".{{cite web|url=http://www.wf-f.org/03-1-France.html|title=France used this pretext to call themselves this|author=wff|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=22 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722112834/http://www.wf-f.org/03-1-France.html|url-status=dead}} The [[Treaty of Verdun]] (843), divided [[Charlemagne]]'s Empire into three parts.{{cite web|url=http://www.francebalade.com/histo/carolin.htm|title=Division of Charlemagne's empire into three parts|author=France Balade|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=19 October 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101019023417/http://www.francebalade.com/histo/carolin.htm|url-status=live}} {{in lang|fr}} The largest area was Western Francia and had borders that were similar to those of modern France. === Kingdom === ==== Middle Ages ==== The [[Carolingian]] [[dynasty]] ruled France until 987, when [[Hugh Capet of France|Hugh Capet]] became [[King of France]]. His descendants, the [[Capetian dynasty|Direct Capetians]], the [[House of Valois]] and the [[House of Bourbon]], unified the country with many wars and dynastic inheritance. One of the most famous kings, [[Louis XIV]], ruled from 1643 to 1715, the longest in French history. ==== Enlightenment ==== The monarchy was the most [[great power|power]]ful during the 17th century and the reign of Louis XIV.{{cite web|url=http://www.uncg.edu/rom/courses/dafein/civ/timeline.htm|title=French History - Le Grand Siècle|author=UNCG|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=1 March 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090301141722/http://www.uncg.edu/rom/courses/dafein/civ/timeline.htm|url-status=dead}} At the time, France had the [[Demographics of France|largest population in Europe]]. The country had a large influence over European politics, economy, and culture. French became the common language of diplomacy in international affairs. Much of the [[Age of Enlightenment]] happened in France. French scientists made big [[Science|scientific]] discoveries in the 18th century. France also [[invasion|conquered]] many [[French overseas collectivities|overseas possessions]] in the Americas and Asia.{{cite web|url=http://www.understandfrance.org/France/History3.html|title=French colonies History|author=Understand France|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=22 September 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100922052426/http://www.understandfrance.org/France/History3.html|url-status=live}} === Republic === ==== Napoleonic Wars ==== France had a monarchy until the [[French Revolution]] caused King [[Louis XVI of France|Louis XVI]] and his wife, [[Marie Antoinette]], to be executed in 1793. [[Maximilien Robespierre]] was a dictator until he was executed himself in 1794.{{cite web|url=http://www.lucidcafe.com/library/95nov/antoinette.html|title=Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette's executions|author=Lucidcafé|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=9 June 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070609055954/http://www.lucidcafe.com/library/95nov/antoinette.html|url-status=dead}} Thousands of other French citizens were killed. [[Napoleon Bonaparte]] took control of the republic in 1799. He later made himself Emperor of the First Empire (1804–1814). His armies conquered most of continental Europe.{{cite web|url=http://www.napoleonguide.com/campind.htm|title=Campaigns of Napoleon Bonaparte|author=Napoleonguide.com|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=23 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100723235623/http://www.napoleonguide.com/campind.htm|url-status=live}} The [[metric system]] was invented by French scientists during the French revolution. That time 3 estates were developed. After Napoleon's final defeat in 1815 at the [[Battle of Waterloo]], the monarchy was restored. An interesting fact is that the French King Louis XIX was king for only 20 minutes from the time his father [[Charles X]] abdicated, to the time the [[July Monarchy]] started in 1830. [[Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte]], Napoleon's nephew, came to power in 1848 and started the Second Empire in 1852. He was removed after the French defeat in the [[Franco-Prussian War]] in 1870. The Third Republic replaced his [[regime]].{{cite web|url=http://www.intellego.fr/soutien-scolaire-3eme/aide-scolaire-Education-civique-juridique-et-sociale/Les-regimes-politiques-de-France-de-1780-a-nos-jours./31424|title=Regimes of France|author=Intellego|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=24 April 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100424200837/http://www.intellego.fr/soutien-scolaire-3eme/aide-scolaire-education-civique-juridique-et-sociale/les-regimes-politiques-de-france-de-1780-a-nos-jours./31424|url-status=live}} {{in lang|fr}} ==== Colonialism ==== The large [[French colonial empire]] in the 19th century included parts of [[West Africa]] and [[Southeast Asia]]. The culture and the politics of those regions were [[influence]]d by France. Many countries that were French [[colony|colonies]] still have French as their official language.{{cite web|url=http://www.alsintl.com/resources/languages/French/|title=French language in Colonies|author=alsintl.com|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=1 September 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100901085645/http://www.alsintl.com/resources/languages/French/|url-status=dead}} ==== World Wars ==== The country actively took part in both the [[World War I]] and [[World War II]], with many battles against Germany taking place on its soil. During World War I, millions were killed in the [[Trench warfare|trenches]], including over a million at the [[Battle of the Somme]].{{cite web|url=http://www.firstworldwar.com/battles/somme.htm|title=Battle of the Somme|author=firstworldwar.com|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=16 March 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150316141435/http://www.firstworldwar.com/battles/somme.htm|url-status=live}} The conditions were extremely difficult for the soldiers on the front. The last surviving veteran was Pierre Picault, who died on 20 November 2008 at the age of 109.[http://dersdesders.free.fr/france.html Ders Des Ders Report - France] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717180723/http://dersdesders.free.fr/france.html |date=17 July 2011 }} {{in lang|fr}} During the World War II, Germany occupied France. The [[Allies of World War II|Allies]] landed in [[Normandy]] on 6 June 1944 and began the [[Battle of Normandy]]. The German forces lost France in just a few months. ==Divisions== The 13 regions and 96 [[departments of France|departments]] of [[metropolitan France]] include [[Corsica]]. France is divided into (administrative) regions: * [[Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes]] * [[Bourgogne-Franche-Comté]] * [[Brittany]] (''Bretagne'') * [[Centre-Val de Loire]] * [[Corsica]] (''Corse'') * [[Grand Est]] * [[Hauts-de-France]] * [[Île-de-France]] * [[Normandy]] (''Normandie'') * [[Nouvelle-Aquitaine]] * [[Occitanie]] * [[Pays de la Loire]] * [[Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur]] Corsica has a different status than the other 12 metropolitan regions. It is called ''[[collectivité territoriale]]''. France also has five [[Overseas Regions of France|overseas regions]]: * [[French Guiana]] (in South America) * [[Guadeloupe]] (in the Caribbean) * [[Martinique]] (in the Caribbean) * [[Mayotte]] (in the Indian Ocean) * [[Réunion]] (in the Indian Ocean) These five overseas regions have the same status as the metropolitan ones. They are like the overseas American states of [[Alaska]] and Hawaii. Then France is divided into 101 [[Departments of France|departments]]. The departments are divided into 342 [[Arrondissements of France|arrondissements]]. The ''arrondissements'' are re-divided into 4,032 [[Cantons of France|cantons]]. The smallest [[Administrative division|subdivision]] is the [[Communes of France|commune]] (there are 36,699 communes). On 1 January 2008, [[INSEE]] counted 36,781 communes in France. 36,569 of them are in [[metropolitan France]] and 212 of them are in [[overseas France]].{{in lang|fr}} {{cite web|url=http://www.insee.fr/fr/methodes/nomenclatures/cog/documentation.asp|title=Code officiel géographique – Présentation|publisher=INSEE|accessdate=27 June 2008|archive-date=4 April 2012|archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/66gU6nxGq?url=http://www.insee.fr/fr/methodes/nomenclatures/cog/documentation.asp|url-status=live}}{{in lang|fr}} {{cite web|url=http://www.insee.fr/fr/methodes/default.asp?page=nomenclatures/cog/outremer.htm|title=Code des collectivités d'outre-mer (COM)|publisher=INSEE|accessdate=27 June 2008|archive-date=4 April 2012|archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/66gU97b9F?url=http://www.insee.fr/fr/methodes/default.asp?page=nomenclatures%2Fcog%2Foutremer.htm|url-status=live}} == Government == The [[government of France]] is a [[semi-presidential system]] determined by the constitution of the [[French Fifth Republic]].{{cite web|url=http://www.absoluteastronomy.com/topics/Semi-presidential_system|title=France's political system|access-date=12 September 2009|archive-date=8 December 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091208120448/http://www.absoluteastronomy.com/topics/Semi-presidential_system|url-status=live}} It provides for a [[separation of powers]].{{cite web|author=Guy Carcassonne|title=Separation of Powers|url=http://www.unc.edu/depts/europe/francophone/principles_en.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100601200220/http://www.unc.edu/depts/europe/francophone/principles_en.pdf|archive-date=1 June 2010|publisher=unc.edu|accessdate=4 August 2010}} The main ideals are expressed in the [[Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen]]. The constitution declares the nation to be "an indivisible, secular, democratic, and social Republic". With a Prime Minister subordinate to the President, this slightly strange system was chosen by General [[Charles de Gaulle]] in 1958. == Military == [[File:Gaule96.jpg|thumb|right|Nuclear [[aircraft carrier]] ''Charles de Gaulle'']] [[File:French Republican Guard Bastille Day 2007 n4.jpg|thumb|upright|French Republican Guard]] The French armed forces has four branches: * The ''Armée de Terre'' (Army) * The ''Marine Nationale'' (Navy) * The ''Armée de l'Air'' (Air Force) * The ''Gendarmerie Nationale'' (a military force which acts as a National Rural Police) France has about 359,000 military personnel.{{cite web|url=http://www.csis.org/media/csis/pubs/060626_asia_balance_powers.pdf|title=Number of military personnel in France, page 32|access-date=26 November 2008|archive-date=26 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226073401/https://www.csis.org/media/csis/pubs/060626_asia_balance_powers.pdf|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=http://www.csis.org/media/csis/pubs/westmb012302%5B1%5D.pdf|title=Number of military personnel in France, page 112|access-date=26 November 2008|archive-date=17 June 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090617081254/http://www.csis.org/media/csis/pubs/westmb012302%5B1%5D.pdf|url-status=live}} France spends 2.6% of its gross domestic product (GDP) on [[defense (military)|defense]]. This is the highest in the [[European Union]]. France and the UK spend 40% of the EU defense [[budget]]. About 10% of France's defense budget is for its [[nuclear weapons]] force. == Economy == [[File:A380 Reveal 2.jpg|thumb|The first completed [[Airbus A380]] in [[Toulouse]] on 18 January 2005. Airbus is a symbol of the [[globalization]] of the French and European economy.]] France is a member of the [[G7]] (previously [[G8]]) , group of [[wikt:lead#Verb|leading]] [[wikt:industry|industrialized]] countries and [[G20]]. France has the eighth-largest economy in the world by [[gross domestic product|Gross domestic product (GDP)]] (which takes into account how much it costs to live in different countries and inflation rates).{{cite web|url=https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2001rank.html|title = CIA World Factbook GDP PPP data update of 2008|publisher = US Government|date = 20 November 2008|access-date = 26 November 2008|archive-date = 27 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200527163315/https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2001rank.html|url-status = live}} France and 11 other [[European Union]] members jointly launched the [[euro]] on 1 January 1999 and started using it in 2002.{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/1845045.stm|title=Euro launched in 12 countries|access-date=12 September 2009|archive-date=27 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927153443/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/1845045.stm|url-status=live}} France's economy has nearly 2.9 million registered companies.{{cite web|url=http://www.journaldunet.com/management/repere/entreprises_france_type.shtml|title=Number of companies in France|access-date=26 November 2008|archive-date=17 December 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081217093527/http://www.journaldunet.com/management/repere/entreprises_france_type.shtml|url-status=live}} The government has a considerable influence over railway, electricity, aircraft, and telecommunications firms (as it owns big companies like [[SNCF]] and [[Électricité de France|EDF]] (French electricity)).{{cite web|url=http://investisseurs.edf.com/the-edf-group/edf-investors/stock-information/shareholding-policy-117065.html|title=Shareholding policy|date=31 December 2007|publisher=Électricité de France|accessdate=5 April 2009|archive-date=9 July 2012|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120709190130/http://investisseurs.edf.com/the-edf-group/edf-investors/stock-information/shareholding-policy-117065.html|url-status=dead}} France has an important aerospace (design of aircraft and [[spacecraft]]) industry led by [[Airbus]].{{in lang|fr}} {{cite web|url=http://www.ademe.fr/midi-pyrenees/documents/a_3/cnes_dossier_presse.pdf| title=France| author=CNES| accessdate=30 May 2007| archive-date=29 June 2007| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070629155229/http://www.ademe.fr/midi-pyrenees/documents/a_3/cnes_dossier_presse.pdf| url-status=dead}} It can also launch [[rocket]]s from [[French Guiana]].{{cite web|url=http://www.russianspaceweb.com/kourou_origin.html|title=Rocket launch site in Kourou|access-date=12 September 2009|archive-date=4 June 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090604112430/http://www.russianspaceweb.com/kourou_origin.html|url-status=live}} France has invested a lot in [[nuclear power]]. This made France the smallest producer of [[Greenhouse gas|carbon dioxide]] among the seven most industrialized countries in the world.{{cite web|url=http://www.bls-frenchcourses.com/french-economy-industry-GB.html|title=France, smallest producer of CO2|access-date=12 September 2009|archive-date=27 June 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090627085127/http://www.bls-frenchcourses.com/french-economy-industry-GB.html|url-status=dead}} As a result, 59 nuclear power plants generate most of the electricity produced in the country (78% in 2006,{{cite web|author=DGEMP / Observatoire de l'énergie|date=April 2007|url=http://www.industrie.gouv.fr/energie/statisti/se_elec.htm|title=Électricité en France: les principaux résultats en 2006.|accessdate=23 May 2007|archive-date=3 June 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070603104111/http://www.industrie.gouv.fr/energie/statisti/se_elec.htm|url-status=live}} up from only 8% in 1973, 24% in 1980, and 75% in 1990). France is the leading agricultural producer and exporter in Europe.{{cite web|url=http://www.ameinfo.com/185827.html|title=France is the leading agricultural producer and exporter in Europe|access-date=12 September 2009|archive-date=13 May 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120513235600/http://www.ameinfo.com/185827.html|url-status=live}} France exports wheat, poultry, dairy products, beef, and pork. It is also famous for its wine industry. France received 10 billion euros in 2006 from the European Community as [[Subsidy|subsidies]] to its farmers.{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/4407792.stm|title = Q&A: Common Agricultural Policy|work = BBC News|date = 20 November 2008|access-date = 6 February 2009|archive-date = 5 February 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090205122234/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/4407792.stm|url-status = live}} At one time, the Factory Act of 1833 limited the workday for women and children to 11 hours a day.{{cite web |url=http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/lesson13.htm |title=1833 Factory Act |accessdate=14 March 2010 |author=Kew|author2=Richmond|author3=Surrey |work=The National Archives |archive-date=10 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140410122152/http://nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/lesson13.htm |url-status=live }} [[File:Chateau de Montsoreau Museum of contemporary art Loire Valley France.jpg|thumb|The [[Château de Montsoreau]] is the only castle in France built in the [[Loire]] river bed.]] == Demographics == On 1 January 2008, it was estimated that 63.8 million people live in France, including in the [[Overseas Regions of France]].{{cite web|url=http://www.insee.fr/en/themes/document.asp?ref_id=ip1170®_id=0|title=Demographic report 2007 - The birth rate remains very high|publisher=Government of France - INSEE|accessdate=15 January 2008|archive-date=21 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210521172701/https://www.insee.fr/en/statistiques|url-status=live}} 61,875,000 of these live in metropolitan France, the part of the country that is within Europe. === Ethnic groups === The major ethnic groups living in France today are descended from [[Celt|Celtic people]] and [[Ancient Rome|Roman people]].{{cite web|url=http://www.state.gov/r/pa/ei/bgn/3842.htm|title = Background Note: France|work = Under Secretary for Public Diplomacy and Public Affairs > Bureau of Public Affairs > Bureau of Public Affairs: Electronic Information and Publications Office > Background Notes - Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs|date = August 2008|publisher = U.S. State Department|accessdate = 24 October 2008|archive-date = 13 September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120913082425/http://www.state.gov/r/pa/ei/bgn/3842.htm|url-status = live}} The significant minority groups living in France are: * Teutonic, that is [[Germanic peoples]] * [[Slavic peoples|Slavic]] * people from North Africa * Sub-Saharan African - people from Africa who live south of the [[Sahara]] desert * people from [[Indochina]] * people from the [[Basque Country (greater region)|Basque Country]] of southwest Europe * [[Roma people|Romani people]] === Racism === Racism takes various forms: discrimination, violence, prejudice, segregation, etc., some on the rise, others on the decline. Moreover, it only takes one attack to succeed, or fail, for the figures for racist violence to skyrocket or, on the contrary, stagnate in France.[https://theconversation.com/la-france-raciste-mieux-construire-les-termes-du-debat-255691 Is France racist? Better constructing the terms of the debate], The Conversation, 2025-05-15 == Culture == [[File:Claude Monet 1899 Nadar.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Claude Monet]], founder of the [[Impressionism|Impressionist]] movement]] === Language === {{main|French language}} French is the official [[language]] of France. It belongs to the [[Romance language]] group, which includes Italian and Spanish. Many regional [[dialect]]s are also used in France. [[Alsatian language|Alsatian]], a German dialect, is spoken in [[Alsace]] and in parts of [[Lorraine]] in eastern France. French was the language of diplomacy and culture in Europe between the 17th and 19th century and is still widely used.{{cite web|url=http://www.history.com/encyclopedia.do?articleId=207636|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080423103843/http://www.history.com/encyclopedia.do?articleId=207636|archivedate=23 April 2008|title=France an important language of diplomacy}} Some people in France also speak [[Basque language|Basque]], [[Breton language|Breton]], [[Catalan language|Catalan]], [[Corsican language|Corsican]], German, [[Flemish language|Flemish]], and [[Occitan language|Occitan]]. There is around 200,000 [[Romani language|Romani]] speakers in France, 950,000 speakers of different [[Arabic]] dialects (plus 220,000 occasional speakers) and 1.5 – 2 million speakers of different Berber dialects.{{cite web|url= https://minorityrights.org/country/france/|title= France - World Directory of Minorities & Indigenous Peoples|date= 2 November 2023}} === Religion === {{bar box |title=France religiosity |titlebar=#ddd |left1=religion |right1=percent |float=right |bars= {{bar percent|Christianity|blue|54}} {{bar percent|Not religious|gray|31}} {{bar percent|Islam|green|5}} {{bar percent|Judaism|pink|1}} {{bar percent|Other religions
or no opinion|brown|10}} }} France is a [[Secularism|secular]] country and the constitution guarantees freedom of religion.{{cite web|url=http://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/connaissance/constitution.asp|title=Constitution of 1958|accessdate=13 August 2010|publisher=Assemblée Nationale|archive-date=6 November 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131106014452/http://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/connaissance/constitution.asp|url-status=live}} {{in lang|fr}} The population is about 51% [[Roman Catholic]], and 31% of people are agnostics or [[Atheism|atheists]]. 5% are [[Muslim]], 3% say they are [[Protestant]] and 1% say they are Jewish. 10% are from other religions or do not have an opinion about religion.{{cite web |author=Catholic World News |year=2003 |url=http://www.catholicculture.org/news/features/index.cfm?recnum=48547 |title=France is no longer Catholic, survey shows |accessdate=11 January 2007 |archive-date=1 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110501035606/http://www.catholicculture.org/news/features/index.cfm?recnum=48547 |url-status=live }}{{in lang|ro}} [http://www.cotidianul.ro/franta_nu_mai_e_o_tara_catolica-20395.html Franţa nu mai e o ţară catolică] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090129144728/http://www.cotidianul.ro/franta_nu_mai_e_o_tara_catolica-20395.html |date=29 January 2009 }}, ''[[Cotidianul]]'' 11 January 2007 There are also [[Zoroastrian]], [[Unitarian Universalism|Unitarian Universalist]], [[Jainism|Jain]] and [[Wicca]]n communities. Religions founded in France include [[Raelism]]. According to a Poll in 2007:{{cite web |url=http://ec.europa.eu/public_opinion/archives/ebs/ebs_225_report_en.pdf | title=Eurobarometer on Social Values, Science and technology 2005 - page 11 | accessdate=5 May 2007 | archive-date=21 August 2011 | archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/616ESNz5H?url=http://ec.europa.eu/public_opinion/archives/ebs/ebs_225_report_en.pdf | url-status=live }} * '''34%''' of French citizens responded that ''"they believe there is a God"''. * '''27%''' answered that ''"they believe there is some sort of [[spirit]] or life force"''. * '''33%''' answered that ''"they do not believe there is any sort of spirit, God, or life force"''. === Literature === {{main|French literature}} [[File:Dartagnan-musketeers.jpg|right|thumb|''The Three Musketeers'' by [[Alexandre Dumas, père|Alexandre Dumas]]]] French literature began in the [[Middle Ages]].{{cite web|url=http://www.discoverfrance.net/France/Literature/DF_literature.shtml|title=French literature started in the Middle Ages|access-date=12 September 2009|archive-date=19 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160419194513/http://www.discoverfrance.net/France/Literature/DF_literature.shtml|url-status=live}} French was divided into several dialects at the time. Some authors [[spelling|spelled]] words differently from one other. During the 17th century, [[Pierre Corneille]], [[Jean Racine]], [[Molière]], [[Blaise Pascal]] and [[René Descartes]] were the main authors.{{cite web|url=http://17emesiecle.free.fr/Auteurs.php|title=French authors of the 17th century|author=17eme siecle|accessdate=2 August 2010|archive-date=26 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100726070006/http://17emesiecle.free.fr/Auteurs.php|url-status=live}} In the 18th and 19th centuries, French literature and poetry reached its best. The 18th century saw writings of authors, essayists and moralists as [[Voltaire]] and [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau]]. As for French children's literature in those times, [[Charles Perrault]] wrote stories such as "[[Little Red Riding Hood]]", "[[Beauty and the Beast]]", "[[Sleeping Beauty]]" and "[[Puss in Boots]]".{{cite web|url=http://www.perraultfairytales.com/en/stories|title=Perrault's tales|accessdate=12 September 2010|publisher=PerraultFairyTales.com|archive-date=15 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110715065339/http://www.perraultfairytales.com/en/stories|url-status=dead}} Many famous French novels were written in the 19th century by authors such as [[Victor Hugo]], [[Alexandre Dumas, père|Alexandre Dumas]] and [[Jules Verne]]. They wrote popular novels like [[The Three Musketeers]], [[The Count of Monte-Cristo]], [[Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea]], [[The Hunchback of Notre-Dame]] and [[Les Misérables]]. Other 19th century fiction writers include [[Emile Zola]], [[Guy de Maupassant]], [[Théophile Gautier]] and [[Stendhal]].{{cite web |url=http://www.discoverfrance.net/France/Literature/DF_literature.shtml |title=French Literature |accessdate=3 August 2010 |last=Boorsch |first=Jean |year=1996 |work=Discoverfrance.net |page=5 |archive-date=19 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160419194513/http://www.discoverfrance.net/France/Literature/DF_literature.shtml |url-status=live }} Famous novels were written during the 20th century by [[Marcel Proust]], [[Antoine de Saint-Exupéry]], [[Albert Camus]], [[Jean-Paul Sartre]] and [[Michel Houellebecq]]. === Sports === [[File:TourDeFrance 2005 07 09.jpg|right|thumb|The ''Peloton'' (means "pack" in French) of the [[Tour de France]]]] The [[Tour de France]] cycling [[Racing|race]] in July is one of the best-known sporting events.{{cite web|url=http://www.weightlossdietinformation.com/the-tour-de-france-the-most-famous-bicycle-race-in-the-world.html|title=Famous tour de France|author=Damian Papworth|accessdate=16 September 2010|archive-date=18 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718024209/http://www.weightlossdietinformation.com/the-tour-de-france-the-most-famous-bicycle-race-in-the-world.html|url-status=dead}} It is a three-week race of around 3,500 km that covers most of France and ends in the center of Paris, on the ''Avenue des Champs-Elysées''. [[association football|Football]] is another popular sport in France. The French team won the [[FIFA World Cup]] in 1998 and 2018. They also won the [[UEFA European Football Championship]] in 1984 and 2000. France also hosts the [[24 Hours of Le Mans]] [[car race]]. France also hosted the [[Rugby World Cup]] in 2007 and finished fourth.{{cite web |url=http://french.lovetoknow.com/Popular_French_Sports |title=Popular French Sports |accessdate=3 August 2010 |last1=Dautaj |first1=Jacqueline |last2=Delp |first2=Valorie |last3=Finley |first3=Amy |work=LoveToKnow Corp. |archive-date=28 May 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100528112941/http://french.lovetoknow.com/Popular_French_Sports |url-status=live }} France is closely associated with the Modern Olympic Games. At the end of the 19th century, the [[Baron]] [[Pierre de Coubertin]] suggested having the Olympic Games again. France hosted the [[Summer Olympics]] twice, in 1900 and 1924, in Paris. France will host the Summer Olympics in 2024, in Paris. France also hosted the [[Winter Olympic Games|Winter Games]] three times: in 1924 in [[Chamonix]], in 1968 in [[Grenoble]], and in 1992 in [[Albertville]]. === Cuisine === [[File:Terrine de saumon au basilic.JPG|thumb|right|230px|Basil salmon [[Terrine (food)|terrine]]]] French cuisine has influenced the style of cooking throughout Europe, and its chefs work in restaurants throughout the world.{{cite web|url=http://www.delices-du-monde.fr/recettes-francaise.html|title=Diversity of French Cuisine|accessdate=1 August 2010|archive-date=23 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100723164351/http://www.delices-du-monde.fr/recettes-francaise.html|url-status=live}}{{in lang|fr}} The roots of modern ''haute cuisine'' lie in chefs like [[François Pierre La Varenne|La Varenne]] (1615–1678) and the notable chef of [[Napoleon]], [[Marie-Antoine Carême]] (1784–1833). These chefs developed a lighter style of food compared to the food of the [[Middle Ages]]. They used fewer spices, and more herbs and creamy ingredients. Typical ingredients like [[roux]] and fish stock, and techniques such as [[marinade|marinading]], and dishes such as [[ragout]], were invented. Carême was an expert pâtissier (pastry-maker), and this is still a mark of French cooking. He developed basic sauces, his 'mother sauces'; he had over a hundred sauces in his repertoire, based on the half-dozen mother sauces. French cuisine was introduced in the 20th century by [[Auguste Escoffier|Georges Auguste Escoffier]] (1846–1935). He was a genius at organization. He worked out how to run large restaurants, as in a big hotel or a palace; how the staff should be organized; how the menu was prepared. He had methods for everything. Escoffier's largest contribution was the publication of ''Le Guide Culinaire'' in 1903, which established the fundamentals of French cookery. Escoffier managed the restaurants and cuisine at the [[Savoy Hotel]] and [[Carlton Hotel]] in London, the [[Hôtel Ritz Paris]], and some of the greatest cruise ships. Escoffier, however, left out much of the culinary character to be found in the [[regions of France]]. Gastro-tourism and the ''[[Guide Michelin]]'' helped to make people familiar with the rich [[bourgeois]] and peasant cuisine of the French countryside in the 20th century. [[Gascony|Gascon]] cuisine has also had great influence over the cuisine in the southwest of France. Many dishes that were once regional have become common all over the country. Cheese and wine are a major part of the cuisine, playing different roles regionally and nationally.{{cite web|url=http://www.goodcooking.com/frcheese.htm|title=French Cheeses|accessdate=1 August 2010|archive-date=10 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171010114424/http://www.goodcooking.com/frcheese.htm|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=http://www.franceway.com/cheese/|title=French Cheese|accessdate=1 August 2010|archive-date=27 August 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100827131743/http://www.franceway.com/cheese/|url-status=dead}}{{cite web|url=http://trifter.com/practical-travel/world-cuisine/top-10-most-tasty-cuisines-in-the-world/|title=The world's best cuisines|accessdate=1 August 2010|archive-date=26 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100726071220/http://trifter.com/practical-travel/world-cuisine/top-10-most-tasty-cuisines-in-the-world/|url-status=dead}} In the north of France, people often prefer to use butter to [[wikt:cook|cook]]. In the south, they prefer [[olive oil]] and garlic.{{cite web|url=http://www.google.com/hostednews/afp/article/ALeqM5jvmxWfyZ2tFVA3qcmC7DkX6SMi5g|title=Butter and oil in French Cuisine|work=Google News |accessdate=1 August 2010|archive-date=25 April 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110425112349/http://www.google.com/hostednews/afp/article/ALeqM5jvmxWfyZ2tFVA3qcmC7DkX6SMi5g|url-status=live}} In France, each [[Regions of France|region]] has its own special [[dish]]; [[choucroute]] in Alsace, [[quiche]] in [[Lorraine]], [[cassoulet]] in the [[Languedoc-Roussillon]], and [[tapenade]] in [[Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur]]. In November 2010, French gastronomy was added by [[UNESCO]] to its lists of the world's 'intangible cultural heritage'.[http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/news/world/stories/DN-culture_17int.ART.State.Edition1.b21e71.html Bon appétit: Your meal is certified by the U.N.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101120234633/http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/news/world/stories/DN-culture_17int.ART.State.Edition1.b21e71.html |date=20 November 2010 }} Dallas Morning News{{Cite web |url=http://www.unesco.org/new/en/media-services/single-view/news/celebrations_healing_techniques_crafts_and_culinary_arts_added_to_the_representative_list_of_the_intangible_cultural_heritage/ |title=Celebrations, healing techniques, crafts and culinary arts added to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage |access-date=5 January 2011 |archive-date=27 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110127080124/http://www.unesco.org/new/en/media-services/single-view/news/celebrations_healing_techniques_crafts_and_culinary_arts_added_to_the_representative_list_of_the_intangible_cultural_heritage/ |url-status=live }} [[File:Chateau-de-versailles-cour.jpg|thumb|The [[Palace of Versailles]] is one of the most popular tourist destinations in France.]] === Tourism === [[File:Paris 06 Eiffelturm 4828.jpg|thumb|right|110px|[[Eiffel Tower]]]] France is the number one tourist destination in the world. In 2007, 81.9 million foreign tourists visited France.{{cite web|url=http://www.tourisme.gouv.fr/fr/z2/stat/tis/att00018288/TIS_EVE2007_2008-5.pdf|title=Le tourisme international en France en 2007|publisher=Direction du Tourisme (French government's tourism agency)|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080624195206/http://www.tourisme.gouv.fr/fr/z2/stat/tis/att00018288/TIS_EVE2007_2008-5.pdf|archivedate=24 June 2008|accessdate=5 June 2008}} {{in lang|fr}} Spain comes second (58.5 million in 2006) and the United States comes third (51.1 million in 2006). Some of the most famous attractions in Paris, are the [[Eiffel Tower]] and the [[Arc de Triomphe]]. Another one is [[Mont Saint Michel]], in [[Normandy]].{{cite web|url=http://www2.culture.gouv.fr/deps/mini_chiff_03/fr/musee.htm|title=Musées et Monuments historiques|access-date=10 November 2008|archive-date=24 December 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071224180811/http://www2.culture.gouv.fr/deps/mini_chiff_03/fr/musee.htm|url-status=live}} A European [[Disneyland]] is located in a suburb east of Paris. The resort opened in 1992 and is also a popular tourist destination in Europe. == Foreign relations == {{see also|European Union|United Nations Security Council}} France is a member of the United Nations.{{cite web|url=http://www.un.org/en/members/index.shtml#f|title=Members of the UN|publisher=United Nations|accessdate=4 August 2010|archive-date=12 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140412154940/http://www.un.org/en/members/index.shtml#f|url-status=live}} It is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council and has veto rights.{{cite web|url=http://www.un.org/sc/members.asp|title=Members of the Security council|publisher=United Nations|accessdate=4 August 2010|archive-date=13 September 2012|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120913181027/www.un.org/sc/members.asp|url-status=live}} It is also a member of the [[World Trade Organization]] (WTO). It hosts the headquarters of the [[Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development|OECD]], [[UNESCO]] and [[Interpol]]. In [[1953]], the United Nations asked France to choose a [[coat of arms]] to represent them internationally. The French emblem is now on their passports. France was a founding member of the European Union.{{cite web|url=http://europa.eu/abc/history/index_en.htm|title=History of the EU|publisher=European Union|accessdate=5 August 2010|archive-date=21 February 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090221102210/http://europa.eu/abc/history/index_en.htm|url-status=live}} In the 1960s, France wanted to exclude the United Kingdom from the organization. It wanted to build its own economic [[Influence|power]] in continental Europe. France and Germany became closer after [[World War II]]. This was to try to become the most influential country in the EU. It limited the influence of the new Eastern European members. France is a member of the [[North Atlantic Treaty Organization]] (NATO).{{cite web|url=http://www.nato.int/cps/en/natolive/nato_countries.htm|title=NATO - Member countries|date=30 July 2010|publisher=Nato.int|accessdate=3 August 2010|archive-date=24 September 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110924014819/http://www.nato.int/cps/en/natolive/nato_countries.htm|url-status=live}} However, under [[Charles de Gaulle|President de Gaulle]], it left the joint military command. In the early 1990s, France received criticism for its underground [[nuclear weapons|nuclear]] tests in [[French Polynesia]]. France vigorously opposed the [[2003 invasion of Iraq]].{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/middle_east/2688117.stm|title=Opposition of the war in Iraq|publisher=BBC|accessdate=5 August 2010|archive-date=5 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181005031037/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/middle_east/2688117.stm|url-status=live}} France retains strong political and economic influence in its former African colonies. For instance it has supplied economic aid and troops for peace-keeping missions in the [[Ivory Coast]] and [[Chad]]. [[France–Russia relations]]. The [[Emmanuel Macron|French president]] was not on the phone with [[Vladimir Putin|Russian president]], for the three first 3 years of the [[Russian invasion of Ukraine]]; In July 2025 they spoke by phone.https://www.vg.no/nyheter/i/73agK3/macron-og-putin-har-snakket-sammen-paa-telefon. According to the Finnish Constitution, the president has no possibility to rule the government without the ministerial approval, and does not have the power to dissolve the parliament under his or her own desire. Finland is actually represented by its prime minister, and not by its president, in the Council of the Heads of State and Government of the European Union. Europe.]] '''Finland''' ([[Finnish language|Finnish]]: ''Suomi'') is a [[country]] in [[Northern Europe]] and is a member state of the [[European Union]] and [[NATO]]. Finland is one of the [[Nordic countries]] and is also part of [[Fennoscandia]]. Finland is located between the 60th and 70th latitudes North. Its neighbours are [[Sweden]] to the west, [[Norway]] to the north, [[Russia]] to the east and [[Estonia]] to the south, beyond the sea called [[Gulf of Finland]]. Most of the western and southern coast is on the shore of the [[Baltic Sea]]. The [[Capital (city)|capital]] of Finland is [[Helsinki]]; the second largest city is [[Tampere]].{{Cite web|last=admin|date=2024-06-21|title=Fascinating things about Tampere (Finland)|url=https://rabeducation.com/fascinating-things-about-tampere-finland/|access-date=2026-07-05|website=RAB Education|language=en-US}} The official [[currency]] of the country is the [[euro]] (EUR); before 2002 it was the [[markka]], the Finnish mark (FIM).{{Cite web|title=Finland and the euro - Economy and Finance - European Commission|url=https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/euro/eu-countries-and-euro/finland-and-euro_en|access-date=2026-07-05|website=economy-finance.ec.europa.eu|language=en}} The [[president]] of Finland is [[Alexander Stubb]]. 5.6 million people live in Finland.{{Cite web|last=information service|first=Guidance and|date=2026-07-05|title=Finland in Figures 2024|url=https://toolbox.finland.fi/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2024/09/finland-in-figures-2024.pdf|website=finland.fi}} [[Finnish language|Finnish]] and [[Swedish language|Swedish]] both are the official [[language]]s of Finland; the most spoken languages is Finnish, mother tongue of about 90% of the population.{{Cite web|title=Languages of Finland and language policy|url=https://en.kotus.fi/on-language/languages-of-finland-and-language-policy/|access-date=2026-07-05|website=Kotus|language=en-GB}}{{Cite web|last=Roux|first=Penelope|date=2026-07-05|title=Notoriously challenging': learning Finnish as a foreign language|url=https://www.britishcouncil.org/voices-magazine/notoriously-challenging-learning-finnish-foreign-language|access-date=2026-07-05|archive-date=2026-05-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518103441/https://www.britishcouncil.org/voices-magazine/notoriously-challenging-learning-finnish-foreign-language|url-status=dead}} Swedish is spoken by the Swedish speaking minority of Finland, called the Finnish Swedes, who make up 5% of the total population. Finland became [[Independence|independent]] of [[Russian Empire|Russia]] on 6 December 1917. The most important cities and towns in Finland are [[Helsinki]], [[Espoo]], [[Tampere]], [[Vantaa]], [[Turku]], [[Oulu]], [[Lahti]], [[Kuopio]], [[Jyväskylä]] and [[Pori]]. Finland is a highly industrialised [[First World]] country. The most important Finnish industrial products are [[paper]], and [[steel]] products such as machines and electronics.{{Cite web|title=Economy and Business Opportunities in Finland, Finnish Economy|url=https://www.globaltenders.com/economy-of-finland|access-date=2026-07-05|website=Global Tenders|language=en}} [[Nokia]] (the mobile company) is originally a company of Finland, named after a small town called [[Nokia, Finland|Nokia]]. Finland has been in the top three on the list of the least corrupt countries on the [[Corruption Perceptions Index]] more times than any other country.{{Cite web|date=2025-02-11|title=Denmark and Finland on top of list of least corrupt countries|url=https://unric.org/en/denmark-and-finland-on-top-of-list-of-least-corrupt-countries/|access-date=2026-07-05|website=United Nations Western Europe|language=en-US}} == People and culture == The people of Finland are called Finns. Most Finns speak [[Finnish language|Finnish]] as their mother tongue. About six percent of Finns have the [[Swedish language]] as their mother tongue. They live mostly in the western part of Finland and on [[Åland]] (Finnish Ahvenanmaa). Finns also study mandatory English and Swedish in school. Most Finns work either in services (that is: shops, banks, offices or businesses) or in factories. Finns often like [[sauna]]s and [[nature]]. Many Finnish families have [[summer cottage]]s, small houses where they go to relax on their summer holidays. The most important [[festival]]s that Finnish people celebrate are [[Midsummer]] and [[Christmas]]. The most popular sports in Finland are [[ice hockey]], [[skiing]], [[track and field]] and [[association football]] (soccer). Finns have also won events in [[swimming]], [[motor sports]] and [[gymnastics]]. There is a group of a few thousand [[Sámi]]s (also called Lapps) in the most northern part of Finland, called [[Lapland]]. Most of the Samis live in [[Norway]] and [[Sweden]]. Many Sami people farm [[reindeer]]s. Originally, Samis were [[hunter-gatherers]]. In the past the Sami were [[nomad]]s, but nowadays they live in regular houses. Minority groups in Finland include Swedish–speakers (5.3 per cent), Russian-speakers (1.4 per cent), [[Estonians]] (0.9 per cent), [[Roma people|Roma]] (0.2 per cent), and Sámi (0.1 per cent). There is a also small number of [[Jews]].{{cite web|url= https://minorityrights.org/country/finland/|title= Finland - World Directory of Minorities & Indigenous Peoples|date= 2 November 2023}} Very few people in Finland are from other countries. In 2016 about 4% of residents were born in another country.{{cite web|last=Bunikowski|first=Dawid|title=Finland's Immigration Crisis|url=https://www.gatestoneinstitute.org/7559/finland-migrant-crisis|publisher=Gatestone Institute|accessdate=27 December 2016|date=March 6, 2016}} == Nature and weather == [[File:Koli hill view.jpg|thumb|250px|This picture is from [[Koli, Finland|Koli]], [[North Karelia]].]] Most of Finland is covered by pine [[forest]]. It is estimated that up to one-third of all wood resources of the [[European Union]] are in Finland. Wood is the most important natural resource of Finland. The national animal of Finland is the [[brown bear]]. The [[swan]], which was considered holy long ago, is the national bird of Finland. The largest animal is the [[elk]], a type of moose, which is a member of the deer family. Other large animals (in the [[wild]]) are [[wolf|wolves]].https://yle.fi/a/74-20094727. Retrieved 2024-06-18 There are hundreds of rivers and thousands of fresh water lakes. [[Fishing]] is a popular [[sport]]. It is estimated there are almost 180,000 lakes in Finland. Many islands in the [[Baltic Sea]] belong to Finland. Thousands of islands are part of the [[Åland]] [[archipelago]]. Tourists from all over the world come to see the fells and the [[northern lights]] in [[Lapland]]. The highest mountain of Finland is Halti, which is 1328 meters high. The largest lake is Saimaa, 4,400 square kilometres. The longest river of Finland is Tornionjoki. The largest river (by watershed) is Kemijoki, 552 kilometres long. The weather in Finland varies widely by season. Summer usually lasts from May to early September, and temperatures can reach up to +30 °C. Autumns are dark and rainy. Winter snow usually begins to fall in Helsinki in early December (in Lapland it can fall as early as October) and in the winter the temperature can drop to -40 °C. Highest temperature recorded in Finland is +37,2 °C and lowest temperature is -51,5 °C. Winter usually lasts to mid-March, when the snow melts in Helsinki (in Lapland the snow usually doesn't melt until early May), and Spring lasts till late May. Spring can be erratic, and the weather can change from frost to sunshine within a matter of days. The famed [[Northern Lights]] are common in Lapland. == History == People first came to Finland 10,000 years ago. That was just after an [[ice age]], after a glacier that covered the ground had receded. Some think the first people in Finland already spoke a language similar to the [[Finnish language]] that is spoken today. It is known that an early form of the Finnish language was spoken in Finland in the [[Iron Age]]. (The Iron Age in Finland was 2,500–800 years ago). The first residents in Finland hunted animals, as "[[hunter-gatherer]]s". Some people started to [[agriculture|farm]] crops about 5,200 years ago. Farming slowly became more and more popular and became the major way of life until the modern age. [[File:Vasarakirves.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Stone [[axe]] from Finland.]] The ancient Finns were [[paganism|pagans]]. The most important god of the Finnish pantheon was [[Ukko]]. He was a god of [[sky]] and [[thunder]], much like [[Odin]], another Scandinavian god-king. These powers were common among the pagan god kings in pantheons ranging from the Finnish Ukko, to the Scandinavian/Germanic/Saxon [[Odin]], all the way east to [[Zeus]] of the Greeks and Jupiter of the Romans. Around a thousand years ago, when most of Europe was adopting Christianity, Finland also began following Christianity. During the [[Reformation]] of Christianity in the 16th century, most Finns became [[Protestant]]s. Some pagan practices still remain amongst the now Christian Finns, such as [[bear worship]]. From the [[Middle Ages]] Finland was a part of [[Sweden]]. Then, in the year 1809, [[Russia]] took Finland from Sweden. Finland was a part of Russia, but after a short period of time it became [[autonomy|autonomous]]. The Finns essentially controlled Finland, though the Tsar was in control officially. Finns could create their own laws and had their own currency, (called the ''[[markka]]''), their own [[stamp]]s and own [[custom]]s. However, Finland did not have its own [[army]]. During the [[1905 Russian Revolution]], in the [[Grand Duchy of Finland]]: the [[Social Democratic Party of Finland|Social Democrats]] organised the [[general strike]] of 1905 ({{OldStyleDate|12–19 November||30 October – 6 November}}). The [[Red Guards (Finland)|Red Guards]] were formed. On {{OldStyleDate|12 August|1906|30 July}}, Russian artillerymen and military engineers [[Sveaborg Rebellion|rose to rebellion]] in the fortress of [[Sveaborg]] (later called [[Suomenlinna]]), Helsinki. The Finnish Red Guards supported the [[Sveaborg Rebellion]] with a general strike, but the mutiny was quelled by loyal troops and ships of the [[Baltic Fleet]] within 60 hours. [[File:Demonstration Pietarsaari 1905.jpg|thumb|right|260px|A [[demonstration]] in 1905 - in [[Jakobstad]].]] ===After independence=== On 6 December 1917, Finland became independent, which meant that it no longer was a part of Russia. There was a [[October Revolution|communist revolution]] in Russia and after 1922 Russia was a part of the [[Soviet Union]]. There were [[Communism|communists]] in Finland too, who tried to create a revolution in Finland This attempt at revolution caused the [[Finnish civil war]]. The communists lost the civil war, and Finland did not change its old capitalist system [[Stalin]], who was the leader of the Soviet Union, did not like having a [[Capitalism|capitalist]] country as its neighbour. Stalin wanted Finland to become a [[communism|communist]] state and be a part of the Soviet Union. The leaders of Finland refused: they wanted to stay independent. The Soviet Union sent many troops across the eastern border of Finland to try to make Finland join them, which resulted in the [[Winter War]]. The Soviet Union eventually won, and took most of [[Karelia]] and other parts of Finland. [[File:Finnish soldiers during the Winter War.jpg|thumb|250px|Finnish soldiers at the time of war.]] [[Adolf Hitler]] was the dictator of Germany, and he wanted to invade the Soviet Union. Finland wanted to retrieve the areas that it had lost, so they joined the German invasion, which started with [[Operation Barbarossa]] in 1941. The Finnish part of the [[Second World War]] is called the [[Continuation War]] in Finland. However, Finland was not a [[fascism|fascist]] or an [[antisemitism|antisemitic]] country. Finns were interested in freedom rather than dictatorship. While Germany was losing the war, Finland had already progressed into the Soviet Union in order to regain the areas lost in the previous peace. Finland wanted to end the war with the Soviet Union, which resulted in peace. Once again Finland had to give up the areas they had conquered. This time, the peace with the Soviet Union made Finland and Germany enemies. Finns fought the Germans, and Germans retreated to [[Norway]], burning down all of Lapland behind them. This is called the [[Lapland War]]. Finland remained independent. After the war, many factories were built in Finland. Many people moved from farms to cities. At that time, big factories manufactured products like [[paper]] and [[steel]]. More and more people worked in more advanced jobs, like [[high technology]]. Also, many people went to universities to get a good education. Finland was one of the first countries where most people had [[Internet]] connections and mobile phones. A well-known company that makes [[mobile phone]]s, [[Nokia]], is from Finland. Finland joined the [[European Union]] in 1995. The Finnish currency was changed to the [[euro]] in 2002. Finland also joined [[NATO]] in 2023, after the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine|Russian invasion of Ukraine]].{{Cite news|last1=Kauranen|first1=Anne|last2=Gray|first2=Andrew|date=2023-04-04|title=Finland joins NATO in historic shift, Russia threatens 'counter-measures'|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/finland-set-join-nato-historic-shift-while-sweden-waits-2023-04-04/|access-date=2023-04-19}} == Economy == Finland has a mixed economy. [[Free market]] controls most of production and sales of goods, but public sector is involved in services. In 2013, taxes were 44% of gross national product. This is 4th largest in Europe, after Denmark, France and Belgium.[http://www.stat.fi/tup/suoluk/suoluk_valtiontalous.html Valtion talous] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210411035857/http://www.stat.fi/tup/suoluk/suoluk_valtiontalous.html |date=2021-04-11 }} National Statistics In 2014 services were 70% of the gross national product.[http://www.stat.fi/tup/suoluk/suoluk_kansantalous.html Kansantalous] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160227052231/http://www.stat.fi/tup/suoluk/suoluk_kansantalous.html |date=2016-02-27 }} National Statistics The largest company in 2014 was oil refinery [[Neste Oil]]. The second largest was [[Nokia]]. Two forest industries [[Stora Enso]] and [[UPM-Kymmene]], were numbers three and four. Number five was [[Kesko]] which sells everyday goods in K-supermarkets.[http://www.talouselama.fi/uutiset/suuryhtiot-puristivat-vahemmasta-liikevaihdosta-enemman-voittoa-3365520 Talouselämä 500, kymmenen suurinta] Talouselämä 27.2.2016 == Politics == The [[head of state]] is the the President, [[Alexander Stubb]] became the [[president of Finland]] in 2024 after winning the [[2024 Finnish presidential election|presidential election]].{{Cite news|date=2024-02-12|title=Finland elects pro-NATO Alexander Stubb as president|language=en|url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2024/02/12/finland-elects-pro-nato-alexander-stubb-as-president_6516908_4.html|access-date=2026-02-21}} He became the president on march 1, 2024.{{Cite web|title=Alexander Stubb|url=https://www.presidentti.fi/en/curriculum-vitae/cai-goran-alexander-stubb/|access-date=2026-07-05|website=Presidentti|language=en-US}} The first president was [[Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg]]. The Prime minister of Finland is [[Petteri Orpo]]. He became the Prime minister on June 20, 2023.{{Cite web|date=2024-03-07|title="This is Europe" debate with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo {{!}} 11-03-2024 {{!}} News {{!}} European Parliament|url=https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/agenda/plenary-news/2024-03-11/23/this-is-europe-debate-with-finnish-prime-minister-petteri-orpo|access-date=2026-07-05|website=www.europarl.europa.eu|language=en}} === Elections === [[Election]]s are [[organize]]d to select 200 [[wikt:member|member]]s to the [[Parliament]] of Finland. Also selected are the [[president]] of Finland, members of [[Town council|town]] and [[city council]]s and Finnish members to the [[European Parliament]]. The [[election]]s are [[secret]] and direct. People [[vote]] directly for the person they want to be elected. In presidential elections votes are only cast for a person, not for a [[political party]]. All the other elections are [[Proportional representation|proportional]]. The system is a combination of voting for individuals and parties.{{cite web |url=http://www.vaalit.fi/en/index/generalinformation/centralprinciplesofholdingelections.html |title=Central Principles of Holding Elections |author= |website=Elections website |publisher=Ministry of Justice |accessdate=6 February 2016 |archive-date=24 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160424101024/http://vaalit.fi/en/index/generalinformation/centralprinciplesofholdingelections.html |url-status=dead }} The right to vote is universal and equal. In general elections everybody has one vote. == Famous Finnish people == {{Div col}} * [[Alvar Aalto]], architect * [[Markku Alen]], 1978 World Rally Champion * [[Valtteri Bottas]], current Formula One driver * [[The Dudesons]], also known as [[Duudsonit]], a four-man stunt group with several TV shows and a movie. title: Fruit
text:
In [[botany]], a '''fruit''' is a plant structure that contains the plant's [[seed]]s. 

To a [[botanist]], the word ''fruit'' is used only if it comes from the part of the [[flower]] which was an [[ovary (botany)|ovary]].<ref>Mauseth, James D. 2003. ''Botany: an introduction to plant biology''. Jones & Bartlett, Boston.</ref> It is an extra layer round the [[seed]]s, which may or may not be fleshy. However, even in the field of botany, there is no general agreement on how fruits should be classified. Many do have extra layers from other parts of the flower.<ref>Schlegel, Rolf 2003. ''Encyclopedic dictionary of plant breeding and related subjects''. Haworth Press. {{ISBN|1-56022-950-0}}.</ref>
[[File:Mature flower diagram.svg|thumb|center|400px|Diagram of flower, cut open, showing the [[ovary (botany)|ovary]]]]

In general speech, and especially in [[cooking]], some fruits are a [[Taste#Sweetness|sweet]] product, but not all fruits are sweet, most fruits are fruity and edible, and many [[Botany|botanical]] fruits are known as [[vegetable]]s. This is how ordinary [[people]] use the words. On this page, we describe what [[botanist]]s call a fruit.

The fleshy part of a fruit is called the mesocarp. It is between the fruit's skin (exocarp) and the seeds. The white part of an [[apple]], for example, is the "fleshy" part of the apple. Usually, when we eat a fruit, we eat the "fleshy" part.

==Types of fruits==
[[File:Grapes.jpg|thumb|left|140px|alt=Grapes hanging on a branch|Diagram of a type of berry]]

===Berry===
If the entire fruit is fleshy, except for maybe a thin skin, the fruit is called a [[berry]]. A berry might contain one seed or many. [[Grape]]s, [[avocado]]s, and [[blueberry|blueberries]] are [[Berry|berries]]. They all have a thin [[skin]], but most of the fruit is fleshy. Don't get confused by the name of fruits like [[Strawberry|strawberries]], because actually they are ''not'' berries. The seeds are on the outside: on a real berry, the seed or seeds are ''inside'' the fruit.

===Pepo===
A pepo (pronounced ''pee' po'') is a [[wikt:modify|modified]] berry. Its skin is hard and thick and is usually called a "rind". [[Pumpkin]]s and [[watermelon]]s, for instance, are pepos.

===Hesperidium===
A hesperidium is another modified berry. It has a [[leather]]y skin that is not as hard as the skin of a pepo. All [[citrus]] fruit like [[Orange (fruit)|oranges]] and [[lemon]] are hesperidiums.[[File:Citrus fruits.jpg|thumb|170px|Citrus fruits are hesperidiums]]

===Pome===
[[File:PearPhoto.jpg|thumb|left|120px|Pears have a core surrounded by flesh, meaning pears are pomes]]

A [[pome]] (pohm) is a fruit that has a [[wikt:core|core]] surrounded by fleshy [[Tissue (biology)|tissue]] that one can eat. The core is usually not eaten. Berries are different - the seeds are ''inside'' the fleshy part, not separated from it by a core. [[Apple]]s and [[pear]]s are pomes.

===Drupe===
[[File:Autumn Red peaches.jpg|thumb|170px|The big hard "pit" in the middle of this peach has a seed inside it]]

[[Stone fruit|Drupes]] are also called [[stone fruit]]. A drupe is a fleshy fruit with a hard stone around the seed. We usually call this 'stone' the 'pit' of the fruit. [[Peach]]es and [[Olive (fruit)|olives]] are drupes. Actually, the [[almond]] fruit is a drupe, too, though we eat the seed that is inside the 'pit' of the [[almond]] fruit.

==Botanical fruits==
Since fruits are produced from fertilised ovaries in [[flower]]s, only [[flowering plant]]s produce fruits. Fruits are an [[evolution]]ary 'invention' which help [[seed]]s get [[wikt:dispersal|dispersed]] by animals.

The botanical term includes many that are not 'fruits' in the common sense of the term. such as the vegetables [[Squash (plant)|squash]], [[pumpkin]]s, [[cucumber]]s, [[tomato]], [[pea]]s, [[bean]]s, [[corn]], [[eggplant]], and [[Capsicum|bell]] [[Capsicum|pepper]] and some spices, such as [[allspice]] and [[Chili pepper|chili]]

.

===Accessory fruits===
[[File:FraiseFruitPhoto.jpg|right|thumb|A [[Strawberry]] fruit: the 'seeds' are each derived from a [[pistil]] of the flower.]]
An accessory fruit or false fruit (pseudocarp) is a fruit in which some of the flesh is derived not from the ovary but from some adjacent tissue.

A [[fig]] is a type of accessory fruit called a syconium. [[Pome]]s, such as [[apple]]s and [[pear]]s, are also accessory fruits: the core is the true fruit.<ref>Esau K. 1977. ''Anatomy of seed plants''. Wiley New York.</ref>

==Non-botanical fruits==
Strictly speaking, these are not botanical fruits: 
* any produced by non-flowering plants, like [[juniper]] berries, which are the seed-containing female cones of conifers.
* fleshy fruit-like growths that develop from other plant tissues (like [[rhubarb]]).
[[File:vaccinium.jpg|thumb|Berries which are simple fleshy fruit. From top right: [[Cranberry|cranberries]], [[lingonberries]], [[blueberries]] red [[Huckleberry|huckleberries]]]]

==Area of agreement==
These are fruits which you can buy in shops, and which are also acceptable as botanical fruits:
* [[berry fruits]]: [[redcurrant]], [[gooseberry]], [[cranberry]], [[blueberry]] Also, but not commonly known as berry fruits, are [[tomato]], [[avocado]], [[banana]].
* [[false berries]]: [[raspberry]], [[strawberry]], [[blackberry]]: they are aggregate fruits (see below). The [[yew]] berry is not a fruit at all because the yew is a [[conifer]].<ref>Note: the seed in a yew "berry" is very poisonous.</ref>
* [[stone fruit]]s or drupes: [[plum]], [[cherry]], [[peach]], [[apricot]], [[Olive (fruit)|olive]].
* [[citrus|citrus fruits]], like [[orange (fruit)|oranges]], [[grapefruit]]s, and [[tangerine]]s.
* [[aggregate fruit]]s: [[raspberry|raspberries]], [[blackberry|blackberries]].
* [[multiple fruit]]s: [[pineapple]]s, [[fig]]s.

Many fruits come from [[tree]]s or [[shrub|bushes]]. For plants, fruits are a means of dispersal, usually by [[animal]]s. When the fruit is eaten, the seed(s) are not digested, and get [[excretion|excreted]]. Where fruits have big stones, just the soft parts are eaten. 

Most fruits we eat contain a lot of [[water]] and [[Nature|natural]] [[sugar]]s, and many are high in [[Vitamin C]]. They have a large amount of [[dietary fibre]]. Fruits are usually low in [[protein]] and [[fat]] content, but avocados and some nuts are exceptions to this. Not only [[human]]s, but our closest living relatives ([[primate]]s) are keen fruit-eaters. So are many other groups of [[herbivorous]] [[mammal]]s and many [[bird]]s.<ref>Lewis, Robert A. 2002. ''CRC dictionary of agricultural sciences''. CRC Press. {{ISBN|0-8493-2327-4}}</ref>

==Seedless fruits==
Seedlessness is an important feature of some fruits of commerce. Commercial bananas, pineapple, and [[watermelon]]s are examples of seedless fruits. Some [[citrus]] fruits, especially oranges, satsumas, mandarin oranges, and [[grapefruit]] are valued for their seedlessness.

Seedless bananas and grapes are [[ploidy|triploids]], and seedlessness results from the abortion of the [[embryo]]nic plant which is produced by fertilisation. The method requires normal pollination and fertilisation.<ref>Spiegel-Roy P. Goldschmidt E.E. 1996. ''The biology of citrus''. Cambridge. {{ISBN|0-521-33321-0}} p87–88</ref>

title: Farm
text:
[[File:Melaka Tropical Fruit Farm - Interior.jpg|thumb|A farm in [[Melaka]], [[Malaysia]].]]
A '''farm''' is a piece of [[land]] used to grow [[crop]]s  and/or [[Animal husbandry|raise animal]]s.

People who grow these plants or raise these animals are called [[farmer]]s. This work is called [[farming]].

Land that is used to grow plants is called farmland.  Land that is used to feed animals with its grass is called [[pasture]].  Land that can be used to grow plants for food is called [[arable land]].

Many farms are very large and can cause damage.  In some places farms are many and small, and can also cause damage.  Farms provides most of the food for people.  Some people farm to eat the food they produce ([[subsistence agriculture]]). Other farms, including large ones, sell their [[Product (consumer goods)|produced]] crops or animals, like [[Horse trading|horses]], to markets far away in [[urban area]]s (commercial or industrial farming). Most subsistence farms are in poorer countries, while industrial farms are in richer countries.

== Kinds of farms ==
[[File:Tea plantation in India02.jpg|thumb|alt=Tea plantation|A [[tea]] plantation in [[India]]]]
* A farm that produces [[fruit]]s or [[Nut (fruit)|nuts]] is called an ''orchard''.
* A farm that produces [[grape]]s is called a ''vineyard''.
* A farm that raises and trains [[horse]]s is called a ''stable''.
* A farm that produces [[milk]] and [[dairy|dairy products]] is called a ''dairy farm''.
* If the animals are raised for [[meat]] it is a [[ranch]].
* A large farm that produces non-essential crops like [[tobacco]], [[coffee]], [[cotton]] or [[sugarcane]] is called a [[plantation]].
* A farm that produces [[rice]] and [[taro]] is called a [[paddy field]].

title: Geography
text:
[[File:Map of the world by the US Gov as of 2016.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Map of [[Earth]] with [[country]] borders and big [[city|cities]] shown]]

'''Geography''' (from [[Ancient Greek|Greek]]: {{lang|el|γεωγραφία}}, ''geographia'', literally  "earth description")<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?term=geography |title=Online Etymology Dictionary |last=Harper |first=Douglas |website=Etymonline.com |publisher=Online Etymology Dictionary |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090212215028/http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?term=geography |archive-date=12 February 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> is the study of earth and its people. It is one of the [[social sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Geography |work=The American Heritage Dictionary/ of the English Language, Fourth Edition |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Company |url=http://dictionary.reference.com/browse/geography |access-date=October 9, 2006}}</ref> Its features are things like [[continent]]s, [[sea]]s, [[river]]s and [[mountain]]s. The 'inhabitants' of Earth are all the people and [[animal]]s that live on it. Its phenomena are the things that happen like [[tide]]s, [[hurricane]]s, [[tornado]]es, [[earthquake]]s and more.

A person who is an expert in geography is called a [[geographer]]. A geographer tries to understand the world and the things that are in it, how they started and how they have changed.<ref>Geography: The Mother of Sciences [http://web.clas.ufl.edu/users/morgans/lecture_2.prn.pdf] [https://web.archive.org/web/20081003084542/http://web.clas.ufl.edu/users/morgans/lecture_2.prn.pdf]</ref>

There are two main parts of geography. These types are [[Physical geography]] and [[human geography]]. Physical geography studies the natural [[environment]] and human geography studies the human [[environment]]. The human [[environmental studies]] includes things such as the [[population]] in a country, how a country's [[economy]] is doing, and more. There is also [[environmental geography]].

[[Map]]s are used in geography to see what land looks like. Geographers spend much time making maps and studying them. Making maps is called [[cartography]], and people who specialize in making maps are called cartographers.

== Branches ==

=== Physical geography ===
{{Main|Physical geography}}
Physical geography (or physiography) focuses on geography as an [[Earth science]]. It tries to understand the physical problems and the issues of [[lithosphere]], [[hydrosphere]], [[Earth's atmosphere|atmosphere]], pedosphere, and global [[flora]] and [[fauna]] (types of plants) patterns ([[biosphere]]).

=== Human geography ===
[[File:Menschentraube.jpg|thumb|220px|A crowd of people around a band.]]
'''[[Human geography]]''' is the [[Social sciences|social science]] that covers the study of people and their communities, cultures, economies, and their interaction with the [[environment]]. [[Geographer|Geographers]] studying the human [[environment]] may look at:
* [[Population]]
* [[Country|Countries of the world]]
* [[Land use]]
* [[Agriculture]]
* [[City]]
* [[Industry]]
* [[Energy]]
* [[Pollution]]

==History==
The oldest known world map dates back to ancient [[Babylon]] from the 9th century BC.<ref name="Kurt A. Raaflaub & Richard J.A. Talbert 2009 147">{{Cite book |title=Geography and Ethnography: Perceptions of the World in Pre-Modern Societies |author=Kurt A. Raaflaub & Richard J.A. Talbert |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |date=2009 |isbn=978-1-4051-9146-3 |page=147 }}</ref> The best known [[Babylonia]]n world map is the ''Imago Mundi'' of 600 BC.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.henry-davis.com/MAPS/Ancient%20Web%20Pages/103.html|title=Slide 103|last=Siebold|first=Jim|website=henry-davis.com|publisher=Henry Davis Consulting Inc.|access-date=10 November 2016|archive-date=29 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180929083127/http://www.henry-davis.com/MAPS/Ancient|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Star chart]]s (maps of the sky) are of a similar age.

During the [[Middle Ages]], people in [[Europe]] made less maps. People in the eastern countries made more maps.<ref name="needham volume 3 512">{{Cite book|last=Needham|first=Joseph|year=1959|title=Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC|journal=Science and Civilization in China|location=Taipei|publisher=Caves Books, Ltd.|volume=3|page=512|isbn=978-0-521-05801-8|access-date=10 November 2016}}</ref> Abū Zayd al-Balkhī created the "Balkhī school" of mapping in [[Baghdad]].<ref name="E61-3">{{Cite journal|last1=Edson|first1=Evelyn|last2=Savage-Smith|first2=Emilie|title=Medieval Views of the Cosmos|journal=International Journal of the Classical Tradition|date=Winter 2007|volume=13|issue=3|pages=61–63|jstor=30222166}}</ref>

[[Western Europe]] became known as the leader of geographic thought during the [[European Renaissance]] and [[Age of Exploration|The Age of Exploration]] (1400–1600). The [[printing press]] made maps and information about the world available to everyone. In 1650, the first edition of ''[[Geographia Generalis]]'' was published.

In the 1700s and 1800s, scientists started to study the relationship between the [[environment]] and its people.
