title: Mass
text:
{{otheruses}}
The '''mass''' of an object is a [[measure]] of how much of it there is.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tsokos |first1=K. A. |title=Physics for the IB Diploma |url=https://archive.org/details/physicsforibdipl0000tsok |date=2005 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, United Kingdom |isbn=9780521604055 |page=[https://archive.org/details/physicsforibdipl0000tsok/page/63 63]}}</ref> For example, A mountain has more mass than a rock. Mass is different from [[weight]]. Weight is the [[Product (mathematics)|product]] of mass times [[gravitational acceleration]]. 

You can measure the mass of an object by using a [[force]] on it. The more mass it has, the less it will change how fast it moves. This is called ''inertial mass'' because it measures the [[inertia]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Physics for scientists and engineers with modern physics : a strategic approach|url=https://archive.org/details/physicsforscient0000knig_i8p4|last=Knight|first=Randall Dewey|date=2003|publisher=Pearson/Addison-Wesley|isbn=0-321-24329-3|location=San Francisco|pages=[https://archive.org/details/physicsforscient0000knig_i8p4/page/n386 349]|oclc=54427199}}</ref>

An object with a lot of mass, like a planet, attracts objects with less mass and keeps them from floating away from the planet. This is called [[gravity]]. a  When measuring the ''force of gravity'' on an object, you can find the object’s ''gravitational mass''. Tests of inertial and gravitational mass show that they are the same or almost the same.<ref name=":0" />

== Units of mass ==
The unit of mass in the [[International System of Units]] is the [[kilogram]], which is represented by the symbol 'kg'. Fractions and multiples of this basic unit include the gram (one thousandth of a kg, symbol 'g') and the [[Metric ton|ton]]ne (one thousand kg), amongst many others.

In some fields or applications, it is convenient to use different units to simplify the discussions or writings. For instance,
* Atomic [[physicist]]s deal with the tiny masses of individual [[atom]]s and measure them in [[atomic mass unit]]s.
* Jewelers normally work with small [[jewel]]s and precious stones where masses are traditionally measured in [[Carat (mass)|carats]], which correspond to 200 mg or 0.2 g.
* The masses of stars are very large and are sometimes expressed in units of [[solar mass]]es.

Traditional units are still in encountered in some countries: [[imperial unit]]s such as the [[ounce]] or the [[Pound (mass)|pound]] were in widespread use within the [[British Empire]]. Some of them are still popular in the United States, which also uses units like the short [[Short ton|ton]] (2,000 pounds, 907 kg) and the long ton (2,240 pounds, 1010 kg), not to be confused with the metric ton (1,000 kg).

== Conservation of mass and relativity ==
{{Main|Conservation of mass}}
Mass is an intrinsic property of the object: it does not depend on its [[volume]], or position in space, for instance. For a long time (at least since the works of [[Antoine Lavoisier]] in the second half of the eighteen century), it has been known that the sum of the masses of objects that interact or of the [[Chemical substance|chemicals]] that react remain conserved throughout these processes. This remains an excellent approximation for everyday life and even most laboratory work.

However, [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]] has shown through his [[Special relativity|special theory of relativity]] that the mass ''m'' of an object moving at speed ''v'' with respect to an observer must be higher than the mass of the same object observed at rest ''m<sub>0</sub>'' with respect to the observer. The applicable formula is

<math>m=\frac{m_0}{\sqrt{1 - (v^2/c^2)}}</math>

where ''c'' stands for the [[speed of light]]. This change in mass is only important when the speed of the object with respect to the observer becomes a large fraction of ''c''.

==The Quantum Concept of Mass==
''For further reference,see the [[Gluon field]] and [[:Higgs boson]]''


In [[Atomic nucleus|atomic nuclei]], example in [[proton]]s and [[neutron]]s,the residual mass comes from the binding kinetic and [[potential energy]] of the quarks and [[gluon]] field. An analogy to go along with is to think of the 3 [[quark]]s as balls with the gluons as a spring connecting the quarks. This mass accounts for 99% of the mass of these [[baryon]]s with the remaining 1% coming from the individual quarks which comes from quantum interactions with the Higgs field.
[[File:Quark_structure_proton.svg|thumb|right|The Quark Structure of the proton. Most hadronic/baryonic mass comes from the binding energy (kinetic&potential) of the gluon field (with the gluons represented as springs binding the quarks.)]]

[[File:Candidate_Higgs_Events_in_ATLAS_and_CMS.png|thumb|right|The ATLAS detection of the mass giving Higgs Boson. The Higgs field gives elementary particles their mass and the corresponding field can be thought of as an infinite source of weak hypercharge and mass.]]

It is the second hottest planet, and the smallest in the [[Solar System]].{{cite web |url= http://nineplanets.org/mercury.html |title= Mercury Facts {{!}} Information, History, Location, Size & Definition |first= |last= |work= nineplanets.org |date= July 2020 |orig-date= last update |accessdate= August 17, 2020 |archive-date= November 24, 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20151124162022/http://nineplanets.org/mercury.html |url-status= live }}{{cite web |url= http://www.bbc.co.uk/science/space/solarsystem/sun_and_planets/mercury_(planet) |title= BBC Solar System - Mercury: A tortured world close to our blazing Sun |first= |last= |work= bbc.co.uk |year= 2012 |orig-date= last update |accessdate= March 7, 2012 |archive-date= October 1, 2011 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111001174346/http://www.bbc.co.uk/science/space/solarsystem/sun_and_planets/mercury_(planet) |url-status= dead }}[[Pluto]] used to be the smallest, but, as of 2006, Pluto is now known as a [[dwarf planet]]. It is also the closest planet to the [[Sun]].{{citation|title=Space Science: Journey to the Innermost Planet|newspaper=Scientific American|pages=26–31|date=March 2011|location=New York|volume=304|issue=3|author1=Murchie, Scott L.|author2=Vervack Jr., Ronald J.|author3=Anderson, Brian J.}} It makes one [[orbit|trip]] around the Sun once every 87.969 days.{{Cite web|url=http://image.gsfc.nasa.gov/poetry/venus/VTratesExt.html|title=Venus year is 224|access-date=August 26, 2010|archive-date=June 7, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100607181651/http://image.gsfc.nasa.gov/poetry/venus/VTratesExt.html|url-status=live}} Mercury is bright when we can see it from [[Earth]]. It has an [[apparent magnitude]] ranging from −2.0 to 5.5. It cannot be seen easily because it is usually too close to the Sun. Because of this, Mercury can only be seen in the morning or evening [[twilight]]{{cite book|title=How it Works Book of Space|url=https://archive.org/details/howitworksbookof0000unse|date=2010|publisher=Imagine Publishing|isbn=9781906078829|page=[https://archive.org/details/howitworksbookof0000unse/page/36 36]-37}} or when there is a [[solar eclipse]]. Less is known about Mercury than about other planets of our Solar System. Even with [[telescope]]s only a small, bright crescent can be seen. It is also hard to put a [[Satellite (artificial)|satellite]] in orbit around it. Two [[spacecraft]] have visited Mercury. The first one was [[Mariner 10|Mariner 10]].{{Cite web |url=http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/masterCatalog.do?sc=1973-085A |title=NASA - NSSDC - Spacecraft - Details |access-date=August 26, 2010 |archive-date=July 30, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090730043759/http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/masterCatalog.do?sc=1973-085A |url-status=dead }} It only made a map of about 45% of the Mercury's surface from 1974 to 1975. The second is the [[MESSENGER]] spacecraft, which finished mapping Mercury in March 2013. Mercury looks like Earth's [[Moon]]. It has many [[crater]]s and smooth plains. It has no moons and little [[atmosphere]] as we know it. However, Mercury does have an extremely thin atmosphere, known as an [[exosphere]]. Mercury has a large [[iron]] [[planetary core|core]]. Because of this Mercury has a [[magnetic field]] about 1% as strong as that of the [[Earth]].{{cite web|url=http://www-spc.igpp.ucla.edu/personnel/russell/papers/merc_mag/|title=Mercury magnetic field|publisher=C. T. Russell & J. G. Luhmann|accessdate=March 16, 2007|archive-date=July 19, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100719051016/http://www-spc.igpp.ucla.edu/personnel/russell/papers/merc_mag/|url-status=dead}} It is a very dense planet because its core is large. Because of it's thin atmosphere, temperature at the surface can be anywhere from about 90 to {{nowrap|700 [[Kelvin|K]]}} (−183 °C to 427 °C, −297 °F to 801 °F),{{cite web|url=http://sci.esa.int/science-e/www/category/index.cfm?fcategoryid=4586|title=Background Science|publisher=European Space Agency|accessdate=May 23, 2008|archive-date=January 17, 2010|archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/5mq2WDgWQ?url=http://sci.esa.int/science-e/www/category/index.cfm?fcategoryid=4586|url-status=dead}} with the [[subsolar point]] being the hottest and the bottoms of craters near the [[Geographical pole|poles]] being the coldest. Known sightings of Mercury date back to at least the first millennium BC. Before the 4th century BC, Greek [[astronomers]] thought that Mercury was two different objects: The one that they were only able to see at sunrise, they called [[Apollo]]; the other one that they were only able to see at sunset, they called [[Hermes]].{{cite book|title=The Voyage of Mariner 10 — Mission to Venus and Mercury|author=Dunne, J. A. and Burgess, E.|chapter-url=http://history.nasa.gov/SP-424/ch1.htm|publisher=NASA History Office|year=1978|chapter=Chapter One|url=http://history.nasa.gov/SP-424/|access-date=August 3, 2009|archive-date=May 24, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110524161325/http://history.nasa.gov/SP-424/|url-status=live}} The English name for the planet is from the [[Ancient Rome|Romans]], who named it after the Roman [[Roman mythology|god]] [[Mercury (mythology)|Mercury]]. The symbol for Mercury is based on Hermes' [[Staff (stick)|staff]].{{cite book|title=Astronomy: A Textbook|url=https://archive.org/details/astronomytextboo0000john|first=John Charles|last=Duncan|year=1946|publisher=Harper & Brothers|pages=[https://archive.org/details/astronomytextboo0000john/page/125 125]|quote=The symbol for Mercury represents the Caduceus, a wand with two serpents twined around it, which was carried by the messenger of the gods.}} Even though Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, it is not the hottest. This is because it has no [[greenhouse effect]]. The heat that the Sun gives it, quickly escapes into space. The hottest planet is [[Venus]].{{cite news | url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/14143062 | title=CBBC Newsround | publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation | accessdate=February 4, 2012 | archive-date=February 24, 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120224035324/http://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/14143062 | url-status=live }} == Inside Mercury == Mercury is one of four [[inner planet]]s in the [[Solar System]]. It is a [[terrestrial planet]] like [[Earth]]. It is the smallest planet in the Solar System, with a [[radius]] of {{cvt|2439.7|km|mi}}. Mercury is even smaller than some of the largest moons in the solar system, such as [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]], the largest moon of [[Jupiter (planet)|Jupiter]] and [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], the largest moon of [[Saturn (planet)|Saturn]]. However, it has in 2.2 times greater mass than Ganymede and around 2 times heavier than Titan. Mercury is made of about 70% [[metal]]lic and 30% [[silicate]] material.{{cite book |title=Exploring Mercury: The Iron Planet |url=https://archive.org/details/exploringmercury00stro |last=Strom |first=Strom, Robert G. |author2=Sprague, Ann L. |year=2003 |page=[https://archive.org/details/exploringmercury00stro/page/52 52] |publisher=Springer |isbn= 1852337311}} Mercury has the second highest [[density]] in the Solar System at 5.427 g/cm³, only slightly less than Earth’s. ==Surface of Mercury== Mercury's [[surface]] resembles the surface of the Moon. It has [[plain]]s that look like [[Lunar mare|mares]] and has lots of [[crater]]s.{{Cite web|title=Mercury's Core Molten, Radar Study Shows|url=https://www.nrao.edu/pr/2007/mercury/|access-date=September 12, 2020|website=www.nrao.edu|archive-date=June 16, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180616103615/https://www.nrao.edu/pr/2007/mercury/|url-status=live}} Mercury was hit by a multitude of [[comet]]s and [[asteroid]]s 4.6 billion years ago. Mercury was also hit during a period called the [[Late Heavy Bombardment]].{{Cite journal|last=Strom|first=RobertG.|date=1979|title=Mercury: A post-Mariner 10 assessment|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF00221842|journal=Space Science Reviews|language=en|volume=24|issue=1|page=3|doi=10.1007/BF00221842|bibcode=1979SSRv...24....3S|s2cid=122563809|issn=0038-6308|via=|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=May 26, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220526123618/https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00221842|url-status=live}} Mercury has many craters because its [[atmosphere]] is too faint to slow foreign objects down.{{Cite journal|last1=Broadfoot|first1=A. L.|last2=Kumar|first2=S.|last3=Belton|first3=M. J. S.|last4=McElroy|first4=M. B.|date=July 12, 1974|title=Mercury's Atmosphere from Mariner 10: Preliminary Results|url=https://www.sciencemag.org/lookup/doi/10.1126/science.185.4146.166|journal=Science|language=en|volume=185|issue=4146|pages=166–169|doi=10.1126/science.185.4146.166|pmid=17810510|bibcode=1974Sci...185..166B|s2cid=7790470|issn=0036-8075|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=May 26, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220526123618/https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.185.4146.166|url-status=live}} Images from ''MESSENGER'' have shown that Mercury may have [[shield volcano]]es.{{Cite journal|last1=Kerber|first1=Laura|last2=Head|first2=James W.|last3=Solomon|first3=Sean C.|last4=Murchie|first4=Scott L.|last5=Blewett|first5=David T.|last6=Wilson|first6=Lionel|date=2009|title=Explosive volcanic eruptions on Mercury: Eruption conditions, magma volatile content, and implications for interior volatile abundances|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0012821X09002611|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|language=en|volume=285|issue=3–4|pages=263–271|doi=10.1016/j.epsl.2009.04.037|bibcode=2009E&PSL.285..263K|via=|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=May 26, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220526123619/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012821X09002611?via%3Dihub|url-status=live}} The surface temperature of Mercury ranges from 100 to 700 K (−173 to 427 °C; −280 to 800 °F) at the most extreme places.{{Cite journal|last=Vasavada|first=A|date=1999|title=Near-surface temperatures on Mercury and the Moon and the stability of polar ice deposits |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0019103599961754|journal=Icarus|language=en|volume=141|issue=2|pages=179–193|doi=10.1006/icar.1999.6175|bibcode=1999Icar..141..179V|via=|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=September 20, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200920023630/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0019103599961754|url-status=live}} Even though the [[temperature]] at the surface of Mercury in the [[day]] is very high, [[observation]]s suggest that there is frozen water on Mercury.{{Cite journal|last1=Ingersoll|first1=Andrew P.|last2=Svitek|first2=Tomas|last3=Murray|first3=Bruce C.|date=1992|title=Stability of polar frosts in spherical bowl-shaped craters on the Moon, Mercury, and Mars|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/001910359290016Z|journal=Icarus|language=en|volume=100|issue=1|pages=40–47|doi=10.1016/0019-1035(92)90016-Z|bibcode=1992Icar..100...40I|via=|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=November 5, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201105231832/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/001910359290016Z|url-status=live}} Mercury is too small and hot for its [[gravity]] to keep any thick atmosphere for a long time. It does have a thin [[exosphere]] that is made up of [[hydrogen]], [[helium]], [[oxygen]], [[sodium]], [[calcium]], [[potassium]].{{Cite journal|last1=Domingue|first1=Deborah L.|last2=Koehn|first2=Patrick L.|last3=Killen|first3=Rosemary M.|last4=Sprague|first4=Ann L.|last5=Sarantos|first5=Menelaos|last6=Cheng|first6=Andrew F.|last7=Bradley|first7=Eric T.|last8=McClintock|first8=William E.|date=2007|title=Mercury's Atmosphere: A Surface-Bounded Exosphere|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s11214-007-9260-9|journal=Space Science Reviews|language=en|volume=131|issue=1–4|pages=161–186|doi=10.1007/s11214-007-9260-9|bibcode=2007SSRv..131..161D|s2cid=121301247|issn=0038-6308|via=|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=May 26, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220526123620/https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11214-007-9260-9|url-status=live}}{{Cite web|date=November 6, 2015|title=Mercury Fact Sheet|url=http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/mercuryfact.html|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151106171436/http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/mercuryfact.html|archive-date=November 6, 2015}} This exosphere is blown away and replenished from lots of sources. Hydrogen and helium may come from the [[solar wind]]. [[Radioactive decay]] of [[Chemical element|elements]] inside the crust of Mercury provide another source of helium, as well as sodium and potassium.{{Cite book|title=Mercury|date=1988|publisher=University of Arizona Press|others=Vilas, Faith., Chapman, Clark R., Matthews, Mildred Shapley., American Astronomical Society. Division for Planetary Sciences., International Astronomical Union. Commission 16., Mercury Conference (1986 : Tucson, Ariz.)|isbn=0-8165-1085-7|location=Tucson|oclc=18557585}} ==Orbit and rotation== [[File:Mercuryorbitsolarsystem.gif|thumb|right|Animation of Mercury and the Earth orbiting the Sun]] Mercury has the most [[Orbital eccentricity|eccentric orbit]] of all the [[planet]]s in the Solar System. It has an eccentricity of 0.21. It ranges from 46,000,000 to 70,000,000 km (29,000,000 to 43,000,000 mi) away from the Sun. Mercury takes 87.969 Earth days to go around the [[Sun]].{{Cite journal|last=Van Hoolst|first=T.|date=2003|title=Mercury's tides and interior structure|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1029/2003JE002126|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|language=en|volume=108|issue=E11|pages=5121|article-number=2003JE002126 |doi=10.1029/2003JE002126|bibcode=2003JGRE..108.5121V|issn=0148-0227}}{{Dead link|date=January 2022 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Mercury's [[axial tilt]] is 0.027 degrees.{{Cite book|title=Cosmic perspectives in space physics|url=https://archive.org/details/cosmicperspectiv0000bisw|last=Biswas, S. (Sukumar)|date=2000|publisher=Kluwer|isbn=0-7923-5813-9|location=Dordrecht|oclc=41319901}}{{Cite journal|last1=Margot|first1=J. L.|last2=Peale|first2=S. J.|last3=Jurgens|first3=R. F.|last4=Slade|first4=M. A.|last5=Holin|first5=I. V.|date=May 4, 2007|title=Large Longitude Libration of Mercury Reveals a Molten Core|url=https://www.sciencemag.org/lookup/doi/10.1126/science.1140514|journal=Science|language=en|volume=316|issue=5825|pages=710–714|doi=10.1126/science.1140514|pmid=17478713|bibcode=2007Sci...316..710M|s2cid=8863681|issn=0036-8075|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=May 26, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220526123621/https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1140514|url-status=live}} While most of Mercury's [[Stellar precession|precession]] is caused by the pull of other planets, the second-largest cause is the warping of [[Theory of relativity|space-time]] around the [[Sun]].{{Cite web|date=January 18, 2018|title=NASA Team Studies Middle-aged Sun by Tracking Motion of Mercury - NASA|url=https://www.nasa.gov/missions/nasa-team-studies-middle-aged-sun-by-tracking-motion-of-mercury/|access-date=October 21, 2025|language=en-US}} In the future, because Mercury's orbit's is very eccentric and [[Jupiter|Jupiter's]] huge gravity, its orbit may become unstable and the following things may happen: * It crashes into the [[Sun]] * It enters the Sun's [[Roche limit]] slowly and is torn apart * It crashes into [[Venus]] * It crashes into [[Earth]] * It is flung out of the [[Solar System]] and becomes a [[rogue planet]] ==List of satellites sent to Mercury== Few [[Satellite (artificial)|man-made satellites]] have been sent to Mercury to study it. They are: ===''Mariner 10''=== {{Main|Mariner 10}} [[File:Mariner_10.jpg|thumb|right|Mariner 10]] The first [[spacecraft]] to visit Mercury was NASA's Mariner 10. It stayed in Mercury's orbit from 1974 to 1975.{{Cite web|title=ch1|url=https://history.nasa.gov/SP-424/ch1.htm|access-date=September 12, 2020|website=history.nasa.gov|archive-date=August 1, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801210338/https://history.nasa.gov/SP-424/ch1.htm|url-status=live}} Mariner 10 took the first close-up [[picture]]s of Mercury's surface. It showed many features, such as the [[crater]]s.{{Cite web|last=Science@NASA|title=NASA - 2006 Transit of Mercury|url=https://www.nasa.gov/vision/universe/solarsystem/20oct_transitofmercury.html|access-date=September 12, 2020|website=www.nasa.gov|language=en|archive-date=April 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403230103/https://www.nasa.gov/vision/universe/solarsystem/20oct_transitofmercury.html|url-status=live}} Unfortunately, the same side of Mercury was day each time Mariner 10 flew close to Mercury. This made observing of both sides of Mercury impossible. In the end, less than 45% of the Mercury's surface was mapped.{{Cite web|title=ESA Science & Technology - Missions to Mercury|url=https://sci.esa.int/web/bepicolombo/-/56015-missions-to-mercury|access-date=September 12, 2020|website=sci.esa.int|archive-date=October 26, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201026045115/https://sci.esa.int/web/bepicolombo/-/56015-missions-to-mercury|url-status=live}}{{Cite web|title=USATODAY.com - MESSENGER to test theory of shrinking Mercury|url=https://usatoday30.usatoday.com/tech/news/2004-08-16-mercury-may-shrink_x.htm|access-date=September 12, 2020|website=usatoday30.usatoday.com|archive-date=July 26, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726231423/http://www.usatoday.com/tech/news/2004-08-16-mercury-may-shrink_x.htm|url-status=live}} Mariner 10 came close to Mercury three times.{{Cite web|title=mariner|url=https://history.nasa.gov/SP-423/mariner.htm|access-date=September 12, 2020|website=history.nasa.gov|archive-date=December 25, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171225233442/https://history.nasa.gov/SP-423/mariner.htm|url-status=live}} At the first time, it found a [[magnetic field]], which surprised [[Planetary geology|planetary geologists]] because Mercury's rotation was too slow to create a magnetic field. The second time was mainly used to take pictures of Mercury's surface. At the third time, it got more information about the magnetic field. It showed that the Mercury's magnetic field is like the Earth's magnetic field.{{Cite journal|last=Ness|first=NormanF.|date=1978|title=Mercury: Magnetic field and interior|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF00240907|journal=Space Science Reviews|language=en|volume=21|issue=5|page=527|doi=10.1007/BF00240907|bibcode=1978SSRv...21..527N|s2cid=120025983|issn=0038-6308|via=|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=May 26, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220526123623/https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00240907|url-status=live}}{{Cite journal|last1=Aharonson|first1=Oded|last2=Zuber|first2=Maria T|last3=Solomon|first3=Sean C|date=2004|title=Crustal remanence in an internally magnetized non-uniform shell: a possible source for Mercury's magnetic field?|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0012821X03006824|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|language=en|volume=218|issue=3–4|pages=261–268|doi=10.1016/S0012-821X(03)00682-4|bibcode=2004E&PSL.218..261A|via=|access-date=September 12, 2020|archive-date=April 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403163043/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0012821X03006824|url-status=live}} On March 24, 1975, eight days after its last close fly by, Mariner 10 ran out of [[fuel]]. Because its orbit could no longer be controlled, mission controllers shut down the probe .{{Cite web|title=ch8|url=https://history.nasa.gov/SP-424/ch8.htm|access-date=September 12, 2020|website=history.nasa.gov|archive-date=August 1, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801210412/https://history.nasa.gov/SP-424/ch8.htm|url-status=live}} Mariner 10 is thought to still be orbiting the Sun.{{Cite web|title=NASA - NSSDCA - Spacecraft - Details|url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1973-085A|access-date=September 12, 2020|website=nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov|archive-date=September 8, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180908063158/https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraftDisplay.do?id=1973-085A|url-status=live}} ===''MESSENGER''=== {{Main|MESSENGER}} [[File:MESSENGER_-_spacecraft_at_mercury_-_atmercury_lg.jpg|thumb|right|MESSENGER]]The second satellite to visit Mercury is NASA's MESSENGER. It stands for MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging. It was launched on August 3, 2004. It made a fly-by of [[Earth]] in August 2005. It made another fly-by of [[Venus]] in October 2006.{{Cite web|title=MESSENGER Engine Burn Puts Spacecraft on Track for Venus|url=http://www.spaceref.com/news/viewsr.html?pid=18956|access-date=September 14, 2020|website=www.spaceref.com}} It made its first fly-by of Mercury happened on January 14, 2008, a second on October 6, 2008, and a third on September 29, 2009.{{Cite web|date=May 13, 2013|title=MESSENGER: MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging|url=http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/gallery/sciencePhotos/image.php?gallery_id=2&image_id=115|access-date=September 14, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130513080731/http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/gallery/sciencePhotos/image.php?gallery_id=2&image_id=115|archive-date=May 13, 2013}}{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=MESSENGER Gains Critical Gravity Assist for Mercury Orbital Observations|url=http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/news_room/details.php?id=136|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130510175510/http://messenger.jhuapl.edu/news_room/details.php?id=136|archive-date=May 10, 2013|access-date=September 14, 2020}} It made a map of most of Mercury that ''Mariner 10'' didn't map. The first image of Mercury orbiting the Sun was gotten on March 29, 2011. MESSENGER was made to study Mercury's high [[density]], the history of Mercury's [[geology]], its magnetic field, the [[structure]] of its core, if it has ice at its poles, and where its thin atmosphere comes from. ''MESSENGER'' crashed into Mercury's surface on April 30, 2015.{{Cite web|last=March 2015|first=Mike Wall 29|title=NASA Mercury Probe Trying to Survive for Another Month|url=https://www.space.com/28948-messenger-mercury-probe-final-days.html|access-date=September 14, 2020|website=Space.com|date=March 29, 2015|language=en|archive-date=September 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200919004135/https://www.space.com/28948-messenger-mercury-probe-final-days.html|url-status=live}}{{Cite news|last=Chang|first=Kenneth|date=April 27, 2015|title=NASA's Messenger Mission Is Set to Crash Into Mercury|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/04/28/science/nasas-messenger-mission-is-set-to-crash-into-mercury.html|access-date=September 14, 2020|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=April 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190401024447/https://www.nytimes.com/2015/04/28/science/nasas-messenger-mission-is-set-to-crash-into-mercury.html|url-status=live}}{{Cite news|last=Corum|first=Jonathan|date=April 30, 2015|title=Messenger's Collision Course With Mercury|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2015/04/30/science/space/messenger-collides-with-mercury.html,%20https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2015/04/30/science/space/messenger-collides-with-mercury.html|access-date=September 14, 2020|issn=0362-4331}}{{Dead link|date=October 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} ===''Bepicolombo''=== {{Main|Bepicolombo}} [[File:BepiColombo_spacecraft_model.png|thumb|right|Bepicolombo]]The [[European Space Agency]] and the [[Japanese Space Agency]] made and launched a spacecraft called ''BepiColombo.'' It will [[orbit]] Mercury with two probes: one to map the planet and the other to study its [[magnetosphere]].{{Cite web|title=ESA gives go-ahead to build BepiColombo|url=http://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/ESA_gives_go-ahead_to_build_BepiColombo|access-date=September 14, 2020|website=www.esa.int|language=en|archive-date=September 15, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200915130227/http://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/ESA_gives_go-ahead_to_build_BepiColombo|url-status=live}} It was launched on October 20, 2018. ''BepiColombo'' is expected to reach Mercury in 2025.{{Cite web|title=ESA Science & Technology - Fact Sheet|url=https://sci.esa.int/web/bepicolombo/-/47346-fact-sheet|access-date=September 14, 2020|website=sci.esa.int|archive-date=September 27, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927173203/https://sci.esa.int/web/bepicolombo/-/47346-fact-sheet|url-status=live}} It will release the probe that will study the magnetosphere into an [[elliptical orbit]]. It will then release the probe the will make a map of Mercury into a [[circular orbit]]. == Related pages == * [[List of planets]] == References == {{reflist}} == Other websites == * {{cite book |url=https://history.nasa.gov/SP-423/sp423.htm |title=Atlas of Mercury |publisher=NASA |date=1978 |id=SP-423 |access-date=August 16, 2020 |archive-date=October 9, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191009033507/https://history.nasa.gov/SP-423/sp423.htm |url-status=dead }} * [http://www.solarviews.com/eng/mercury.htm SolarViews.Com] * [http://www.planetfacts.net/Mercury-Facts.html www.planetfacts.net] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111129074113/http://www.planetfacts.net/Mercury-Facts.html |date=November 29, 2011 }} {{Solar System}} {{authority control}} [[Category:Mercury (planet)| ]]

''Top row, left to right'': The [[MacBook Neo]], [[MacBook Air]], and [[MacBook Pro]] laptops
''Bottom row, left to right'': The [[iMac]], [[Mac Mini]], and [[Mac Studio]] desktops }} | lifespan = 1984–present | aka = Macintosh | website = {{URL|https://www.apple.com/mac/|apple.com/mac}} }} [[File:M1 iMac vector.svg|thumb|An [[iMac]]. Unlike most computers, it has a computer system with the screen inside it.]] The '''Apple Macintosh''' or just '''Mac''' is a line of [[personal computer]]s made by the American company [[Apple Inc.|Apple Inc]]. The Macintosh was one of the first computers in which the people could use a mouse for pointing on a screen which had icons. This new way of working with a computer ([[interface]]) was known as [[graphical user interfaces and consoles|graphical user interface]]. It was this feature of the Macintosh that made it so popular. == History == === Processor history === The '''Apple–Intel transition''' was when Apple changed the [[CPU]] of Macintosh computers from [[PowerPC]] processors to Intel [[x86]] processors.{{cite web|url=https://www.apple.com/pr/library/2005/06/06Apple-to-Use-Intel-Microprocessors-Beginning-in-2006.html|title=Press Info - Apple to Use Intel Microprocessors Beginning in 2006|date=2005-06-06|publisher=Apple|accessdate=2011-11-01}}{{cite web|url=http://www.macworld.com/article/45176/2005/06/oranges.html|title=Apple faithful learning to like oranges|publisher=Macworld|accessdate=2011-11-01}}{{Dead link|date=December 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} It was announced at the 2005 [[WWDC|World Wide Developers Conference]].{{cite web|url=https://www.wired.com/gadgets/mac/commentary/cultofmac/2005/06/67767?currentPage=all|title=Apple and Intel OK With Coders|author=Daniel Terdiman|publisher=Wired.com|accessdate=2011-11-01}} [[Steve Jobs]] announced it. Macintoshes were different than other personal computers for many years based on their [[central processing unit]] (CPU). At the start, Macs used [[Motorola 68000]] chips instead of [[Intel]] chips. Later, Macs used [[PowerPC]] chips. In 2006, Macs started to use Intel chips. In 2020, Macs started to use Apple Silicon chips. Today, Macs are sold with [[Apple M1]] chips. == Macintoshes == {| class="wikitable" |- | || '''Compact''' (portable) || '''Consumer''' ([[wikt:end user|end user]]) || '''Professional''' |- | '''Desktop''' || [[Mac Mini]] || [[iMac]] || [[Mac Pro]]; [[Mac Studio]] |- | '''Portable''' ([[MacBook]]) || [[MacBook]] || [[MacBook Air]] || [[MacBook Pro]] |- | '''Server''' || [[Mac Mini]] (server) || [[Mac Mini]] (server) || [[Mac Pro]] (server) |} === Software === The Mac does not have the [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] operating system installed on it. It has its own range of operating systems, known as [[macOS]]. The newest operating system is known as “Tahoe". Macs can run both Windows and macOS at the same time with help of a program called “Boot Camp”, which comes on every [[:en:MacBook Pro (Intel-based)|Intel-based]] Mac. In general, Macintosh computers cost more than other computers of the same speed. ==Related pages== * [[iMac]] * [[MacBook]] * [[MacBook Air]] * [[MacBook Pro]] * [[Macintosh 128K]] * [[Macintosh Classic]] * Other popular products of Apple include [[iPod]], [[iPhone]] and [[iPad]]. ==References== {{Commons}} {{reflist}} {{Tech-stub}} [[Category:Apple hardware|Macintosh]]

title: Metre
text:
[[File:5 metres (8349446738) (2).jpg|thumb|right|This giraffe is nearly five metres tall.]]
The '''metre''' (British spelling) or '''meter''' (American spelling) (symbol: '''m''') is the basic [[units of measurement|unit]] of [[length]] in the [[SI]] measurement system. The [[symbol]] for the metre is '''m'''. The first meaning (in the [[French Revolution]]) was one ten-millionth of the [[distance]] between the [[Earth]]'s [[equator]] and the [[North Pole]] along the [[Paris]] [[meridian]].<ref name=NIST>{{cite web|url=http://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/meter.html|title=Historical context of the SI|publisher=US Government - National Institute of Standards and Technology}}</ref> The metre is now defined as the [[distance]] [[light]] travels in a [[vacuum]] in 1/299,792,458 of a [[second]].<ref name=NIST/>

In the [[Imperial unit|imperial]] system of measurement, one yard is 0.9144 metres (after international agreement in 1959), so a metre is very near to 39.37 [[inch]]es: about 3.281 [[Foot (unit of length)|feet]], or 1.0936 [[US yard|yards]].

[[File:Platinum-Iridium meter bar.jpg|thumb|right|The bar (made of [[platinum]] and [[iridium]]) that defined the length of a metre until 1960.]]

title: Magnifying glass
text:
[[File:Magnifying glass2.jpg|upright|thumb|240px|<small>A magnifying glass used to look at a [[postage stamp]]</small>]]
A '''magnifying glass''' is a [[Lens (optics)|lens]] through which can be used to make things appear bigger, so you can see them better. It is used in many applications and manual operations, e.g., for examining [[postage stamps]] in [[philately]].

The magnifying glass consists of a piece of convex<ref>[http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/convex convex in English Wiktionary].</ref>-shaped glass or plastic. It has to be held at the right distance between the eye and the object for the object to be in [[Focus (optics)|focus]]. The magnifying glass usually comes with a handle. A [[telescope]] is a more advanced kind of magnifying glass and consists of at least two glass lenses. 

A pair of [[binoculars]] is like a telescope for each eye. ''Spectacles'' or [[eyeglasses]] also use lenses to correct a person's vision.

title: Molecule
text:
{{one source|date=April 2021}}
[[File:Glucose.PNG|200px|thumb|right|This is a [[sugar]] molecule. Carbon atoms are made blue, oxygen atoms are made red and hydrogen atoms are made white to show the difference. In reality atoms do not have a color.]]
A '''molecule''' is the smallest amount of a [[chemical substance]] that can exist. If a molecule were split into smaller pieces, it would be a different [[substance]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://goldbook.iupac.org/|title=The IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology: The Gold Book|date=2019|publisher=International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC)|editor-last=Gold|editor-first=Victor|edition=4|location=Research Triangle Park, NC|language=en|doi=10.1351/goldbook.m04002}}</ref>

Molecules are made up of [[atom]]s that are stuck together in a particular shape or [[form]].  Not all combinations of atoms are equally possible; atoms make certain shapes in preference to others.  Also, they have different [[valency]].   For example, [[oxygen]] atoms always have two bonds with other atoms, [[carbon]] atoms always have four bonds with other atoms, and [[nitrogen]] atoms always have three bonds with other atoms.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Chemistry : the central science.|date=2002|publisher=Prentice Hall|others=Theodore L. Brown, Theodore L. Brown|isbn=0-13-066997-0|edition=9th|location=Upper Saddle River, NJ|oclc=47953855}}</ref> <ref>{{Citation|title=Quark|date=2025-06-09|url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Quark&oldid=1294786786|work=Wikipedia|language=en|access-date=2025-07-04}}</ref>

In the [[w:Kinetic theory of gases|kinetic theory of gases]], the term ''molecule'' is often used for any gaseous [[particle]] regardless of its composition. According to this definition, [[noble gas]] atoms are considered molecules as they are in fact monoatomic molecules.<ref>{{cite book| last= Chandra| first= Sulekh| title= Comprehensive Inorganic Chemistry| date= 2005| publisher= New Age Publishers| isbn= 81-224-1512-1}}</ref>

In [[gas]]es like [[air]], the molecules are just flying around. In [[liquid]]s like [[water]], the molecules are stuck together but they can still move. In [[solid]]s like [[sugar]], the molecules can only [[vibrate]].  In the fourth [[state of matter]] known as [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]], the atoms are [[Ionization|ionized]] and cannot form molecules.

With a [[molecular formula]], you can write down the numbers of all atoms in a molecule. For example, the molecular formula of [[glucose]] is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>. That means that one molecule of glucose is made up of six carbon atoms, twelve hydrogen atoms and six oxygen atoms.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Chemistry|url=https://archive.org/details/chemistry0006chan|last=Chang|first=Raymond|date=1998|publisher=McGraw-Hill|isbn=0-07-115221-0|edition=6th|location=Boston, Mass.|oclc=711906521}}</ref>

== Bonding ==

For a molecule to exist, [[atoms]] have to stick together. This happens when two atoms share [[electron]]s. Instead of circling just one atom, the electron now circles around two. This is called a [[covalent bond]].  Sometimes, more than one electron is shared. The more [[electron]]<nowiki/>s are shared, the stronger the bond gets and the stronger the atoms stick together.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Chemical structure and bonding|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780935702613|last=DeKock|first=Roger L.|date=1989|publisher=University Science Books|others=Harry B. Gray|isbn=0-935702-61-X|edition=2nd|location=Mill Valley, Calif.|oclc=20570258}}</ref>

Bonds can also be broken apart. Since most bonds require energy to form, they also give off [[energy]] when they are broken. But before most bonds break, the molecule has to be heated. Then the atoms start to move, and when they move too much, the bond breaks. Molecules that require less energy to break than they give off when broken are called [[Fuel|fuels]]. For example, a candle will just sit there and nothing happens. But when you use a match to light it, it will burn for a long time. The match brings the energy to break the first bonds, which release enough energy to break the bonds below them, until the candle has burned down. There are also [[ionic bond]]s.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Biology : exploring life|url=https://archive.org/details/biologyexploring0000camp|last=Campbell|first=Neil A.|date=2006|publisher=Pearson/Prentice Hall|others=Brad Williamson, Robin J. Heyden, Pearson/Prentice Hall|isbn=0-13-250882-6|location=Boston, Mass.|oclc=75299209}}</ref>

title: Moral reasoning
text:
'''Moral reasoning''' is a topic [[education|studied]] in [[psychology]] and in moral [[philosophy]]. It studies how people think about moral issues, problems, and questions. [[Psychologist]]s who have studied it include [[Lawrence Kohlberg]] and Elliot Turiel. Kohlberg said that [[moral]] understanding develops in three main stages as a person gets older, but Turiel said that there are three domains of moral understanding that develop at the same time as a person gets older.

Moral philosophy, or [[ethics]], is a major branch of [[philosophy]]. It is the study of value or quality. It covers the [[Philosophical analysis|analysis]] and use of [[concept]]s such as [[wikt:right#Adjective|right]], [[wikt:wrong|wrong]], [[Good (philosophy)|good]], [[evil]], and [[moral responsibility|responsibility]].
