Scientific research uses [[hypotheses]] based on ideas or earlier knowledge, which can be categorized through different topics. Then those hypotheses are tested by [[experiments]]. People who study and research science and try to find out everything about it are called [[scientist]]s. Scientists [[Research|study]] things by [[sight|looking]] at them very carefully, by [[measure|measuring]] them, and by doing [[experiment]]s and [[test]]s. Scientists try to [[wikt:explain|explain]] why things act the way they do, and [[predict]] what will happen. The [[history of science]] is thousands of years old. The beginnings of modern science can be found in [[ancient Egypt]] and [[Mesopotamia]] (around 3000–1200 BCE). They developed early ideas in [[Mathematics|math]], [[astronomy]], and [[medicine]]. They influenced the [[Ancient Greece|Greeks]], who tried to explain what happened in our world using natural causes. Later, during [[Golden Age of India|India’s Golden Age]], more progress was made. This included the creation of the Hindu–Arabic number system.{{Cite book|title=India: a history|url=https://archive.org/details/indiahistory00keay|last=Keay|first=John|date=2000|publisher=Atlantic Monthly Press|isbn=978-0-87113-800-2|edition=1st|location=New York}}{{Cite book|title=A history of natural philosophy: from the ancient world to the nineteenth century|url=https://archive.org/details/historyofnatural0000gran|last=Grant|first=Edward|date=2007|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-68957-1|location=Cambridge New York}}{{Cite book|title=The beginnings of western science: the European scientific tradition in philosophical, religious, and institutional context, prehistory to A.D. 1450|url=https://archive.org/details/beginningsofwest0000lind_d9a5|last=Lindberg|first=David C.|date=2007|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-48205-7|edition=2nd|location=Chicago, Ill.}} After the [[Western Roman Empire]] fell during the [[Early Middle Ages]] (400–1000 CE), scientific progress in [[Europe]] slowed down. But progress started up again during certain periods. In the [[Islamic world]], [[scholars]] kept, studied, and made Greek science better during the [[Islamic Golden Age]].{{Cite book|title=The beginnings of western science: the European scientific tradition in philosophical, religious, and institutional context, prehistory to A.D. 1450|url=https://archive.org/details/beginningsofwest0000lind_d9a5|last=Lindberg|first=David C.|date=2007|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-48205-7|edition=2nd|location=Chicago, Ill.}} Later, when the [[Byzantine Empire]] got weaker, its scholars took Greek books to Western Europe, helping start the [[Renaissance]].{{Cite book|title=A history of natural philosophy: from the ancient world to the nineteenth century|url=https://archive.org/details/historyofnatural0000gran|last=Grant|first=Edward|date=2007|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-68957-1|location=Cambridge New York}} From the 10th to 13th centuries, Europe re-learned Greek and Islamic science. This helped cause the [[scientific revolution]] in the 16th century. Science began to change a lot. New discoveries removed old ideas.{{Cite book|title=The beginnings of western science: the European scientific tradition in philosophical, religious, and institutional context, prehistory to A.D. 1450|url=https://archive.org/details/beginningsofwest0000lind_d9a5|last=Lindberg|first=David C.|date=2007|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-48205-7|edition=2nd|location=Chicago, Ill.}}{{Cite book|title=The scientific revolution: a very short introduction|url=https://archive.org/details/scientificrevolu0000prin|last=Principe|first=Lawrence|date=2011|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-956741-6|edition=1st|series=Very short introductions|location=Oxford}} [[The scientific method]] became more important. By the 19th century, science became more professional and organized.{{Cite book|title=From natural philosophy to the sciences: writing the history of nineteenth-century science|url=https://archive.org/details/fromnaturalphilo0000unse|date=2003|publisher=Univ. of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-08928-7|editor-last=Cahan|editor-first=David|location=Chicago, Ill. London}} Instead of calling it “natural philosophy”, it was called “natural science”.{{Cite book|title=The territories of science and religion|last=Harrison|first=Peter|date=2015|publisher=The University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-18451-7|location=Chicago London}} ==Etymology and Terminology== The history of the word “science” and the terms used in science tell us a lot about how the subject has changed over [[time]] and what it means in different [[culture]]s and [[Philosophy|philosophies]]. The word “science” comes from the [[Latin]] word “scientia,” which means “knowledge.” That word came from the verb “scire,” which means “to know.”{{Cite web|title=Science - Etymology, Origin & Meaning|url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/science|access-date=2025-07-17|website=etymonline|language=en-US}} In [[ancient Rome]], scientia just meant any kind of [[knowledge]] you could get through [[learning]] or [[experience]]. It included many subjects like [[philosophy]], [[Rhetoric|speaking (rhetoric)]], and [[Mathematics|math]]. But back then, it did not mean what we now think of as science.{{Cite web|last=Cartwright|first=Mark|date=2016-09-06|title=Roman Science|url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Roman_Science/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=World History Encyclopedia|language=en}} In ancient Greece, a similar idea was called “epistēmē” (ἐπιστήμη). Philosophers like [[Aristotle]] and [[Plato]] used this word to mean knowledge that could be proven through [[reason]]. They saw it as different from “doxa,” which meant [[opinion]], something that might not be true or could change.{{Citation|last=Parry|first=Richard|title=Episteme and Techne|date=2024|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2024/entries/episteme-techne/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Winter 2024|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2025-07-17|editor2-last=Nodelman|editor2-first=Uri}} The meaning of “science” started to change during the [[Scientific Revolution]] in the 1500s and 1600s. During this time, famous thinkers like [[Galileo Galilei]], [[Johannes Kepler]], [[Francis Bacon]], and [[Isaac Newton]] began to create a new way of learning about the world. They used [[observation]], [[experiment]]s, and [[Mathematics|math]] to find answers. This method helped form the basis of what we now call modern science.{{Cite web|title=STEAM News - The Precursor to Modern Science: The Scientific Revolution|url=https://www.steamnews.org/articles/science/the-precursor-to-modern-science-the-scientific-revolution|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.steamnews.org|language=en-US}} Back then, people did not call it “science”, they called it “natural philosophy”, especially when studying the physical world like [[motion]], [[planet]]s, or [[light]].{{Citation|last=Blair|first=Ann|title=Natural Philosophy|date=2006|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cambridge-history-of-science/natural-philosophy/F1FD6F16ACFC81FF69E7B62B013C6FF0|work=The Cambridge History of Science: Volume 3: Early Modern Science|volume=3|pages=363–406|editor-last=Park|editor-first=Katharine|series=The Cambridge History of Science|place=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-57244-6|access-date=2025-07-17|editor2-last=Daston|editor2-first=Lorraine}} The word “scientist” was not even invented until 1834. A man named [[William Whewell]], who studied the [[History of science|history]] and [[philosophy of science]], came up with it. He suggested “scientist” in a book review to describe someone who studies the natural world in a careful, organized way, just like the word “artist” describes someone who creates [[art]].{{Cite web|title=scientist - Quick search results {{!}} Oxford English Dictionary|url=https://www.oed.com/search/dictionary/?q=scientist|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.oed.com|language=en}}{{Cite journal|last=Ross|first=Sydney|date=1962|title=Scientist: The story of a word|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00033796200202722|journal=Annals of Science|language=en|volume=18|issue=2|pages=65–85|doi=10.1080/00033796200202722|issn=0003-3790}} Science words (or scientific terms) have changed and grown over time, just like science itself. In the past, many science terms came from [[Greek language|Greek]] and [[Latin]], because those were the main [[language]]s used by educated people in [[Europe]] for many centuries.{{Cite web|title=Latinus Scientificus: The History and Culture of Scientific Latin by Barry Wood|url=https://jbh.journals.villanova.edu/article/download/2403/2325?inline=1|access-date=2025-07-17|website=jbh.journals.villanova.edu}} For example, the word “biology” comes from the Greek words bios (which means “life”) and logos (which means “study”), so [[biology]] means “the study of life.”{{Cite web|title=Biology - Etymology, Origin & Meaning|url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/biology|access-date=2025-07-17|website=etymonline|language=en-US}} The word “physics” comes from the Greek word physis, meaning “nature.”{{Cite web|title=Physics - Etymology, Origin & Meaning|url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/physics|access-date=2025-07-17|website=etymonline|language=en-US}} “Chemistry” likely comes from the Arabic word al-kīmiyāʾ, which has roots in ancient Egyptian and Greek (Hellenistic) [[alchemy]], a practice that tried to change substances and discover how materials work.{{Cite web|title=Chemistry - Etymology, Origin & Meaning|url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/chemistry|access-date=2025-07-17|website=etymonline|language=en-US}} Scientific terms are very important because they help scientists be precise (use exact meanings), communicate clearly, and organize ideas and information. Each area of science has its own set of special words to describe things it studies. For example, in [[physics]], words like “momentum,” “entropy,” and “quantum” have very specific meanings that are different from how they are used in everyday language.{{Cite journal|date=2023|title=What's in a name?|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-023-02185-2|journal=Nature Physics|language=en|volume=19|issue=8|pages=1065|doi=10.1038/s41567-023-02185-2|bibcode=2023NatPh..19.1065. |issn=1745-2481}} In [[biology]], scientists name [[living thing]]s using a system called [[Binomial nomenclature|Linnaean binomial nomenclature]]. This system gives each organism a Latin name made of two parts: the [[genus]] and [[species]].{{Cite web|date=2025-07-14|title=Carolus Linnaeus - Taxonomy, Binomial Nomenclature, Systematics {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Carolus-Linnaeus/Classification-by-natural-characters|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} For example, [[human]]s are called Homo sapiens.{{Cite web|date=2025-06-16|title=Homo sapiens {{!}} Meaning, Characteristics, & Evolution {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Homo-sapiens|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} Having standardized scientific words is important for making sure experiments can be repeated correctly ([[Reproducibility|replicability]]), letting scientists check each other’s work ([[peer review]]), and helping scientists from all over the world work together, even if they speak different languages.{{Citation|last=Glantz|first=Meyer D.|title=Chapter 2 - The Terminology of Addictive Behavior|date=2013-01-01|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123983367000024|work=Principles of Addiction|pages=13–22|editor-last=Miller|editor-first=Peter M.|place=San Diego|publisher=Academic Press|doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-398336-7.00002-4|isbn=978-0-12-398336-7|access-date=2025-07-17}} Many words used in science today come from the history and culture of the time when they were first used. Some scientific terms actually started out as jokes, creative ideas, or simple descriptions, but they became official because people started using them so much. For example, the term “[[Big Bang]]” was first used by astronomer [[Fred Hoyle]] in a radio broadcast in 1949. He did not believe in the Big Bang theory and actually used the name to make fun of it. But, the name caught on and is now the main word we use for how the [[universe]] began.{{Cite journal|last=Kragh|first=Helge|date=2024-03-25|title=How did the Big Bang get its name? Here's the real story|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-00894-z|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=627|issue=8005|pages=726–728|doi=10.1038/d41586-024-00894-z |pmid=38528166 |bibcode=2024Natur.627..726K }} Another example is the word “[[quark]],” which is used for tiny particles that make up [[proton]]s and [[neutron]]s. Physicist [[Murray Gell-Mann]] chose this word from a line in a book called Finnegans Wake by James Joyce. This shows how [[creativity]] and [[language]] play a role in science.{{Cite web|title=What Does 'Quark' Have to Do with Finnegans Wake?|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/quark|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.merriam-webster.com|language=en}} Scientific words often come from metaphors or comparisons to help people understand complex ideas. For example, the word “[[cell]]” in [[biology]] was first used by [[Robert Hooke]] in 1665. When he looked at [[Cork (material)|cork]] under a [[microscope]], he saw tiny box-like spaces that reminded him of the small rooms (cells) where monks lived. That is how the name “cell” was born.{{Cite web|title=What is a cell? {{!}} British Society for Cell Biology|url=https://bscb.org/learning-resources/softcell-e-learning/what-is-a-cell/|access-date=2025-07-17|language=en-US}} In computer science, the word “[[Computer virus|virus]]” is used to describe a program that can copy itself and infect other programs, just like real [[virus]]es do in the [[human body]]. Scientists used this name because it helped people understand how these harmful programs behave. These examples show that scientific words often come from real-world ideas, and they help us understand new or difficult concepts by connecting them to things we already know.{{Cite web|title=Fred Cohen & Associates|url=http://all.net/books/virus/index.html|access-date=2025-07-17|website=all.net}}{{Cite web|title=Professor Len Adleman explains how he coined the term "computer virus"|url=https://www.welivesecurity.com/2017/11/01/professor-len-adleman-explains-computer-virus-term/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.welivesecurity.com|language=en}} The language used in science is always changing to become more fair, clear, and inclusive. In the past, many scientific terms were based on ideas that focused too much on [[human]]s, [[Europe]], or one [[gender]]. Over time, scientists have worked to replace these words with ones that are more neutral and accurate. For example, in [[astronomy]], the word “[[planet]]” was officially redefined in 2006 by the [[International Astronomical Union|International Astronomical Union (IAU)]]. Because of this change, [[Pluto]] was no longer called a full planet, but instead a [[dwarf planet]], which caused a lot of debate.{{Cite web|date=2023-07-22|title=What is a Planet?|url=https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/what-is-a-planet/|access-date=2025-07-17|language=en-US}} In everyday science language, people now often say “human” instead of “man”, and “humankind” instead of “mankind”. These changes help make science feel more welcoming to everyone, no matter their background or identity.{{Cite news|title=Man, mankind or people ?|language=en|url=https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/man-mankind-or-people|access-date=2025-07-17}} As science keeps moving forward, new inventions and discoveries also bring new words. For example, scientists discovered [[CRISPR]], a tool that can edit [[gene]]s. The word CRISPR is an acronym (a short word made from initials) for “Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats.” It shows how scientists create short terms to explain big, complex ideas.{{Cite web|title=CRISPR|url=https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/CRISPR|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.genome.gov|language=en}} New fields like [[machine learning]], [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence (AI)]], and [[quantum computing]] are also creating new words. These words need to be defined very clearly, so scientists from different areas can understand each other and work together without confusion.{{Cite web|title=Top scientific discoveries and breakthroughs for 2025|url=https://www.cas.org/resources/cas-insights/scientific-breakthroughs-2025-emerging-trends-watch|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.cas.org|language=en}} ==History== ===Prehistoric science=== [[File:Stonehenge2007 07 30.jpg|thumb|[[Stonehenge]] was a [[megalith]] built by prehistoric humans]] The period of prehistoric science includes the [[Palaeolithic]], [[Mesolithic]], and [[Neolithic|Neolithic age]]s, which lasted from about 2.5 million years ago to around 3000 BCE. Even though these early efforts were not "science" the way we know it today, they showed careful observation, experiments, and the start of organized thinking. One of the first and most important forms of early science was making [[stone tool]]s. It started with a human ancestor called [[Homo habilis]] and continued through different prehistoric cultures like the [[Acheulean]], [[Mousterian]], and [[Upper Paleolithic]]. People made tools like [[hand axe]]s, [[Scraper (archeology)|scraper]]s, [[Bone tool|awl]]s (used for poking holes), and [[Clacton Spear|spear tip]]s. To do this, they had to understand how [[stone]]s break, what kinds of [[rock]]s work best, and how to hit them with the right amount of [[force]]. [[Archeology|Archaeologists]] (scientists who study ancient human history) have found evidence that these early humans learned by [[trial and error]], and they shared their knowledge with others. Over time, they improved their tools to make them stronger and more useful. This kind of hands-on learning and passing down of skills is one of the earliest examples of using science to solve problems, especially in understanding materials and how to use them, what we now call [[materials science]].{{Cite journal|last=Tine|first=Shalon van|date=2017|title=Prehistory|url=https://press.rebus.community/historyoftech/front-matter/prehistory/|journal=Rebus|language=en}} Early humans also showed basic knowledge of [[astronomy]], the study of the [[sky]]. This can be seen in archaeological discoveries like the [[Blanchard bone]] (around 30,000 BCE) and the [[Lascaux|Lascaux Cave paintings]] (around 17,000 BCE). These objects and drawings may show that early people were watching the Moon’s phases or recognizing star groups like the [[Pleiades|Pleiades constellation]].{{Cite web|title=The Ishango and Blanchard Bones - PlanetQuest|url=https://www.planetquest.org/learn/ishango.html|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.planetquest.org}}{{Cite web|last=Cottier|first=Cody|date=2023-01-17|title=Ancient humans and their early depictions of the universe|url=https://www.astronomy.com/science/ancient-humans-and-their-early-depictions-of-the-universe/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Astronomy Magazine|language=en-US}} One of the earliest sky-watching structures is the [[Nabta Playa]] stone circle in [[Egypt|southern Egypt]], built around 6000 BCE. It is one of the oldest known examples of people using [[megalith]]s (large stones) to line up with the [[Summer solstice|summer solstice sunrise]], the longest day of the year. It may also have helped track seasonal rains, which were very important for survival in that dry area.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of archaeoastronomy and ethnoastronomy|date=2014|publisher=Springer Reference|isbn=978-1-4614-6140-1|editor-last=Ruggles|editor-first=C. L. N.|location=New York}} These structures show that early people spent years carefully watching the sky, noticing patterns, and trying to predict natural cycles, like when [[rain]] or [[season]]s would come. This was an early step toward the science of astronomy.{{Cite web|title=Astronomy Lecture Notes - Early History|url=http://www.phy.olemiss.edu/~luca/astr/Topics-Introduction/Ancient-N.html|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.phy.olemiss.edu}} Another major scientific step happened during the [[Neolithic Revolution]], around 10,000 BCE, when humans started [[farming]]. This time period was extremely important because people learned to grow [[plant]]s and raise [[animal]]s. They had to understand [[soil]], [[water]], and [[Weather|weather pattern]]s to grow [[food]] successfully. Early farmers in places like the [[Fertile Crescent]] (in the [[Middle East]]), [[Yellow River civilization|China’s Yellow River valley]], and [[Mesoamerica]] ([[Central America]]) grew [[crop]]s like [[wheat]], [[barley]], [[millet]], [[rice]], and [[Maize|maize (corn)]].{{Cite web|title=Early Agricultural Communities|url=https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/early-agricultural-communities|access-date=2025-07-17|website=education.nationalgeographic.org|language=en}} They watched how these plants grew over many generations and chose the ones with the best traits, like more food, better taste, or the ability to survive without much water. This careful choosing is the beginning of [[genetics]] (even though they did not know that word), and their work helped people settle down, build villages, and eventually start [[civilization]]s. These farming skills are the beginning of what we now call [[agricultural science]].{{Cite web|title=Neolithic Revolution|url=https://www2.nau.edu/~gaud/bio301/content/neolth.htm|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www2.nau.edu}}{{Cite web|date=2025-07-17|title=What was the Neolithic Revolution?|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/neolithic-agricultural-revolution|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Culture|language=en}}{{Cite journal|last1=Bowles|first1=Samuel|last2=Choi|first2=Jung-Kyoo|date=2019|title=The Neolithic Agricultural Revolution and the Origins of Private Property|url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/701789|journal=Journal of Political Economy|volume=127|issue=5|pages=2186–2228|doi=10.1086/701789|issn=0022-3808}} Even though prehistoric people did not write things down, they still had surprisingly advanced [[Medicine|medical knowledge]]. One of the most amazing examples is [[Trepanning|trepanation]], a kind of [[surgery]] where people removed parts of the [[skull]]. Scientists have found skulls from as far back as 7000 BCE in [[Europe]], [[Africa]], and [[South America]] that show signs of this surgery, and some of the skulls even show [[healing]], which means people survived the operation.{{Cite journal|last1=Alt|first1=Kurt W.|last2=Jeunesse|first2=Christian|last3=Buitrago-Téllez|first3=Carlos H.|last4=Wächter|first4=Rüdiger|last5=Boës|first5=Eric|last6=Pichler|first6=Sandra L.|date=1997|title=Evidence for stone age cranial surgery|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/387360a0|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=387|issue=6631|pages=360|doi=10.1038/387360a0|pmid=9163419 |bibcode=1997Natur.387..360A |issn=1476-4687}} This suggests that early humans had basic knowledge of the body, special tools, and may have used natural medicines, like [[herb]]s, to reduce [[pain]] or stop [[infection]]. Another example is [[Ötzi the Iceman]], a frozen body found in the [[Alps]] from around 3300 BCE. His body had [[tattoo]]s that lined up with places used in [[acupuncture]], a method of healing still used today. He was also carrying a medicinal fungus called [[Fomitopsis betulina]], which may have been used to fight infection.{{Cite web|title=5000-year-old 'Iceman' may have benefited from a sophisticated health care system|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/5000-year-old-iceman-may-have-benefited-sophisticated-health-care-system|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.science.org|language=en}}{{Cite journal|last1=Pleszczyńska|first1=Małgorzata|last2=Lemieszek|first2=Marta K.|last3=Siwulski|first3=Marek|last4=Wiater|first4=Adrian|last5=Rzeski|first5=Wojciech|last6=Szczodrak|first6=Janusz|date=2017|title=Fomitopsis betulina (formerly Piptoporus betulinus): the Iceman's polypore fungus with modern biotechnological potential|journal=World Journal of Microbiology & Biotechnology|volume=33|issue=5|pages=83|doi=10.1007/s11274-017-2247-0|issn=1573-0972|pmc=5380686|pmid=28378220}} People in prehistoric times also began using [[Mathematics|math]] and [[measurement]]. They made tools like tally sticks to help them count. One of the oldest is the [[Lebombo bone]] from about 35,000 BCE, and another is the [[Ishango bone]] from around 20,000 BCE. These bones have carved marks that might show number patterns, multiples, or even prime numbers. Some scientists think they may also have tracked lunar cycles (the [[Phases of the Moon|phases of the moon]]).{{Cite book|title=Numbers and the making of us: counting and the course of human cultures|url=https://archive.org/details/numbersmakingofu0000ever|last=Everett|first=Caleb|date=2017|publisher=Harvard University press|isbn=978-0-674-50443-1|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts}}{{Cite journal|last1=d'Errico|first1=Francesco|last2=Doyon|first2=Luc|last3=Colagé|first3=Ivan|last4=Queffelec|first4=Alain|last5=Le Vraux|first5=Emma|last6=Giacobini|first6=Giacomo|last7=Vandermeersch|first7=Bernard|last8=Maureille|first8=Bruno|date=2018-02-19|title=From number sense to number symbols. An archaeological perspective|journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences|language=en|volume=373|issue=1740|article-number=20160518|doi=10.1098/rstb.2016.0518|pmid=29292345 |issn=0962-8436|pmc=5784044}} Later, in places like [[Mesopotamia]] and the [[Indus Valley civilization|Indus Valley]], early people started using standard measurements. They needed these for storing [[grain]], trading goods, and building things. They created systems to measure [[volume]] and [[weight]], which helped them with [[farming]], [[business]], and early forms of [[engineering]].{{Cite web|title=Old Babylonian metrology|url=https://myslu.stlawu.edu/~dmel/mesomath/obmetrology.html|access-date=2025-07-17|website=myslu.stlawu.edu}}{{Citation|last=Iwata|first=Shigeo|title=Weights and Measures in the Indus Valley|date=2016|url=https://link.springer.com/rwe/10.1007/978-94-007-7747-7_8938|encyclopedia=Encyclopaedia of the History of Science, Technology, and Medicine in Non-Western Cultures|pages=4473–4474|publisher=Springer, Dordrecht|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-94-007-7747-7_8938|isbn=978-94-007-7747-7|access-date=2025-07-17}} In prehistoric times, early people showed amazing skills in building large stone structures, which we now call megalithic architecture. One of the oldest examples is [[Göbekli Tepe]], built around 9600 BCE in what is now [[Turkey]]. It has huge stone pillars carved with [[animal]]s, arranged in circles. These stones are very heavy, and moving and placing them would have taken many people working together, using simple tools and their understanding of leverage (how to move heavy things using [[force]] and [[angle]]s). They probably also used basic measuring tools to plan where to put the stones.{{Cite web|last=Centre|first=UNESCO World Heritage|title=Göbekli Tepe|url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1572/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre|language=en}} Other examples, like [[Stonehenge]] in [[England]] (about 3000 BCE) and the stone lines at [[Carnac]] in [[France]], show that people in different places had similar building knowledge. These projects needed not just strength, but also careful planning, measuring, and even watching the sky to line up stones with seasons or sunrise points. This shows early knowledge of [[engineering]] and [[astronomy]].{{Cite web|title=Building Stonehenge|url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/stonehenge/history-and-stories/building-stonehenge/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=English Heritage}}{{Cite web|title=Megaliths of Carnac: Introduction|url=https://menhirs.tripod.com/intro.html|access-date=2025-07-17|website=menhirs.tripod.com}}{{Dead link|date=May 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}{{Cite web|title=Carnac Stones - Carnac, France|url=http://www.sacred-destinations.com/france/carnac-stones|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.sacred-destinations.com}} Early humans were also smart about taking care of the [[environment]]. They used [[fire]] in helpful ways. For example, [[Australian Aboriginals]] practiced something called [[fire-stick farming]]. They burned certain areas on purpose to help new plants grow, bring animals to the area, and make the land easier to manage.{{Cite journal|last1=Bliege Bird|first1=R.|last2=Bird|first2=D. W.|last3=Codding|first3=B. F.|last4=Parker|first4=C. H.|last5=Jones|first5=J. H.|date=2008-09-30|title=The "fire stick farming" hypothesis: Australian Aboriginal foraging strategies, biodiversity, and anthropogenic fire mosaics|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=105|issue=39|pages=14796–14801|doi=10.1073/pnas.0804757105|pmid=18809925 |doi-access=free |pmc=2567447 |bibcode=2008PNAS..10514796B }} In the [[Andes Mountains]] (in [[South America]]), ancient farming communities built [[Terrace farming|terrace]]s (step-like farms on hills) and [[Irrigation|irrigation system]]s to control [[water]]. This helped them farm on steep land and stop [[soil]] from washing away. These people understood how to manage [[natural resources]], like water and soil, in ways that are similar to today’s ideas of [[sustainability]] (protecting the environment while meeting human needs).{{Cite web|title=Laraos Terraces|url=https://www.wmf.org/projects/laraos-terraces|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Laraos Terraces|language=en}}{{Cite web|title=How did the Inka control erosion and grow crops in the steep Andes terrain? {{!}} Engineering the Inka Empire|url=https://americanindian.si.edu/inkaroad/engineering/question/how-did-inka-control-erosion-and-grow-crops-steep-andes-terrain.html#:~:text=steep%20Andes%20terrain?-,How%20did%20the%20Inka%20control%20erosion%20and%20grow%20crops%20in,the%20force%20of%20the%20current.&text=The%20Inka%20avoided%20erosion%20by%20controlling%20the%20destructive%20force%20of%20water.&text=Place%20materials%20in%20the%20correct%20order%20to%20create%20a%20stable%20terrace.|access-date=2025-07-17|website=americanindian.si.edu}} People also started to create ways to record and share information. Early forms of writing included [[cave art]], [[petroglyph]]s (pictures carved in rock), and [[Prehistoric token|token]]s (small clay objects used for counting). In [[Mesopotamia]], around 8000 BCE, people used clay tokens to keep track of food and goods. Over time, this system turned into writing, known as [[cuneiform]]. Writing allowed people to store [[knowledge]], like farm records and star charts, and pass it on to future generations. This step, moving from oral traditions (speaking stories and knowledge) to writing things down, helped humans build on knowledge over time. It was the beginning of being able to record science and discoveries so they would not be forgotten.{{Cite web|title=The Evolution of Writing {{!}} Denise Schmandt-Besserat|url=https://sites.utexas.edu/dsb/tokens/the-evolution-of-writing/|access-date=2025-07-17|language=en-US}} ===Ancient science=== [[File:Plimpton_322.jpg|thumb|The [[Plimpton 322|Plimpton 322 tablet]] by the [[Babylonia]]ns records [[Pythagorean triple]]s, written {{circa|1800 BCE}}|alt=Clay tablet with markings, three columns for numbers and one for ordinals]] Ancient science was the early scientific knowledge and inventions created by some of the first civilizations in places like [[Mesopotamia]], [[Egypt]], [[Indus Valley civilization|the Indus Valley]], [[ancient China]], and [[Mesoamerica|Mesoamerica (Central America)]]. This period lasted from around 3000 BCE to 600 BCE.{{Cite book|title=The Near East: archaeology in the "Cradle of Civilization"|last=Maisels|first=Charles Keith|date=1993|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-415-04742-5|series=The Experience of archaeology|location=London ; New York}} In [[Mesopotamia]], one of the first places where civilization began, science was used in areas like [[farming]], [[government]], and [[astronomy]]. The [[Sumerians]] and [[Babylonian]]s created number systems, including one based on [[Sexagesimal|60 (sexagesimal)]]. This is why we still use 60 minutes in an [[hour]] and 360 degrees in a [[circle]] today.{{Cite journal|last=Friberg|first=Jöran|date=2019-03-01|title=Three thousand years of sexagesimal numbers in Mesopotamian mathematical texts|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00407-019-00221-3|journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences|language=en|volume=73|issue=2|pages=183–216|doi=10.1007/s00407-019-00221-3|issn=1432-0657}} They were also great at studying the sky. On clay tablets written in cuneiform writing, they recorded things like [[star chart]]s, [[calendar]]s, and math problems. Babylonian astronomers carefully watched the [[Moon]] and [[planet]]s, and used math to predict [[eclipse]]s (when the [[Moon]] or [[Sun]] is covered) and planet alignments.{{Cite web|last=Hays|first=Jeffrey|title=Ancient Babylonian and Mesopotamian Astronomy {{!}} Middle East And North Africa — Facts and Details|url=https://africame.factsanddetails.com/article/entry-1027.html|access-date=2025-07-17|website=africame.factsanddetails.com|language=en}} One of their most important discoveries was the [[Metonic cycle]], which is a 19-year cycle where the Moon’s phases happen on the same days of the calendar again.{{Cite web|title=The Babylonian Calendar|url=https://webspace.science.uu.nl/~gent0113/babylon/babycal.htm|access-date=2025-07-17|website=webspace.science.uu.nl}}{{Citation|last=Steele|first=John M.|title=Mesopotamian Calendars|date=2015|url=https://link.springer.com/rwe/10.1007/978-1-4614-6141-8_189|work=Handbook of Archaeoastronomy and Ethnoastronomy|pages=1841–1845|publisher=Springer, New York, NY|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-6141-8_189|bibcode=2015hae..book.1841S |isbn=978-1-4614-6141-8|access-date=2025-07-17}} [[History of science|Ancient Egyptian science]] was closely tied to [[farming]], [[timekeeping]], and building large [[monument]]s. The Egyptians created a 365-day calendar by watching the star Sirius (which they called Sopdet). Every year, [[Sirius]] rose in the sky just before the Nile River flooded. This was a very important event that made the [[soil]] good for growing [[crop]]s. To prepare for this, the Egyptians had to be good at measuring the sky and water levels.{{Cite web|title=Sirius|url=https://www.gautschy.ch/~rita/archast/sirius/siriuseng.htm|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.gautschy.ch}}{{Dead link|date=July 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} They also used science to build huge structures like the [[pyramid]]s. These amazing buildings needed careful [[planning]], [[geometry]] (math involving shapes), and knowledge of [[material]]s and [[surveying]] (measuring land). Egyptian engineers were skilled at all of these things.{{Cite web|date=2020-11-09|title=11.2: The pyramids of Egypt|url=https://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Introductory_Engineering/EGR_1010%3A_Introduction_to_Engineering_for_Engineers_and_Scientists/11%3A_Historical_case_studies_in_Engineering/11.02%3A_The_pyramids_of_Egypt|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Engineering LibreTexts|language=en}} A famous document called the [[Rhind Mathematical Papyrus]], written around 1650 BCE, shows that Egyptian students learned math such as [[fraction]]s, [[area]]s, [[volume]]s, and [[ratio]]s.{{Cite web|title=Rhind papyrus {{!}} math, hieroglyphics, scribes {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Rhind-papyrus|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}}{{Cite web|title=Rhind Mathematical Papyrus|url=https://sites.math.washington.edu//~greenber/Rhind.html|access-date=2025-07-17|website=sites.math.washington.edu}} The [[Indus Valley civilization|Indus Valley Civilization]] (around 2600 to 1900 BCE) also had amazing science and technology, even though we still do not fully understand it because their writing system has not been decoded yet.{{Cite journal|last=Robinson|first=Andrew|date=2015-10-22|title=Ancient civilization: Cracking the Indus script|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/526499a|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=526|issue=7574|pages=499–501|doi=10.1038/526499a|pmid=26490603 |bibcode=2015Natur.526..499R |issn=0028-0836}} Cities like [[Mohenjo-Daro]] and [[Harappa]] were built in neat grid patterns, had advanced [[Drainage|drainage system]]s, and used standard sizes for things like [[Weight (object)|weight]]s and [[brick]]s.{{Cite web|title=Indus River Valley civilization|url=https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/world-history/world-history-beginnings/ancient-india/a/the-indus-river-valley-civilizations|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.khanacademy.org|language=en}} At a site called [[Lothal]], scientists found a [[Shipyard|dockyard]], which shows that people there understood how tides worked and how to build for the [[sea]]. The use of uniform bricks and measuring tools also shows they had organized production and possibly government systems to manage it. All of this points to high-level technical knowledge and careful planning.{{Cite web|last=Centre|first=UNESCO World Heritage|title=Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal|url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5918/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre|language=en}}{{Cite web|title=World's First Port Discovered in Red Sea|url=https://hic-mena.org/activitydetails.php?id=pWtpag|access-date=2025-07-17|website=hic-mena.org}}{{Cite journal|last1=Leshnik|first1=Lawrence S.|last2=Junghans|first2=K. H.|date=1968|title=The Harappan "Port" at Lothal: Another View 1|url=https://anthrosource.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1525/aa.1968.70.5.02a00070|journal=American Anthropologist|language=en|volume=70|issue=5|pages=911–922|doi=10.1525/aa.1968.70.5.02a00070|issn=0002-7294}} In [[ancient China]], science grew together with [[philosophy]] and [[government]]. People studied nature because they wanted to understand it better and use that knowledge to rule wisely. One early book called the [[I Ching]] (also called the Book of Changes) was written by at least the late 2nd millennium BCE. It used patterns and binary logic (ideas based on two choices, like yes/no or dark/light) to explain natural cycles and how the [[universe]] worked.{{Cite book|title=The Cambridge history of Chinese literature edited by Kang-i Sun Chang and Stephen Owen|last1=Sun|first1=Kangyi|last2=Owen|first2=Stephen|date=2010|publisher=Cambridge university press|isbn=978-0-521-11677-0|location=Cambridge}}{{Cite book|title=Ancient and early medieval Chinese literature: a reference guide|last1=Knechtges|first1=David Richard|last2=Chang|first2=Tai ping|date=2010|publisher=Brill|isbn=978-90-04-18016-1|series=Handbook of oriental studies|location=Leiden}} By the time of the [[Zhou Dynasty]] (around 1046–256 BCE), Chinese scientists had invented many useful tools and ideas. They created early earthquake detectors (called [[Seismometer|seismographs]]),{{Cite web|date=2016-10-27|title=What was the first instrument that actually recorded an earthquake? {{!}} U.S. Geological Survey|url=https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/what-was-first-instrument-actually-recorded-earthquake|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.usgs.gov|language=en}} studied the [[star]]s ([[astronomy]]),{{Cite web|last=Devonshire|first=John|date=2025-01-19|title=Ancient Astronomy: The Remarkable Contributions of China|url=https://www.hamiltonrasc.ca/ancient-astronomy-china/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=RASC Hamilton|language=en}} used [[plant]]s as [[Drug|medicine]] ([[herbal medicine]]),{{Cite journal|last=Gaur|first=Rishabh|date=2024-03-01|title=A brief history: Traditional Chinese medicinal system|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667142524000320|journal=Pharmacological Research - Modern Chinese Medicine|volume=10|article-number=100387|doi=10.1016/j.prmcm.2024.100387|issn=2667-1425}} and learned how to work with [[metal]]s and [[chemical]]s ([[metallurgy]]). They also made a complex calendar based on both the Moon’s phases and solar seasons. This calendar used a 60-part cycle (called the [[sexagenary cycle]]) and showed that they had a very advanced way of measuring time using math.{{Cite journal|last=Smith|first=Adam Daniel|date=2010|title=The Chinese Sexagenary Cycle and the Ritual Origins of the Calendar|url=https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/10.7916/D8891CDX|journal=Oxford|doi=10.7916/D8891CDX}}{{Cite book|url=http://archive.org/details/the-triennial-huong-exam-deducing-laureates-birth-years-2024.05.12|title=The Triennial Hương Exam Deducing Laureates' Birth Years|last=Loc Vu-Quoc|first=Hung Vu|date=2024-07-21}} The Chinese were also experts in bronze casting, making tools and objects out of melted [[metal]]. They made [[alloy]]s (mixtures of metals) that had the same recipe every time, using careful control of [[heat]] and basic understanding of [[chemistry]].{{Cite web|title=Bronze Age Casting|url=https://asia-archive.si.edu/learn/ancient-chinese-bronzes/bronze-age-casting/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art|language=en-US}} In [[Mesoamerica]], the [[Olmec]] (around 1500–400 BCE) and later the [[Maya]] made amazing discoveries in astronomy, math, and building. The Maya used a base-20 number system (instead of base-10 like we use).{{Cite journal|last=Batz|first=J. Mucía|date=2021-01-25|title="Nik" — The Zero in Vigesimal Maya Mathematics|url=https://baas.aas.org/pub/2021n1i336p03/release/2|journal=Bulletin of the AAS|language=en|volume=53|issue=1}}{{Cite web|title=Maya Numerals|url=http://www.saxakali.com/historymam2.htm|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.saxakali.com|archive-date=2006-07-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060714025120/http://www.saxakali.com/historymam2.htm|url-status=dead}} They invented long count [[calendar]]s that could track time for thousands of years.{{Cite web|date=2025-06-05|title=Maya calendar {{!}} System, Mesoamerica, & Astronomy {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Maya-calendar|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} They watched the sky carefully and recorded things like the movements of [[Venus]], [[eclipse]]s, [[solstice]]s, and planet alignments. Some of this information was written in books called [[Codex|codices]], like the [[Dresden Codex]]. The Maya used these observations to plan religious festivals, decide when to plant crops, and even schedule political events. They built [[pyramid]]s and [[temple]]s that lined up perfectly with events in the sky. They were constantly watching the sky and collecting data, just like modern scientists.{{Cite journal|last=Aldana|first=Gerardo|date=2022-02-11|title=Maya Calendar and Mesoamerican Astronomy|url=http://ethos.lps.library.cmu.edu/article/id/520/|journal=Encyclopedia of the History of Science|volume=4|issue=1|doi=10.34758/qyyd-vx23}} In all of these ancient civilizations, [[medicine]] was based on practical [[experience]] and [[observation]], even though it was often connected to [[religion]] or spiritual beliefs. In [[Ancient Egypt]], a medical text called the [[Edwin Smith Papyrus]] (written around 1600 BCE) showed that Egyptian doctors had a logical and scientific approach to treating injuries. It includes detailed instructions for doing [[surgery]] and describes how to treat injuries to the [[head]], [[spine]], and [[arm]]s or [[leg]]s. It even gave predictions (called [[prognosis]]) about how serious the injuries were and what might happen to the patient, depending on where the injury was.{{Cite news|title=Edwin Smith papyrus {{!}} Ancient Egyptian, Medical Texts, Surgery {{!}} Britannica|language=en|work=Encyclopedia Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Edwin-Smith-papyrus|access-date=2025-07-17}} In [[Mesopotamia]], doctors used a book called the Diagnostic Handbook by a man named [[Esagil-kin-apli]] (around 1069 BCE). This book helped doctors figure out what was wrong with a [[patient]] by looking at their [[symptom]]s, then choosing [[treatment]]s. These treatments might include [[herbal medicine]], [[chant]]s or [[prayer]]s, and physical treatments like [[bandage]]s or surgeries.{{Cite book|title=Knowledge and rhetoric in medical commentary: ancient Mesopotamian commentaries on a handbook of medical diagnosis (Sa-gig)|last=Wee|first=John Z.|date=2020|publisher=Brill|isbn=978-90-04-41756-4|series=Cuneiform monographs|location=Leiden Boston}} In [[Ancient China]], a book called the [[Shennong Bencaojing]] (written in the first millennium BCE) listed hundreds of medicinal herbs and their effects on the body. This book became the base of Traditional Chinese Medicine. It showed how Chinese doctors tested herbs, classified their properties, and wrote down their results, which helped build knowledge over many generations.{{Cite book|title=Medicine in China: a history of pharmaceutics|url=https://archive.org/details/medicineinchinah0000unsc_h6r2|last=Unschuld|first=Paul U.|date=1986|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-05025-9|series=Comparative studies of health systems and medical care|location=Berkeley}}{{Cite book|title=Herbal medicine: Biomolecular and clinical aspects|date=2011|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-4398-0713-2|editor-last=Benzie|editor-first=Iris F. F.|edition=2nd|series=Oxidative stress and disease|location=Boca Raton|editor-last2=Wachtel-Galor|editor-first2=Sissi}} These early sciences also depended on good recordkeeping, which allowed people to share and pass on knowledge over time. Each civilization created its own writing system, including [[cuneiform]] in Mesopotamia, [[hieroglyph]]s in Egypt, [[oracle bone script]] in China, and [[Maya script]] in Mesoamerica. These writing systems helped people write down important information, like [[star chart]]s and [[astronomy]], [[Mathematical table|math table]]s, medical recipes, and instructions for building things Because this knowledge was written down, it could be passed from one generation to the next, even if science back then was usually done by priests, scribes, or royal advisors, not scientists like we think of today.{{Cite web|title=Early writing systems {{!}} EBSCO Research Starters|url=https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/early-writing-systems|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.ebsco.com|language=en}} ===Classical antiquity=== [[File:MANNapoli 124545 plato's academy mosaic.jpg|left|thumb|[[Plato's Academy mosaic]], made between 100 BCE and 79 CE, shows many Greek philosophers and scholars|alt=Framed mosaic of philosophers gathering around and conversing]] Classical science started in [[ancient Greece]], especially in a city called [[Miletus]]. There, early thinkers like [[Thales]] (around 624–546 BCE) tried to explain how the world works without using stories about [[gods]] or [[magic]]. Thales believed that [[water]] was the basic substance that everything came from. This idea started a new way of thinking called [[natural philosophy]], which focused on finding natural causes for things we observe in the world.{{Cite web|title=Thales of Miletus {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy|url=https://iep.utm.edu/thales/|access-date=2025-07-17|language=en-US}} After Thales, other thinkers from Miletus also had big ideas. [[Anaximander]] said everything came from something called the apeiron (which means “the boundless” or unlimited). Anaximenes thought [[air]] was the most important element.{{Cite web|title=Anaximander {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy|url=https://iep.utm.edu/anaximander/|access-date=2025-07-17|language=en-US}} Another important thinker was [[Pythagoras]] (around 570–495 BCE). He believed that [[number]]s and [[Mathematics|math]] were the true key to understanding the [[universe]]. His school studied [[geometry]], [[music]], and [[number]]s. They discovered that when strings of certain lengths were plucked, they made sounds that matched simple number [[ratio]]s. This showed a connection between music and math, and supported the idea that the whole universe had a kind of mathematical harmony, a concept called the “music of the spheres.”{{Citation|last=Huffman|first=Carl|title=Pythagoras|date=2024|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2024/entries/pythagoras/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Spring 2024|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2025-07-17|editor2-last=Nodelman|editor2-first=Uri}} In [[medicine]], a famous Greek named [[Hippocrates]] (around 460–370 BCE) made big changes. He said that [[illness]] was not caused by angry gods or magic, but by natural causes like [[diet]], [[environment]], and the balance of fluids in the body. He taught doctors to carefully observe patients, keep records, and study the effects of things like [[climate]] and [[food]] on [[health]]. Hippocrates also created the [[Humorism|four-humor theory]], which said the body had four fluids: [[blood]], phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile. People believed for many centuries that staying healthy meant keeping these in balance. He also introduced ethical rules for doctors, such as those in the [[Hippocratic Oath]], which is still remembered today. Because of Hippocrates, medicine became more scientific and professional.{{Cite web|title=Hippocrates {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy|url=https://iep.utm.edu/hippocra/|access-date=2025-07-17|language=en-US}} [[Aristotle]] (384–322 BCE) was one of the most important thinkers in ancient science. He was a student of Plato and later became the teacher of [[Alexander the Great]]. Aristotle wrote about many subjects, including [[biology]], [[physics]], [[astronomy]], [[psychology]], and [[logic]]. In biology, [[Aristotle]] studied sea animals and did some of the first [[dissection]]s (cutting open bodies to learn how they work). He grouped [[animal]]s by their physical traits, which helped create early classification systems. In physics and astronomy, he believed the [[Earth]] was at the center of the [[universe]] ([[geocentric model]]), and that everything in the sky moved in perfect circles made of a special substance called [[aether]]. He thought the heavens were unchanging, unlike Earth, which was made of [[Soil|earth]], [[water]], [[air]], and [[fire]], things that could decay and change. Aristotle also created a famous way of thinking about why things happen, called the four causes. The material cause was what something is made of, the formal cause was the shape or structure of the thing, the efficient cause was what caused it to happen, and the final cause was its purpose or goal.{{Citation|last=Shields|first=Christopher|title=Aristotle|date=2023|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2023/entries/aristotle/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Winter 2023|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2025-07-17|editor2-last=Nodelman|editor2-first=Uri}} One of Aristotle’s students, [[Theophrastus]] (around 371–287 BCE), took these ideas further, especially in [[Botany|plant science]]. He wrote books like Enquiry into Plants and On the Causes of Plants, where he tried to classify and describe [[plant]]s in a clear and organized way. He noticed details like where plants grow, how they reproduce, and how people use them. He divided plants into groups like [[tree]]s, [[shrub]]s, and [[herb]]s, and because of his work, he is known as the “father of botany”. His ideas about plants were so good that scientists still read them over a thousand years later.{{Citation|last=Ierodiakonou|first=Katerina|title=Theophrastus|date=2020|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2020/entriesheophrastus/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Winter 2020|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2025-07-17}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} After Alexander the Great died, Greek science continued to grow during the [[Hellenistic period]] (323–31 BCE). One of the most famous centers of learning was [[Alexandria]], in [[Egypt]]. It had a huge [[library]], scholars from many cultures, and support from powerful leaders. One of the most important scientists there was [[Euclid]] (around 300 BCE). He wrote a book called The Elements, which organized everything known about [[geometry]] into 13 books. He proved shapes and math rules using logic and step-by-step thinking. This method, called the [[Axiomatic system|axiomatic method]], became the model for how scientists and mathematicians would work for thousands of years.{{Cite web|date=2025-07-10|title=Euclid - Geometry, Elements, Mathematics {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Euclid-Greek-mathematician/Renditions-of-the-Elements|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} [[Archimedes of Syracuse]] (about 287–212 BCE) was a brilliant ancient scientist and inventor. He made important discoveries in [[physics]], [[engineering]], and [[Mathematics|math]]. One of his most famous ideas is called [[Archimedes' principle]]. It says that when you put something in [[water]] (or another [[liquid]]), the liquid pushes up on it with a [[force]] equal to the [[weight]] of the liquid the object pushes out of the way. This explains why some things float and others sink. Archimedes also studied [[lever]]s, [[pulley]]s, and other [[machine]]s, helping to create the basic rules of [[mechanical engineering]]. He figured out how to calculate the [[area]] and [[volume]] of different shapes and came up with a very good estimate for the number [[Pi|pi (π)]].{{Cite web|date=2025-06-21|title=Archimedes {{!}} Facts & Biography {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Archimedes|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} [[Eratosthenes]] (about 276–194 BCE) was the head librarian at the [[Library of Alexandria]], one of the greatest learning centers of the ancient world. He was good at math, astronomy, and geography, and used these skills to measure the size of the [[Earth]] very accurately. He did this by comparing shadows in two cities at the same time during the [[summer solstice]] (the longest day of the year). He also invented a system of [[latitude]] and [[longitude]] to map [[location]]s, just like the grid system used in maps today. Eratosthenes tried to create a [[map]] of the entire known world.{{Cite web|last=Mark|first=Joshua J.|date=2022-03-03|title=Eratosthenes|url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Eratosthenes/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=World History Encyclopedia|language=en}} [[Aristarchus of Samos]] (about 310–230 BCE) was an early astronomer who had a bold idea: the [[Sun]] is at the center of the [[solar system]], not the Earth. This idea is called the [[Heliocentrism|heliocentric model]]. At the time, most people believed the Earth was at the center, so his theory was not accepted, partly because they did not have strong [[telescope]]s or enough evidence. Even though his idea was ignored back then, his work later inspired scientists like [[Copernicus]], who helped start the modern understanding of the solar system.{{Cite web|last=Mark|first=Joshua J.|date=2022-02-16|title=Aristarchus of Samos|url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Aristarchus_of_Samos/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=World History Encyclopedia|language=en}} [[Claudius Ptolemy]] (about 100–170 CE) lived in Roman Egypt and was a famous ancient astronomer and scientist. He believed that the [[Earth]] was at the center of the [[universe]], and he wrote a big book called the [[Almagest]], where he explained this idea using a model called the [[geocentric model]]. To explain how the Sun, Moon, and planets move in the sky, he used epicycles, deferents, and equants, complicated ways of showing [[orbit]]s that looked like circles within circles. Even though this model was wrong (we now know the Sun is at the center), Ptolemy’s system worked well for making predictions and was used for over 1,400 years. Ptolemy did not just study [[Outer space|space]], he also worked on [[optics]] (how [[light]] and [[Sight|vision]] work), [[map]]s, and [[music]]. He even wrote about [[astrology]].{{Cite web|last=Cartwright|first=Mark|date=2023-09-07|title=Claudius Ptolemy|url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Claudius_Ptolemy/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=World History Encyclopedia|language=en}} The Romans were more focused on practical science than on theories. They were great engineers and used science to build things like [[aqueduct]]s (which carried [[water]]), [[road]]s, [[bridge]]s, and [[Building|concrete building]]s. They understood how water flows, how to balance weight, and how to use strong building materials.{{Cite web|last=Cartwright|first=Mark|date=2016-09-06|title=Roman Science|url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Roman_Science/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=World History Encyclopedia|language=en}} A Roman engineer named [[Vitruvius]] wrote a book called De Architectura in the 1st century BCE, where he talked about [[architecture]], [[Body proportion|human body proportion]]s, and [[machine]]s. He combined art and science to show how buildings should look beautiful but also work well.{{Cite web|last=Babbs|first=Sean|title=Research Guides: HIST 1061, The Rise and Fall of Ancient Rome (Jobin) - Rare Books Collection: Vitruvius' de Architectura: the Roman World in Renaissance Architecture|url=https://libguides.colorado.edu/c.php?g=1084056&p=7902486|access-date=2025-07-17|website=libguides.colorado.edu|language=en}} In medicine, a Roman doctor named [[Galen]] (around 129–200 CE) became very important. He studied how the body works by examining [[animal]]s, learning about [[organ]]s, [[bone]]s, and how [[disease]]s spread. He believed in the four humors (like Hippocrates) and thought that keeping these in balance kept people healthy. Galen’s medical ideas were used in Europe and the Islamic world for many hundreds of years.{{Cite web|date=2025-06-03|title=Galen {{!}} Biography, Achievements, & Facts {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Galen|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} ===Islamic Golden Age=== [[File:Hunayn ibn-Ishaq al-'Ibadi Isagoge.jpg|thumb|upright|The Christian physician [[Hunayn ibn Ishaq]] led the translation of works.]] [[File:Astrolabe planisférique closeup800x600x300.jpg|thumb|215px|Improvements to the [[astrolabe]] were one of the achievements of this era]] Science during the [[Islamic Golden Age]] (from about the 8th to the 14th century CE) was one of the most creative and important times in history. During this period, Muslim scholars made huge advances in [[astronomy]], [[Mathematics|math]], [[medicine]], [[physics]], [[chemistry]], [[geography]], and [[engineering]].{{Cite journal|last=King|first=David A.|date=1983|title=The Astronomy of the Mamluks|url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/353360|journal=Isis|language=en|volume=74|issue=4|pages=531–555|doi=10.1086/353360|issn=0021-1753}}{{Cite web|title=History Of Science And Technology In Islam|url=http://www.history-science-technology.com/Articles/articles%208.html|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.history-science-technology.com|language=en}} This progress happened because of several things which included leaders supported science, especially the [[Abbasid Caliphate|Abbasid caliph]]s who helped fund [[research]] and [[learning]].{{Cite web|title=BBC Radio 4 - In Our Time, Al-Kindi|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b01k2bv8|access-date=2025-07-17|website=BBC|language=en-GB}} Books from [[Greece]], [[India]], [[Persia]], and [[China]] were translated into Arabic, allowing people to learn from many different cultures,{{Cite book|title=Greek thought, Arabic culture: the Graeco-Arabic translation movement in Baghdad and early ʻAbbāsid society (2nd-4th/8th-10th centuries)|url=https://archive.org/details/greekthoughtarab0000guta|last=Gutas|first=Dimitri|date=1998|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-415-06132-2|location=London ; New York}} and Islamic culture encouraged learning (called ‘ilm in Arabic) and logical thinking.{{Cite book|title=Renaissance of sciences in Islamic countries|last1=Salam|first1=Abdus|last2=Dalafi|first2=H. R.|last3=Hassan|first3=Mohamed|date=1994|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-9971-5-0946-0|location=Singapore ; River Edge, NJ}} One of the most important places during this time was the [[House of Wisdom]] (Bayt al-Hikma) in [[Baghdad]], created by Caliph [[Harun al-Rashid]] and expanded by his son [[Al-Ma'mun]]. It was a major center where scholars gathered to translate, study, and improve scientific knowledge. They translated famous works from Greek, Persian, and Indian scientists, like [[Aristotle]], [[Galen]], [[Euclid]], and [[Ptolemy]], into Arabic.{{Cite book|title=Medieval Islamic civilization: an encyclopedia|date=2006|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-415-96691-7|editor-last=Meri|editor-first=Josef W.|series=Routledge encyclopedias of the Middle Ages|location=New York|editor-last2=Bacharach|editor-first2=Jere L.}}{{Cite web|title=Bayt al-Hikmah {{!}} House of Wisdom, Islam, Time Period, Significance, & Baghdad {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Bayt-al-Hikmah|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} One key figure was [[Hunayn ibn Ishaq]], who translated over 100 medical books.{{Cite book|title=The map of knowledge: how classical ideas were lost and found: a history in seven cities|url=https://archive.org/details/mapofknowledgeth0000moll|last=Moller|first=Violet|date=2019|publisher=Doubleday|isbn=978-0-385-54177-0|edition=1st American|location=New York}} In [[astronomy]], Muslim scientists made many improvements to older models from Greece and India. [[Al-Battani]] (also known as Albatenius, around 858–929 CE) carefully studied the [[Sun]] and calculated the length of the [[year]] as 365.2422 days, almost exactly what is known today.{{Cite web|title=Al-Battani - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Al-Battani/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} [[Al-Zarqali]] (also called Arzachel) made the [[Toledan Tables]], which helped European scientists and even influenced Copernicus hundreds of years later.{{Cite web|title=al-Zarqali - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Al-Zarqali/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} [[Al-Tusi]] (1201–1274 CE), working at the [[Maragheh observatory]], invented a math model called the [[Tusi couple]], which helped improve future ideas about how planets move.{{Cite web|title=Nasir al-Din al-Tusi - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Al-Tusi_Nasir/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} Muslim astronomers also built observatories (places to study the stars) in cities like [[Baghdad]], [[Maragheh]], [[Samarkand]], and [[Shiraz]]. They invented tools like the [[astrolabe]], [[sextant]], and spherical instruments to measure [[star]]s and [[planet]]s very precisely. These tools were used to find the correct times for prayer, determine the direction of [[Mecca]] (Qibla), and create Islamic calendars.{{Cite web|title=Theme: Islamic astronomy|url=https://web.astronomicalheritage.net/show-theme?idtheme=15|website=UNESCO}} In the field of mathematics, Islamic scholars made major breakthroughs, especially in [[algebra]], [[arithmetic]], [[geometry]], and [[trigonometry]]. One important mathematician, [[Al-Khwarizmi|Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi]] (around 780–850 CE), wrote a book called Al-Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala. This book laid the foundation for [[algebra]]. The word "algebra" actually comes from al-jabr, meaning "completion." Al-Khwarizmi also created step-by-step ways to solve quadratic equations and methods for doing calculations. In fact, the word “[[algorithm]]” comes from his name.{{Cite web|title=Al-Khwarizmi - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Al-Khwarizmi/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} Another scholar, [[Omar Khayyam]] (1048–1131), figured out how to solve [[cubic equation]]s using geometry.{{Cite web|title=Omar Khayyam - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Khayyam/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} [[Jamshid al-Kashi|Al-Kashi]] (died 1429) calculated the number [[pi]] to 16 decimal places and improved the way decimal numbers were used, something very important for modern math.{{Cite web|title=al-Kashi - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Al-Kashi/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} In [[trigonometry]], scientists like [[Al-Biruni]] and [[Nasir al-Din al-Tusi]] made accurate tables for [[sine]], [[cosine]], and [[tangent]], helping to turn trigonometry into its own branch of mathematics.{{Cite web|title=Al-Biruni - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Al-Biruni/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} In medicine, Islamic scientists made great progress by using ideas from ancient Greek thinkers and combining them with careful observation and testing. A famous doctor named [[Al-Razi]] (also known as Rhazes, 854–925) wrote a huge 25-volume medical book called Kitab al-Hawi. He was the first to clearly tell the difference between [[smallpox]] and [[measles]] and believed in learning through watching and testing patients.{{Cite journal|last1=Amr|first1=Samir S.|last2=Tbakhi|first2=Abdulghani|date=2007|title=Abu Bakr Muhammad Ibn Zakariya Al Razi (Rhazes): Philosopher, Physician and Alchemist|journal=Annals of Saudi Medicine|language=en|volume=27|issue=4|pages=305–307|doi=10.5144/0256-4947.2007.305|pmid=17684438 |issn=0256-4947|pmc=6074295}} Another well-known doctor, [[Avicenna|Ibn Sina]] (also called Avicenna, 980–1037), combined medical knowledge from [[Greece]], [[Persia]], and [[India]] in his book The Canon of Medicine. This book was used as a guide in both Europe and the Islamic world for more than 600 years. He introduced important medical ideas like testing medicines, using [[quarantine]] to stop [[disease]]s from spreading, checking a patient’s [[pulse]], and understanding how infections work.{{Cite journal|last1=Amr|first1=Samir S.|last2=Tbakhi|first2=Abdelghani|date=2007|title=Ibn Sina (Avicenna): The Prince Of Physicians|journal=Annals of Saudi Medicine|language=en|volume=27|issue=2|pages=134–135|doi=10.5144/0256-4947.2007.134|pmid=17420624 |issn=0256-4947|pmc=6077049}} Muslim doctors also invented [[Surgical instrument|surgical tool]]s, used [[antiseptics]] to stop [[infection]]s, and developed special treatments for eye problems.{{Cite journal|last=Majeed|first=Azeem|date=2005-12-24|title=How Islam changed medicine|journal=BMJ|language=en|volume=331|issue=7531|pages=1486–1487|doi=10.1136/bmj.331.7531.1486|pmid=16373721 |issn=0959-8138|pmc=1322233}} One doctor, [[Ammar al-Mawsili|Ammar ibn Ali al-Mawsili]], even invented a [[syringe]] to remove [[cataract]]s from the eye.{{Cite journal|last1=Laios|first1=Konstantinos|last2=Moschos|first2=Marilita M.|last3=George|first3=Androutsos|date=2016|title=Ammar ibn Ali al-Mawsili and His Innovating Suction Method for the Treatment of Cataract|url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1553350615618289|journal=Surgical Innovation|language=en|volume=23|issue=4|pages=433|doi=10.1177/1553350615618289|pmid=26603693 |issn=1553-3506}} In the study of [[light]] and [[physics]], [[Ibn al-Haytham]] (also called Alhazen, 965–1040) made discoveries that helped shape modern science. In his book Book of Optics, he showed that the Greek idea of [[Sight|vision]], where light was thought to come out of the eyes, was wrong. He explained that light bounces off objects and goes into the eye, and he correctly described how the [[retina]] and [[Lens (anatomy)|lens]] work. Ibn al-Haytham tested his ideas with experiments using things like [[mirror]]s, [[lens]]es, and a camera obscura (an early version of a [[camera]]). He believed in forming hypotheses, testing them, and repeating experiments. These are ideas that are important to the modern [[scientific method]]. He also studied [[motion]], [[mechanics]], and [[inertia]], and his work influenced later scientists in Europe, like [[Roger Bacon]] and [[Kepler]].{{Cite web|title=Ibn al-Haytham - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Al-Haytham/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} In early Islamic times, [[chemistry]] was called [[alchemy]], and Muslim scientists made big discoveries while trying to understand how materials change. One of the most important alchemists was [[Jabir ibn Hayyan]] (also called Geber), who lived in the 8th century. He wrote hundreds of books about how to heat, purify, and mix substances using methods like [[distillation]] and [[crystallization]]. He even described how to make [[aqua regia]], a powerful [[acid]] that can dissolve [[gold]]. Jabir believed in testing ideas through careful experiments and recording results, which helped move alchemy closer to real, practical chemistry. He also used special lab tools like [[alembic]]s (for distilling liquids), [[crucible]]s (for heating substances), and [[furnace]]s, helping to shape the way modern chemistry labs would work.{{Cite journal|last1=Amr|first1=Samir S.|last2=Tbakhi|first2=Abdelghani|date=2007|title=Jabir ibn Hayyan|journal=Annals of Saudi Medicine|language=en|volume=27|issue=1|pages=52–53|doi=10.5144/0256-4947.2007.53|pmid=17337999 |issn=0256-4947|pmc=6077026}} Muslim scientists also made great progress in [[geography]], which is the study of the [[Earth]] and how it is measured. They traveled, observed nature, and made better maps. A brilliant scholar named [[Al-Biruni]] (973–1048) used [[Mathematics|math]] and [[trigonometry]] to measure the size of the Earth from the top of a [[mountain]], and his answer was very close to what we know today. He also collected the exact locations ([[latitude]] and [[longitude]]) of over 600 cities and even suggested that the Earth spins, hundreds of years before scientists in [[Europe]] did. Another scholar, [[Al-Khwarizmi]], corrected mistakes in older maps from the Greek scientist [[Ptolemy]]. Later, [[Muhammad al-Idrisi|Al-Idrisi]] made a famous world map in 1154 for a European king, using [[knowledge]] from Arab traders, sailors, and explorers.{{Cite web|title=al-Idrisi|url=https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/al-idrisi|access-date=2025-07-17|website=education.nationalgeographic.org|language=en}} Islamic scientists also made amazing progress in engineering and building machines. They designed clever devices like early [[robot]]s (called [[automata]]), [[water clock]]s, and [[machine]]s that used [[water]] and [[air]] to move. In the 9th century, three brothers known as the [[Banū Mūsā brothers|Banu Musa]] wrote The Book of Ingenious Devices, which described over 100 inventions using [[gear]]s, [[valve]]s, and [[tube]]s called [[siphon]]s. Later, a brilliant inventor named [[Ismail al-Jazari|Al-Jazari]] (1136–1206) built fancy water clocks, [[mechanical toy]]s that could be programmed to move, and one of the first [[crankshaft]]s, a tool still used in [[engine]]s today. These machines were not just for show; they were used in palaces, public fountains, and farming systems to help people in everyday life.{{Cite web|title=Machines from the East: Mechanical innovations from Muslim Civilisation|url=https://artsandculture.google.com/story/machines-from-the-east-mechanical-innovations-from-muslim-civilisation/pQWBwUIF15iiLQ|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Google Arts & Culture|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=Nizamoglu|first=Cem|date=2016-10-24|title=The Journey of Automatic Machines in Muslim Civilisation|url=https://muslimheritage.com/journey-of-automatic-machines/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Muslim Heritage}} To spread knowledge, the Islamic world created many places for [[learning]]. These included [[school]]s called [[madrasa]]s, [[hospital]]s known as [[bimaristan]]s, [[Library|libraries]], and [[Observatory|observatories]] where people could study the [[star]]s. Famous schools like the [[Nezamiyeh]] in [[Baghdad]], [[University of al-Qarawiyyin|Al-Qarawiyyin]] in [[Fez, Morocco|Fez]] ([[Morocco]]), and [[Al-Azhar University|Al-Azhar]] in [[Cairo]] became major centers for science and [[education]]. [[Scholar]]s traveled from place to place, shared ideas, and copied books so they could be studied in different parts of the world. From [[Spain]] and [[North Africa]] all the way to [[Central Asia]] and [[India]], science and learning were an important part of Islamic culture.{{Cite journal|last=Bulliet|first=Richard W.|date=1983|title=The Age Structure of Medieval Islamic Education|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1595484|journal=Studia Islamica|issue=57|pages=105–117|doi=10.2307/1595484|jstor=1595484 |issn=0585-5292}} ===Medieval and Renaissance Europe=== [[File:De Revolutionibus manuscript p9b.jpg|thumb|Drawing of the heliocentric model as proposed by the Copernicus's ''{{lang|la|[[De revolutionibus orbium coelestium]]}}''|alt=Drawing of planets' orbit around the Sun]] During the [[early Middle Ages]] (around the 5th to 10th centuries), science in [[Western Europe]] slowed down after the fall of the [[Western Roman Empire]]. Many ancient books and ideas were at risk of being lost. Luckily, monks in [[monasteries]] helped save this knowledge by copying old texts written in [[Latin]]. These included the works of famous thinkers like [[Aristotle]], [[Pliny the Elder]], [[Galen]], and [[Boethius]].{{Cite book|title=The beginnings of western science: the European scientific tradition in philosophical, religious, and institutional context, prehistory to A.D. 1450|url=https://archive.org/details/beginningsofwest0000lind_d9a5|last=Lindberg|first=David C.|date=2007|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-48205-7|edition=2nd|location=Chicago}} One important [[scholar]] from this time was [[Isidore of Seville]] (around 560–636), who tried to collect and organize all human [[knowledge]] into one big book called Etymologiae. People at the time believed that studying [[nature]] helped them better understand God’s creation.{{Cite web|title=Saint Isidore of Sevilla {{!}} Biography & Works {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Isidore-of-Sevilla|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} Even though science was limited during this period, learning started to improve under [[Charlemagne]] (who ruled from 768–814). He supported [[education]] and helped start cathedral schools, which taught subjects like [[Mathematics|math]], [[geometry]], [[music]], and [[astronomy]] (called the quadrivium), along with [[grammar]], [[logic]], and [[writing]] (the trivium).{{Cite web|date=2025-06-06|title=Charlemagne - Emperor, Franks, Holy Roman Empire {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charlemagne/Emperor-of-the-Romans|access-date=2025-07-17|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}} Between the 11th and 13th centuries, science in [[Europe]] came back to life thanks to a big effort to translate ancient books. In places like [[Spain]], [[Sicily]], and parts of the [[Middle East]], European scholars came in contact with the [[Islamic world]] and the [[Byzantine Empire]]. From them, they got access to many old Greek and Roman ideas, now improved by Arabic scholars. Translators like [[Gerard of Cremona]] worked hard to turn important Arabic and Greek books by [[Aristotle]], [[Avicenna]], [[Ibn al-Haytham|Alhazen]], and [[Galen]] into [[Latin]] so more people in Europe could understand them. These books taught about [[astronomy]], [[medicine]], [[Mathematics|math]], and [[optics]].{{Cite web|title=Gherard - Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Gherard/|access-date=2025-07-17|website=Maths History|language=en}} This sparked the rise of universities in cities like [[Bologna]], [[Paris]], [[Oxford]], and [[Salamanca]].{{Cite journal|last1=de la Croix|first1=David|last2=Docquier|first2=Frédéric|last3=Fabre|first3=Alice|last4=Stelter|first4=Robert|date=2024-08-01|title=The Academic Market and The Rise of Universities in Medieval and Early Modern Europe (1000–1800)|url=https://doi.org/10.1093/jeea/jvad061|journal=Journal of the European Economic Association|volume=22|issue=4|pages=1541–1589|doi=10.1093/jeea/jvad061|issn=1542-4766}} A new way of thinking called scholasticism became popular. Scholastic thinkers like [[Thomas Aquinas]] mixed Greek philosophy with Christian beliefs,{{Citation|last=Pasnau|first=Robert|title=Thomas Aquinas|date=2024|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2024/entries/aquinas/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Winter 2024|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2025-07-17|editor2-last=Nodelman|editor2-first=Uri}} and others like [[Albertus Magnus]] and [[Roger Bacon]] encouraged people to observe [[nature]] and do [[experiment]]s to learn how the world works.{{Cite web|title=Albertus Magnus 1193?-1282 – A History of Speech – Language Pathology|url=https://ubwp.buffalo.edu/history-of-cds/middle-ages/key-players-in-the-medieval-period/albertus-magnus/|access-date=2025-07-17|language=en-US}}{{Cite journal|last=Sidebottom|first=Eric|date=2013|title=Roger Bacon and the beginnings of experimental science in Britain|journal=Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine|language=en|volume=106|issue=6|pages=243–245|doi=10.1177/0141076813488482|pmid=23761584 |issn=0141-0768|pmc=3705416}} By the 14th century, some smart thinkers in [[Europe]] were starting to question old ideas about how things move. Two of these thinkers, [[Nicole Oresme]] and [[Jean Buridan]], worked at the [[University of Paris]] and had new ideas about [[physics]]. Jean Buridan came up with a theory called impetus, which was an early idea similar to what we now call [[inertia]]. He said that once something is moving, it can keep moving on its own. It does not need to be pushed forever. This was a big change from the old belief (by [[Aristotle]]) that something had to keep being pushed to keep moving.{{Citation|last=Zupko|first=Jack|title=John Buridan|date=2024|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2024/entries/buridan/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Spring 2024|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2025-07-17|editor2-last=Nodelman|editor2-first=Uri}} [[Nicole Oresme]] did not agree with the old idea that [[Earth]] was the center of the [[universe]] (geocentric model).
