Publishing|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-66659-4_4|isbn=978-3-319-66657-0|access-date=2025-07-19|last2=Eilks|first2=Ingo|editor2-last=Mevarech|editor2-first=Zemira R.|editor3-last=Baker|editor3-first=Dale R.}} [[Government]]s use science to make rules, spend money wisely, and protect people and nature.{{Cite book|title=The fifth branch: science advisers as policymakers|last=Jasanoff|first=Sheila|date=1994|publisher=Harvard University Press [u.a.]|isbn=978-0-674-30062-0|edition=2. print|location=Cambridge, Mass}} Many big science projects, like [[CERN]] (which studies tiny particles), the [[IPCC]] (which studies climate change), or the [[Human Genome Project]] (which mapped all human genes), show how countries and scientists work together around the world to learn and make progress.{{Cite journal|last1=Collins|first1=Francis S.|last2=Morgan|first2=Michael|last3=Patrinos|first3=Aristides|date=2003-04-11|title=The Human Genome Project: Lessons from Large-Scale Biology|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1084564|journal=Science|language=en|volume=300|issue=5617|pages=286–290|doi=10.1126/science.1084564|pmid=12690187 |bibcode=2003Sci...300..286C |issn=0036-8075}}{{Cite web|title=IPCC — Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|url=https://www.ipcc.ch/|access-date=2025-07-19}}{{Cite web|title=Home {{!}} CERN|url=https://home.cern/|access-date=2025-07-19|website=home.cern}} ==Core Principles and Characteristics== ===Empiricism=== [[Empiricism]] is a basic idea in science. It says that we learn things by using our senses, like [[Vision|seeing]], [[hearing]], or [[Measurement|measuring]], not just by guessing or following tradition.{{Cite web|title=The Project Gutenberg eBook of An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume I., by John Locke|url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/10615/10615-h/10615-h.htm#link2H_4_0002|access-date=2025-07-19|website=www.gutenberg.org}} Instead of relying only on what people believe or think is true, science depends on what we can actually observe, test, and measure. This is why scientists use special tools like [[telescope]]s, [[microscope]]s, and [[sensor]]s, to help them see things that are too small, too far, or otherwise invisible to the [[human eye]].{{Cite journal|last1=Bogen|first1=James|last2=Woodward|first2=James|date=1988|title=Saving the Phenomena|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2185445|journal=The Philosophical Review|volume=97|issue=3|pages=303|doi=10.2307/2185445 |jstor=2185445 }} For example, when scientists look for [[planet]]s outside our [[solar system]], called [[exoplanet]]s, they cannot see the planets directly. Instead, they look at tiny changes in the [[brightness]] of a [[star]]. If the star gets a little dimmer at regular times, it might mean a planet is passing in front of it. This method is based on careful observation, which is what empiricism is all about.{{Cite book|title=The exoplanet handbook|last=Perryman|first=M. A. C.|date=2018|publisher=New York, NY : Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-108-41977-2|edition=2nd|location=Cambridge}}{{Cite web|date=2023-06-07|title=Exoplanets - NASA Science|url=https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanets/|access-date=2025-07-19|language=en-US}} Empiricism also means that scientific results should be [[Reproducibility|reproducible]]. This means that if someone does an [[experiment]] again, they should get the same results. A good example is Gregor Mendel’s pea plant experiments, where he discovered how traits are passed down from parents to offspring. Scientists were able to repeat his work and get the same [[pattern]]s, showing that the results were reliable.{{Cite book|title=Origins of Mendelism|last=Olby|first=Robert C.|date=1985|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-62592-8|edition=2nd|location=Chicago}} The idea of empiricism was supported by philosophers like [[John Locke]], who believed that people are not born with [[knowledge]]. Instead, he said the mind starts out like a blank slate, and everything we learn comes from experience. This idea is different from [[rationalism]], which says we are born with certain ideas or that we can learn everything through [[logic]] alone.{{Cite web|title=Meditations on First Philosophy by Rene Descartes|url=https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/descartes/1639/meditations.htm|access-date=2025-07-19|website=www.marxists.org}} In science, empiricism helps make sure our knowledge is based on real-world [[evidence]]. Empirical methods in science are not just about watching things happen, they also include doing careful [[experiment]]s to test ideas. These experiments are done in a controlled way to help scientists figure out which things cause certain results. For example, when [[Alexander Fleming]] saw that a certain type of [[mold]] killed [[bacteria]], it was not enough just to notice it. Scientists had to do more experiments to prove that the mold, later called [[Penicillium notatum]], could really fight [[infection]]s. This led to the discovery of [[penicillin]], an important medicine.{{Cite journal|last=Fey|first=Paul|date=2005-02-01|title=The mold in Dr. Florey's coat The story of the penicillin miracle|url=http://www.jci.org/articles/view/24342|journal=Journal of Clinical Investigation|language=en|volume=115|issue=2|pages=199|doi=10.1172/JCI24342|issn=0021-9738}}{{Dead link|date=May 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} This kind of testing is how scientists confirm what works and what does not. Galileo also used experiments with ramps ([[inclined plane]]s) to show that objects do not need a force to keep moving, which went against the old ideas from [[Aristotle]].{{Cite web|title=Galileo: The Telescope & The Laws of Dynamics|url=https://www.pas.rochester.edu/~blackman/ast104/galileo12.html#:~:text=Perhaps%20Galileo's%20greatest%20contribution%20to,external%20force%20acts%20on%20it.|access-date=2025-07-19|website=www.pas.rochester.edu}} In more recent times, scientists used special detectors at [[LIGO]] to find [[gravitational wave]]s, tiny ripples in space predicted by [[General relativity|Einstein’s theory of general relativity]] 100 years earlier. This discovery was another example of how scientists use careful [[observation]] and testing to confirm or disprove [[Scientific theory|scientific theories]].{{Cite journal|last1=Abbott|first1=B. P.|last2=Abbott|first2=R.|last3=Abbott|first3=T. D.|last4=Abernathy|first4=M. R.|last5=Acernese|first5=F.|last6=Ackley|first6=K.|last7=Adams|first7=C.|last8=Adams|first8=T.|last9=Addesso|first9=P.|last10=Adhikari|first10=R. X.|last11=Adya|first11=V. B.|date=2016-02-11|title=Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.061102|journal=Physical Review Letters|language=en|volume=116|issue=6|article-number=061102 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.061102|pmid=26918975 |arxiv=1602.03837 |bibcode=2016PhRvL.116f1102A |issn=0031-9007}} Empirical methods are also used in big, complex areas like [[climate science]]. Scientists collect information from things like [[ice core]]s, [[satellite]]s, and even [[tree ring]]s to learn about Earth’s climate over time. These different sources of [[data]] help build models to understand and predict how the planet is changing. Even though empiricism, the idea that [[knowledge]] comes from [[observation]] and [[experience]], is a key part of science, it is not always simple. One challenge is deciding what counts as a valid observation and how to understand what we see. Sometimes, what scientists notice or pay attention to depends on the theories they already believe in. This idea is called “theory-laden observation.” Philosopher [[Thomas Kuhn]] explained that scientists often use models or ideas they already have to decide what to look for and how to explain it. For example, early astronomers had trouble understanding why planets sometimes seemed to move backward in the sky (called [[Retrograde and direct motion|retrograde motion]]) until they used models like the Ptolemaic system or the later Copernican model, which helped them interpret what they were seeing. In some parts of science, such as [[quantum physics]], things get even harder. Scientists cannot always observe tiny particles directly. Instead, they have to use [[mathematical model]]s and [[experiment]]s to figure out what is happening. Phenomena like [[quantum entanglement]] or [[wavefunction collapse]] are known through indirect evidence and complex data.{{Cite web|title=What Is Quantum Physics?|url=http://scienceexchange.caltech.edu/topics/quantum-science-explained/quantum-physics|access-date=2025-07-19|website=Caltech Science Exchange|language=en}} In the [[social science]]s (like [[psychology]] or [[sociology]]), empiricism works a bit differently. Scientists use tools like [[survey]]s, [[interview]]s, and [[experiment]]s with people to gather data. But this kind of research can have its own problems. For example, people might give answers they think are expected (this is called [[social desirability bias]]), or they might act differently because they know they are being watched (called the [[Hawthorne effect]] or [[observer bias]]).{{Cite book|title=Bryman's social research methods|url=https://archive.org/details/nlsiu.300.72.cla.40484|last1=Clark|first1=Tom|last2=Foster|first2=Liam|last3=Sloan|first3=Luke|last4=Bryman|first4=Alan|last5=Bryman|first5=Alan|date=2021|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-879605-3|edition=6th|location=Oxford}} ===Rationality and Logic=== [[Rationality]] and [[logic]] are very important in science. They help scientists make sure their ideas make sense, their theories fit together, and their conclusions are based on good reasoning. Rational thinking in science means using reason carefully. Scientists use it to come up with ideas (called [[Hypothesis|hypotheses]]), to plan [[experiment]]s, to understand results, and to compare different explanations. This helps make sure that conclusions come from real evidence, not just guesses. Logic gives rules for how to go from one idea to another. It helps scientists check if their arguments are valid.{{Cite book|title=Philosophy of logics|url=https://archive.org/details/philosophyoflogi0000haac|last=Haack|first=Susan|date=1978|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-21988-4|location=Cambridge [Eng.] ; New York}} For example, in [[biology]], if all [[mammal]]s are warm-blooded and [[whale]]s are mammals, then whales must be warm-blooded. This is a basic kind of [[Critical thinking|logical thinking]] called [[deductive reasoning]].{{Cite journal|last=Johnson-Laird|first=Phil|date=2010|title=Deductive reasoning|url=https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wcs.20|journal=WIREs Cognitive Science|language=en|volume=1|issue=1|pages=8–17|doi=10.1002/wcs.20|pmid=26272833 |issn=1939-5078}} Science also uses the [[Law of noncontradiction|rule of non-contradiction]]. This means something cannot be both true and not true at the same time. For example, a [[chemical]] cannot both contain and not contain the same [[Chemical element|element]] under the same conditions. This helps scientists make clear and reliable chemical models.{{Citation|last=Gottlieb|first=Paula|title=Aristotle on Non-contradiction|date=2023|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2023/entries/aristotle-noncontradiction/|encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|editor-last=Zalta|editor-first=Edward N.|edition=Winter 2023|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|access-date=2025-07-20|editor2-last=Nodelman|editor2-first=Uri}} There are also formal types of logic, like [[propositional logic]], [[predicate logic]], and [[modal logic]]. These are used in areas like [[computer science]], [[artificial intelligence]], and [[mathematical biology]]. They help scientists build computer programs, design experiments, and understand complex systems.{{Cite book|title=Language, proof, and logic|url=https://archive.org/details/languageprooflog0000bark|last1=Barker-Plummer|first1=Dave|last2=Barwise|first2=Jon|last3=Etchemendy|first3=John|last4=Liu|first4=Albert|last5=Murray|first5=Michael|last6=Pease|first6=Emma|date=2011|publisher=CSLI Publ|isbn=978-1-57586-632-1|edition=2nd|location=Stanford, Calif}} Logic and rational thinking are important in science not just to support good ideas, but also to find [[mistake]]s, hidden [[problem]]s, or wrong [[assumption]]s in [[Scientific theory|scientific theories]]. In [[physics]], the discovery of [[quantum mechanics]] made scientists question old ideas. For example, [[classical physics]] said that objects behave in clear, predictable ways (called [[determinism]]) and that things far apart cannot affect each other instantly (called [[locality]]). But quantum mechanics showed that very small particles often behave in strange and random ways, so scientists had to use new kinds of logic to understand them. There is also a big problem between two important theories: [[general relativity]] and [[quantum field theory]]. Relativity explains how big things like planets and galaxies work, while quantum theory explains tiny particles. But the two theories do not fully agree with each other. This has led scientists to search for a new theory that combines both, such as [[string theory]] or [[loop quantum gravity]].{{Cite news|last=Powell|first=Corey S.|date=2015-11-04|title=Relativity versus quantum mechanics: the battle for the universe|language=en-GB|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2015/nov/04/relativity-quantum-mechanics-universe-physicists|access-date=2025-07-20|issn=0261-3077}}{{Cite web|last=Outreach|first=Research|date=2019-12-19|title=Unifying quantum mechanics with Einstein's general relativity|url=https://researchoutreach.org/articles/unifying-quantum-mechanics-einstein-general-relativity/|access-date=2025-07-20|website=Research Outreach|language=en-GB}}{{Cite book|title=The fabric of the cosmos: space, time, and the texture of reality|url=https://archive.org/details/fabricofcosmossp00gree|last=Greene|first=Brian|date=2005|publisher=Vintage Books|isbn=978-0-375-72720-7|edition=1st|location=New York}} Science often uses a method called [[hypothetico-deductive reasoning]]. This means scientists start with a theory, then use logic to make predictions that can be tested. If experiments agree with the prediction, the theory is stronger. If not, the theory may need to change. For example, we know that [[antibiotic]]s kill [[bacteria]], not [[virus]]es. This logical idea helps doctors avoid giving antibiotics for viral infections, which helps prevent [[antibiotic resistance]].{{Cite journal|last1=Davies|first1=Julian|last2=Davies|first2=Dorothy|date=2010|title=Origins and Evolution of Antibiotic Resistance|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_microbiology-and-molecular-biology-reviews_2010-09_74_3/page/416|journal=Microbiology and Molecular Biology Reviews|language=en|volume=74|issue=3|pages=417–433|doi=10.1128/MMBR.00016-10|pmid=20805405 |pmc=2937522 |issn=1092-2172}} In [[social science]]s, logic is also important. [[Game theory]] is a tool that uses logic and reasoning to study how people make choices in situations where others are also making [[decision]]s. It helps explain things like [[voting]], [[diplomacy]] between countries, and even how [[government]]s sell licenses for things like radio frequencies. Game theory helps people make better decisions by thinking logically about the actions of others.{{Cite book|title=Playing for real: a text on game theory|url=https://archive.org/details/playingforrealte0000binm|last=Binmore|first=K. G.|date=2007|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-530057-4|location=Oxford ; New York}}{{Cite book|title=An introduction to game theory|url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoga0000osbo|last=Osborne|first=Martin J.|date=2004|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-512895-6|location=New York}} Scientific thinking also includes the idea of parsimony, which is often called [[Occam's Razor]]. This idea says that if there are different explanations for something, the simplest one that still explains the [[fact]]s should be chosen. This rule helps scientists choose the best theories in many fields, such as [[biology]] and [[climate science]]. For example, a long time ago, people believed that the [[Earth]] was at the center of the universe (the [[Geocentrism|geocentric model]]). But this model needed many complicated parts, like epicycles, to explain how planets moved. Later, Copernicus suggested that the [[Sun]] was at the center instead (the [[Heliocentrism|heliocentric model]]). This simpler idea explained the same facts more easily, so it became the better choice.{{Cite book|title=Ockham's razors: a user's manual|last=Sober|first=Elliott|date=2015|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-107-69253-4|location=Cambridge}} In [[Neuroscience|brain science]], a new idea called the [[Bayesian brain hypothesis]] says that the [[brain]] works by using [[probability]] to update what it believes. This means the brain uses logic and evidence, like a smart guesser. This idea is also used in computer fields like [[robotics]] and [[machine learning]].{{Cite journal|last1=Knill|first1=David C.|last2=Pouget|first2=Alexandre|date=2004|title=The Bayesian brain: the role of uncertainty in neural coding and computation|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0166223604003352|journal=Trends in Neurosciences|language=en|volume=27|issue=12|pages=712–719|doi=10.1016/j.tins.2004.10.007 |pmid=15541511 }} Logic is also very important in doing science in a fair and careful way. For example, [[decision theory]] is a part of logic that helps scientists decide how to run medical studies. It helps them think clearly about risks, benefits, and what is unknown when testing new treatments.{{Citation|last=Berger|first=James O.|title=Statistical Decision Theory|date=1989|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-349-20181-5_26|work=Game Theory|pages=217–224|editor-last=Eatwell|editor-first=John|place=London|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan UK|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-349-20181-5_26|isbn=978-1-349-20181-5|access-date=2025-07-20|editor2-last=Milgate|editor2-first=Murray|editor3-last=Newman|editor3-first=Peter}} == Scientific method == Today, "science" usually refers to a way of pursuing [[knowledge]], not just the knowledge itself. It is mainly about the [[phenomena]] of the material world. The Greek works into Western Europe from the 6th to 7th century B.C. revived "[[Philosophy]]".Oxford English Dictionary In the 17th and 18th centuries scientists increasingly sought to formulate knowledge in terms of ''[[scientific law|laws of nature]]'' such as [[Newton's laws of motion]]. And during the 19th century, the word "science" became more and more associated with the [[scientific method]] itself. It was seen as a way to study the natural world, including [[physics]], [[chemistry]], [[geology]] and [[biology]]. It was also in the 19th century that the term ''[[scientist]]'' was created by [[William Whewell]]. He meant it to tell the difference between those who looked for knowledge on nature from those who looked for other types of knowledge.The ''Oxford English Dictionary'' dates the origin of the word "scientist" to 1834. The [[scientific method]] is the name given to the methods used by scientists to find knowledge. The main [[wikt:feature|feature]]s of the scientific method are: # Scientists identify a question or a problem about nature. Some problems are simple, such as "how many legs do flies have?" and some are very deep, such as "why do objects fall to the ground?" # Next, scientists investigate the problem. They work at it, and collect facts. Sometimes all it takes is to look carefully. # Some questions cannot be answered directly. Then scientists suggest ideas, and test them out. They do [[experiment]]s and collect [[data]]. # Eventually, they find what they think is a good answer to the problem. Then they tell people about it. # Later, other scientists may agree or not agree. They may suggest another answer. They may do more experiments. Anything in science might be revised if we find out the previous solution was not good enough. === An example === A famous example of science in action was the [[expedition]] led by [[Arthur Eddington]] to [[Principe Island]] in [[Africa]] in 1919. He went there to record where the stars were around the Sun during a [[solar eclipse]]. The observation of where the stars were shown that the apparent star positions close to the Sun were changed. In effect, the light passing the Sun was pulled towards the Sun by [[gravitation]]. This confirmed predictions of [[gravitational lensing]] made by [[Albert Einstein]] in the [[general theory of relativity]], published in 1915. Eddington's observations were considered to be the first solid proof in favour of Einstein's theory. === Practical impacts of scientific research === Discoveries in fundamental science can be world-changing. [[Vaccines]] for [[viruses]] are built by genomics. |} ==Philosophy of science== [[File:Epicycle and deferent.svg|thumb|For [[Thomas Kuhn|Kuhn]], the addition of [[epicycles]] in Ptolemaic astronomy was "normal science" within a paradigm, whereas the [[The Structure of Scientific Revolutions#Copernican Revolution|Copernican Revolution]] was a paradigm shift|alt=Depiction of epicycles, where a planet orbit is going around in a bigger orbit]] The [[philosophy of science]] is a subject that looks closely at how science works and what it really means. It asks big questions like: How do we know something is true in science? How do scientific ideas change over time? Can science truly be objective? People who study the philosophy of science try to understand the methods scientists use, the rules they follow, and how their discoveries affect the world.{{Cite book|title=Philosophy of science: a very short introduction|url=https://archive.org/details/apu.501.oka.49362|last=Okasha|first=Samir|date=2016|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-874558-7|edition=2nd|location=Oxford, United Kingdom}} This field connects to other areas of [[philosophy]], such as [[epistemology]] (the study of [[knowledge]]), [[metaphysics]] (the study of what exists), [[ethics]], and [[logic]].{{Cite book|title=Theory and reality: an introduction to the philosophy of science|last=Godfrey-Smith|first=Peter|date=2021|publisher=The University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-77113-7|edition=2nd|location=Chicago London}} It also looks at how science is actually done in both [[natural science]]s (like [[physics]] and [[biology]]) and [[social science]]s (like [[psychology]] and [[sociology]]).{{Cite book|title=What is this thing called science?|last1=Chalmers|first1=Alan F.|last2=Chalmers|first2=Alan F.|date=1999|publisher=Hackett Publ. Company Inc|isbn=978-0-87220-452-2|edition=3. ed., reprinted|location=Indianapolis}} One of the biggest questions in the philosophy of science is called the [[demarcation problem]]. This means trying to figure out what counts as real science and what does not, like [[pseudoscience]], which pretends to be scientific but doesn't follow the same rules.{{Cite web|title=Pseudoscience and the Demarcation Problem {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy|url=https://iep.utm.edu/pseudoscience-demarcation/|access-date=2025-07-19|language=en-US}} A famous philosopher named [[Karl Popper]] said that real science should be [[Falsifiability|falsifiable]]. This means a scientific idea must make clear predictions that could be proven wrong with evidence. For example, [[General relativity|Einstein’s theory of general relativity]] predicted that [[light]] would bend during a [[solar eclipse]]. Scientists tested this and confirmed it, showing the theory was falsifiable. On the other hand, Popper criticized things like [[Psychoanalysis|Freud’s psychoanalysis]], which tried to explain human behavior in ways that could not really be tested or proven wrong, because it could twist its explanations to fit any situation.{{Cite web|title=Popper, Karl: Philosophy of Science {{!}} Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy|url=https://iep.utm.edu/pop-sci/|access-date=2025-07-19|language=en-US}} Some later philosophers, like [[Imre Lakatos]] and [[Paul Feyerabend]], said that science is not always so simple. They pointed out that many great scientific ideas started out as vague or hard to test. So, the question of what counts as real science is still debated, and there may not be one easy answer.{{Citation|last=Ladyman|first=James|title=The History of Philosophy of Science|date=2019|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cambridge-history-of-philosophy-19452015/history-of-philosophy-of-science/C6579516684BD38320C503F154931F3C|work=The Cambridge History of Philosophy, 1945–2015|pages=189–209|editor-last=Thomson|editor-first=Iain D.|place=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|doi=10.1017/9781316779651.017|isbn=978-1-107-17303-3|access-date=2025-07-19|editor2-last=Becker|editor2-first=Kelly}} [[Scientific realism]] and [[anti-realism]] are two different ways of thinking about what science is really doing. People who support scientific realism, like [[Hilary Putnam]] and [[Richard Boyd]], believe that scientific theories describe the world as it actually is, even the parts we cannot see, like [[electron]]s or [[black hole]]s.{{Cite book|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/mathematics-matter-and-method/B3078C1C0AF323299F65D5DAFD046DC0|title=Mathematics, Matter and Method: Philosophical Papers|last=Putnam|first=Hilary|date=1979|publisher=Cambridge University Press|edition=2|volume=1|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511625268 |isbn=978-0-521-22553-3 }}{{Citation|last=Boyd|first=Richard N.|title=On the Current Status of the Issue of Scientific Realism|date=1983|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-015-7676-5_3|work=Methodology, Epistemology, and Philosophy of Science: Essays in Honour of Wolfgang Stegmüller on the Occasion of His 60th Birthday, June 3rd, 1983|pages=45–90|editor-last=Hempel|editor-first=Carl G.|place=Dordrecht|publisher=Springer Netherlands|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-94-015-7676-5_3|isbn=978-94-015-7676-5|access-date=2025-07-19|editor2-last=Putnam|editor2-first=Hilary|editor3-last=Essler|editor3-first=Wilhelm K.}} They argue that science works so well, like making accurate predictions and helping us build amazing technology, because its ideas are mostly true, or at least close to the truth.{{Cite journal|last=Boyd|first=Richard|date=1990|title=Realism, approximate truth, and philosophical method|url=https://hdl.handle.net/11299/185718|journal=University of Minnesota Digital Conservancy|hdl=11299/185718 |language=en}} On the other side, anti-realists, like [[Bas van Fraassen]], believe something different. They say the job of science is not to find the absolute truth, but to come up with ideas and models that correctly predict what we can observe. This is called [[empirical adequacy]].{{Cite book|title=The scientific image|url=https://archive.org/details/scientificimage0000vanf|last=Van Fraassen|first=Bas C.|date=1980|publisher=Clarendon Press ; Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-824424-0|series=Clarendon library of logic and philosophy|location=Oxford : New York}} For example, in [[quantum mechanics]] (the science of very tiny particles), the math can predict things very well, but different scientists have totally different beliefs about what is really happening. Some realists believe in things like the [[Many-worlds Interpretation]],{{Cite journal|last=Barrett|first=Jeffrey|date=1998-06-03|title=Everett's Relative-State Formulation of Quantum Mechanics|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archIves/win2013/entries/qm-everett/|journal=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|language=en}}{{Cite book|url=https://academic.oup.com/book/25622|title=The Emergent Multiverse: Quantum Theory according to the Everett Interpretation|last=Wallace|first=David|date=2012-05-24|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-954696-1|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199546961.001.0001}} while anti-realists prefer ideas like the [[Copenhagen Interpretation]], which focus only on what we can measure and see.{{Cite journal|last1=Einstein|first1=A.|last2=Podolsky|first2=B.|last3=Rosen|first3=N.|date=1935-05-15|title=Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.47.777|journal=Physical Review|volume=47|issue=10|pages=777–780|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.47.777 |bibcode=1935PhRv...47..777E }}{{Cite book|url=https://academic.oup.com/book/27275|title=Quantum Mechanics|last=Fraassen|first=Bas C. van|date=1991-09-26|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-823980-2|doi=10.1093/0198239807.001.0001}} Another big idea in the philosophy of science is how science explains things. One early idea was the [[deductive-nomological model]], created by [[Carl Hempel]]. He said that to explain something scientifically, you had to show how it follows from general laws and starting conditions. For example, explaining why a [[planet]] moves in an [[ellipse]] (oval shape) using Newton's laws of gravity and motion.{{Cite journal|last1=Hempel|first1=Carl G.|last2=Oppenheim|first2=Paul|date=1948|title=Studies in the Logic of Explanation|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S003182480002273X/type/journal_article|journal=Philosophy of Science|language=en|volume=15|issue=2|pages=135–175|doi=10.1086/286983|issn=0031-8248}} But not everyone agreed with this model. Some philosophers thought it did not explain things in everyday life or in complicated sciences like biology.{{Cite book|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt5vkdm7|title=Four Decades of Scientific Explanation|last=Salmon|first=Wesley C.|date=1990|publisher=University of Pittsburgh Press|isbn=978-0-8229-5926-7|doi=10.2307/j.ctt5vkdm7 |jstor=j.ctt5vkdm7 }} So, newer thinkers, like [[Nancy Cartwright]] and [[James Woodward]], introduced different ways to explain things, especially using causes and mechanisms.{{Cite book|url=https://academic.oup.com/book/27605|title=How the Laws of Physics Lie|last=Cartwright|first=Nancy|date=1983-06-09|publisher=Oxford University PressOxford|isbn=978-0-19-824704-3|edition=1|language=en|doi=10.1093/0198247044.001.0001}}{{Cite book|url=https://academic.oup.com/book/4324|title=Making Things Happen: A Theory of Causal Explanation|last=Woodward|first=James|date=2004-01-08|publisher=Oxford University PressNew York|isbn=978-0-19-515527-3|edition=1|language=en|doi=10.1093/0195155270.001.0001}} In this newer view, a good explanation tells us how something works step by step. For instance, if we want to explain how the [[heart]] pumps [[blood]], we do not just give a [[Scientific law|law]], we show how parts like [[pacemaker cell]]s, [[ion channel]]s, and [[Muscle|muscle fiber]]s all work together to make the heart beat. This kind of explanation is especially useful in subjects like [[neuroscience]] and [[medicine]], where understanding the parts and how they interact is key.{{Cite book|url=https://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/2860/Discovering-ComplexityDecomposition-and|title=Discovering Complexity: Decomposition and Localization as Strategies in Scientific Research|last1=Bechtel|first1=William|last2=Richardson|first2=Robert C.|date=2010-08-06|publisher=The MIT Press|isbn=978-0-262-28917-7|language=en|doi=10.7551/mitpress/8328.001.0001}} One big question in the philosophy of science is called the problem of [[induction]]. This idea was first brought up by a philosopher named [[David Hume]] in the 1700s. He asked: How do we really know that what happened in the past will keep happening in the future? For example, we believe the sun will rise tomorrow because it has always done so. But Hume pointed out that we do not have a perfect reason to believe that, just past experience.{{Cite web|title=The Project Gutenberg eBook of An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, by David Hume.|url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9662/9662-h/9662-h.htm|access-date=2025-07-19|website=www.gutenberg.org}} Science often depends on these kinds of [[pattern]]s, but there is no absolute [[proof]] that they will always hold true. Later on, a philosopher named [[Nelson Goodman]] added to this [[puzzle]]. He showed that it is not always easy to decide which patterns are meaningful. He created a strange example using the [[color]] “grue,” which means something is [[green]] before a certain time and [[blue]] after. This example showed that choosing which patterns to trust is harder than it seems.{{Cite book|title=Fact, fiction, and forecast|last=Goodman|first=Nelson|date=1983|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-29071-6|edition=4th|location=Cambridge, Mass}} Today, some philosophers and scientists try to solve this problem using [[probability]]. This is called [[Bayesian reasoning]], where people adjust their beliefs based on how likely something is and what they already know.{{Cite book|title=Scientific reasoning: the Bayesian approach|last1=Howson|first1=Colin|last2=Urbach|first2=Peter|date=2005|publisher=Open Court|isbn=978-0-8126-9578-6|edition=3rd|location=Chicago}} But even this method has challenges, like being hard to calculate and including some personal judgment.{{Cite book|title=Bayes or bust? a critical examination of Bayesian confirmation theory|url=https://archive.org/details/bayesorbustcriti0000earm|last=Earman|first=John|date=1992|publisher=MIT Press|isbn=978-0-262-51900-7|series=A Bradford book|location=Cambridge, Mass.}} Another important thinker was [[Thomas Kuhn]], who wrote a famous book in 1962 called The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. He said that science does not always grow in a straight line by slowly adding new facts. Instead, he said science works through [[paradigm]]s, big ideas or frameworks that shape how scientists think, what they study, and what evidence they trust. Scientists work within a paradigm for a long time during “normal science,” but eventually they find anomalies, things that do not fit. When enough of these build up, a [[scientific revolution]] happens, and the old paradigm is replaced with a new one. For example, when scientists moved from [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|Newton’s laws]] to [[General relativity|Einstein’s theory of relativity]], or from [[Geocentrism|Ptolemy’s geocentric model]] ([[Earth]] at the center) to [[Heliocentrism|Copernicus’s heliocentric model]] ([[Sun]] at the center), these were paradigm shifts.{{Cite book|title=The structure of scientific revolutions|url=https://archive.org/details/structureofscien0003kuhn_k955|last=Kuhn|first=Thomas S.|date=1996|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-45807-6|edition=3rd|location=Chicago, IL}} Kuhn also said that different paradigms can be incommensurable, meaning they are so different that they cannot easily be compared. This idea was controversial. Philosophers like Karl Popper and Imre Lakatos disagreed with Kuhn. [[Karl Popper]], for example, believed that science moves forward by [[falsification]]. This means that scientists should constantly test their ideas and try to prove them wrong. If a [[Scientific theory|theory]] fails the test, it should be rejected. Popper thought that a good scientific theory must be one that could be proven false if the evidence does not support it. For example, saying “All swans are white” is a scientific idea because it can be tested, and even disproven by finding just one black [[swan]]. Another philosopher, [[Imre Lakatos]], offered a different view. He did not think science was as dramatic as Kuhn’s idea of sudden "paradigm shifts," but he also did not fully agree with Popper. Lakatos said that science works through research programmes, groups of theories and ideas that develop over time. These programmes may face [[problem]]s and make [[mistake]]s, but if they keep improving and helping us understand more, then they are still making [[progress]]. Lakatos believed science should still be rational and goal-directed, even if it changes slowly and builds on earlier [[idea]]s.{{Cite book|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/methodology-of-scientific-research-programmes/8DBCEFE34A59BAD3D393FB958A4DC5FC|title=The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes: Philosophical Papers|last=Lakatos|first=Imre|date=1978|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-28031-0|editor-last=Worrall|editor-first=John|volume=1|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511621123|editor-last2=Currie|editor-first2=Gregory}} The philosophy of science does not just focus on how we know things or what [[reality]] is made of. It also asks important questions about [[ethics]] (what is right or wrong) and [[politics]] (how science affects society). These questions are especially important in fields like [[environmental science]], [[artificial intelligence]], [[biotechnology]], and how we respond to [[pandemic]]s.{{Cite book|title=Science, policy, and the value-free ideal|url=https://archive.org/details/sciencepolicyval0000doug|last=Douglas|first=Heather E.|date=2009|publisher=University of Pittsburgh Press|isbn=978-0-8229-6026-3|location=Pittsburgh, Pa}}{{Cite book|title=Science in a democratic society|url=https://archive.org/details/scienceindemocra0000kitc|last=Kitcher|first=Philip|date=2011|publisher=Prometheus books|isbn=978-1-61614-407-4|location=Amherst (N.Y.)}} For example, when scientists or [[government]]s use computer models to make decisions about [[public health]] or [[climate change]], philosophers ask: Are these models reliable? Are they being used fairly?{{Cite book|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/philosophy-and-climate-science/6ED745AB77E4388C2966265C5B28B328|title=Philosophy and Climate Science|last=Winsberg|first=Eric|date=2018|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-107-19569-1|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/9781108164290}} Scientists also have to think about responsibility, how their discoveries might help or harm people.{{Cite journal|last=Douglas|first=H.|date=2003|title=The moral responsibilities of scientists (tensions between autonomy and responsibility)|url=http://www.ohri.ca/newsroom/seminars/SeminarUploads/1973/Douglas%202003%20The%20Moral%20Responsibilities%20of%20Scientists.pdf|journal=American Philosophical Quarterly|volume=40|issue=1 |pages=59–68}} One idea that comes up is called the [[precautionary principle]]. This means that if a new technology might be dangerous and we do not fully understand the risks, we should be careful and not rush into using it.{{Cite book|title=Protecting public health & the environment: implementing the precautionary principle|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781559636889|date=1999|publisher=Island Press|isbn=978-1-61091-303-4|editor-last=Raffensperger|editor-first=Carolyn|location=Washington, D.C|editor-last2=Tickner|editor-first2=Joel A.}} This idea is based on [[epistemic humility]], which means recognizing the limits of our [[knowledge]].{{Cite book|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/philosophy-and-the-precautionary-principle/FB666B607B8A87E3075A235F2F1530AB|title=Philosophy and the Precautionary Principle: Science, Evidence, and Environmental Policy|last=Steel|first=Daniel|date=2014|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-107-07816-1|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/cbo9781139939652}} A good example is [[CRISPR]], a powerful gene-editing tool. While it can be used to treat diseases, it also raises big questions: Should we change human DNA? Should we allow “designer babies”? These are not just scientific questions, they are philosophical and ethical ones, too.{{Cite journal|last=Sun|first=Bob Z.|date=2020|title=Review of Altered inheritance: CRISPR and the ethics of human genome editing by Françoise Baylis|url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s40592-020-00106-0|journal=Monash Bioethics Review|language=en|volume=38|issue=1|pages=91–93|doi=10.1007/s40592-020-00106-0|pmid=32314277 |issn=1321-2753}} Philosophers also talk about whether there is only one correct way to do science. Some thinkers, like [[Paul Feyerabend]], believed that there is no single method that all science must follow. He called this idea [[epistemological anarchism]], which means that even unusual or untraditional approaches can lead to progress.{{Cite book|title=Against method|last=Feyerabend|first=Paul|date=2010|publisher=Verso|isbn=978-1-84467-442-8|edition=4th|location=London; New York}} This way of thinking is called [[pluralism]], and it accepts that different fields of science may need different tools and ways of thinking.{{Cite book|title=The fate of knowledge|url=https://archive.org/details/fateofknowledge0000long|last=Longino|first=Helen E.|date=2002|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-08876-1|location=Princeton, N.J}}{{Cite book|title=Scientific pluralism|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780816647637|date=2006|publisher=University of Minnesota Press|isbn=978-0-8166-4763-7|editor-last=Kellert|editor-first=Stephen H.|series=Minnesota studies in the philosophy of science|location=Minneapolis, MN|editor-last2=Longino|editor-first2=Helen E.|editor-last3=Waters|editor-first3=C. Kenneth}} For instance, in [[climate science]], scientists use a mix of [[physics]], [[statistics]], and [[information]] about [[human behavior]] to make [[prediction]]s. In [[medicine]], both controlled [[experiment]]s and [[patient]] stories give useful, but very different, kinds of [[evidence]]. This shows that science does not always follow just one path. Instead, different methods can work together to give us a better understanding of the world.{{Cite book|title=Social empiricism|url=https://archive.org/details/socialempiricism0000solo|last=Solomon|first=M.|publisher=MIT Press|year=2001|isbn=9780262264648}} ==Science and society== [[File:Covid-19 SP - UTI V. Nova Cachoeirinha.jpg|thumb|During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], groups like the [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization (WHO)]] and the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)]] gave advice based on science. They told people how to stay safe using masks, vaccines, and social distancing.]] Scientific discoveries have played a big role in changing the world. They have helped improve how people live, work, and communicate. Some important examples include the invention of the [[printing press]], the rise of [[Factory|factories]] during the [[Industrial Revolution]], and modern tools like [[electricity]], [[antibiotic]]s, and the [[internet]]. These discoveries changed not only technology, but also how societies are organized.{{Cite book|title=The Gifts of Athena: Historical Origins of the Knowledge Economy|last=Mokyr|first=Joel|date=2011|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-12013-3|location=Princeton}} For example, in the 1700s, [[James Watt]] improved the [[steam engine]]. This invention made it easier to move goods and power machines. It helped build large cities and connect countries through trade.{{Citation|last=Hills|first=Richard L.|title=James Watt. 1: His time in Scotland, 1736 - 1774|date=2002|edition=1st|place=Ashbourne|publisher=Landmark|isbn=978-1-84306-045-1}} In 1928, [[Alexander Fleming]] discovered [[penicillin]], the first [[antibiotic]]. This medicine saved many lives by treating [[infection]]s and changed the way doctors and hospitals work all over the world. Science also helps [[government]]s make better [[decision]]s. When leaders use evidence and facts, they can solve big problems like climate change, diseases, and food shortages. For example, the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)]] studies thousands of scientific papers to give advice about [[global warming]]. In 1987, the [[Montreal Protocol]] helped protect the [[ozone layer]] by banning harmful gases called [[CFC]]s. Scientists showed that CFCs were damaging the atmosphere, and the agreement helped the ozone layer begin to heal.{{Cite web|title=The Montreal Protocol on Substances That Deplete the Ozone Layer|url=https://www.state.gov/the-montreal-protocol-on-substances-that-deplete-the-ozone-layer/|access-date=2025-07-20|website=United States Department of State|language=en}}{{Cite web|title=Saving the Ozone Layer - Celebrating 30 Years of the Montreal Protocol|url=https://2017-2021.state.gov/saving-the-ozone-layer-celebrating-30-years-of-the-montreal-protocol/|access-date=2025-07-20|website=United States Department of State|language=en-US}} During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], groups like the [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization (WHO)]] and the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)]] gave advice based on science. They told people how to stay safe using masks, vaccines, and social distancing.{{Cite web|title=Coronavirus|url=https://www.who.int/health-topics/coronavirus|access-date=2025-07-20|website=www.who.int|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=CDC|date=2020-02-11|title=Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19)|url=https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/science/science-briefs/masking-science-sars-cov2.html|access-date=2025-07-20|website=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|language=en-us}} However, not everyone followed or trusted this advice equally.{{Cite journal|last1=van der Linden|first1=Sander|last2=Roozenbeek|first2=Jon|last3=Compton|first3=Josh|date=2020-10-23|title=Inoculating Against Fake News About COVID-19|journal=Frontiers in Psychology|language=English|volume=11|article-number=566790 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2020.566790|pmid=33192844 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-1078|pmc=7644779}} Science also helps countries work together. This is called [[science diplomacy]]. Projects like the [[International Space Station|International Space Station (ISS)]] or joint research in the [[Arctic]] bring scientists from different countries together. These efforts can build peace and cooperation between nations.{{Citation|last1=Turekian|first1=Vaughan C.|title=The Emergence of Science Diplomacy|date=2012-09-05|url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789814440073_0001|work=Science Diplomacy|pages=3–24|publisher=WORLD SCIENTIFIC|doi=10.1142/9789814440073_0001|isbn=978-981-4440-06-6|access-date=2025-07-20|last2=Macindoe|first2=Sarah|last3=Copeland|first3=Daryl|last4=Davis|first4=Lloyd S.|last5=Patman|first5=Robert G.|last6=Pozza|first6=Maria}} The connection between science and society goes both ways. Science changes the world, but society also shapes how science is done. People's [[value]]s, [[culture]], [[money]], and [[politics]] all influence what research is supported and how results are used. For example, during the [[Cold War]], the [[U.S.]] focused heavily on space research after the [[Soviet Union]] launched [[Sputnik 1]] in 1957. This led to the creation of NASA and more investment in science and engineering education. Politics and fear of falling behind in space technology drove this big push.{{Cite book|title=The heavens and the earth: a political history of the space age|last=McDougall|first=Walter A.|date=1997|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|isbn=978-0-8018-5748-5|edition=Johns Hopkins paperbacks|location=Baltimore, Md}}{{Cite book|title=Competing with the Soviets: science, technology, and the state in Cold War America|url=https://archive.org/details/competingwithsov0000wolf|last=Wolfe|first=Audra J.|date=2013|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|isbn=978-1-4214-0769-2|series=Johns Hopkins introductory series in the history of science|location=Baltimore}} Social movements can also change science. In the 1970s, feminist groups pointed out that medical research mostly focused on [[men]]. Because of this, rules changed so [[women]] had to be included in [[clinical trial]]s. This helped scientists understand how treatments can work differently in men and women.{{Cite web|title=History of Women's Participation in Clinical Research|url=https://orwh.od.nih.gov/toolkit/recruitment/history|access-date=2025-07-20|website=orwh.od.nih.gov |date=24 April 2024 }} In farming, many people worry about [[Genetically modified organisms|genetically modified organisms (GMOs)]]. This public concern has led to different rules in different places. For example, [[Europe]] uses the [[precautionary principle]], which means being more careful about approving new GMO products than in countries like the U.S.{{Cite journal|last=Tait|first=Joyce|date=2001-04-01|title=More Faust than Frankenstein: the European debate about the precautionary principle and risk regulation for genetically modified crops|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/13669870010027640|journal=Journal of Risk Research|volume=4|issue=2|pages=175–189|doi=10.1080/13669870010027640|issn=1366-9877}} Even the way [[Scientific literature|scientific paper]]s are shared is shaped by [[money]] and [[business model]]s. Many journals charge people to read studies, which has caused debates about whether scientific knowledge should be free and open to everyone.{{Cite book|title=Open access|url=https://archive.org/details/9780262517638OpenAccess|last=Suber|first=Peter|date=2012|publisher=MIT Press|isbn=9780262517638|series=MIT Press essential knowledge series|location=Cambridge, Mass}}{{Cite journal|last1=Himmelstein|first1=Daniel S|last2=Romero|first2=Ariel Rodriguez|last3=Levernier|first3=Jacob G|last4=Munro|first4=Thomas Anthony|last5=McLaughlin|first5=Stephen Reid|last6=Greshake Tzovaras|first6=Bastian|last7=Greene|first7=Casey S|date=2018-03-01|title=Sci-Hub provides access to nearly all scholarly literature|journal=eLife|language=en|volume=7|article-number=e32822 |doi=10.7554/eLife.32822|pmid=29424689 |doi-access=free |pmc=5832410 |issn=2050-084X}} Science also helps grow economies and create new jobs. Many big industries, like [[biotechnology]], [[renewable energy]], [[artificial intelligence]], and [[aerospace]], are based on years of [[scientific research]].{{Cite book|title=The entrepreneurial state: debunking public vs. private sector myths|url=https://archive.org/details/entrepreneurials0000mazz_g0r9|last=Mazzucato|first=Mariana|date=2014|publisher=Anthem Press|isbn=978-0-85728-252-1|edition=Revised|series=Anthem frontiers of global political economy|location=London ; New York}} For example, the [[semiconductor industry]], which makes [[computer chip]]s, came from early work in [[solid-state physics]]. Today, it is a global industry worth trillions of dollars.{{Cite book|title=Crystal fire: the birth of the information age|url=https://archive.org/details/crystalfirebirth00rior|last1=Riordan|first1=Michael|last2=Hoddeson|first2=Lillian|date=1997|publisher=Norton|isbn=978-0-393-04124-8|edition=1st|location=New York}} Governments often help science and technology grow by giving [[tax break]]s, supporting [[patent]]s, and creating partnerships between public and private groups.{{Cite web|title=Main Science and Technology Indicators|url=https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/main-science-and-technology-indicators_2304277x.html|access-date=2025-07-20|website=OECD|language=en}} In countries like [[South Korea]] and [[Israel]], spending more than 4% of the country’s income on research and development (R&D) has helped build strong technology industries.{{Cite web|title=UNESCO science report: The race against time for smarter development|url=https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000377250|access-date=2025-07-20|website=unesdoc.unesco.org}} However, new [[technology]] can also cause problems. These discussions are not just for scientists. They also involve ethicists, lawyers, religious leaders, and the general public. This helps make sure that science is used in ways that are fair and good for everyone.{{Cite journal|last=Jasanoff|first=Sheila|date=2003-09-01|title=Technologies of Humility: Citizen Participation in Governing Science|url=https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1025557512320|journal=Minerva|language=en|volume=41|issue=3|pages=223–244|doi=10.1023/A:1025557512320|issn=1573-1871}} Many of today’s biggest problems, like [[disease]]s, [[climate change]], and [[Food security|food shortage]]s, affect the whole world. Wealthy countries usually lead in science. They have more money for research, better equipment, and more universities.{{Cite journal|last1=Chan|first1=Leslie|last2=Kirsop|first2=Barbara|last3=Arunachalam|first3=Subbiah|date=2011|title=Towards open and equitable access to research and knowledge for development|journal=PLOS Medicine|volume=8|issue=3|article-number=e1001016|doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.1001016|doi-access=free |issn=1549-1676|pmc=3066136|pmid=21483470}} In contrast, many low- and middle-income countries struggle with problems like not enough funding, [[brain drain]] (when scientists leave to work in richer countries), and limited access to scientific tools and journals.{{Cite journal|last=Gaillard|first=Jacques|date=2010-03-01|title=Measuring Research and Development in Developing Countries: Main Characteristics and Implications for the Frascati Manual|url=https://doi.org/10.1177/097172180901500104|journal=Science, Technology and Society|language=EN|volume=15|issue=1|pages=77–111|doi=10.1177/097172180901500104|issn=0971-7218}}{{Cite journal|last=Tijssen|first=Robert J. W.|date=2007-05-01|title=Africa's contribution to the worldwide research literature: New analytical perspectives, trends, and performance indicators|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-007-1658-3|journal=Scientometrics|language=en|volume=71|issue=2|pages=303–327|doi=10.1007/s11192-007-1658-3|issn=1588-2861}} Some groups are working to close this gap. For example, [[The World Academy of Sciences|TWAS (The World Academy of Sciences)]] and [[International Network for the Availability of Scientific Publications|INASP (International Network for the Availability of Scientific Publications)]] help support science in developing countries. They promote regional cooperation, open-access publishing, and training programs to build research skills.{{Cite web|title=Home {{!}} INASP|url=https://www.inasp.info/|access-date=2025-07-22|website=www.inasp.info}}{{Cite web|last=Sciences (TWAS)|first=The World Academy of|date=2025-07-31|title=Home {{!}} TWAS|url=https://twas.org/|access-date=2025-07-22|website=twas.org|language=en}} The idea of [[open science]], supported by [[UNESCO]], says that scientific knowledge should be freely available to everyone. It also encourages scientists to work together, share results, and be transparent about how they do their research.{{Cite news|title=UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science|language=en|url=https://www.unesco.org/en/open-science/about|access-date=2025-07-22}} A good example of open science is what happened during the COVID-19 pandemic. Scientists around the world used platforms like [[GISAID]] to quickly share data about the virus’s genes. This helped track new versions of the [[SARS-CoV-2|virus]] and develop better responses faster.{{Cite journal|last1=Shu|first1=Yuelong|last2=McCauley|first2=John|date=2017-03-30|title=GISAID: Global initiative on sharing all influenza data - from vision to reality|journal=Euro Surveillance: Bulletin Europeen Sur les Maladies Transmissibles = European Communicable Disease Bulletin|volume=22|issue=13|article-number=30494|doi=10.2807/1560-7917.ES.2017.22.13.30494|issn=1560-7917|pmc=5388101|pmid=28382917}}{{Cite journal|last=Reardon|first=Sara|date=2021-07-21|title=How the Delta variant achieves its ultrafast spread|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-021-01986-w|journal=Nature|language=en|doi=10.1038/d41586-021-01986-w|pmid=34290423 |issn=0028-0836}} However, there are still challenges. Sometimes, patents and intellectual property rules make it hard for poorer countries to get important technologies, like vaccines or medical treatments.{{Cite book|title=Plagues and the paradox of progress: why the world is getting healthier in worrisome ways|url=https://archive.org/details/plaguesparadoxof0000boll|last=Bollyky|first=Thomas J.|date=2018|publisher=The MIT Press|isbn=978-0-262-03845-4|location=Cambridge, MA}}{{Cite book|url=https://www.southcentre.int/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/RP47_WTO-role-in-IP-and-access-to-medicines_EN.pdf|title=Access to Medical Technologies in Developing Countries: The Role of Intellectual Property|last=Correa|first=C.|publisher=South Centre|year=2021}} This shows that fairness in science is not just about sharing [[knowledge]], it is also about making sure everyone can use it.{{Cite web|title=Global strategy on digital health 2020-2025|url=https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020924|access-date=2025-07-22|website=www.who.int|language=en}} ==Criticisms and limitations== [[File:Spurious correlations - spelling bee spiders.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|This funny image is an example of data dredging or p-hacking, where people find patterns in data that do not really mean anything. It shows a fake connection between the number of letters in the winning word of the Scripps National Spelling Bee and the number of people in the U.S. who died from venomous spider bites. These two things have nothing to do with each other, but the graph makes it look like they do. It shows how data can be misleading if not used carefully.]] Science is the best tool humans have for understanding and predicting how [[nature]] works. But it is not perfect. Science has limits, and it is not always free from [[mistake]]s or [[bias]].{{Cite book|title=Science as social knowledge: values and objectivity in scientific inquiry|url=https://archive.org/details/scienceassocialk0000long|last=Longino|first=Helen E.|date=1990|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-07342-2|location=Princeton, N.J}}{{Cite book|title=The price of truth: how money affects the norms of science|url=https://archive.org/details/priceoftruthhowm0000resn|last=Resnik|first=David B.|date=2007|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-530978-2|series=Practical and professional ethics series|location=Oxford ; New York}} Science depends on observation, testing, and the idea that ideas should be [[Falsifiability|falsifiable]], which means they can be proven wrong if new evidence shows up. Because of this, science cannot answer questions that are metaphysical (about things beyond the physical world), emotional, or based on personal values. These kinds of questions cannot be tested or measured with tools and experiments.{{Cite book|title=Philosophy of pseudoscience: reconsidering the demarcation problem|date=2013|publisher=The University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-05179-6|editor-last=Pigliucci|editor-first=Massimo|location=Chicago|editor-last2=Boudry|editor-first2=Maarten}} For example, science can study what happens in the [[brain]] during [[meditation]], but it cannot fully explain what a person feels during that experience. This is part of a big question in [[philosophy]] and [[Neuroscience|brain science]] called the [[problem of consciousness]]. Scientists also disagree about how best to explain complex systems. Some believe that everything can be broken down into smaller parts ([[reductionism]]), while others think that new properties appear when parts come together ([[Emergence|emergentism]]). This is an important debate in areas like [[neuroscience]] and [[systems biology]].{{Cite journal|last=Anderson|first=P. W.|date=1972-08-04|title=More Is Different|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.177.4047.393|journal=Science|volume=177|issue=4047|pages=393–396|doi=10.1126/science.177.4047.393 |pmid=17796623 |bibcode=1972Sci...177..393A }} Some philosophers have said that science is not as objective as it may seem. For example, [[Thomas Kuhn]] argued that what scientists observe is affected by the theories they already believe. This idea is called [[theory-ladenness]]. In his famous book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), Kuhn said that science does not always move forward step by step. Instead, it goes through big changes called [[paradigm shift]]s, times when one way of thinking is replaced by another. A good example is how Einstein’s relativity replaced Newton’s mechanics. Kuhn also said that during these shifts, scientists working under different theories may not agree on what counts as proof or even what questions are important. This makes it hard to compare old and new ideas fairly. Another thinker, [[Paul Feyerabend]], said that there is no single "scientific method" that always works. In his book Against Method (1975), he said that in the [[history of science]], sometimes “anything goes.” He believed that too many strict rules in science can actually stop progress. One example is how Galileo’s telescope was at first seen as untrustworthy by many scientists of his time. People did not trust what it showed because it was new and did not fit their existing ideas. This shows that new tools and ideas are sometimes rejected, not because they are wrong, but because they challenge the way people already think.{{Cite book|title=Galileo, courtier: practice of science in the culture of absolutism|last=Biagioli|first=Mario|date=2006|publisher=Univ. of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-04560-3|edition=Paperback ed., [Nachdr.]|series=Science and its conceptual foundations|location=Chicago}} One basic problem in science is called the [[problem of induction]]. It was explained by philosopher [[David Hume]] in the 1700s. The problem asks: how can we be sure that something will always happen just because it has happened many times before? For example, the sun has risen every day in history, but that does not guarantee it will rise tomorrow. Yet, science often assumes that nature follows regular patterns like this. Philosopher [[Karl Popper]] tried to solve this problem by saying that science should focus on proving ideas false, not just confirming them. This is called [[falsifiability]]. According to Popper, science moves forward by getting rid of wrong theories. But this approach also has problems. If an experiment gives unexpected results, scientists do not always throw out the theory. Sometimes they blame the tools, the way the data was read, or unknown factors. For example, if a [[telescope]] shows strange [[data]] about a [[planet]], the issue might be with the [[telescope]], not the [[Scientific theory|theory]]. So it is not always clear when a theory has truly been disproven. This shows that scientific ideas are not final truths. They can change when new evidence appears or when old evidence is understood in a new way. Social and cultural factors also affect science. They influence what gets studied, who gets to do the research, and how results are shared. Most science today is led by institutions in the Western world, and it is often written in [[English]]. This has raised concerns about [[epistemic colonialism]], where knowledge from non-Western cultures, like Indigenous traditions or ancient medical systems, is ignored or only accepted when explained in Western scientific terms.{{Cite web|title=Epistemologies of the South: Justice Against Epistemicide|url=https://www.routledge.com/Epistemologies-of-the-South-Justice-Against-Epistemicide/Santos/p/book/9781612055459|access-date=2025-07-22|website=Routledge & CRC Press|language=en}} For example, [[Ayurveda]] and [[Traditional Chinese medicine]] have been used for thousands of years. But in modern science, they are often not taken seriously unless specific parts of them are tested in lab conditions or [[clinical trial]]s.{{Cite book|title=Other-worldly: making Chinese medicine through transnational frames|url=https://archive.org/details/otherworldlymaki0000zhan|last=Zhan|first=Mei|date=2009|publisher=Duke university press|isbn=978-0-8223-4363-9|location=Durham}}{{Cite journal|last=Patwardhan|first=Bhushan|date=2014|title=Bridging Ayurveda with evidence-based scientific approaches in medicine|journal=The EPMA Journal|volume=5|issue=1|article-number=19|doi=10.1186/1878-5085-5-19|doi-access=free |issn=1878-5077|pmc=4230501|pmid=25395997}} There are also problems inside the scientific community. Many researchers are under pressure to publish lots of papers to keep their jobs. This is called "[[publish or perish]]." It can lead to rushed studies, weak results, and even bad practices like [[Data dredging|p-hacking]] (changing data to get the desired result).{{Cite journal|last=Ioannidis|first=John P. A.|date=2005|title=Why most published research findings are false|journal=PLOS Medicine|volume=2|issue=8|article-number=e124|doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124|doi-access=free |issn=1549-1676|pmc=1182327|pmid=16060722}}{{Cite journal|last1=Head|first1=Megan L.|last2=Holman|first2=Luke|last3=Lanfear|first3=Rob|last4=Kahn|first4=Andrew T.|last5=Jennions|first5=Michael D.|date=2015|title=The extent and consequences of p-hacking in science|journal=PLOS Biology|volume=13|issue=3|article-number=e1002106|doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1002106|doi-access=free |issn=1545-7885|pmc=4359000|pmid=25768323}} These issues are part of what's known as the [[replication crisis]], when other scientists try to repeat a study but do not get the same results. One big study in 2015, called the Open Science Collaboration, tried to repeat 100 famous psychology experiments. Only 36% of them gave similar results. This showed that many scientific findings may not be as reliable as once thought.{{Cite journal|last=Open Science Collaboration|date=2015-08-28|title=Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aac4716|journal=Science|volume=349|issue=6251|article-number=aac4716|doi=10.1126/science.aac4716 |pmid=26315443 }} Science works best when it is honest and independent. But sometimes, economic and political pressures can affect what scientists study, how results are shared, and whether the truth is told. For example, in the 1900s, [[Tobacco industry|tobacco companies]] paid for studies that made [[smoking]] look safer than it really was. They tried to hide the fact that smoking causes [[cancer]]. This delayed laws to protect people and led to millions of deaths. The [[fossil fuel industry]] has done something similar. By funding certain research groups and articles, they tried to make people doubt the strong scientific agreement that human actions are causing [[climate change]]. These actions are examples of corporate influence over science, which can reduce public trust and keep people from knowing the full truth.{{Cite book|title=Merchants of doubt: how a handful of scientists obscured the truth on issues from tobacco smoke to climate change|last1=Oreskes|first1=Naomi|last2=Conway|first2=Erik M.|date=2022|publisher=Bloomsbury|isbn=978-1-60819-394-3|edition=Paperback edition, Nachdruck|location=New York London Oxford New Delhi Sydney}}{{Cite book|title=Bending science: how special interests corrupt public health research|url=https://archive.org/details/bendingscienceho0000mcga|last1=McGarity|first1=Thomas O.|last2=Wagner|first2=Wendy|date=2008|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=978-0-674-02815-9|location=Cambridge, Mass}} [[Government]]s can also interfere with science. During the early [[COVID-19 pandemic]], some leaders delayed sharing important data or ignored the advice of health experts. This may have made the [[pandemic]] worse and hurt people’s trust in science and government decisions.{{Cite journal|last1=Sachs|first1=Jeffrey D|last2=Karim|first2=Salim S Abdool|last3=Aknin|first3=Lara|last4=Allen|first4=Joseph|last5=Brosbøl|first5=Kirsten|last6=Colombo|first6=Francesca|last7=Barron|first7=Gabriela Cuevas|last8=Espinosa|first8=María Fernanda|last9=Gaspar|first9=Vitor|last10=Gaviria|first10=Alejandro|last11=Haines|first11=Andy|date=2022|title=The Lancet Commission on lessons for the future from the COVID-19 pandemic|journal=The Lancet|language=en|volume=400|issue=10359|pages=1224–1280|doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(22)01585-9 |pmid=36115368 |pmc=9539542 |bibcode=2022Lanc..400.1224S }}{{Cite journal|last1=Gollust|first1=Sarah E.|last2=Nagler|first2=Rebekah H.|last3=Fowler|first3=Erika Franklin|date=2020-12-01|title=The Emergence of COVID-19 in the US: A Public Health and Political Communication Crisis|url=https://read.dukeupress.edu/jhppl/article/45/6/967/165291/The-Emergence-of-COVID-19-in-the-US-A-Public|journal=Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law|language=en|volume=45|issue=6|pages=967–981|doi=10.1215/03616878-8641506|pmid=32464658 |issn=0361-6878}} To keep science honest, there must be transparency (open sharing of methods and results) and safeguards that protect scientists from outside pressure.{{Cite journal|last=Ioannidis|first=John P. A.|date=2014|title=How to make more published research true|journal=PLOS Medicine|volume=11|issue=10|article-number=e1001747|doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.1001747|doi-access=free |issn=1549-1676|pmc=4204808|pmid=25334033}} Science often uses controlled experiments to find clear answers. But some problems are too complex for this method to work perfectly. Fields like [[climate science]], [[epidemiology]] (the study of diseases), and [[ecology]] deal with systems that have many parts working together. Because of this, scientists must use models and probabilities to make predictions. For example, [[climate model]]s look at how things like [[greenhouse gas]]es, [[ocean current]]s, and [[Weather|weather pattern]]s interact. These models can show possible future trends, but they cannot predict exactly what will happen in a specific place at a specific time many years ahead. Sometimes people misunderstand this. They think that if science is uncertain, it must be wrong. But in complex systems, uncertainty is normal. It does not mean the science is bad. The same problem appears in [[nutritional science]]. It is hard to study [[diet]] because people eat many things at once, and other factors (like [[sleep]] or [[exercise]]) affect [[health]] too. This can lead to confusing or changing advice about what is healthy.{{Cite journal|last1=Vitolins|first1=Mara Z.|last2=Case|first2=Talsi L.|date=2020|title=What Makes Nutrition Research So Difficult to Conduct and Interpret?|journal=Diabetes Spectrum: A Publication of the American Diabetes Association|volume=33|issue=2|pages=113–117|doi=10.2337/ds19-0077|issn=1040-9165|pmc=7228817|pmid=32425447}} Even in areas with experiments, like genetics, scientists have learned that things are more complicated than they once thought. Many diseases cannot be explained by a single [[gene]]. Instead, they are caused by interactions between many genes and environmental factors. This shows that [[reductionism]], studying only small parts of a problem, can miss the bigger picture when dealing with [[complex system]]s.{{Cite journal|last1=Manolio|first1=Teri A.|last2=Collins|first2=Francis S.|last3=Cox|first3=Nancy J.|last4=Goldstein|first4=David B.|last5=Hindorff|first5=Lucia A.|last6=Hunter|first6=David J.|last7=McCarthy|first7=Mark I.|last8=Ramos|first8=Erin M.|last9=Cardon|first9=Lon R.|last10=Chakravarti|first10=Aravinda|last11=Cho|first11=Judy H.|date=2009|title=Finding the missing heritability of complex diseases|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=461|issue=7265|pages=747–753|doi=10.1038/nature08494|pmid=19812666 |pmc=2831613 |bibcode=2009Natur.461..747M |issn=1476-4687}} Science is a powerful way to learn about the natural world, but it has limits. Some important questions cannot be answered by science alone. These include [[Normativity|normative]] (what we should do), [[Existentialism|existential]] (why we exist), and [[Metaphysics|metaphysical]] (beyond the physical world) questions. For example, science cannot fully answer “What is the meaning of life?”, “Is there a God?”, “What is morally right or wrong?”, or “What is consciousness?”. Science can study things we can see and test, like how the brain works. For instance, [[neuroscience]] can show how parts of the brain light up when we make [[choice]]s. But it cannot tell us what we should do [[Morality|morally]]. This is known as the [[is–ought problem]], explained by philosopher [[David Hume]]. In the same way, [[evolutionary biology]] can explain how helping others ([[altruism]]) may have developed in humans. But it cannot say whether we should be kind from a moral point of view. These types of questions are explored through [[philosophy]], [[religion]], [[ethics]], and the [[humanities]] (like [[history]] and [[literature]]). Thinking that science is the only way to gain knowledge is called the [[Scientism|scientism fallacy]]. It ignores the important insights from other areas of human thought, like art, culture, and spiritual traditions.{{Cite book|title=Defending science - within reason: between scientism and cynicism|last=Haack|first=Susan|date=2007|publisher=Prometheus Books|isbn=978-1-59102-458-3|edition=Paperback|location=Amherst, NY}} People’s trust in science is not the same everywhere. It depends on their background, politics, and past experiences. In some places, people see science as something only for experts or something that does not care about their real-life problems. This is especially true in communities that have been treated unfairly by scientific institutions in the past.{{Cite journal|last1=Cologna|first1=Viktoria|last2=Mede|first2=Niels G.|last3=Berger|first3=Sebastian|last4=Besley|first4=John|last5=Brick|first5=Cameron|last6=Joubert|first6=Marina|last7=Maibach|first7=Edward W.|last8=Mihelj|first8=Sabina|last9=Oreskes|first9=Naomi|last10=Schäfer|first10=Mike S.|last11=van der Linden|first11=Sander|date=2025|title=Trust in scientists and their role in society across 68 countries|journal=Nature Human Behaviour|language=en|volume=9|issue=4|pages=713–730|doi=10.1038/s41562-024-02090-5|pmid=39833424 |pmc=7617525 |issn=2397-3374}} One well-known case is that of [[Henrietta Lacks]], an African-American woman whose cancer cells were taken without her permission in the 1950s. Her cells were used in many scientific breakthroughs, but her family was never asked or informed. This case is still discussed today in conversations about [[bioethics]] (the ethics of medical and scientific research) and trust in science.{{Cite book|title=The immortal life of Henrietta Lacks|url=https://archive.org/details/unset0000unse_h0q7|last=Skloot|first=Rebecca|date=2010|publisher=Crown Publishers|isbn=978-1-4000-5217-2|location=New York}} To build trust, it is not enough to just explain science better. Scientists also need to include different communities, listen to their concerns, and make research more open and fair.{{Cite journal|last=Wynne|first=Brian|date=2006|title=Public Engagement as a Means of Restoring Public Trust in Science – Hitting the Notes, but Missing the Music?|url=https://karger.com/article/doi/10.1159/000092659|journal=Public Health Genomics|language=en|volume=9|issue=3|pages=211–220|doi=10.1159/000092659|pmid=16741352 |issn=1662-4246}} People also get confused when scientific advice changes. For example, during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], guidelines about wearing masks changed as scientists learned more. Some people saw this as a sign that science was unreliable. But in reality, this shows how science works, it updates when new [[evidence]] becomes available. That is a strength, not a weakness, but it must be clearly explained so the public understands why advice sometimes changes.{{Cite journal|last=Ioannidis|first=John P. A.|date=2020|title=Coronavirus disease 2019: The harms of exaggerated information and non-evidence-based measures|journal=European Journal of Clinical Investigation|language=en|volume=50|issue=4|article-number=e13222 |doi=10.1111/eci.13222|pmid=32191341 |issn=0014-2972|pmc=7163529}} == References == {{reflist}} == Other websites == * [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yk5IWzTfWeM "How Do We Know What Is True?" (animated video; 2:52)] {{Outline footer}} [[Category:Basic English 850 words]] [[Category:Science| ]] [[Category:Observation]]

The '''Saint Lawrence River''' ({{lang-fr|fleuve Saint-Laurent}}; [[Tuscarora language|Tuscarora]]: ''Kahnawáʼkye'';<ref>Rudes, B. ''Tuscarora English Dictionary'' Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1999</ref> [[Mohawk language|Mohawk]]: ''Kaniatarowanenneh'', meaning "big waterway") is a big [[river]] in eastern [[North America]]. It flows between the [[Canada|Canadian]] [[province]] of [[Quebec]] & [[Ontario]] and the [[United States|American]] [[state]] of [[New York (state)|New York]], and through the major Canadian city of [[Montreal]]. It is the third-largest river in Canada.

The river drains water from the [[Great Lakes]] into the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. It is more than {{convert|1600|NM|abbr=off}} long. The river meets the Atlantic Ocean in a big "[[estuary]]" or bay, the biggest in the world; this is called the [[Gulf of Saint Lawrence]].

The Canadian cities of [[Kingston, Ontario|Kingston]], [[Montreal]], [[Trois-Rivières]], and [[Quebec City]] are on this river. The [[Saint Lawrence Seaway]] allows [[ship]]s to go up the river and through the Great Lakes right into the middle of North America.
