Even though the planets follow paths around the Sun, the distances between them are huge compared to how big the planets are.{{Cite web|title=Distances Between the Planets of the Solar System • The Planets|url=https://theplanets.org/distances-between-planets/|access-date=2025-07-09|website=The Planets|language=en-US}} For example, Earth is about 12,700 kilometers wide, but the closest it ever gets to Mars is around 96 million kilometers away.{{Cite web|date=2023-05-30|title=Facts About Earth|work=NASA Science |url=https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/|access-date=2025-07-09|language=en-US}}{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=2025-01-12|title=Mars closest to Earth on January 12, 2025|url=https://earthsky.org/tonight/mars-closest-to-earth/|access-date=2025-07-09|website=earthsky.org|language=en-US}} Because of these huge distances, even fast [[spacecraft]] take a long [[time]], months or years, to travel between planets. The farther you go, the longer it takes.{{Cite web|date=2025-02-19|title=How Long Does it Take to Get to the Moon... Mars... Jupiter? We Asked a NASA Expert: Episode 51 - NASA|url=https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/smd/how-long-does-it-take-to-get-to-the-moon-mars-jupiter-we-asked-a-nasa-expert-episode-51/|access-date=2025-07-09|language=en-US}} For instance, [[light]] from the Sun takes only 8 minutes to reach Earth, but it takes over 4 hours to reach Neptune.{{Cite web|date=2024-04-12|title=How long does it take for light from the Sun to reach Earth?|url=https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/how-take-light-from-sun-reach-earth|access-date=2025-07-09|website=BBC Sky at Night Magazine|language=en}}{{Cite web|date=2017-11-10|title=Neptune: Facts - NASA Science|url=https://science.nasa.gov/neptune/neptune-facts/|access-date=2025-07-09|language=en-US}} All this [[Outer space|space]] makes it harder to explore and communicate with the outer planets. Sending missions to places like Neptune or beyond is a big challenge and a major achievement for [[science]] and [[engineering]].{{Cite web|title=Challenges of space travel - Space exploration - National 5 Physics Revision|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/guides/zqm4fcw/revision/3|access-date=2025-07-09|website=BBC Bitesize|language=en-GB}} Some [[Scientific model|model]]s of the Solar System are made to help people understand just how big and spread out everything really is. Since the real Solar System is way too large to picture easily, scientists and educators sometimes build scale models to shrink it down while keeping the sizes and distances in the right proportion. Some of these models are small and mechanical, like [[Orrery|orreries]], which are devices that show planets moving around the Sun.{{Cite web|title=Orrery|url=https://www.hsm.ox.ac.uk/orrery|access-date=2025-07-09|website=www.hsm.ox.ac.uk|language=en}} Others are huge and can stretch across cities or even entire regions. One of the biggest models is the [[Sweden Solar System]].{{Cite web|title=Sweden Solar System|url=https://www.swedensolarsystem.se/en/|access-date=2025-07-09|website=www.swedensolarsystem.se}} In it, the [[Avicii Arena]] in [[Stockholm]] represents the Sun, and it is about 110 meters wide (361 feet). In this model, Jupiter is a 7.3-meter ball (about 24 feet wide) located at an [[airport]] 40 kilometers (25 miles) away. [[Sedna]], an object far out in the Solar System, is shown as a 10-centimeter ball (about 4 inches) placed 810 kilometers (500 miles) away.{{Cite web|title=Luleå är Sedna - Lokalt den 17 november 2005 - Arkiv - Norrbottens-Kuriren|url=http://www.kuriren.nu/arkiv/2005/11/17/Lokalt/1510647/Lule%C3%A5-%C3%A4r-Sedna.aspx|access-date=2025-07-09|website=www.kuriren.nu}}{{Cite web|title=Tours of Model Solar Systems|url=http://www.psych.illinois.edu/~wbrewer/solarmodel.html|access-date=2025-07-09|website=www.psych.illinois.edu|archive-date=2010-07-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100724064517/http://www.psych.illinois.edu/~wbrewer/solarmodel.html|url-status=dead}} If we shrank the distance from the Sun to Neptune down to just 100 meters (about the length of a soccer field), then the Sun would only be about 3 centimeters wide (a little bigger than a [[marble]]), the [[Giant planet|giant planets]] would be all smaller than about 3 mm (0.12 in), and Earth and the other small planets would be tiny dots, smaller than a [[flea]]. These kinds of models help us understand that even though planets can be big, they are still tiny compared to the space between them.{{Cite web|title=Solar System Scale|url=https://www.nasa.gov/audience/foreducators/5-8/features/F_Solar_System_Scale.html|access-date=2025-07-09|website=www.nasa.gov|archive-date=2023-03-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230328021134/https://www.nasa.gov/audience/foreducators/5-8/features/F_Solar_System_Scale.html|url-status=dead}} ===Mass and Composition Distribution=== [[File:Solar_system_mass_distribution_ppm_chart.svg|thumb|Solar system mass distribution]] The Solar System’s mass and the way its parts are spread out tell us a lot about how it formed and changed over time. Most of the Solar System’s [[mass]], about 99.86%, is in the [[Sun]], which is a huge ball made mostly of [[hydrogen]] and [[helium]]. The Sun’s gravity controls the movement of all the planets, asteroids, comets, and space dust. It’s incredibly massive, weighing about 1.989 × 10³⁰ kilograms. This huge mass creates a strong gravitational pull that keeps everything else in the Solar System in [[orbit]], and it also helps determine how things spin and move.{{Cite web|date=2023-05-31|title=Sun - NASA Science|url=https://science.nasa.gov/sun/|access-date=2025-07-15|language=en-US}}{{Cite web|title=Sun Fact Sheet|url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html|access-date=2025-07-15|website=nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov|archive-date=1998-02-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19980222081658/https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html|url-status=dead}} Only about 0.14% of the Solar System’s total mass is in everything else, like the eight [[planet]]s, [[dwarf planet]]s, [[Natural satellite|moon]]s, [[asteroid]]s, objects in the [[Kuiper Belt]], and the [[Oort cloud|Oort Cloud]].{{Cite web|date=2023-07-20|title=Chapter 1: The Solar System - NASA Science|url=https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter1-1/|access-date=2025-07-15|language=en-US}} Out of this small portion, more than 70% is found in [[Jupiter]], the largest planet. Jupiter weighs about 1.9 × 10²⁷ kilograms, which is 318 times heavier than [[Earth]].{{Cite web|title=Jupiter |url=https://www.dlr.de/en/research-and-transfer/projects-and-missions/juice/jupiter-gas-giant-and-ringed-planet/jupiter|access-date=2025-07-15|website=www.dlr.de|language=en}} Because of its size, Jupiter has a very strong gravitational pull. It affects the movement of asteroids, helps keep the orbits of other planets stable, and played a big role in clearing out leftover space rocks when the Solar System was still forming.{{Cite web|date=2023-05-31|title=Jupiter|url=https://science.nasa.gov/jupiter/|access-date=2025-07-15|language=en-US}} The [[giant planet]]s, [[Jupiter]], [[Saturn]], [[Uranus]], and [[Neptune]], make up about 99% of the total mass of all the planets in the Solar System. This shows that the Solar System has a bimodal structure, meaning most of the mass is in these large [[Gas giant|gas]] and [[ice giant]]s, not the smaller rocky planets closer to the Sun.{{Cite book|url=https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/13117/chapter/10|title=Read "Vision and Voyages for Planetary Science in the Decade 2013-2022" at NAP.edu|language=en}} Saturn is the second largest planet, with a mass about 95 times that of Earth. Like Jupiter, it is mostly made of hydrogen and helium, but Saturn has more ices and heavier elements deep inside.{{Cite web|date=2023-05-31|title=Saturn|url=https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/|access-date=2025-07-15|language=en-US}} Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants. They also have atmospheres made of hydrogen and helium, but inside they have a lot of [[water]], [[ammonia]], and [[Methane|methane ices]]. Each of them has a mass between 14 and 17 times the mass of Earth.{{Cite web|title=Uranus/Neptune|url=https://pages.uoregon.edu/jschombe/ast121/lectures/lec20.html#:~:text=Neptune%20is%2017%20times%20the,could%20contain%20nearly%2060%20Earths.|access-date=2025-07-15|website=pages.uoregon.edu}} On the other hand, the [[Terrestrial planet|terrestrial (rocky) planet]]s, [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]], [[Venus]], [[Earth]], and [[Mars]], have only a tiny amount of the Solar System’s mass. Earth makes up more than half of the total mass of these four rocky planets because it’s the biggest and densest. These inner planets are made mostly of [[Silicate|silicate rock]] and [[metal]], with common elements like [[iron]], [[oxygen]], [[silicon]], and [[magnesium]]. They do not have much hydrogen or helium because, when the Solar System was forming, the area close to the Sun was too hot for light gases to stick around. The Sun’s heat pushed those gases away, so only heavier materials like rock and metal were left behind to form the inner planets.{{Cite web|title=Planets and How They Formed|url=https://lco.global/spacebook/solar-system/planets-and-how-they-formed/|access-date=2025-07-15|website=lco.global|language=en}} Besides the major planets, the Solar System has many smaller objects. Even though these objects have only a small amount of mass compared to the planets, they are very important for helping scientists understand how the planets formed. One group of these small objects is the [[asteroid belt]], which is found between Mars and Jupiter. The asteroid belt has less than 4% of the Moon’s mass, but it contains materials that were part of the early building blocks of the rocky planets. The biggest object in the belt is [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]], which is about 940 kilometers wide. Ceres makes up about one-third of the asteroid belt’s total mass and is made mostly of [[rock]] and [[Ice|water ice]].{{Cite journal|last=Krasinsky|first=G|date=2002|title=Hidden Mass in the Asteroid Belt|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0019103502968375|journal=Icarus|language=en|volume=158|issue=1|pages=98–105|doi=10.1006/icar.2002.6837|bibcode=2002Icar..158...98K}}{{Cite journal|last1=Pitjeva|first1=E. V.|last2=Pitjev|first2=N. P.|date=2018|title=Masses of the Main Asteroid Belt and the Kuiper Belt from the Motions of Planets and Spacecraft|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1134/S1063773718090050|journal=Astronomy Letters|language=en|volume=44|issue=8–9|pages=554–566|doi=10.1134/S1063773718090050|arxiv=1811.05191 |bibcode=2018AstL...44..554P |issn=1063-7737}} Farther away from the Sun is the Kuiper Belt, which holds thousands of icy objects. Some of the best-known are [[Pluto (dwarf planet)|Pluto]], [[Eris (dwarf planet)|Eris]], [[Haumea (dwarf planet)|Haumea]], and [[Makemake (dwarf planet)|Makemake]]. These objects are much smaller than the giant planets, but their mix of rock and ices like [[methane]], [[nitrogen]], and [[carbon monoxide]] helps scientists learn about the chemistry of the early outer Solar System. The total mass of the Kuiper Belt is only a small fraction of Earth’s mass, between 0.01 and 0.1 times the mass of Earth, because over billions of years, much of its mass was lost in space due to collisions and gravitational forces.{{Cite journal|last1=Romanishin|first1=W.|last2=Tegler|first2=S. C.|last3=Rettig|first3=T. W.|last4=Consolmagno|first4=G.|last5=Botthof|first5=B.|date=2001-10-09|title=1998 SM165: A large Kuiper belt object with an irregular shape|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=98|issue=21|pages=11863–11866|doi=10.1073/pnas.211147998 |pmid=11572937 |pmc=59815 |doi-access=free }}{{Cite journal|last1=Pitjeva|first1=E. V.|last2=Pitjev|first2=N. P.|date=2018|title=Masses of the Main Asteroid Belt and the Kuiper Belt from the Motions of Planets and Spacecraft|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1134/S1063773718090050|journal=Astronomy Letters|language=en|volume=44|issue=8–9|pages=554–566|doi=10.1134/S1063773718090050|arxiv=1811.05191 |bibcode=2018AstL...44..554P |issn=1063-7737}} Even farther out is the [[Oort cloud|Oort Cloud]], which scientists think is a huge, round shell of icy objects surrounding the Solar System. It is believed to contain trillions of comets made mostly of water ice, [[carbon dioxide]] ice, and other frozen gases. The total mass of the Oort Cloud is not known for sure, but it might be several times the mass of Earth. It stretches as far as 100,000 [[Astronomical unit|astronomical units (AU)]] from the Sun (1 AU is the distance from Earth to the Sun). The Oort Cloud is thought to be the source of [[Comet|long-period comet]]s, comets that take hundreds or thousands of years to orbit the Sun and sometimes come close enough to be seen from Earth. [[Natural satellite|Moon]]s and [[Planetary ring|ring]]s around planets add a little bit of mass to the Solar System, but not very much compared to the planets. For example, [[Moon|Earth’s Moon]] is the fifth largest moon in the Solar System. It is pretty big compared to Earth, with a mass that is about 1.2% of Earth’s mass. The Moon is mostly made of [[Silicate|silicate rock]], which is similar to the material found in [[Earth's crust|Earth’s crust]] and [[Earth's mantle|mantle]].{{Cite web|date=2017-11-15|title=Moon Facts - NASA Science|url=https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/|access-date=2025-07-16|language=en-US}} The outer planets have some very large moons too, like [[Ganymede (moon)|Ganymede]], [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], [[Callisto (moon)|Callisto]], and [[Io (moon)|Io]]. These moons are made of a mix of rock and ice. Some of them, like [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] and [[Enceladus (moon)|Enceladus]], even have [[ocean]]s beneath their icy surfaces, which shows that there are many different kinds of icy, possibly habitable places beyond Earth. The types of [[Chemical element|element]]s found in different parts of the Solar System also tell us a lot about how it formed. These elements were created in earlier generations of [[star]]s and then spread out into [[Outer space|space]]. In the outer Solar System, there are more volatile elements (which are lighter and can turn into gas easily), while the inner Solar System has more refractory materials (which are heavier and can stay solid at high [[temperature]]s). This difference shows how temperature, [[sunlight]], and the movement of planets affected where different materials could collect and form planets.{{Cite book|title=Encyclopedia of the solar system|url=https://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofso0000unse_m9q5|date=2014|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-12-415845-0|editor-last=Spohn|editor-first=Tilman|edition=3rd|location=Amsterdam ; Boston|editor-last2=Breuer|editor-first2=Doris|editor-last3=Johnson|editor-first3=T. V.}} == Orbits of the planets == The [[Earth's orbit]] around the Sun is nearly a perfect circle, but in a very slightly oval shaped orbit, an [[orbit|elliptical orbit]]. The other [[planet]]s in the Solar System also orbit the Sun in slightly elliptical orbits. [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] has a more elliptical orbit than the others, and there is obviously some explanation for this. Some of the smaller objects orbit the Sun in very [[orbit|eccentric orbits]]. The planets all orbit the Sun in the same direction.{{Cite book|title=From dust to life : the origin and evolution of our solar system|url=https://archive.org/details/fromdusttolifeor0000cham|last1=Chambers|first1=John|last2=Mitton|first2=Jacqueline|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2014|isbn=978-0-691-14522-8|location=Princeton, New Jersey|oclc=859181634}}{{rp|4-5}} A full account of the planetary motion needs an account of the ''n''-body problem, which is not treated on this wiki. A page can be found on En wiki. == Discovery and exploration == {{Main|History of astronomy}} For thousands of years, people had no need for a name for the "Solar System". They thought the Earth stayed still at the center of everything ([[geocentrism]]). The Greek philosopher [[Aristarchus of Samos]] suggested that there was a special order in the sky.{{cite journal|title= The astronomical system of Copernicus|author=WC Rufus|journal=Popular Astronomy|year=1923|volume=31|pages=510|bibcode=1923PA.....31..510R|url=http://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1923PA.....31..510R|accessdate=2009-05-09}} [[Nicolaus Copernicus]] was the first to develop a [[Mathematical model|mathematical system]] that described what we now call the "Solar System". This was called a "new system of the world". In the 17th century, [[Galileo Galilei]], [[Johannes Kepler]] and [[Isaac Newton]] began to understand [[physics]] more clearly. People began to accept the idea that the Earth is a planet that moves around the Sun, and that the planets are worlds, and that all worlds are governed by the same [[physical law]]s. More recently, telescopes and [[space probe]]s sometimes let us see details directly. All inner planets have surface features. The gas giants (as the name suggests) have surfaces whose make-up is gradually being discovered. == The eight planets == [[File:Uklad Sloneczny 2006.png|thumb|Planetary distances, not to scale]] In their order from the Sun: #[[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] #[[Venus]] #[[Earth]] #[[Mars]] #[[Jupiter]] #[[Saturn (planet)|Saturn]] #[[Uranus]] #[[Neptune]] The planets are the biggest objects that go around the Sun. It took people many years of using [[telescope]]s to find the objects that were farthest away. [[Planets beyond Neptune|New planets]] might still be found, and more small objects are found every year. Most of the planets have [[Satellite (natural)|moons]] that orbit around them just as the planets orbit the Sun. There are over 400 of these moons in the Solar System. == Dwarf planets == {{Main|Dwarf planet}} Pluto was discovered by American astronomer [[Clyde Tombaugh]] in 1930. It was declared the ninth planet of the Solar System. Pluto's planet status changed in 2006, when the [[International Astronomical Union]] (IAU) decided on a definition of the word "planet" for the first time. By this definition, Pluto was not a planet due to its irregular orbit and size. Thus, Pluto lost its planet status. Eris was first announced in 2005. It was found to be 27% more massive than Pluto. Pluto did not fit in with the rest of the planets. So, the IAU defined a new category called "dwarf planet", into which Pluto did fit, along with some other small Solar System bodies. These small bodies are sometimes called [[plutino]]s.{{cite web|title=IAU 2006 General Assembly: Result of the IAU Resolution votes|url=https://www.iau.org/news/pressreleases/detail/iau0603/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140429212224/https://www.iau.org/news/pressreleases/detail/iau0603/|archive-date=2014-04-29|publisher=IAU|accessdate=2018-09-04}} There is an unknown number of dwarf planets in the Solar System. As of 2025, these nine small Solar System bodies are often called dwarf planets: * [[Pluto]] * [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] * [[Haumea (dwarf planet)|Haumea]] * [[Eris (dwarf planet)|Eris]] * [[Makemake (dwarf planet)|Makemake]] * [[50000 Quaoar|Quaoar]] * [[90377 Sedna|Sedna]] * [[90482 Orcus|Orcus]] * [[225088 Gonggong|Gonggong]] == Structure == There are a few main parts of the Solar System. Here they are in order from the Sun, with the planets numbered, and [[dwarf planet]]s marked with letters. === Inner solar system === [[File:Terrestrial planet size comparisons.jpg|thumb|The inner planets. From left to right: [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]], [[Venus]], [[Earth]], and [[Mars]]]] The first four planets closest to the Sun are called the inner planets. They are small and dense terrestrial planets, with solid surfaces. They are made up of mostly rock and metal with a distinct internal structure and a similar size. Three also have an [[atmosphere]]. The study of the four planets gives information about [[geology]] outside the Earth. * [[Terrestrial planet|Terrestrial planets]] region contains the four planets closest to the sun, all are rocky planets ** '''(1)''' [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] ** '''(2)''' [[Venus]] ** '''(3)''' [[Earth]] ** '''(4)''' [[Mars]] * [[Asteroid belt]] region contains; ** ''(a)'' [[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]] (the only '''[[dwarf planet]]''' in this region) ** [[Asteroid]]s === Outer solar system === [[File:Gas planet size comparisons.jpg|thumb|The outer planets: From left to right: [[Jupiter]], [[Saturn]], [[Uranus]], and [[Neptune]]]] * [[Giant planet]]s region contains the four largest planets. Jupiter and Saturn are [[gas giant]]s, while Uranus and Neptune are [[ice giant]]s; ** '''(5)''' [[Jupiter]] ** '''(6)''' [[Saturn (planet)|Saturn]] ** '''(7)''' [[Uranus]] ** '''(8)''' [[Neptune]] === Trans-Neptune region === * [[Kuiper belt]] region contains; ** ''(b)'' [[Pluto]] ** ''(c)'' [[90482 Orcus|Orcus]] ** ''(d)'' [[Haumea (dwarf planet)|Haumea]] ** ''(e)'' [[Makemake (dwarf planet)|Makemake]] ** ''(f)'' [[Quaoar]] ** [[Kuiper belt|Kuiper belt objects]] and possibly other dwarf planets ** short-period [[comet]]s * [[Scattered disc]] region contains; ** ''(g)'' [[90377 Sedna|Sedna]] ** ''(h)'' [[225088 Gonggong|Gonggong]] ** ''(i)'' [[Eris (dwarf planet)|Eris]] ** [[Scattered disc|Scattered disk objects]] and possibly other dwarf planets === Oort Cloud === The [[Oort cloud]] is separate from the '''trans-Neptune region''', and much farther out. It contains the long-period [[comet]]s. == Ecliptic plane == The ''plane of the [[ecliptic]]'' is defined by the Earth's orbit around the Sun. All of the planets orbit the Sun roughly around this same [[Orbital plane (astronomy)|orbital plane]]. The farther away from this plane a planet orbits, the more ''inclined'' is its orbit to the ecliptic. If you could look at the Solar System "edge on" then all the planets would be orbiting more or less in the plane of the ecliptic. {{clear}} == References == {{Reflist}} == More reading == * {{cite book|first=Kenneth R.|last=Lang|title=The Cambridge Guide to the Solar System|url=https://archive.org/details/cambridgeguideto0000lang_r9p2|publisher=Cambridge University Press|edition=2nd|date=2011|isbn=978-0521198578}} * {{cite book |last1=Iggulden |first1=Hal |last2=Iggulden |first2=Conn |title=The Dangerous Book for Boys |url=https://archive.org/details/dangerousbookfor0000iggu_u2s8 |date=2007 |publisher=HarperCollins |location=New York |isbn=978-0061243585 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/dangerousbookfor0000iggu_u2s8/page/216 217]–224 |chapter=The Solar System (a quick reference guide) }} * Thierry Montmerle; Jean-Charles Augereau; Marc Chaussidon 2006. ''Solar System formation and early evolution: the first 100 million years. Earth, Moon, and Planets''. Springer. [[98 (number)|98]] (1–4): 39–95. Bibcode:2006EM&P...98...39M. doi:10.1007/s11038-006-9087-5. S2CID 120504344. == Other websites == {{commons category}} * [http://www.solarviews.com/eng/homepage.htm Views of the Solar System] * [http://www.exploratorium.edu/ronh/weight/index.html Your Weight on Other Worlds] * [https://www.gsupdate.online/2021/07/the-planets-in-the-solar-system.html The Planets in the Solar System] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210710070248/https://www.gsupdate.online/2021/07/the-planets-in-the-solar-system.html |date=2021-07-10 }} {{wikibooks|Wikijunior:Solar System}} {{Solar System}} {{authority control}} [[Category:Solar System| ]]

title: Saturn
Slavery
text:
{{Slavery}}
[[File:Punishing Slaves in Cuba.tif|thumb|[[Black people|Black]] slaves in [[Cuba]] being [[torture]]d during the [[19th century]].]]

'''Slavery''' is when a person is treated as the [[property]] of another person. This person is usually called a slave, and the owner is called a slavemaster. It often means that slaves are forced to work, or else they will be punished by the [[law]] (if slavery is legal in that place) or by their master. There is [[evidence]] that even before there was [[writing]], there was slavery.<ref>''Tribe and Polity in Late Prehistoric Europe'', eds. D. Blair Gibson; M.N. Geselowitz (New York: Plenum Press, 1988), p. 179</ref> Almost all [[culture]]s and [[continent]]s have a history of slavery.<ref name="Slavery">[http://www.britannica.com/blackhistory/article-24156 Historical survey > Slave-owning societies]. ''Encyclopædia Britannica.''</ref> Some societies had laws about slavery or had an [[economy]] that was built on it. [[Ancient Greece]] and [[Ancient Rome]] had many slaves.
[[File:Entraves esclave.jpg|thumb|Chains such as these were used to stop slaves from escaping]]
In the [[20th century]], almost all [[countries]] made laws making slavery illegal. The [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] says that slavery is wrong. Slavery is now banned by [[international law]], including [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]] and [[Supplementary Convention on the Abolition of Slavery]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ohchr.org/EN/ProfessionalInterest/Pages/SlaveryConvention.aspx |title=Slavery Convention |author= |website= |publisher=The United Nations |accessdate=4 November 2015}}</ref> Despite this, there are still different forms of slavery in some countries.<ref name="BBC Millions 'forced into slavery'">{{Cite news|date=2002-05-27|title=Millions 'forced into slavery'|language=en-GB|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/2010401.stm|access-date=2024-06-02}}</ref> The [[Islamic Republic of Mauritania]] was the last country in the world to officially ban slavery.<ref name="NYER-2014">{{cite magazine|last1=Okeowo|first1=Alexis|date=September 8, 2014|title=Freedom Fighter: A slaving society and an abolitionist's crusade|url=http://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2014/09/08/freedom-fighter|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180106081042/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2014/09/08/freedom-fighter|archive-date=January 6, 2018|access-date=October 16, 2014}}</ref> In 2007, "under international pressure", its government passed a law allowing slaveholders to be prosecuted.<ref name="a">{{cite web|last=Corrigan|first=Terence|date=September 6, 2007|title=Mauritania: Country Made Slavery Illegal Last Month|url=http://www.saiia.org.za/governance-and-aprm-opinion/mauritania-made-slavery-illegal-last-month.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110804032958/http://www.saiia.org.za/governance-and-aprm-opinion/mauritania-made-slavery-illegal-last-month.html|archive-date=August 4, 2011|access-date=January 21, 2008|publisher=The East African Standard}}</ref> However, in 2019, approximately 40 million people, were still enslaved throughout the world despite slavery being illegal. About 26% of these were children. In the modern world, more than half of the people who are slaves provide [[forced labour]], usually in the factories and [[sweatshop]]s of the private sector of a country's economy.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Hodal|first1=Kate|date=May 31, 2016|title=One in 200 people is a slave. Why?|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2019/feb/25/modern-slavery-trafficking-persons-one-in-200|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430012324/https://www.theguardian.com/news/2019/feb/25/modern-slavery-trafficking-persons-one-in-200|archive-date=April 30, 2019|work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> 

In [[Industrialized|industrialised]] countries, [[human trafficking]] is a modern form of the slave trade. In non-industrialised countries, enslavement by [[debt bondage]] is a common form of enslaving a person.<ref name="newint">{{cite web|title=Slavery in the 21st century|url=http://www.newint.org/issue337/facts.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527095857/http://www.newint.org/issue337/facts.htm|archive-date=May 27, 2010|access-date=August 29, 2010|publisher=Newint.org}}</ref> There are many types of modern slavery. Some of these include captured [[Domestic worker|domestic servants]], people in [[Forced marriage|forced marriages]], and [[Military use of children|child soldiers]].<ref name="modernslavery">{{cite web|date=January 30, 2007|title=Religion & Ethics – Modern slavery: Modern forms of slavery|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/ethics/slavery/modern/modern_1.shtml#section_2|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140106012011/http://www.bbc.co.uk/ethics/slavery/modern/modern_1.shtml#section_2|archive-date=January 6, 2014|access-date=June 16, 2009|publisher=[[BBC]]}}</ref>

==Origin of the word==
The English word ''slave'' comes from the [[Middle English]] word {{lang|enm|sclave}}. {{lang|enm|Sclave}} came from the [[Old French]] word ''{{lang|fro|esclave}}''.  The French word came from [[Late Latin]] ''sclavus''.<ref name="OED">{{Cite dictionary|title=slave|date=2022|encyclopedia=[[Oxford English Dictionary]]|doi=10.1093/OED/4545849469}}</ref>  There are many theories for where the word ''sclavus'' came from. A common theory is that the word came from [[Slavic peoples]] in [[Central Europe]] and [[Eastern Europe]] who were often put into slavery.<ref>{{citation |title=slave |encyclopedia=Online Etymology Dictionary |url=http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?term=slave |accessdate=26 March 2009}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=Merriam-Webster's |url=http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/slave |accessdate=18 August 2009}}</ref> Another theory is that ''sclavus'' came from [[Byzantine Greek]] {{lang|grc-x-byzant|σκυλάειν}}. The Greek word means to steal from an enemy that was killed in war. <ref name="OED"/> 

==History of slavery==
{{main|History of slavery}}
=== Early civilizations ===
Slavery has existed in various forms since antiquity.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://unesdoc.unesco.org/images/0013/001337/133738e.pdf#page=9 |title=Struggles against slavery |author= |date=2004 |website= |publisher=UNESCO |accessdate=4 February 2016}}, p. 44</ref> The earliest records of slavery can be traced to Babylon 18th Century BC, in texts such as the ''[[Code of Hammurabi]]'' (c. 1760 BC), which codifies slavery as law.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wsu.edu/~dee/MESO/CODE.HTM |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110514033802/http://www.wsu.edu/~dee/MESO/CODE.HTM |archivedate=14 May 2011 |title= Mesopotamia: The Code of Hammurabi|quote=e.g. Prologue, "the shepherd of the oppressed and of the slaves" Code of Laws No. 307, "If any one buy from the son or the slave of another man".}}</ref>

In the Ancient [[Near East]], slaves were often prisoners of war, which was determined as lawful by the book of [[Deuteronomy]]. There were many distinctions made to categorize those by factors such as class, gender, age and race. For example, [[Israelites]] were not allowed to enslave other Israelites. The Deuteronomic Code calls for the [[death penalty]] for the [[crime]] of [[kidnapping]] Israelites to enslave them.{{fact|date=May 2025}}

In [[Ancient Egypt]], slaves were mainly [[Prisoner of war|prisoners of war]]. Many times, slaves inherited the status of their slave parents. Others became slaves over unpaid [[debt]]s. Some slaves were poor [[peasant]]s who offered themselves into servitude in exchange for [[food]] and [[shelter]]. The lives of slaves were normally better than that of peasants.<ref name="touregypt1">{{cite web|url=http://www.touregypt.net/featurestories/slaves.htm |title=Slaves and Slavery in Ancient Egypt |publisher=Touregypt.net |date=2011-10-24 |accessdate=2015-10-18}}</ref> Young slaves could not be put to hard work, and had to be brought up by the mistress of the [[household]]. Not all slaves went to houses. Some sold themselves to [[temple]]s, or were assigned to temples by the [[king]]. 

In many places, [[citizen]]s were partly or fully protected from being enslaved, so most slaves were foreigners.

===Ancient Rome ===
[[File:Adamo Ghisi - Alegorija ropstva, 1573.jpg|thumb|Adamo Ghisi: [[Allegory]] of Slavery, etching, 1573.]][[File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Vente d'esclaves à Rome, 1884.jpg|thumb|''[[Slave Market in Ancient Rome]]'', a painting by [[Jean-Léon Gérôme]]]]

Slaves were important in [[society]] and the economy of ancient Rome. They did simple manual labor and [[Domestic worker|domestic services]], but also could have complex jobs and [[profession]]s. [[Teacher]]s, [[accountant]]s, and [[physician]]s were often slaves. [[Greece|Greek]] slaves were often well [[education|educated]]. Most slaves, such as those who were made slaves as [[punishment]], worked on [[farm]]s, in [[Mining|mines]], and at [[mill (grinding)|mills]]. Their living conditions were very bad, and they did not live for very long.{{cn}}

Slaves were considered property under [[Roman law]] and were not legally people. Unlike Roman [[Citizenship|citizens]], they could suffer [[corporal punishment]], [[Sexual abuse|sexual exploitation]] ([[sex work]]ers were often slaves), [[torture]], and [[Execution|summary execution]]. A slave's [[testimony]] could not be accepted in a [[court of law]] unless the slave was tortured. This was because they thought that slaves would be too loyal to their masters to reveal damaging evidence unless [[coercion|coerced]]. Over time, however, slaves gained some legal protection, including the right to file complaints against their masters. Attitudes changed in part because of the influence among the educated elite of the [[Stoicism|Stoics]], whose [[Egalitarianism|egalitarian]] views of humanity extended to slaves, and also because of slave [[rebellion]]s. Better treatment meant fewer rebellions.{{cn}}

Roman slaves could hold [[property]] which, even though it belonged to their [[wikt:master|master]]s, they were allowed to use as if it were their own. Upper class slaves were allowed to earn their own [[money]]. With enough money they could buy their freedom.<ref>Kehoe, Dennis P. 2011. ''The Oxford Handbook of Social Relations in the Roman World''. Oxford University Press, pp. 147–148</ref>

After the Roman Empire broke up, slavery gradually changed into [[serfdom]]. Serfdom was similar to slavery but the worker received a set amount of wages and had certain civil rights and could leave the employment of the master.{{cn}}
===Asian slavery===
Both non-Muslims and Muslims in Southeast Asia during the 18th century bought Japanese girls who came by sea.<ref>{{cite book |last=Clarence-Smith  |first=William Gervase |author-link= |date=2006  |title=Islam and the Abolition of Slavery |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=nQbylEdqJKkC&dq=japanese+girls+sold+slaves+muslims&pg=PA15|edition=illustrated|location= |publisher=Oxford University Press|page=15 |isbn=0195221516}}</ref> Japanese slave girls were still owned by India-based Portuguese (Lusitanian) families according to [[Francisco De Sousa]], a Jesuit who wrote about that in 1698. This was long after the 1636 [[edict]] by [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokguawa]] Japan had expelled Portuguese people.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kowner  |first=Rotem |author-link= |date=2014  |volume= 63 of McGill-Queen's Studies in the History of Ideas|title=From White to Yellow: The Japanese in European racial thought, 1300-1735 |edition=reprint|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DgudBQAAQBAJ&dq=japanese+girls+sold+slaves+muslims&pg=PA432 |location= |publisher=McGill-Queen's Press - MQUP|page=431, 432 |isbn=978-0773596849}}</ref>

China imported Korean slaves and Indochinese slaves.<ref>{{cite book |last=Wright  |first=Robert E. |author-link= |date= 2017 |title=The Poverty of Slavery: how unfree labor pollutes the economy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-gYpDgAAQBAJ&dq=japanese+girls+sold+slaves+muslims&pg=PA56 |edition=illustrated|location= |publisher=Springer|page=56 |isbn=978-3319489681}}</ref> Japanese children in medieval Japan could be taken as slaves if debts were not repaid by their parents.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Campbell |first1=Gwyn |last2= Stanziani|first2=Alessandro |author-link= |date=2015 |title=Bonded labour and debt in the Indian Ocean world |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RolECgAAQBAJ&dq=japanese+girls+sold+slaves+muslims&pg=PA6|location= |publisher= Routledge |page=6 |isbn=978-1317320081|chapter=INTRODUCTION |edition=reprint|volume=1 of Financial History}}</ref> Japanese parents sold their daughters to Portuguese in Kyushu. Japanese children and women from the Bungo domain were sold as slaves to Europeans in Higo after Bungo was attacked in 1586 by the Satsuma domain.<ref>{{cite book |last= Moran |first= J.F. |date=2012  |title= The Japanese and the Jesuits: Alessandro Valignano in sixteenth century Japan |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=TNwqBgAAQBAJ&dq=japanese+girls+sold+slaves+muslims&pg=PA106|location= |publisher=Routledge|page=106 |isbn=978-1134881130}}</ref>

=== Arab slave trade ===
{{main|Arab slave trade}}

[[File:'Cargo of Newly released Slaves on board H.M.S. London' RMG E9085 (cropped) (cropped).tiff|left|thumb|300x300px|Black slaves, mostly [[children]], after being taken from slavers, 1880.]]
Historians estimate that between 650 [[AD]] and the 1960s, 10 to 18 million people were enslaved by Arab slave traders. They were taken from Europe, Asia and Africa across the [[Red Sea]], [[Indian Ocean]], and [[Sahara]] desert. Male slaves were often employed as [[servant]]s, [[soldier]]s, or workers by their owners. Many male slaves were [[Castration|castrated]] and became [[eunuch]]s.<ref name="MooreABS">{{cite web |url=http://atlantablackstar.com/2014/06/02/10-facts-about-the-arab-enslavement-of-black-people-not-taught-in-schools/ |title=10 facts about the Arab enslavement of black people not taught in schools |author=A. Moore |date=2 June 2014 |website= |publisher=Atlanta Black Star |accessdate=30 January 2016}}</ref> It has been claimed that as many as six out of every ten boys [[Bleeding|bled]] to death during the process, though the source may not be reliable.<ref name="MooreABS" /> [[Eunuch]]s fetched a higher price: that made castration worthwhile. According to Ronald Segal, author of ''Islam’s Black Slaves: the other black diaspora'' (2002), "The calipha in Baghdad at the beginning of the 10th Century had 7,000 black eunuchs and 4,000 white eunuchs in his palace”.<ref name="MooreABS" /> Women and children taken as slaves were mainly used as servants and [[Concubinage|concubines]]. While the later Atlantic slave trade concentrated on men for labor, the Arab slave trade started with men and boys, but shifted over time to concentrate more on woman and young girls for [[sex]]ual purposes. By the 1900s, Arab slave traders had taken between 10 and 18 million slaves out of Africa.<ref name="MooreABS" />

=== The Atlantic slave trade ===
{{main|Atlantic slave trade|African slave trade|slave trade}}

[[File:Slavecontract doc.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Slave contract [[Lima]]/[[Peru]] 13/10/[[1794]]]]
For four [[centuries]], beginning in the late [[15th century]], [[million]]s of [[Africa]]ns were taken as slaves by [[Europe]]ans.<ref name="EM">{{cite web |url=https://mondediplo.com/1998/04/02africa |title=The impact of the slave trade on Africa |author=Elikia M’bokolo |website= |date=April 1998 |publisher=Le Monde diplomatique |accessdate=4 November 2015}}</ref> Europeans began exporting Africans to the New World as a source of cheap labor on colonial plantations.<ref name="EM" />

Between 1452 and 1455, [[Pope Nicolas V]] issued a series of [[papal bull]]s authorizing the [[Portugal|Portuguese]] to take African slaves.<ref name="LDL">{{cite web |url=http://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/exhibits/show/african_laborers_for_a_new_emp/pope_nicolas_v_and_the_portugu |title=African Laborers for a New Empire: Iberia, Slavery, and the Atlantic World |author= |website= |publisher=Lowcountry Digital Library |accessdate=4 November 2015}}</ref> At first slave traders raided coastal areas and carried black people off. But the mines and fields of the colonies needed more and more slaves. In the early 1700s, Spain began to issue [[license]]s and [[contract]]s to supply slaves. By the 1750s, large slaving companies were established. Most of Europe at the time was involved in the slave trade.<ref name="LDL" />

=== In the United States ===
[[File:Woman with enslaved girl, New Orleans 1850s.jpg|thumb|An enslaved black child with a white slave owner in [[New Orleans]] during the 1850s.]]
{{Main|Slavery in the United States}}

Many [[Europe]]ans who arrived in [[North America]] during the [[17th century|17th]] and [[18th century|18th centuries]] came under contract as [[indentured servant]]s.<ref>[http://mertsahinoglu.com/research/indentured-servitude-colonial-america/ Indentured Servitude in Colonial America] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180117075542/http://mertsahinoglu.com/research/indentured-servitude-colonial-america/ |date=2018-01-17 }}. Deanna Barker, ''Frontier Resources''.</ref> The change from indentured servitude to slavery was a gradual process in Virginia. The earliest legal documentation of such a shift was in 1640. This is where an African, [[John Punch (slave)|John Punch]], was sentenced to lifetime slavery for attempting to run away. This case also marked the disparate treatment of [[Africa]]ns as held by the Virginia County Court, where two [[Caucasian|white]] runaways received far lesser sentences.<ref>{{Cite book |title=In the Matter of Color: Race and the American Legal Process: The Colonial Period |first=A. Leon |last=Higginbotham |publisher=Greenwood Press  |year=1975 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ErPg7VegkcMC&dq=%22john+punch%22&pg=PR7 |isbn=9780195027457}}</ref> 

After 1640, planters started to ignore the expiration of indentured [[contract]]s. They kept their servants as slaves for life. This was demonstrated by the case Johnson v. Parker. The court ruled that [[John Casor]], an indentured servant, be returned to Johnson who claimed that Casor belonged to him for his life.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Foner|first=Philip S.|year=1980|title=History of Black Americans: From Africa to the emergence of the cotton kingdom|url=http://testaae.greenwood.com/doc_print.aspx?fileID=GR7529&chapterID=GR7529-747&path=books/greenwood|url-status=dead|journal=Greenwood Publishing Group|publisher=Oxford University Press|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131014135617/http://testaae.greenwood.com/doc_print.aspx?fileID=GR7529&chapterID=GR7529-747&path=books%2Fgreenwood|archive-date=2013-10-14|access-date=2020-12-31}}</ref><ref>[http://www.americanheritage.com/articles/magazine/ah/1993/1/1993_1_90.shtml Selling Poor Steven] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060507112026/http://www.americanheritage.com/articles/magazine/ah/1993/1/1993_1_90.shtml |date=2006-05-07 }}. Philip Burnham, ''American Heritage Magazine. ''</ref> According to the [[1860 United States Census|1860 U. S. census]], 393,975 individuals, representing 8% of all US families, owned 3,950,528 slaves.<ref>[http://www.civil-war.net/pages/1860_census.html 1860 Census Results] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040604075834/http://www.civil-war.net/pages/1860_census.html |date=2004-06-04 }}, The Civil War Home Page.</ref> One-third of Southern families owned slaves.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Coates|first=Ta-Nehisi|date=2010-08-09|title=Small Truth Papering Over a Big Lie|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/national/archive/2010/08/small-truth-papering-over-a-big-lie/61136/|access-date=2024-06-02|website=The Atlantic|language=en}}</ref> Slavery in United States was legally abolished by the [[Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution]] in 1865.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ashbrook.org/publications/respub-v6n1-boyd/ |title= A look into the constitutional understanding of slavery |author=Susan L. Boyd |date=April 1995 |website= |publisher=Ashbrook Center at Ashland University |accessdate=February 1, 2017}}</ref> That year, [[Gordon Granger]] (a military [[officer]]) and his men, set the last slaves free in [[Galveston, Texas]].

===In the Middle East===
In the 2010s, [[ISIL]] (or [[Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant]]), were taking part in slave trade (of non-Muslim women), on the largest territory that they controlled.{{fact|date=September 2023}}
Scholars of Islamic law have condemned the revival of the slave trade of non-Muslim women by the [[Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant]]. ISIL had to flee (later in the 2010s), from most of the areas that they once controlled.

== Modern-day slavery ==
{{main|Slavery in the 21st century}}

Slavery has officially been abolished, in all countries of the world. Slave-like conditions still exist, but talking about 'slavery' has become more difficult, because people no longer agree on the terms. Things like threats, violence, the use of force, abuse of power and trickery are used to get or keep people in a situation where they can easily be exploited.  Common forms of modern-day slavery include:

* Keeping people on fishing boats. These boats often stay at sea for weeks or months, and the people on the boats can easily be exploited
* [[Domestic servant|Domestic servants]] are often treated badly, and receive almost no payment for the work they do
* People are [[Forced prostitution|forced into prostitution]]. Things like [[Forced marriage|forced marriages]], or [[Child marriage|marriages of children]] are often used to hide the fact that they are slaves. Sometimes they are used as [[Sexual slavery|sex slaves]]. 
* People who are [[migrants]] often fall into the hands of people engaged in [[human trafficking]]. Children get victims of [[trafficking of children]].
* Children are [[Child labour|forced to work like adults]], and sometimes get used as [[Child soldier|child soldiers]]. [[Child prostitution]] also happens. 
* People are [[Fraud factory|forced to defraud others]].
* People who are prisoners are forced to work, as part of their sentence. Usually, they get paid very little for the work they do.



Millions of people are still slaves in some parts of the world, mostly in [[South Asia]] and [[Africa]]. It is less common in the [[First World|developed world]] partly because of differences in financing [[law enforcement]], but it still happens there as well.<ref name="BBC Millions 'forced into slavery'" /> The ways in which it is done have changed.

Some of the countries where there is still slavery are in [[Africa]], the [[Middle East]], and [[South Asia]].<ref name="antislaverysociety">{{cite web |url=http://www.anti-slaverysociety.org/slavery.htm |title=Does Slavery Still Exist? |accessdate=2008-01-04 |last= |first= |publisher=Anti-Slavery Society |archive-date=2018-08-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180808135831/http://www.anti-slaverysociety.org/slavery.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

While people are still bought at sold, like beforehand, this is less common today. Today, people get trapped in slave-like conditions in other ways.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3humDwAAQBAJ|title=Addressing Modern Slavery (Sydney: UNSW Press, 2019)|last1=Nolan|first1=Justine|last2=Boersma|first2=Martijn|date=September 2019|publisher=University of New South Wales Press|isbn=9781742244631|access-date=2020-02-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028025858/https://books.google.com/books?id=3humDwAAQBAJ|archive-date=2020-10-28|url-status=live}}</ref> Modern slavery is often linked with [[poverty]]. There are countries and areas, where people are poorly-educated, and where there is little or no [[rule of law]]. This can create a setting where slavery is seen as acceptable. It is commonly seen in impoverished countries, and those where there are vulnerable minorities. Tens of thousands of people work in slave-like conditions in industries such as mining, farming, and factories; they produce goods for consumption inside the country or export to more [[wikt:prosperous|prosperous]] nations.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Modern Slavery: Its Root Causes and the Human Toll|url=https://www.cfr.org/interactives/modern-slavery|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190421211352/https://www.cfr.org/interactives/modern-slavery/|archive-date=2019-04-21|access-date=2019-05-13|website=Council on Foreign Relations}}</ref> 

In the older form of slavery, slave-owners spent more on getting slaves. It was more difficult for them to be disposed of. The cost of keeping them healthy was considered a better investment than getting another slave to replace them. In modern slavery people are easier to get at a lower price so replacing them when exploiters run into problems becomes easier.{{cn}}

Modern slavery can be quite profitable.<ref>Siddarth Kara, Sex Trafficking: Inside the Business of Modern Slavery (New York: Columbia University Press, 2010).</ref> Total annual revenues of traffickers were estimated in 2014 to over $150 billion,<ref>{{cite web|date=December 7, 2017|title=Human Trafficking Numbers|url=https://www.humanrightsfirst.org/resource/human-trafficking-numbers|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190507064607/https://www.humanrightsfirst.org/resource/human-trafficking-numbers|archive-date=May 7, 2019|access-date=May 13, 2019|website=Human Rights First}}</ref> though profits are substantially lower.

[[Corruption|Corrupt]] governments [[wikt:tacitly|tacitly]] allow it, even though it is outlawed by international treaties such as [[Supplementary Convention on the Abolition of Slavery]] and local laws.  

Today, slaves may work because of things like a high [[debt]]. Many victims are told that their families will be harmed if they report the slave owners. Many slaves are forced to be domestic servants. In some cases, their families sell their children because of poverty.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bina|first=Anna Coren,Jessie Yeung,Abdul Basir|date=2021-11-01|title=She was sold to a stranger so her family could eat as Afghanistan crumbles|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/11/01/asia/afghanistan-child-marriage-crisis-taliban-intl-hnk-dst/index.html|access-date=2023-10-14|website=CNN|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Rigby|first=Jennifer|date=2020-09-28|title=Children for sale: How the pandemic is forcing poverty-stricken parents to make desperate choices|language=en-GB|work=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/global-health/climate-and-people/children-sale-pandemic-forcing-poverty-stricken-parents-make/|access-date=2023-10-14|issn=0307-1235}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=CNN witnesses 9-year-old being sold for marriage to 55-year-old man {{!}} CNN|date=2021-11-01|url=https://www.cnn.com/videos/world/2021/11/01/afghan-girls-for-sale-lead-coren-pkg-vpx.cnn|language=en|access-date=2023-10-14}}</ref> Some slaves have been trafficked from one part of the world to another. These people are illegally in their host country, and therefore do not report the abuse. Forced [[prostitution]] is a type of slavery. Another form of slavery still happening today is forced [[child labor]]. Some children have to work in [[Mining|mines]] or in [[plantation]]s, or they have to fight wars as [[child soldier]]s.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Rakela|first=Mirjana|date=2008-11-16|title=Child Warriors Around The World -- Manipulation Without End|language=en|work=Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty|url=https://www.rferl.org/a/Child_Warriors_Around_The_World__Manipulation_Without_End/1349622.html|access-date=2023-10-14}}</ref>

One study says that there are 27 million people (but others say there could be as many as 200 million) in slavery today.<ref>Kevin Bales, ''Disposable People''</ref> Other terms that describe the recruitment of laborers, and that may have similarities to slavery are [[Blackbirding]], [[Impressment]] and [[Shanghaiing]].{{cn}}

On some fishing boats, there are slaves. The boats fish in [[international water]]s. Media has said that officials in some countries have accepted [[bribe]]s, so that officials can use power to keep [[law enforcement]] from stopping slaves from working on fishing boats.<ref>{{cite web |title=Modern slavery in Thailand |url=https://www.walkfree.org/global-slavery-index/country-studies/thailand/?utm_source=chatgpt.com |website=walkfree.org |accessdate=28 July 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Trapped at Sea: Blood, Sweat, and Tears of Thailand's Fishing Industry |url=https://hir.harvard.edu/thailand-fishing-industry/ |website=Harvard International Review |date=9 March 2018 |accessdate=28 July 2025}}</ref>


In 1809, American slaves were sold for around the equivalent of [[US$]]40,000 in today's money.<ref name="Economics and Slavery2">{{cite web|date=2013-05-19|title=Slavery Today|url=https://www.freetheslaves.net/our-model-for-freedom/slavery-today/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180918033125/https://www.freetheslaves.net/our-model-for-freedom/slavery-today/|archive-date=2018-09-18|access-date=2013-08-18|website=Free The Slaves}}</ref> A slave can be bought for $90–$100 (as of 2017).<ref>{{Cite news|last=Batha|first=Emma|date=2017-11-16|title=How much is a life worth, ask activists fighting slavery?|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-slavery-conference-lives-idUSKBN1DG2O4|url-status=live|access-date=2021-04-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422142812/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-slavery-conference-lives-idUSKBN1DG2O4|archive-date=2021-04-22}}</ref>{{Where}} Bales explains, "This is an economic crime ... People do not enslave people to be mean to them; they do it to make a profit."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bales|first=Kevin|date=March 2010|title=Kevin Bales {{!}} Speaker {{!}} TED|url=https://www.ted.com/speakers/kevin_bales|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220418023959/https://www.ted.com/speakers/kevin_bales|archive-date=2022-04-18|access-date=2019-05-13|website=www.ted.com|language=en}}</ref>

===Africa===
{{main|Slavery in contemporary Africa}}

[[Child slavery]] has commonly been used when making [[cash crop]]s and [[mining]]. According to the [[United States Department of State]], more than 109,000 children were working on [[cocoa]] farms alone in [[Côte d'Ivoire]] (Ivory Coast) in 'the worst forms of [[child labour]]' in 2002.<ref>[http://www.state.gov/g/drl/rls/hrrpt/2005/61565.htm U.S. Department of State Country Reports on Human Rights Practices], 2005 Human Rights Report on Côte d'Ivoire</ref>

In [[Mauritania]], it is thought that up to 600,000 men, women and children, or 20% of the population, are{{when}} slaves, and that many of them are used as [[bonded labour]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.saiia.org.za/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=635:mauritaniamadeslaveryillegallastmonth&catid=62:governance-a-aprm-opinion&Itemid=159 |title=Mauritania made slavery illegal last month |access-date=2008-07-08 |archive-date=2010-11-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101121020916/http://www.saiia.org.za/governance-and-aprm-opinion/mauritania-made-slavery-illegal-last-month.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=BBC World Service {{!}} The Abolition season on BBC World Service|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/worldservice/specials/1458_abolition/page4.shtml|access-date=2024-06-02|website=www.bbc.co.uk}}</ref> Slavery in Mauritania was made illegal in 2007.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/6938032.stm|title=Mauritanian MPs pass slavery law|date=August 9, 2007|via=news.bbc.co.uk}}</ref> 

In [[Niger]], there is also much slavery. A Nigerien study has found that more than 800,000 people are slaves, almost 8% of the population.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|title=The Shackles of Slavery in Niger|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Nightline/story?id=813618&page=1|access-date=2024-06-02|website=ABC News|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/programmes/from_our_own_correspondent/4250709.stm|title=Born to be a slave in Niger|date=February 11, 2005|via=news.bbc.co.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/worldservice/specials/1357_slavery_today/page3.shtml|title=BBC World Service | Slavery Today|website=www.bbc.co.uk}}</ref>
===Asia===
In summer 2007, 570 people were found to be slaves for brick makers in [[China]].<ref name="brickkiln">{{cite news |first= |last= |authorlink= |title=Convictions in China slave trial |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/asia-pacific/6902459.stm |work= |publisher=BBC |date=July 17, 2007 |accessdate=2008-01-04 }}</ref> They included 69 children.<ref>{{cite news |first=Zhu |last=Zhe |title=More than 460 rescued from brick kiln slavery
|url=http://www.chinadaily.com.cn/china/2007-06/15/content_894802.htm |newspaper=China Daily |date=June 15, 2007 |accessdate=2008-01-04 }}</ref> The Chinese government made a force of 35,000 police check northern Chinese brick [[kiln]]s for slaves, and sent lots of kiln supervisors and officials to prison and sentenced one kiln foreman to death for killing a worker who was a slave.<ref name="brickkiln"/>
====Myanmar (formerly Burma)====
In November 2006, the [[International Labour Organization]] said that it would prosecute members of the [[junta]] that rules [[Myanmar]] (also called Burma) at the [[International Court of Justice]] for "Crimes against Humanity". This is because the military makes some [[citizens]] do [[forced labour]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://in.today.reuters.com/news/newsArticle.aspx?type=worldNews&storyID=2006-11-16T163442Z_01_NOOTR_RTRJONC_0_India-276537-1.xml&archived=False |title=ILO seeks to charge Myanmar junta with atrocities |publisher=Reuters |date=2006-11-16 |accessdate=2006-11-17 }}{{Dead link|date=December 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/asiaCrisis/idUSL14863912|title=ILO asks Myanmar to declare forced labour banned |work=Reuters }}</ref> The International Labour Organisation says that it thinks that about 800,000 people are forced to work this way.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.atimes.com/atimes/Southeast_Asia/GC29Ae02.html |title=ILO cracks the whip at Yangon |access-date=2008-07-08 |archive-date=2017-11-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171119044024/http://www.atimes.com/atimes/Southeast_Asia/GC29Ae02.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.suntimes.com/news/world/926083,thailand050108.article |title=Critics: Myanmar biofuel drive uses forced labor |access-date=2008-07-08 |archive-date=2010-12-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101204150428/http://www.suntimes.com/news/world/926083,thailand050108.article |url-status=dead }}</ref>

As of 2025, there are claims that groups of online [[scammer]]s (in Myanmar), includes slaves; The [[BGF]]'s "involvement in Chinese-run online scams, illegal casinos, and online gambling operations in Myawaddy [was shown] in May" 2024, according to media.<ref>https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/general/2961315/karen-border-guard-force-to-help-nail-scammers. Retrieved 2025-02-15</ref><ref>https://www.bangkokpost.com/opinion/opinion/2959308/dystopia-of-slavery. Retrieved 2025-02-12</ref>

== People in favor of slavery ==
{{Main|Proslavery thought}}
Some people have been in favor of slavery, others were opposed to it. Before and during the [[American Civil War]], some thinkers thought that slavery was good for people, They said that some people were [[Natural slavery|natural slaves]]. These people needed supervision, and would not do well if they were free.

== Stopping slavery ==
{{Main|Abolitionism}}
Starting in the 18th century, there were ideas of stopping or banning slavery. Many of these were done in territories that were part of the [[British Empire]], or in its sphere of influence. The movement of wanting to stop slavery is called abolitionism. People such as [[William Wilberforce]], [[John Newton]], and [[Olaudah Equiano]] were well-known in the movement. About 1815, the [[Congress of Vienna]] had a statement that slavery is bad.

In 1833, the British Empire stopped slavery. Laws in Britain stopped the [[atlantic slave trade]]. The [[American Civil War]] ended [[slavery in the United States]] in 1865.<ref>{{cite web|date=September 19, 2015|title=Soldiers and Sailors Database – The Civil War (U.S. National Park Service)|url=http://www.itd.nps.gov/cwss/manassas/social/introsoc.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070714073725/http://www.itd.nps.gov/cwss/manassas/social/introsoc.htm|archive-date=July 14, 2007|access-date=September 29, 2015|publisher=Itd.nps.gov}}</ref> There was the [[Emancipation Proclamation]]. In 1865, when the North won, all slaves were made free. Still more countries abolished slavery afterwards. [[Pedro II of Brazil]] abolished it in 1888. Forced labor however continued, either against the law or by debt [[peon]]age or other methods which the laws of the various countries did not count as slavery. France abolished slavery in 1794 during the Revolution.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cbNNFxiAMeAC|title=The Abolitions of Slavery: From L. F. Sonthonax to Victor Schoelcher, 1793, 1794, 1848|date=2003|publisher=UNESCO Publishing|isbn=978-1-57181-432-6|editor1-last=Dorigny|editor1-first=Marcel|location=Paris|page=vi|access-date=August 16, 2022|via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref> In 1802, it was restored under [[Napoleon]];<ref name="dwyer">{{cite journal|last=Dwyer|first=Philip|year=2008|title=Remembering and Forgetting in Contemporary France: Napoleon, Slavery, and the French History Wars|journal=French Politics, Culture & Society|publisher=[[Berghahn Books]]|volume=26|issue=3|pages=110–122|doi=10.3167/fpcs.2008.260306|jstor=42843569 |issn = 1537-6370 }}</ref> Slavery has not been allowed in France since April 27, 1848.

title: Soul
text:
[[File:SoulCarriedtoHeaven.jpg|thumb|Soul carried to Heaven by William Bouguereau]]
{{for|the music genre|Soul music}}
Many [[philosophy|philosophies]] and [[religion]]s say that a '''soul''' is a [[supernatural]] essence of a [[life|living]] [[human being]] that lives after [[human death|death]]. It is usually said to be [[immortal]]. It cannot be discovered by science, because it cannot be tested in any controlled way. Many different opinions exist as to what happens to personal [[experience]] after death. 

[[Reincarnation]] is a belief that after the body dies, the soul will be born again in another body. It is important to [[Hinduism]]. [[Buddhist]]s understand the idea of an eternal soul, and the idea of simple annihilation as delusion; they say that there is no unchanging, permanent self, soul or essence in phenomena.  Buddhists believe in [[transmigration]], or [[rebirth]] in samsara or other [[planes of existence]], based on how they understand kamma (Pāli; karma in Sanskrit), and nibbana (nirvana in Sanskrit) for Enlightened ones. In [[Jainism]] the soul is sometimes called jiva.<ref>Jagmanderlal Jaini. [https://books.google.com/books?id=B7sKgdtJcisC&q=jiva#v=onepage&q=jiva%20soul%2084&f=false Outlines of Jainism]. (2013). Page 84. Cambridge University Press.</ref>

[[Resurrection]] is the Christian belief that a soul returns in the same body. In most Christian denomination this was realized in Jesus Christ but is also the promise for all souls; see [[heaven]], [[hell]], and [[Final Judgement]].

Most [[Atheism|atheists]] say that there is no such thing as a soul, and that the body is the only part of a person.

== Popular culture ==
In popular culture, soul usually means deep feeling and commitment. It is in this sense that the word appears in the term [[soul music]]. However that music was also influenced by [[gospel music]] which was religious.

One popular idea about souls that is easy to express, is that a person ''is'' a soul, and ''has'' a body.<ref>Miller, Walter M. Jr. (1960). ''A Canticle for Leibowitz.''</ref> The soul is the "I" in "I exist" that feels and lives life. What people call the [[mind]] could be ''part'' of the soul: one soul started this article, other souls have edited it, and another soul is reading it. This view, however, implies that the [[human body]] is a possession, and seems to devalue bodies that do not have souls as defined or understood by the speaker (some people say that [[animal]]s, [[heretic]]s, and people of another [[religion]] do not have souls). Like most uses of the verb [[to be]], there is an ideology in these simple words.

Christianity teaches that all humans have an immortal soul.<ref name=mayled>{{cite book|title=GCSE Religious Studies: Philosophy and Applied Ethics for OCR B: Revision Guide|url=https://archive.org/details/gcsereligiousstu0000mayl_a2d6|first=Jon|last=Mayled|publisher=Hodder Education|date=2010|page=[https://archive.org/details/gcsereligiousstu0000mayl_a2d6/page/17 17]|isbn=978-1-444-11071-5}}</ref> This means that it is a part of them which does not die when their physical body dies, but lives on with them to [[heaven]] or to [[hell]]. Christians believe that the soul is the 'breath of life' which God gave to Adam.<ref name=mayled />

In [[Japan]] the soul is believed to weigh 21 grams. This belief may have been influenced by the observations of [[:en:Duncan MacDougall (doctor)|Dr. McDougall]] in the early 1900s.{{cn|date=June 2013}} <!-- citation needed tag includes both sentences -->

=== Characteristics ===
One distinction often made is between soul, which is distinct from other souls, and [[spirit]], which may be combined with that of other beings. The idea of the [[Holy Spirit]] in [[Christianity]], for example, is a universal and shared spirit many souls are part of, and which is expressed on Earth in that faith by "the Church" meaning "the body of Christ" meaning "all bodies that follow Jesus." This could be more inclusive than the is/has view of souls and bodies.

title: Soap
text:
[[File:Tualetsapo.jpg|thumb|right|A bar of soap]]
[[File:Collage-furfur.jpg|thumb|Liquid soap]]
'''Soap''' is a [[chemical compound]] resulting from the reaction of an alkali (commonly [[Sodium hydroxide|sodium]] or [[potassium hydroxide]]) with a [[fatty acid]]. Soaps are the metallic salts of long chain fatty acids. When mixed with [[water]] during [[bath]]ing, cleansing, or [[washing]], they help people and clothes get [[hygiene|clean]] by lowering the chance of [[dirt]] and [[oil]] to get to the skin or [[fabric]]. Soaps are made from [[animal]] [[fat]]s or [[vegetable oil]]s. There are two basic steps in making soap. They are called Saponification and Salting-out of soap. Some people like to make their own soap.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wikihow.com/Make-Your-Own-Soap|title=How to Make Your Own Soap|website=wikiHow|language=en|access-date=2018-12-28}}</ref>

Soap cleans very well in [[soft water]]. It is not [[Toxicity|toxic]] to water life. It can be broken down by [[bacteria]]. However, it is slightly [[Solubility|soluble]] in water, so it is not often used in [[washing machine]]s. It does not work well in [[hard water]]. It cannot be used in strongly [[acid]]ic [[solution]]s. Mild hand soaps are only [[Base (chemistry)|basic]] enough to remove unwanted skin oils. For other forms of oil, dishwashing soap is strong enough to remove almost all forms of oil without damaging petroleum products such as [[plastic]]s. It does not damage skin either. Soap suds physically capture and lift [[Microorganism|germs]] (a virus, bacteria etc.) off of the surface of the skin and then water rinses them into the sink. 

Soap has been made in many ways. Humanity has used soap-like things for thousands of [[year]]s. The earliest recorded evidence of the making of soap-like materials dates back to around 2800 BC in Ancient [[Babylon]]<ref>{{cite book | last = Willcox | first = Michael | editor = Hilda Butler
 | title = Poucher's Perfumes, Cosmetics and Soaps | url = https://archive.org/details/pouchersperfumes00pouc | edition = 10th
 | year = 2000 | publisher = Kluwer Academic Publishers | location = Dordrecht
 | pages = [https://archive.org/details/pouchersperfumes00pouc/page/n467 453] | chapter = Soap
 | isbn = 9780751404791 | quote =The earliest recorded evidence of the production of soap-like materials dates back to around 2800 BCE in ancient Babylon.}}</ref> and [[Sumer]]ia.<ref name="Caveman">{{cite book|chapter=Ancient Technology|title=From Caveman to Chemist|url=https://archive.org/details/fromcavemantoche0000salz|pages=[https://archive.org/details/fromcavemantoche0000salz/page/6 6]–7|author=Hugh W. Saltzberg|isbn=0-8412-1787-4|year=1991|publisher=American Chemical Society}}</ref> They were soap solutions, or soapy water.  People made them by mixing ashes with water and fat and boiling them.<ref name="Caveman" /> The Babylonians used [[water]], [[alkali]] and [[Cinnamomum aromaticum|cassia]] to make soap.<ref name="ZME">{{cite news|author=Alexandra Gerea|title=A soapy affair – The science of homemade soap making|url=https://www.zmescience.com/other/feature-post/making-soap-home/|accessdate=July 19, 2020|publisher=ZME Science|date=January 9, 2016}}</ref>

Ancient Gauls added salt to the soap solution to make the solid soap [[Chemical precipitation|fall out]].<ref name="Caveman" />

The [[Ebers papyrus]] (Egypt, 1550 BC) suggests that [[ancient Egypt]]ians bathed often and had animal and vegetable oils with alkaline [[salt]]s to make a soap-like substance. Egyptian [[document]]<nowiki/>s say that a soap-like substance was used in the preparation of [[wool]] for [[weaving]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=First Soap - Old Soaps and The First Recorded Evidence of Soap Making|url=http://www.soaphistory.net/soap-history/first-soap/|access-date=2022-06-10|website=www.soaphistory.net}}</ref>

title: Summary
text:
{{wikt}}
A '''summary''' is a condensed explanation of an event, story, document, etc.. i.e. "summing up the facts." They are not constrained to any medium or topics. Not to be confused with [[abstract]], which is a summary of a document. There are many different levels of summarization that can be done. The summarizer may choose any length, but the sumarees may not appreciate anything more than absolutely necessary to get the required facts.

Summaries help to spread information fast. They also help people make decisions on if it is something worth looking further into.

EXAMPLES

A quick "good/bad" can suffice in some situations. In other situations, the summary may rival the length of the original.

"This book was really cool. This guy drives a pickup to work everyday, and has a dangerous job."

Many [[science|scientific]] [[journal]]s [[Publishing|publish]] a summary for every large article so people who do not have much time can read the main information quickly without spending too much time reading the article.

title: Service economy
text:
A '''service''' is a job or work done for someone else. All the service trades form a '''service economy'''. 

Good examples are:
*[[Government]] is perhaps the largest example. 
*[[Hospital|Hospitals]] and the health services generally.
*[[Bank|Banks]] and financial services.
*[[Engine|Motor]] trade services. All services except actual products such as parts and petrol (which are obviously goods or products).
*[[Painting]] a house as opposed to building it.

The old split between product and service is now often a service–product continuum.<ref>Victor R., Fuchs 2011. Who shall live?: health, economics and social choice. ISBN 9789814365642</ref> Many products are being transformed into services.<ref>Goods/service continuum.[https://mbastudymaterial.com/goods-service-continuum/] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220522010713/https://mbastudymaterial.com/goods-service-continuum/ |date=2022-05-22 }}</ref>
An example is [[IBM]], which made computers, now is mainly a consultancy for businesses which use computers. That has been so at least for the past 40 years.<ref>Bauer, Roy A. and others. 1992. The Silverlake Project: transformation at IBM (AS/400). Oxford University Press.
</ref>

The person or company which gives the service will get something in return for the service, obviously. Who gives the service usually gets money in return. Who gives the service may get goods in return. Who gives the service can get another service in return. This is a type of [[trade]].

title: Sense
text:
There are several meanings of the word '''sense'''.  This page is for [[wikipedia:disambiguation|disambiguation]] - there are more detailed articles on each meaning:

When a word has several meanings, one can refer to it as being used "in the sense of..." some context or other.  In [[Basic English|Simple English]] for instance we avoid using words in unusual senses.

== The sensory system of animals ==
The human [[sensory system]] is usually said to have six senses:
*[[Hearing]] is the sense of sound that comes into our [[ear]]s. 
*[[Sight]] is the sense of seeing things with our [[eye]]s.  
*[[Touch]] is the sense of feeling things with our [[skin]].  
*[[Taste]] is the sense of the flavor of things with our [[tongue]]s
*[[Olfaction|Smell]] is the sense of smelling things with our [[nose]]s.  
*[[Kinesthetic]] sense is knowing where your whole [[body]] is and where it is not.
Other animals may have other senses. [[Fish]] have [[lateral line]]s which detect changes in the water pressure around them, and some can detect changes in [[electric field]]s around them.

== Sense in language ==
Sense in this context is the [[wikt:meaning|meaning]] conveyed by language. 

Another use is to flag whether an [[argument]] or [[statement]] is correct and understood.  "That makes '''no sense'''" or "That is '''nonsense'''" are examples from everyday [[speech]].  

A variation of this is to say that something does not make "[[economic sense]]".  Usually these words signal a [[political]] [[dispute]] or some failure to define terms correctly.

The term "[[common sense]]" is thinking based on a wide experience of life. It used to mean practical [[wikt:wisdom|wisdom]]. It has a long history of being used in [[politics]], often to mean that some idea will be accepted or rejected because of [[human nature]] (what people are like).

title: Synagogue
text:
{{Judaism}}
[[File:Great Synagogue Jerusalem.jpg|thumb|220px|right|The Great Synagogue in Jerusalem]]
A '''synagogue''' is a place where [[Judaism|Jews]] meet to [[worship]] and [[pray]] to [[God]].

In [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]], a synagogue is called ''beit knesset'', which means, a "house of gathering". The word "synagogue" comes from ''sunagoge'', which is a [[Greek language|Greek]] word. In a synagogue, Jews carry out the [[Jewish services]], which consist of prayers, sometimes with special actions.

A synagogue will usually have a large room for prayers. There might be some smaller rooms for studying. There will be some offices. There will also usually be a big room for special events. 

The front of a synagogue faces towards [[Jerusalem]] in [[Israel]].  In the front is the holiest part of the synagogue, the [[Ark]]. This is a closet which has the [[Torah]] scrolls inside.  The Torah scrolls have the holy writings of Judaism on them.  The Ark usually has a curtain in front of it.

On top of the Ark is light which is always lit, called the “[[Eternal Lamp]]”. It is a symbol which means that God is always there.
Every synagogue has a raised platform called the “[[Bimah]]”. The person who reads the Torah scroll stands there when he reads. The Bimah is either in the middle of the hall, or in front of the Ark.

In some synagogues men and women sit in different places. Some synagogues even have a short wall so that they can not see each other. This is so that the people will think about the prayers better.

Jews may call synagogues by different names. Many [[Orthodox Judaism|Orthodox]] and [[Conservative Judaism|Conservative]] Jews living in [[English language|English]]-speaking countries use the name "synagogue" or the word "shul", which is [[Yiddish]]. Jews who speak [[Spanish language|Spanish]] or [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]] call synagogues ''esnoga''. Some Jews call the synagogue a [[temple]]. 

Jewish worship does not have to be carried out in a synagogue.  It can be wherever a [[minyan]] of ten Jews are. It could be in someone's home or anywhere such as a cruise liner or an airplane. Some synagogues have a separate room or torah study, this is called the "beth midrash" meaning house of study. Some kinds of Jewish worship can be done alone or with fewer than ten people.
Synagogues are places were Jews can worship.

title: Scarcity
text:
'''Scarcity''' in [[economics]] is the lack of various forms of [[capital (economics)|capital]]. Scarcity can be used to describe an economic [[wikt:situation|situation]] in economics, or it can be used to describe more general situations.

In economics, scarcity is the result of [[wikt:people|people]] having "Unlimited Wants and Needs," or always wanting something new, and having "Limited [[Resource]]s." Limited Resources means that there are never enough resources, or [[material]]s, to [[satisfaction|satisfy]], or fulfill, the wants and needs that every person have. Scarcity is called the "basic economic problem," meaning that it always [[existence|exists]].

Scarcity exists due to the effects of [[nature]] such as [[drought]], [[flood]]s, storms, pest infestation, [[fire]] and other things.  Real scarcity can also exist by over use of [[non-renewable resources]].  Goods (things) and [[service]]s are also scarce because there are only a [[Constraint|limited]] [[number]] of things in the [[world]] and due to the limits of [[technology]] and our own [[priority|priorities]].

More scarce goods and services have higher prices, because of [[supply and demand]]. [[Gold]] is used less than [[iron]], but the price of gold is much higher, because gold is more scarce. [[Lawyers]] are paid more than [[Janitor|janitors]], because there is scarcity of qualified lawyers.

Scarcity of capital is the main constraint in [[economic development]] of [[Developing country|developing countries]]. Economic growth is an increase in the production and consumption of goods and services. It entails increasing population or per capita consumption. It is represented by increasing [[Gross domestic product|Gross Domestic Product]] (GDP). Scarcity refers to limited resources. These resources are the inputs of production i.e., land, labor and capital.

== Artificial scarcity ==
[[File:Solitary ring and diamond.JPG|thumb|[[Diamond|Diamonds]] are an example of artificial scarcity.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Nace|first=Trevor|title=De Beers Gives In And Begins Selling Lab Made Diamonds|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/trevornace/2018/05/30/de-beers-gives-in-and-begins-selling-lab-made-diamonds/|access-date=2021-04-06|website=Forbes|language=en}}</ref>]]
Artificial scarcity is when somebody limits the amount of goods or services that are available, although it would be simple to make more. Artificial scarcity can increase profits for a business. Some people will pay more for something that is scarce, because it shows that they are rich (a status symbol). [[Copyrights]], [[patents]], [[Monopoly|monopolies]], [[Cartel|cartels]], [[planned obsolescence]] can make artificial scarcity.
