The seats are red, and the words "Manchester United" are written in white seats. The roof of the stand is supported by a cantilever structure. On the lip of the roof, it reads "Old Trafford Manchester".}} === 1878–1893: North Road === Newton Heath first played on a field on [[North Road (football ground)|North Road]]. This was close to the railway. At first, the capacity (number of people who could watch) was about 12,000. However, club officials said the [[wikt:facilities|facilities]] were not good enough for a club that wanted to join The Football League.White, Jim (2008) p. 21. They made it bigger in 1887. In 1891, Newton Heath bought two [[Grandstand|grandstands]]. Each held 1,000 people.James (2008), p. 392. Attendances (the number of people watching) were not recorded for many of the early matches at North Road. However, the highest attendance was about 15,000. This was for a First Division match against [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]] on 4 March 1893.Shury & Landamore (2005), p. 54. There was a similar attendance for a friendly match (not competitive) against Gorton Villa on 5 September 1889.Shury & Landamore (2005), p. 51. === 1893–1910: Bank Street === In June 1893, Manchester Deans and Canons, the owner of North Road, [[wikt:eviction|evicted]] the team. They did not think that the club was right to make people pay to get into the ground. The club secretary, [[A. H. Albut]], [[wikt:procure|procured]] the use of the [[Bank Street (football ground)|Bank Street ground]] in [[Clayton, Greater Manchester|Clayton]].Shury & Landamore (2005), pp. 21–22. At first it had no [[Bleacher|stands]]. By the start of the [[1893–94 Newton Heath F.C. season|1893–94 season]], there were two stands. One stand was along the whole length of the pitch on one side. The other stand was behind the goal at the "Bradford end". At the opposite end, the "Clayton end", the [[Soil|ground]] had been "built up, thousands thus being provided for". Newton Heath's first league match at Bank Street was against [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]] on 1 September 1893. 10,000 people watched and [[Alf Farman]] scored a [[hat-trick]]. Newton Heath's won 3–2. The club added other stands for the next league game against [[Nottingham Forest F.C.|Nottingham Forest]], three weeks later. In October 1895, before the visit of Manchester City, the club bought a 2,000-capacity stand. This was from the [[Broughton Rangers]] [[rugby league]] club. Newton Heath also put up another stand on the "reserved side" (as opposed to the "popular side"). However, bad weather meant only 12,000 could watch the match against Manchester City.Shury & Landamore (2005), p. 24. [[Bailiff|Bailiffs]] closed the Bank Street ground for a time in 1902. The club captain, Harry Stafford, [[Fundraising|raised]] enough money to pay for the club's next away game at Bristol City. He also helped to find a ground at [[Harpurhey]] for the next reserves game against Padiham.Shury & Landamore (2005), pp. 33–34. After [[Investment|investors]] gave the club more money, the new club president John Henry Davies paid £500 for a new 1,000-seat stand at Bank Street.Inglis (1996), p. 234. Within four years, the stadium had [[Roof|cover]] on all four sides. It was also able to hold about 50,000 people. Some of them could watch from the [[viewing gallery]] on top of the Main Stand. === 1910–present: Old Trafford === {{main|Old Trafford}} Manchester United won its first league title in 1908. It won the FA Cup a year later. Davies decided that the Bank Street was too small for his [[wikt:ambition|ambitions]]. In February 1909, six weeks before the club's first FA Cup title, [[Old Trafford]] became the home of Manchester United. The club bought the land for around £60,000. Architect [[Archibald Leitch]] had about £30,000 to build the stadium. The original plans were for a [[capacity]] of 100,000 people. However, this changed to 77,000 because it was too expensive. Brameld and Smith of Manchester built the stadium.{{Cite web|date=2024-04-10|title=Old Trafford – MUSCSA|url=https://manutd.co.za/old-trafford/|access-date=2024-05-06|language=en-US}} The stadium's record attendance was on 25 March 1939. It was for an [[FA Cup]] semi-final between [[Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C.|Wolverhampton Wanderers]] and [[Grimsby Town F.C.|Grimsby Town]]. 76,962 people watched the match.Rollin and Rollin, pp. 254–255. [[Bomb|Bombing]] in the [[World War II|Second World War]] [[wikt:destruction|destroyed]] much of the stadium. The central tunnel in the South Stand was the only part left of that stand. After the war, the club got money from the [[War Damage Commission]]. They got £22,278. The team played its "home" games at Manchester City's [[Maine Road]] ground while Old Trafford was being built again. Manchester United had to pay £5,000 per year, and a small percentage of gate receipts (tickets sold).White, John (2007), p. 11. The club made the stadium better over the years. It added roofs, first to the Stretford End and then to the North and East Stands. Pillars supported (held) the roofs. This blocked the view of many fans. To make this better, the club built a [[Cantilever|cantilevered]] [[wikt:structure|structure]] instead. The Stretford End was the last stand to get a cantilevered roof. This was finished before the [[1993–94 Manchester United F.C. season|1993–94 season]] started.Barnes et al. (2001), p. 19. The club built four {{convert|180|ft|m|adj=on}} [[Transmission tower|pylons]] for [[lighting]]. Each pylon had 54 individual floodlights. The club used them for the first time on 25 March 1957. The pylons cost £40,000. In 1987, the club stopped using these pylons. They used a new lighting system inside in the roof of each stand instead. This is the same system used today.Barnes et al. (2001), pp. 44–45. The [[Taylor Report]] said that clubs needed to have a stadium with only seats. This meant that Old Trafford could only have 44,000 fans at the same time in 1993. In 1995, the North Stand changed into three [[wikt:tier|tiers]] (levels). After this, about 55,000 people could watch the games. At the end of the 1998–99 season, the club built second tiers for the East and West Stands. 67,000 people could watch the games after this. Between July 2005 and May 2006, they added 8,000 more seats with second tiers in the north-west and north-east quadrants (corners). Fans used some of the new seating for the first time on 26 March 2006. This set a new attendance record of 69,070. This was the most for a Premier League match.{{cite news|date=26 March 2006|title=Man Utd 3–0 Birmingham|work=BBC Sport|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_prem/4820120.stm|accessdate=29 January 2011}} The record slowly went up. It was highest on 31 March 2007. 76,098 fans saw Manchester United beat [[Blackburn Rovers F.C.|Blackburn Rovers]] 4–1. Only 114 seats (0.15 percent of the total capacity of 76,212) were empty.{{cite news|last=Coppack|first=Nick|date=31 March 2007|title=Report: United 4 Blackburn 1|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|url=http://www.manutd.com/en/Fixtures-And-Results/Match-Reports/2007/Mar/Report-United-4-Blackburn-1.aspx|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111216043425/http://www.manutd.com/en/Fixtures-And-Results/Match-Reports/2007/Mar/Report-United-4-Blackburn-1.aspx|archive-date=16 December 2011|accessdate=3 December 2010}} In 2009, the seating changed. This meant there were 255 fewer seats. The new capacity became 75,957.Morgan (2010), pp. 44–48.{{cite news|last=Bartram|first=Steve|date=19 November 2009|title=OT100 #9: Record gate|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|url=http://www.manutd.com/en/News-And-Features/The-OT-100-News/2009/Nov/OT100-9-Record-gate.aspx|accessdate=3 December 2010}} Manchester United has the second highest average attendance of European football clubs.{{Cite news|date=3 May 2013|title=Barclays Premier League Stats: Team Attendance – 2012–13|work=ESPN FC|publisher=ESPN Internet Ventures|url=http://www.espnfc.com/barclays-premier-league/23/statistics/performance?season=2012|accessdate=11 May 2013}}{{cite web|title=German Bundesliga Stats: Team Attendance – 2012–13|url=http://www.espnfc.com/german-bundesliga/10/statistics/performance?season=2012|work=ESPN FC|publisher=ESPN Internet Ventures|accessdate=11 May 2013}}{{cite web|title=Spanish La Liga Stats: Team Attendance – 2012–13|url=http://www.espnfc.com/spanish-primera-division/15/statistics/performance?season=2012|work=ESPN FC|publisher=ESPN Internet Ventures|accessdate=11 May 2013}} This is behind only [[Borussia Dortmund]]. == Support == Manchester United is one of the most [[Popularity|popular]] football clubs in the world. It has one of the highest average home attendances (the most people that go to the stadium to watch) in Europe.{{cite news|last=Rice|first=Simon|date=6 November 2009|title=Manchester United top of the 25 best supported clubs in Europe|work=The Independent|publisher=Independent Print|location=London|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/news-and-comment/manchester-united-top-of-the-25-best-supported-clubs-in-europe-1816245.html|accessdate=6 November 2009}} The club says that there are more than 200 officially recognised groups of the Manchester United Supporters Club (MUSC). They are in at least 24 countries.{{cite web|title=Local Supporters Clubs|url=http://www.manutd.com/en/Fanzone/Local-Supporters-Clubs.aspx|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110807033724/http://www.manutd.com/en/Fanzone/Local-Supporters-Clubs.aspx|archive-date=7 August 2011|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|accessdate=3 December 2010}} The club goes on summer tours every year. These are very popular. [[Accounting|Accountancy firm]] and sports [[industry]] [[Consultant|consultants]] [[Deloitte]] says that they believe that Manchester United has 75 million fans in the world.Hamil (2008), p. 126. The club has the third most people in the world following them on social media among sports teams. The first and second are [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] and [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]]. It has over 73 million Facebook fans as of December 2019.[http://www.marca.com/en/2014/11/13/en/football/barcelona/1415913827.html "Barça, the most loved club in the world"]. Marca. Retrieved 15 December 2014[http://fanpagelist.com/category/top_users/view/list/sort/fans/page1 "Top 100 Facebook fan pages"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150209081114/http://fanpagelist.com/category/top_users/view/list/sort/fans/page1 |date=2015-02-09 }}. FanPageList.com. Retrieved 23 November 2015 A 2014 [[Research|study]] showed that Manchester United had the loudest fans in the Premier League.{{cite news|date=24 November 2014|title=Manchester United fans the Premier League's loudest, says study|work=ESPN FC|publisher=ESPN Internet Ventures|url=http://www.espnfc.com/barclays-premier-league/story/2162036/manchester-united-the-premier-leagues-loudest-fanssays-study|accessdate=20 February 2015}} Two independent [[Institution|bodies]] help the fans: the [[Independent Manchester United Supporters' Association]] (IMUSA), which has close links to the club through the MUFC Fans Forum,{{cite web|title=Fans' Forum|url=http://www.manutd.com/en/Club/Fans-Forum.aspx|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110814003417/http://www.manutd.com/en/Club/Fans-Forum.aspx|archive-date=14 August 2011|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|accessdate=3 December 2010}} and the [[Manchester United Supporters' Trust]] (MUST). After the Glazer family bought the club in 2005, a group of fans formed another club. This club is called [[F.C. United of Manchester]]. The West Stand of Old Trafford is called the "[[Stretford End]]". It is the home end(where the local fans sit) and the loudest part of the stadium.Barnes et al. (2001), p. 52. === Rivalries === Manchester United has [[Rival|rivalries]] with [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]], [[Leeds United A.F.C.|Leeds United]], [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]], and [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]].{{cite news|last=Smith|first=Martin|date=15 April 2008|title=Bitter rivals do battle|work=The Daily Telegraph|location=London|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/2297404/Wolves-v-West-Brom-Bitter-rivals-do-battle.html|accessdate=24 June 2010}}{{cite news|last=Stone|first=Simon|date=16 September 2005|title=Giggs: Liverpool our biggest test|work=Manchester Evening News|url=http://menmedia.co.uk/manchestereveningnews/sport/football/manchester_united/s/174/174381_giggs_liverpool_our_biggest_test.html|url-status=dead|accessdate=31 March 2010|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110814034532/http://menmedia.co.uk/manchestereveningnews/sport/football/manchester_united/s/174/174381_giggs_liverpool_our_biggest_test.html|archivedate=14 August 2011}} The club plays in the [[Manchester derby]] against Manchester City. [[File:2009-3-14_ManUtd_vs_LFC_Ronaldo_Tackling.JPG|thumb|[[Cristiano Ronaldo]] on the ball in a 2009 Premier League game between Manchester United and [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]]]] The rivalry with Liverpool comes from the competition between the two cities during the [[Industrial Revolution]]. At the time, Manchester was famous for its [[Textile|textile industry]] and [[Liverpool]] was an important [[port]].{{cite news|last=Rohrer|first=Finlo|date=21 August 2007|title=Scouse v Manc|work=BBC Sport|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/magazine/6956608.stm|accessdate=24 June 2010}} The two clubs are the most successful English teams in both domestic (in England) and international competitions. Between them they have won [[List of English football champions|39 league titles]], 9 [[UEFA Champions League|European Cups]], 4 [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cups]], 5 [[UEFA Super Cup|UEFA Super Cups]], 20 [[FA Cup|FA Cups]], 14 [[EFL Cup|League Cups]], 2 [[FIFA Club World Cup|FIFA Club World Cups]], 1 [[Intercontinental Cup (football)|Intercontinental Cup]] and 37 [[FA Community Shield|FA Community Shields]].{{cite web|last=Smith|first=Adam|date=30 November 2016|title=Leeds United England's 12th biggest club, according to Sky Sports study|url=http://www.skysports.com/football/news/11715/10676765/leeds-united-englands-13th-biggest-club-according-to-sky-sports-study|work=Sky Sports}}{{Cite news|date=21 September 2012|title=Liverpool v Manchester United: The bitter rivalry|newspaper=BBC Sport|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/0/football/19653230}}{{cite web|date=13 August 2015|title=Which club has won the most trophies in Europe|url=http://talksport.com/football/which-club-has-won-most-trophies-europe-most-successful-clubs-best-leagues-revealed|accessdate=26 September 2015|archive-date=26 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150926210603/http://talksport.com/football/which-club-has-won-most-trophies-europe-most-successful-clubs-best-leagues-revealed|url-status=dead}} It is one of the biggest rivalries in the football world. It is also one of the most famous matches in English football.{{cite news|date=20 March 2015|title=The 20 biggest rivalries in world football ranked – Liverpool vs Manchester Utd|work=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/picturegalleries/11484651/The-20-biggest-rivalries-in-world-football-ranked.html?frame=3239123|accessdate=7 November 2015}}{{cite news|last=Aldred|first=Tanya|date=22 January 2004|title=Rivals uncovered|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2004/jan/22/newsstory.sport11|accessdate=7 November 2015}}{{cite news|date=22 March 2008|title=Interview: Ryan Giggs|work=[[Football Focus]]|publisher=[[BBC|British Broadcasting Corporation]]|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/football_focus/7308778.stm|accessdate=22 March 2008}}{{cite news|date=6 December 2012|title=Liverpool remain Manchester United's 'biggest rival' says Ryan Giggs|newspaper=The Independent|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/premier-league/liverpool-remain-manchester-uniteds-biggest-rival-says-ryan-giggs-8390079.html|accessdate=7 November 2015}}{{cite web|date=26 November 2013|title=The 7 Greatest Rivalries in Club Football: From Boca to the Bernabeu|url=http://bleacherreport.com/articles/1867347-the-7-greatest-rivalries-in-club-football-from-boca-to-the-bernabeu/page/4|website=The Bleacher Report|accessdate=7 November 2015}} The "Roses Rivalry" with Leeds comes from the [[Wars of the Roses]]. These were wars between the [[House of Lancaster]] and the [[House of York]], with Manchester United part of Lancashire and Leeds part of Yorkshire.Dunning (1999), p. 151. The rivalry with Arsenal comes from the two teams, and managers [[Alex Ferguson]] and [[Arsène Wenger]], often fighting for the [[Premier League]] title. They have 33 league trophies between them (20 for Manchester United, 13 for Arsenal). This has become one of the biggest Premier League rivalries in history.{{cite web|title=Arsenal v Manchester United head-to-head record|url=http://www.arsenal-world.co.uk/head_to_head/arsenal/vs/manchester_united/index.shtml|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161101140857/http://www.arsenal-world.co.uk/head_to_head/arsenal/vs/manchester_united/index.shtml|archive-date=1 November 2016|publisher=Arsenal official web|accessdate=24 April 2013}}{{Cite news|last1=Hayward|first1=Paul|date=31 January 2010|title=Rivalry between Arsène Wenger and Sir Alex Ferguson unmatched in sport|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2010/jan/31/sir-alex-ferguson-arsene-wenger-rivalry|accessdate=24 April 2013}} == Club identity and support == Manchester United is one of the most popular and widely supported football clubs in the world. The club is often known by the nickname '''"the Red Devils"''', which comes from its traditional red shirts.{{cite web | title=Manchester United | History, Records & Achievements | Britannica | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Manchester-United }} The club has built a large global fan base over many years due to its success and history. It has won a record 20 English top-division league titles and many other major trophies.{{cite web | title=Manchester United | History, Records & Achievements | Britannica | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Manchester-United }} Because of this, Manchester United is considered one of the most successful and valuable football clubs in the world.{{cite web | title=Manchester United | History, Records & Achievements | Britannica | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Manchester-United }} Manchester United is also known for developing young players through its youth system. Many famous footballers began their careers at the club’s academy before becoming professional players.{{cite web | title=Manchester United | History, Records & Achievements | Britannica | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Manchester-United }} == Global brand == Manchester United has been called a global [[Trademark|brand]].{{Cite news|last=Gibson|first=Owen|date=2010-01-12|title=The Glazers' London operation|language=en-GB|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2010/jan/12/manchester-united-finances|access-date=2024-05-06|issn=0261-3077}}{{Cite web|last=Pilger|first=Sam|title=How Manchester United Exploit Their Global Brand Like Nobody Else|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1687727-how-manchester-united-exploit-their-global-brand-like-nobody-else|access-date=2024-05-06|website=Bleacher Report|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=Fletcher-Jones|first=Matthew|date=2021-11-30|title=Why brand Manchester United keeps them hooked|url=https://www.cityam.com/why-brand-manchester-united-keeps-them-hooked/|access-date=2024-05-06|website=CityAM|language=en-GB}}{{Cite web|date=2024-04-24|title=The Global Brand Power Of Manchester United {{!}} Business Manchester|url=https://www.businessmanchester.co.uk/2024/04/24/the-global-brand-power-of-manchester-united/|access-date=2024-05-06|language=en-GB}} In 2011, [[Brand Finance]] said the club's [[Trademark|trademarks]] and [[intellectual property]] was worth £412 million. This was £39 million more than the year before. It was also £11 million more than the second best brand, Real Madrid. It gave the brand a strength [[wikt:rating|rating]] of AAA (Extremely (very) Strong).{{cite web|date=September 2011|title=Top 30 Football Club Brands|url=http://www.brandfinance.com/images/upload/top_30_european_football_brands_2011_final_website.pdf|publisher=Brand Finance|accessdate=4 October 2011}} In July 2012, ''[[Forbes]]'' magazine placed Manchester United first in its list of the ten most valuable (worth the most money) sports team brands. It said that the Manchester United brand was worth $2.23 billion.{{cite news|last=Badenhausen|first=Kurt|date=16 July 2012|title=Manchester United Tops The World's 50 Most Valuable Sports Teams|work=Forbes|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/kurtbadenhausen/2012/07/16/manchester-united-tops-the-worlds-50-most-valuable-sports-teams/|accessdate=16 July 2012}} The club is third in the Deloitte Football Money League (behind Real Madrid and Barcelona).{{cite news|date=2 March 2010|title=Real Madrid becomes the first sports team in the world to generate €400m in revenues as it tops Deloitte Football Money League|work=Deloitte|url=http://www.deloitte.com/view/en_GB/uk/industries/sportsbusinessgroup/|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110614035034/http://www.deloitte.com/view/en_GB/uk/industries/sportsbusinessgroup/d039400401a17210VgnVCM100000ba42f00aRCRD.htm|accessdate=22 June 2010|archivedate=14 June 2011}} In January 2013, the club became the first sports team in the world to be [[wikt:value|valued]] at $3 billion.{{cite news|last=Ozanian|first=Mike|date=27 January 2013|title=Manchester United Becomes First Team Valued At $3 Billion|work=Forbes|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/mikeozanian/2013/01/27/manchester-united-becomes-first-team-valued-at-3-billion/|accessdate=29 January 2013}} ''Forbes'' magazine valued the club at $3.3 billion. This was $1.2 billion more than the next most valuable sports team. Real Madrid were first for the next four years, but Manchester United returned to the top of the ''Forbes'' list in June 2017. It had a valuation of $3.689 billion.{{Cite news|last=Ozanian|first=Mike|date=6 June 2017|title=The World's Most Valuable Soccer Teams 2017|work=Forbes|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/mikeozanian/2017/06/06/the-worlds-most-valuable-soccer-teams-2017/|access-date=13 October 2017}} [[File:Turkish_Airlines_Boeing_737-800_ManU_Karakas.jpg|left|thumb|An official partner of the club, [[Turkish Airlines]] in Manchester United livery]] Many say that the strength of Manchester United's global brand is thanks to Matt Busby. He built the team again after the Munich air disaster.Barnes et al. (2001), p. 52. Bobby Charlton and Nobby Stiles (both won the World Cup with England in 1966), Denis Law and George Best played in this team. The team had an attacking style of play and "captured the imagination of the English footballing public".Hamil (2008), p. 116. Busby's team also became linked to the [[Liberalism|liberalisation]] of [[Western world|Western society]] during the 1960s. George Best was known as the "[[Fifth Beatle]]" because of his [[Hairstyle|haircut]]. He was the first footballer to be important in the media away from football. Manchester United was the second English football club to [[Initial public offering|float]] on the London Stock Exchange in 1991. The club had a lot of money after this. This helped with its [[Commercial management|commercial strategy]]. The club focused on both commercial and sporting success. This brought high [[Profit|profits]] whereas the football industry often brings large losses.Hamil (2008), p. 124. The Manchester United brand became stronger because the media were very interested in player's personal lives. The most famous example is David Beckham (who also made his own [[wikt:global|global]] brand). This attention often makes people more interested in the football. This gives the club more chances for [[Sponsor|sponsorship]], which becomes more valuable when it is on television often.Hamil (2008), p. 121. During his time with the club, Beckham became more popular across Asia. This was very important for the club's commercial success in that part of the world.{{cite news|date=18 June 2003|title=Beckham fever grips Japan|work=BBC Sport|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/asia-pacific/2999514.stm|accessdate=20 June 2010}} When a club finishes in a better position in the league it gets more money from television [[Transaction|rights]]. This means that if a teams wins more matches, the club also gets more money. Since the Premier League started, Manchester United has had the most [[revenue]] from the [[BSkyB]] television rights.Hamil (2008), p. 120. Manchester United has also had the highest [[Income|commercial income]] of any English club. In 2005–06, the club's commercial operation made £51 million. This was £42.5 million at Chelsea, £39.3 million at Liverpool, £34 million at Arsenal and £27.9 million at Newcastle United. An important sponsorship [[Interpersonal relationship|relationship]] was with sports company [[Nike, Inc.|Nike]]. They looked after the club's [[Product (business)|merchandising]] operation as part of a £303 million 13-year [[partnership]] between 2002 and 2015.Hamil (2008), p. 122. There are many branded products and [[Service sector|services]] to buy through Manchester United Finance and the club's membership scheme. There are also Manchester United-branded media services. For example, the club has its own television channel, [[MUTV (Manchester United F.C.)|MUTV]]. This has helped the club get more fans who aren't able to got to Old Trafford.Hamil (2008), p. 126. === Sponsorship === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;margin-left:1em;float:right" |- !scope="col"| Period !scope="col"| Kit manufacturer !scope="col"| Shirt sponsor (chest) !scope="col"| Shirt sponsor (sleeve) |- |1945–1975 |[[Umbro]] |rowspan="3"| — |rowspan="11"| — |- |1975–1980 |[[Admiral Sportswear|Admiral]] |- |1980–1982 |rowspan="2"|[[Adidas]] |- |1982–1992 |rowspan="2"|[[Sharp Corporation|Sharp Electronics]] |- |1992–2000 |rowspan="2"|[[Umbro]] |- |2000–2002 |rowspan="2"|[[Vodafone]] |- |2002–2006 |rowspan="4"|[[Nike, Inc.|Nike]] |- |2006–2010 |[[American International Group|AIG]] |- |2010–2014 |[[Aon (company)|Aon]] |- |2014–2015 |rowspan="3"|[[Chevrolet]] |- |2015–2018 |rowspan="4"|[[Adidas]] |- |2018–2021 |rowspan="2"|[[Kohler Co.|Kohler]] |- |2021–2022 |rowspan=2|[[TeamViewer]] |- |2022– |[[DXC Technology]] |} [[Sharp Corporation|Sharp Electronics]] was the club's first shirt sponsor. They first signed a five-year deal worth £500,000. This was at the beginning of the 1982–83 season. This relationship lasted until the end of the 1999–2000 season. In 2000, [[Vodafone]] agreed a four-year, £30 million deal.{{cite news|last=Ducker|first=James|date=4 June 2009|title=Manchester United show financial muscle after signing record £80m shirt contract|work=The Times|publisher=Times Newspapers|location=London|url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/premier_league/manchester_united/article6426463.ece|accessdate=9 July 2010}}{{Dead link|date=September 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Vodafone then agreed to pay £36 million to make the deal four years longer. However, after two seasons it stopped being the sponsor to focus on its sponsorship of the Champions League. For the 2006–07 season, American insurance corporation [[American International Group|AIG]] was the shirt sponsor. They signed a four-year £56.5 million deal. In September 2006, it was the biggest shirt sponsorship deal in the world.{{cite news|date=7 September 2006|title=Oilinvest to renegotiate Juventus sponsorship|publisher=SportBusiness (SBG Companies)|url=http://www.sportbusiness.com/oilinvest-renegotiate-juventus-sponsorship|url-access=subscription|accessdate=28 May 2007}}{{cite news|date=6 April 2006|title=Man Utd sign £56m AIG shirt deal|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/4882640.stm|accessdate=24 June 2010}} In 2010, American reinsurance company [[Aon plc|Aon]] became the club's shirt sponsor. They signed a four-year deal worth about £80 million. It became the most expensive shirt sponsorship deal in football history.{{cite news|last1=Smith|first1=Ben|last2=Ducker|first2=James|date=3 June 2009|title=Manchester United announce £80 million sponsorship deal with Aon|work=The Times|publisher=Times Newspapers|location=London|url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/premier_league/manchester_united/article6422090.ece|accessdate=9 July 2010}}{{Dead link|date=September 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} In August 2011, Manchester United announced their first training kit sponsor. They agreed a four-year deal with [[DHL Express|DHL]]. Reports say it was worth £40 million. Reports also say it was the first training kit sponsorship deal in English football.{{cite news|date=22 August 2011|title=DHL delivers new shirt deal|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|url=http://www.manutd.com/en/News-And-Features/Club-News/2011/Aug/DHL-delivers-ground-breaking-deal.aspx|accessdate=22 August 2011}}{{cite news|date=22 August 2011|title=Manchester United unveils two new commercial deals|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-14615711|accessdate=22 August 2011}} The DHL contract lasted for just over a year. The club cancelled the contract in October 2012. DHL stayed the club's official [[logistics]] partner.{{cite news|date=26 October 2012|title=Manchester United buy back training kit sponsorship rights from DHL|work=The Guardian|publisher=Guardian News and Media|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2012/oct/26/manchester-united-training-kit-sponsorship|accessdate=12 September 2014}} United then sold the contract for the training kit sponsorship to Aon in April 2013. The deal was worth £180 million over eight years. This was also for the naming rights (Aon were allowed to use their name) for the [[Trafford Training Centre]] (also called Carrington).{{cite news|last=Ogden|first=Mark|date=7 April 2013|title=Manchester United to sign £180m Aon deal to change name of Carrington training base|newspaper=The Telegraph|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/teams/manchester-united/9977438/Manchester-United-to-sign-180m-Aon-deal-to-change-name-of-Carrington-training-base.html|accessdate=28 January 2014}} The club's first kit [[Manufacturing|manufacturer]] was [[Umbro]]. In 1975, United agreed a five-year deal with [[Admiral Sportswear]].{{cite web|title=Admiral: Heritage|url=http://www.admiralsportswear.com/heritage.htm|work=Admiral Sportswear|accessdate=11 July 2010|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090228182703/http://www.admiralsportswear.com/heritage.htm|archivedate=28 February 2009}} [[Adidas]] received the new contract in 1980.Devlin (2005), p. 149. Umbro became the manufacturer again in 1992.Devlin (2005), p. 148. Umbro's sponsorship lasted for ten years. After this, [[Nike, Inc.|Nike]] signed a record £302.9 million deal. This that lasted until 2015. The club sold 3.8 million [[wikt:replica|replica]] shirts in the first 22 months with the company.Hamil (2008), p. 127.{{cite news|date=3 November 2000|title=Man Utd in £300m Nike deal|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/1005794.stm|accessdate=24 June 2010}} The club also had other sponsors such as Aon and [[Budweiser]].{{cite news|last=Wachman|first=Richard|date=24 April 2010|title=Manchester United fans call on corporate sponsors to back fight against Glazers|work=The Guardian|publisher=Guardian News and Media|location=London|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2010/apr/24/manchester-united-corporate-sponsors-glazers-red-knights|accessdate=14 July 2010}} On 30 July 2012, United signed a seven-year deal with American [[Car|automotive]] [[corporation]] [[General Motors]]. They became the shirt sponsor after Aon, from the 2014–15 season. The deal was worth about $80m-a-year or $559m over seven years. The club used the logo of General Motors brand [[Chevrolet]] on the shirts.{{cite web|last=Edgecliffe|first=Andrew|date=4 August 2012|title=GM in record Man Utd sponsorship deal|url=http://www.ft.com/cms/s/0/776d0ba2-ddb6-11e1-aa7b-00144feab49a.html#axzz2Ahv4xupV|publisher=FT.com|accessdate=29 October 2012}}{{cite news|date=30 July 2012|title=Chevrolet signs seven-year deal|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|url=http://www.manutd.com/en/News-And-Features/Club-News/2012/Jul/chevrolet-signs-seven-year-shirt-deal-beginning-in-2014.aspx|accessdate=30 July 2012}} Nike said that they would not sign a new kit deal with Manchester United after the 2014–15 season. They said this was because it was becoming more expensive.{{cite web|title=Premier League: Sportswear giants Nike to end Manchester United sponsorship|url=http://www1.skysports.com/football/news/12040/9375980/premier-league-sportswear-giants-nike-to-end-manchester-united-sponsorship|publisher=Sky Sports|accessdate=9 July 2014}}{{cite news|last=Bray|first=Chad|date=9 July 2014|title=Nike and Manchester United Set to End Equipment Partnership|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/07/10/business/international/nike-and-manchester-united-set-to-end-partnership.html|accessdate=9 July 2014}} In 2015, Adidas became the new kit sponsor for Manchester United. They signed a world-record 10-year deal worth at least £750 million.{{cite news|last=Jackson|first=Jamie|date=14 July 2014|title=Manchester United sign record 10-year kit deal with Adidas worth £750m|work=theguardian.com|publisher=Guardian News and Media|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2014/jul/14/manchester-united-kit-deal-adidas|accessdate=14 July 2014}}{{cite news|last=De Menezes|first=Jack|date=14 July 2014|title=Manchester United and adidas announce record £75m-per-year deal after Nike pull out|work=independent.co.uk|publisher=Independent Print|url=http://www.flicksfromthepast.com/article/manchester-united-and-adidas-announce-record---75m-per-year-deal-after-nike-pull-out|url-status=dead|accessdate=14 July 2014|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160101074719/http://www.flicksfromthepast.com/article/manchester-united-and-adidas-announce-record---75m-per-year-deal-after-nike-pull-out|archivedate=1 January 2016}} [[Plumbing]] products manufacturer [[Kohler Co.|Kohler]] became the club's first [[sleeve]] sponsor at the start of the 2018–19 season.{{cite news|date=12 July 2018|title=Kohler Unveiled as Shirt Sleeve Sponsor|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|url=https://www.manutd.com/en/news/detail/kohler-unveiled-as-man-united-principal-partner-and-shirt-sleeve-sponsor|accessdate=12 July 2018}} The deal with General Motors ended in 2021. Manchester United then signed a five-year deal with [[TeamViewer]]. The deal is worth £235m.{{Cite web|date=19 March 2021|title=Manchester United agree £235m shirt sponsorship contract with TeamViewer from next season in five-year deal|url=https://www.skysports.com/football/news/11667/12250656/manchester-united-agree-235m-shirt-sponsorship-contract-with-teamviewer-from-next-season-in-five-year-deal|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709190722/https://www.skysports.com/football/news/11667/12250656/manchester-united-agree-235m-shirt-sponsorship-contract-with-teamviewer-from-next-season-in-five-year-deal|archive-date=9 July 2021|access-date=4 July 2021|website=Sky Sports}} == Ownership and finances == The Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company first [[Money|funded]] the club. The club became a [[Private company|limited company]] in 1892. It sold [[Share (finance)|shares]] to its supporters for £1. It used an application form.Barnes et al. (2001), p. 9. In 1902, the four local businessmen who invested £500 to save the club from [[bankruptcy]] became the main owners. John Henry Davies was among these. He became the club president. After his death in 1927, the club was at risk of bankruptcy again. James W. Gibson saved it in December 1931. He took control of the club after investing £2,000.Barnes et al. (2001), p. 12. Gibson [[wikt:promote|promoted]] his son, Alan, to the [[Board of directors|board]] in 1948.Crick & Smith (1990), p. 181. James Gibson died three years later. The Gibson family stayed as the owner of the club through James' wife, Lillian.Crick & Smith (1990), p. 92. However, the former player [[Harold Hardman]] became the [[Chairperson|chairman]] .White, Jim (2008), p. 92. Louis Edwards, a friend of Matt Busby, became part of the board a few days after the Munich air disaster. He started to buy shares in the club. He spent about £40,000. He had a 54 percent [[Shareholder|shareholding]] and took control in January 1964.Dobson & Goddard (2004), p. 190. When Lillian Gibson died in January 1971, Alan Gibson got her shares. He sold some of his shares to Louis Edwards' son, Martin, in 1978. [[Martin Edwards]] became chairman when his father died in 1980.{{cite news|date=18 August 1989|title=1989: Man U sold in record takeover deal|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/august/18/newsid_2499000/2499267.stm|accessdate=24 June 2010}} Media [[Businessperson|tycoon]] [[Robert Maxwell]] tried to buy the club in 1984. However, he did not want to pay the price Edward wanted. In 1989, chairman Martin Edwards tried to sell the club to [[Michael Knighton]] for £20 million. The sale did not happen. Knighton joined the [[board of directors]] instead. Manchester United was floated on the stock market in June 1991 (raising £6.7 million).Dobson & Goddard (2004), p. 191. Another businessman wanted to buy them in 1998. This time it was [[Rupert Murdoch]] and his [[BSkyB|British Sky Broadcasting]] Corporation. As a result ''Shareholders United Against Murdoch'' – now the ''Manchester United Supporters' Trust'' – [[wikt:encourage|encouraged]] fans to buy shares in the club to stop any [[hostile takeover]]. The Manchester United board accepted a £623 million offer.Bose (2007), p. 157. However, the [[Competition Commission (United Kingdom)|Monopolies and Mergers Commission]] stopped the deal at the last stage in April 1999.Bose (2007), p. 175. A few years later, there was a power struggle (different people wanted control) at the club. The club manager, Alex Ferguson disagreed with his [[Horse racing|horse-racing]] [[Partnership|partners]], [[John Magnier]] and [[J. P. McManus]]. They had slowly become the largest [[Shareholder|shareholders]]. They had an argument about who owned the horse [[Rock of Gibraltar (horse)|Rock of Gibraltar]]. Magnier and McManus didn't want Ferguson to be manager anymore. The board then looked for new [[Investment|investors]] to try to make the Irishmen's [[majority]] smaller.Bose (2007), pp. 234–235. In May 2005, [[Malcolm Glazer]] bought the 28.7 percent stake from McManus and Magnier. This meant he had a controlling interest through his company Red Football Ltd. He [[Loan|borrowed]] a lot of money to buy the club and become the owner. The club's value was about £800 million (at the time about $1.5 billion).{{cite news|date=16 May 2005|title=Glazer Man Utd stake exceeds 75%|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/4550141.stm|accessdate=11 August 2007}} After this, the club was not on the stock exchange anymore.{{cite news|date=23 June 2005|title=Glazer gets 98% of Man Utd shares|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/4629401.stm|accessdate=24 June 2010}} In July 2006, the club announced a £660 million [[Refinancing|debt refinancing]] package (deal). This meant there was 30 percent less [[interest]] to pay every year. It was then about £62 million a year.{{cite news|date=8 July 2006|title=Glazers Tighten Grip on United With Debt Refinancing|work=The Political Economy of Football|url=http://www.footballeconomy.com/archive/archive_2006_jul_08.htm|accessdate=11 August 2008}}{{cite news|date=18 July 2006|title=Manchester United reveal refinancing plans|publisher=RTÉ (Raidió Teilifís Éireann)|url=http://www.rte.ie/sport/soccer/2006/0718/manunited2.html|url-status=dead|accessdate=24 June 2010|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100105215252/http://www.rte.ie/sport/soccer/2006/0718/manunited2.html|archivedate=5 January 2010}} In January 2010, the club had debts of £716.5 million ($1.17 billion).{{cite news|date=20 January 2010|title=Manchester United debt hits £716m|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/8470595.stm|accessdate=26 January 2010}} Manchester United refinanced more through a [[Bond (finance)|bond issue]] worth £504 million. This meant the club could pay most of the £509 million it [[wikt:owe|owed]] to [[Bank|international banks]].{{cite news|date=11 January 2010|title=Manchester United to raise £500m|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/8451848.stm|accessdate=26 January 2010}} The club had to pay interest of about £45 million per year on the bonds.{{cite news|last=Wilson|first=Bill|date=22 January 2010|title=Manchester United raise £504m in bond issue|work=BBC News|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/business/8475317.stm|accessdate=26 January 2010}} The bonds were to [[Maturity (finance)|mature]] on 1 February 2017. The club's debt made fans angry. They staged a protest on 23 January 2010, at Old Trafford and at the club's [[Trafford Training Centre]].{{cite news|last=Hughes|first=Ian|date=23 January 2010|title=Man Utd 4–0 Hull|work=BBC Sport|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_prem/8472354.stm|accessdate=26 January 2010}}{{cite news|date=25 January 2010|title=Prime Minister Gordon Brown warns football over debts|work=BBC Sport|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_prem/8479331.stm|accessdate=26 January 2010}} Supporter groups told fans who went to the match to wear green and gold, the colours of Newton Heath. On 30 January, reports said that the Manchester United Supporters' Trust had held meetings with a group of rich fans. These fans were [[Nickname|nicknamed]] the "Red Knights". They had plans to buy the club from the Glazers.{{cite news|last1=Hassan|first1=Nabil|last2=Roan|first2=Dan|date=30 January 2010|title=Wealthy Man Utd fans approach broker about takeover|work=BBC Sport|publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/m/man_utd/8488910.stm|accessdate=4 March 2010}} In August 2011, reports said the Glazers went to [[Credit Suisse]] to start a $1 billion (approx. £600 million) [[initial public offering]] (IPO) on the [[Singapore Exchange|Singapore stock exchange]]. This meant the value of the club would be more than £2 billion.{{cite news|last=Gibson|first=Owen|date=16 August 2011|title=Manchester United eyes a partial flotation on Singapore stock exchange|work=The Guardian|publisher=Guardian News and Media|location=London|url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2011/aug/16/manchester-united-glazers-flotation-singapore|accessdate=17 August 2011}} However, in July 2012, the club announced plans to list its IPO on the [[New York Stock Exchange]] instead.{{cite news|last1=1Hrishikesh|first1=Sharanya|last2=Pandey|first2=Ashutosh|date=3 July 2012|title=Manchester United picks NYSE for U.S. public offering|publisher=Thomson Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/2012/07/04/us-manchesterunited-ipo-idUSBRE86219520120704|accessdate=4 July 2012|archive-date=4 July 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120704122552/http://www.reuters.com/article/2012/07/04/us-manchesterunited-ipo-idUSBRE86219520120704|url-status=dead}} The share price was going to be between $16 and $20 each. The price fell to $14 by the launch of the IPO on 10 August. This was because of bad comments from [[New York Stock Exchange|Wall Street]] [[wikt:analyst|analysts]]. It was also because [[Facebook]] had a bad start on the stock market in May 2012. Even with the lower share price, Manchester United was valued at $2.3 billion. This made is most valuable football club in the world.{{cite news|last=Rushe|first=Dominic|date=10 August 2012|title=Manchester United IPO: share prices cut before US stock market flotation|work=The Guardian|publisher=Guardian News and Media|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2012/aug/10/manchester-united-ipo-share-prices|accessdate=24 August 2012}} There are two different types of shares for the club. The people who own the shares have different voting rights (to make decisions) at the club. The public have "Class A" share. These shares have 10 times lesser voting rights than the Glazers own. Those shares are called "Class B" shares.{{cite news|last1=Jolly|first1=Richard|date=1 August 2012|title=Manchester United IPO - Q&A|work=[[ESPN]]|url=https://www.espn.com/soccer/columns/story/_/id/1128842/richard-jolly%3A-manchester-united-ipo---q%26a|url-status=live|access-date=30 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220131055144/https://www.espn.com/soccer/columns/story/_/id/1128842/richard-jolly%3A-manchester-united-ipo---q%26a|archive-date=31 January 2022}} At the start in 2012, the public could only buy 10% of the shares.{{cite news|date=10 August 2017|title=Glazers to sell two percent of Manchester United shares - sources|work=[[ESPN]]|url=https://www.espn.com.sg/soccer/manchester-united/story/3176288/glazers-to-sell-two-percent-of-manchester-united-shares-on-new-york-stock-exchange-sources|url-status=live|access-date=30 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211124222746/https://www.espn.com.sg/soccer/manchester-united/story/3176288/glazers-to-sell-two-percent-of-manchester-united-shares-on-new-york-stock-exchange-sources|archive-date=24 November 2021}} As of 2019, the Glazers still had control over the club. They had over 70% of shares. They had even higher voting power.{{cite news|last1=Rudge|first1=Dean|date=25 September 2019|title=The truth behind claims Manchester United owners the Glazers are set to sell millions of shares|work=[[Manchester Evening News]]|url=https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/man-utd-glazers-shares-woodward-16977534|url-status=live|access-date=30 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921101850/https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/man-utd-glazers-shares-woodward-16977534|archive-date=21 September 2020}} In 2012, ''[[The Guardian]]'' [[Estimation|estimated]] that the club had paid over £500 million in debt interest and other fees for the Glazers.{{cite news|last1=Conn|first1=David|date=22 February 2012|title=Cost of Glazers' takeover at Manchester United reaches £500m|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/david-conn-inside-sport-blog/2012/feb/22/manchester-united-glazers-debt|access-date=26 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200409100918/https://www.theguardian.com/sport/david-conn-inside-sport-blog/2012/feb/22/manchester-united-glazers-debt|archive-date=9 April 2020}} In 2019, ''The Guardian'' reported that this sum was now £1 billion. At the end of 2019, the club had a [[Debt|net debt]] of nearly £400 million.{{cite news|last1=Jackson|first1=Jamie|date=25 February 2020|title=Manchester United's net debt rises £73.6m to £391.3m in three months|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2020/feb/25/manchester-uniteds-net-debt-rises-736m-to-3913m-in-three-months-solskjaer-woodward|url-status=live|access-date=30 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201008035329/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2020/feb/25/manchester-uniteds-net-debt-rises-736m-to-3913m-in-three-months-solskjaer-woodward|archive-date=8 October 2020}} In 2023, the Glazers were interested in selling some shares. Different investors were interested. [[Jim Ratcliffe|Sir Jim Ratcliffe]], who owns [[Ineos|INEOS]], and [[Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani]], a [[Qatar|Qatari]] [[sheikh]], both said they were interested in investing in the club.{{cite news|date=23 March 2023|title=Man Utd takeover: Sir Jim Ratcliffe & Sheikh Jassim to submit new bids as deadline extended amid confusion|website=BBC Sport|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/65043304|url-status=live|access-date=23 March 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230322201910/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/65043304|archive-date=22 March 2023}} In March 2023, [[Finland|Finnish]] [[entrepreneur]] [[Thomas Zilliacus]] also said he was interested.{{cite news|date=25 March 2023|title=Man Utd takeover latest: Sheikh Jassim also submits second bid after Sir Jim Ratcliffe|website=BBC Sport|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/65054294|url-status=live|access-date=4 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230405115401/https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/65054294|archive-date=5 April 2023}} On 24 December 2023, the club said that Ratcliffe had bought 25 per cent of Manchester United.{{Cite web|date=24 December 2023|title=Club statement|url=https://www.manutd.com/en/news/detail/man-utd-reaches-agreement-for-sir-jim-ratcliffe-to-acquire-25-per-cent-shareholding|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231224161701/https://www.manutd.com/en/news/detail/man-utd-reaches-agreement-for-sir-jim-ratcliffe-to-acquire-25-per-cent-shareholding|archive-date=24 December 2023|access-date=24 December 2023|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United}} It also said that his INEOS Sport company was going to look after football operations. The Glazers are still the biggest shareholders. They own over 40% of the shares.{{Cite web|last=Alencar|first=Mauricio|date=2024-01-09|title=Who owns Manchester United? How much did the Glazers pay?|url=https://www.cityam.com/who-owns-manchester-united-now-how-much-did-the-glazers-pay-in-2005-how-much-does-sir-jim-ratcliffe-own/|access-date=2024-05-06|website=CityAM|language=en-GB}} Sir Jim Ratcliffe completed the deal to buy shares in the club on 21 February 2024.{{Cite web|title=Sir Jim Ratcliffe completes deal to buy Manchester United minority stake|url=https://www.skysports.com/football/news/11667/13071401/sir-jim-ratcliffe-completes-deal-to-buy-manchester-united-minority-stake|access-date=2024-05-06|website=Sky Sports|language=en}} As of 2024, he owns 27.7% of the club (25% of the Class A shares and 25% of the Class B shares).{{Cite web|date=2024-02-21|title=Man Utd investment finalised as Ratcliffe buys 27.7% stake|url=https://www.proactiveinvestors.co.uk/companies/news/1041410/man-utd-investment-finalised-as-ratcliffe-buys-27-7-stake-1041410.html|access-date=2024-05-06|website=Proactiveinvestors |Director of football insights & innovation |Richard Hawkins |- |Director of data science |Dominic Jordan |- |} ==Honours== Manchester United has won more trophies than most clubs in Europe.{{cite news|last=Bloomfield|first=Craig|date=13 August 2015|title=Which club has won the most trophies in Europe? The most successful clubs from the best leagues revealed|publisher=talkSPORT|url=http://talksport.com/football/which-club-has-won-most-trophies-europe-most-successful-clubs-best-leagues-revealed|accessdate=30 October 2015|archive-date=26 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150926210603/http://talksport.com/football/which-club-has-won-most-trophies-europe-most-successful-clubs-best-leagues-revealed|url-status=dead}} The club's first trophy was the Manchester Cup. It won this as Newton Heath LYR in 1886.Shury & Landamore (2005), p. 8. In 1908, the club won its first league title. It won the [[FA Cup]] for the first time the year after. Since then, it has won a record 20 first division titles. This includes a record 13 Premier League titles. Its 13 FA Cups is second only to [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] (14). They have also played a record 30 times in the [[FA Community Shield]] (which used to be called the FA Charity Shield). This is a game at the start of each season between the winners of the league and the FA Cup from the season before. Out of those 30 games, Manchester United won 21. This counts four times when the match was a draw and the two clubs shared the trophy. The club won a lot under manager [[Matt Busby]]. This started with the FA Cup in [[1948 FA Cup Final|1948]]. The high point was becoming the first English club to win the [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] in [[1968 European Cup Final|1968]], and winning five league titles in the years before. However, the club's best decade was in the 1990s when [[Alex Ferguson]] was the manager. In the 1990s, he helped the club win five league titles, four FA Cups, one [[Football League Cup|League Cup]], five Charity Shields (one shared), one UEFA Champions League, one [[UEFA Cup Winners' Cup]], one [[UEFA Super Cup]] and one [[Intercontinental Cup (football)|Intercontinental Cup]]. The club also won the [[Double (association football)|Double]] (winning the [[Premier League]] and [[FA Cup]] in the same season) three times during the 1990s. Before their first double in 1993–94, it had only happened five times in English football. When they won a second double in 1995–96, it was called the "Double Double". They were the first team to win the double twice.{{cite news|date=11 May 2020|title=On This Day: United's Historic 'Double Double'|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|url=https://www.manutd.com/en/news/detail/glory-days-story-of-the-1996-fa-cup-win-for-man-utd|accessdate=13 May 2020}} They won the European Cup (now the UEFA Champions League) for a second time in [[1999 UEFA Champions League Final|1999]], and the Premier League and FA Cup. This means they became the first English club to win the [[Treble (association football)|Treble]]. That Champions League title meant they could play in the Intercontinental Cup (which doesn't exist anymore). They also won this. They are the only British team to win the Intercontinental Cup. They won another Champions League title in [[2008 UEFA Champions League Final|2008]]. This meant they qualified for the [[2008 FIFA Club World Cup]]. They also won this cup. Until 2019, they were the only British team to win that competition. Liverpool then won it in 2019. The club's won the [[UEFA Europa League]] in [[2016–17 UEFA Europa League|2016–17]]. By winning that title, United became the fifth club to win the "[[UEFA club competition records and statistics#List of teams to have won the three main European club competitions|European Treble]]" of [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup/UEFA Champions League]], [[UEFA Cup Winners' Cup|Cup Winners' Cup]], and [[UEFA Europa League|UEFA Cup/Europa League]] after [[Juventus F.C.|Juventus]], [[AFC Ajax|Ajax]], [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] and [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]].{{cite news|date=24 May 2017|title=Manchester United win the UEFA Europa League|website=ManUtd.com|publisher=Manchester United|url=http://www.manutd.com/en/News-And-Features/Football-News/2017/May/Manchester-United-win-the-Europa-League-after-beating-Ajax-in-the-final-in-Stockholm-24-May-2017.aspx|accessdate=26 May 2017|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20180601015225/http://www.manutd.com:80/en/News-And-Features/Football-News/2017/May/Manchester-United-win-the-Europa-League-after-beating-Ajax-in-the-final-in-Stockholm-24-May-2017.aspx|archivedate=1 June 2018}}{{cite web|date=23 May 2017|title=Europa League final: Manchester United on the brink of unique achievement no other English club could ever match|url=http://talksport.com/football/europa-league-final-manchester-united-brink-unique-achievement-no-other-english-club-could|publisher=talkSPORT|accessdate=28 May 2017|archive-date=27 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170527015722/http://talksport.com/football/europa-league-final-manchester-united-brink-unique-achievement-no-other-english-club-could|url-status=dead}} The club's won its 2022–23 EFL Cup in February 2023. [[Ole Gunnar Solskjær|Ole Gunnar Solksjær]] v Nottingham Forest, Premiership, 6 February 1999 == Manchester United Women == {{Main|Manchester United W.F.C.}} A team called Manchester United Supporters Club Ladies started in the late 1970s. It was [[wikt:unofficial|unofficially]] [[wikt:recognise|recognised]] as the club's women's team. It helped start the [[North West Women's Regional Football League]] in 1989.{{cite web|last=Wigmore|first=Tim|title=Why Do Manchester United Still Not Have a Women's Team?|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2742131-why-do-manchester-united-still-not-have-a-womens-team|website=Bleacher Report}} The team made an official [[partnership]] with Manchester United in 2001. It became the club's official women's team. However, in 2005, after [[Malcolm Glazer]] became the owner, the club was [[wikt:disband|disbanded]]. This was because it was seen to be "unprofitable" (not good for making money).{{cite news|last=Leighton|first=Tony|date=21 February 2005|title=United abandon women's game to focus on youth|work=The Guardian|publisher=Guardian News and Media|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2005/feb/21/newsstory.sport2|accessdate=21 August 2019}} In 2018, Manchester United formed a new [[Manchester United W.F.C.|women's football team]]. It started in the [[FA Women's Championship|second division of women's football in England]] in its first season.{{cite news|date=28 May 2018|title=Manchester United get Women's Championship licence; West Ham join top flight|work=BBC Sport|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/44279069|accessdate=28 May 2018}}{{cite news|date=28 May 2018|title=Manchester United granted place in Women's Championship by FA|work=The Independent|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/womens_football/manchester-united-women-championship-football-association-fa-a8372731.html|accessdate=28 May 2018}}{{cite news|date=28 May 2018|title=Manchester United Women to play in FA Women's Championship next season|work=ESPN|url=http://www.espn.com/espnw/sports/article/23629758/manchester-united-women-play-fa-women-championship-season|accessdate=28 May 2018}}{{cite news|date=28 May 2018|title=Manchester United granted FA Women's Championship place with West Ham in Super League|work=Sky Sports|url=http://www.skysports.com/football/news/28508/11388053/manchester-united-granted-fa-womens-championship-place-with-west-ham-in-super-league|accessdate=28 May 2018}}{{cite news|date=28 May 2018|title=West Ham the big winners, Sunderland key losers in women's football revamp|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2018/may/28/west-ham-winners-sunderland-losers-womens-football-super-league|accessdate=28 May 2018}} It won the championship that season. The season after, it joined the first division, the [[FA Women's Super League|Women's Super League]]. == Related pages == * [[List of Manchester United F.C. players]] == Notes == {{reflist|group=nb}} == References == {{reflist}} {{Premier League}} [[Category:1878 establishments in England]] [[Category:Manchester United F.C.| ]]

The club plays in the [[English Premier League|Premier League]]. The manager is Chris Wilder.

Newcastle play in the [[English Premier League|Premier League]]. The club is currently managed by [[Eddie Howe]], and has been managing since 2021. == History == Newcastle United was formed in [[1892]] after the two rival clubs Newcastle West End and Newcastle East End grouped together. They have played their matches at the ground St.James' Park ever since. This ground holds 52,000 people, and is one of the biggest in England. It is located just inside the centre of Newcastle. Newcastle originally played in red shirts and white shorts. In fact, there was a kit clash in their very first League match, away to the then-named Woolwich Arsenal. The home side wore red, so Newcastle played in their change kit of black and white stripes. A permanent switch to black and white soon followed, most likely to reduce kit clashes, and perhaps as a further attempt to appease West End fans. The decision was taken in 1894, as the minutes from the club meeting reveal: ‘It was agreed that the Club’s colours should be changed from red shirts and white knickers to black and white shirts (two inch stripe) and dark shorts.’.{{Cite web|url=https://stuffbypaulbrown.com/2011/03/25/a-short-history-of-newcastle-uniteds-black-and-white-stripes/|title=A short history of Newcastle United's black and white stripes|date=2011-03-25|website=Stuff by Paul Brown|language=en|access-date=2019-08-13|archive-date=2019-08-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190813030713/https://stuffbypaulbrown.com/2011/03/25/a-short-history-of-newcastle-uniteds-black-and-white-stripes/|url-status=dead}} On the 24th day of May 2009 which was also the last day of the season, Newcastle were relegated to the second tier of English football, the Coca-Cola Championship. They returned to the top flight of English football, winning the Championship in the 2009/10 season. In the 2010/11 season, they finished mid-table. The club then went on to finish 5th place in the 2011/12 season. On 17 July 2019, former [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]] manager [[Steve Bruce]] was made manager on a three-year contract.{{Cite web|date=2019-07-17|title=Sheffield Wednesday take legal advice after Newcastle appoint Steve Bruce|url=http://www.theguardian.com/football/2019/jul/17/newcastle-appoint-steve-bruce-manager-rafael-benitez|access-date=2021-10-13|website=the Guardian|language=en}} Bruce oversaw 13th and 12th-placed finishes during his first two seasons in charge, both of which were affected by the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. On 7 October 2021, after 14 years as owner, Ashley sold the club to a new group of owners. The group was made up of Saudi Arabia's [[Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund|Public Investment Fund]], [[RB Sports & Media]] and [[PCP Capital Partners]].{{Cite web|title=PIF, PCP Capital Partners and RB Sports & Media acquire Newcastle United Football '''Portsmouth F.C.''' is an [[England|English]] [[Association football|football]] club. They play in [[EFL League One]]. Their home stadium is called [[Fratton Park]].

Portsmouth's manager is John Mousinho. The most famous manager was probably [[Harry Redknapp]] who took the team to an [[FA Cup]] victory in 2008 which subsequently got the team into the [[UEFA Europa League]] (then called the UEFA Cup) for the first time. The club has since been hit with financial problems and see themselves in the fourth tier of English football.

They have a big rivalry with a team called [[Southampton F.C.]] They are also from [[Hampshire]].

'''Tottenham Hotspur Football Club''' is an [[England|English]] [[Association football|football]] club. The club plays in the [[English Premier League|Premier League]]. 

Their current [[stadium]] is the [[Tottenham Hotspur Stadium]] in [[North London]]. 

Famous Tottenham Hotspur players include [[Pat Jennings]], [[Paul Gascoigne]], [[Glenn Hoddle]], [[Dave Mackay]], [[Gary Lineker]], [[Danny Blanchflower]], [[Teddy Sheringham]] and [[Jimmy Greaves]]. 

They have many rivals in London, but their most famous rivals are [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]]. [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] are widely regarded as Tottenham's second biggest rival. 

Tottenham were the first winners of the UEFA Cup tournament, and the first team in the 20th century to achieve the league and cup double. 

In the [[2016–17 Premier League]], they finished in second position and earned a place in the [[European Champions League]]. They reached the Champions League final in the 2018–2019 season, but ultimately lost 0–2 to [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]].

There is also a [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C. Women|Tottenham Hotspur women's football club]].

==History==
===Early years===

The club was formed in 1884 by players from Derbyshire County [[Cricket]] Club who wanted something to do in the winter. They started out by playing at the Racecourse Ground, Derby.

The Rams, as Derby County are known, were one of the first members of The Football League when it started in 1888. Back in 1895 the club moved to a new stadium, The Baseball Ground.  It was  called this because [[baseball]] had been played there much earlier beforehand, and it became their home for the next 102 years.  When they moved, Derby County had changed their club colours to the black and white they still use today at matches.

In 1898, Derby got to their first [[FA Cup]] final, but lost. The same happened again in 1899 and 1903. Derby's went down to the Football League's Second Division for the first time in 1907, but they came back up to the First Division in 1911.

In 1914, they were relegated again, but won the Second Division the next year to get promoted. [[World War I]] meant that they had to wait until 1919 to play First Division football again. After just two seasons, they were relegated yet again in 1921.

After Derby's next promotion in 1926 the club got much better, and were one of the top teams from the late 1920s all the way through to the 1939-1940 season, which was interrupted when  [[World War II]] broke out.

===FA Cup win===
The FA Cup restarted in the 1945-1946 season. Derby got to the final again, but this time they beat [[Charlton Athletic F.C.|Charlton Athletic]] 4-1 to win the Cup. Some people had thought the reason Derby kept losing in the FA Cup was that they were cursed by gypsies, as the Baseball Ground was built on the site of a gypsy camp. Some players even thought so, and before the final they asked the gypsies to lift the curse.

The Football League began again the next season, but Derby did not play well and were relegated in 1953. Things went from bad to worse and in 1955 they were relegated to the [[Football League Third Division]] (North) for the first time in their history.  Derby were too good for that league though, and finished second at the first try.  Then they did even better next season by finishing first, and going back up to the top division.

===The Clough years===

In 1967, [[Brian Clough]] took over Derby County with Peter Taylor helping him.  Derby were back in Division Two, but Clough got them promoted to the First Division in 1969.  He led them to their first ever Championship in 1972. Derby could not win the title again the next season, but they did get to the semi-finals of the [[European Cup]], but they lost to [[Juventus F.C.|Juventus]].  A lot of people in England thought after the match that the Italian club had paid money to the referee as a bribe.  This was never proved.  Clough left the club after an argument with Derby's chairman Sam Longson.  Clough later became manager of [[Nottingham Forest F.C.]], where he went on to win a First Division championship and two European Cups.

===After Clough===

Derby won the league again in 1974-1975, this time with [[Dave Mackay]] as manager. He used to play for the club, as captain, under Clough.  When Mackay left in 1976, Derby got slowly worse until they went down in 1980.

Derby's stay in the Second Division was not a happy one and they were relegated to the Football League Third Division in 1984.  It was exactly 100 years since the club formed, and just nine years after their last Championship.

The club made Arthur Cox manager. After a two-year stay in the Third Division, they were promoted to the Second Division.  They won that league the next year, going back up to the First Division in 1987.

The club managed to finish 5th in 1989, but it was owned by businessman Robert Maxwell, who was having money problems.  He stopped spending money on new players, and sold the club not long before his death.  The club was relegated back to the Second Division in 1991 (which changed its name to the First Division a year later when the First Division clubs left to form the FA Premier League).

Jim Smith became Derby's manager in 1995.  Before the end of the season, Smith took the Rams   up to the Premier League for the first time.

===Back to the Premier League and relegation to the Championship===

Derby County did well in the 1996-97 season, finishing 12th in the final table with international  players like Aljosa Asanovic and Igor Stimac playing well. The club moved into the new 33,000-seat Pride Park Stadium for the 1997-98 season, and went on to finish ninth.  Next year they did even better, finishing eighth, but the season after that Derby struggled, and finished 16th. Another bad season followed in 2000-01, as Derby finished 17th in the Premiership - just one place clear of going down.

Jim Smith left the club in October 2001 and his assistant manager Colin Todd took over.  He kept his job for just 3 months before he was sacked. At the end of January 2002, John Gregory got the manager's job. Derby started well, but then lost seven of their last eight matches and were relegated again after six seasons in a row in the Premiership.

It was a bad time to go down.  Money owed to the Football League teams by the TV company ITV Digital was never paid, and Derby were one of the clubs to suffer worst.  They had to sell their best players and rebuild a team with mostly very young players.  They finished 18th after a difficult season.  In late March, Gregory was suspended and George Burley came in as a temporary manager. At the end of the season Gregory was sacked and Burley took over fully.  Owner Lionel Pickering lost control of the club and a new board of John Sleightholme, Jeremy Keith and Steve Harding came in.  Derby finished 20th in the 2003-2004 First Division campaign, but did much better in the 2004-05 season and finished 4th in the Division which was now called the Football League Championship.  This meant they won a promotion play-off spot, but lost in the semi-finals to [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]]. Soon after losing, Burley left.  Derby then employed Phil Brown for a short period who was then replaced by the Academy Coach, Terry Westley, who kept the club up in the 2005-06 season.

Before the final game of the 2005-06 season a local consortium led by Peter Gadsby, took over the Rams and gave the manager's job to Billy Davies, who left Preston after compensation was agreed by both clubs for his services.  The new changes and fresh activity in the transfer market promise a bright future for this founder member of the football league.

Following a poor start to the 2007-2008 season which saw Derby achieve just one win in 14 matches Billy Davies left Derby County FC.<ref>{{Cite web|last=BBC|title=Billy Davies leaves Derby County|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/derby/content/articles/2007/11/26/davies_departure_2007_feature.shtml#:~:text=Billy%20Davies%27s%2018%20months%20in,the%20chairman%20in%20three%20weeks.|access-date=2021-08-24|website=www.bbc.co.uk|language=en-gb}}</ref> Derby were promoted to the Premier League after defeating [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]] 1-0 in the finals of the promotion playoffs.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2007-05-28|title=Derby 1-0 West Brom|language=en-GB|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/eng_div_1/6689971.stm|access-date=2021-08-24}}</ref>

==Famous players==

Many people think the best Rams player ever was Steve Bloomer, one of the highest scoring players in the history of English football.  He played for Derby from the late 19th century to just before the First World War. Other top players include the FA Cup winners Peter Doherty, Jackie Stamps and Raich Carter. In more recent years players like Roy McFarland, Archie Gemmill, Colin Todd, Kevin Hector, Steve Powell, Ron Webster, Alan Hinton and [[Dave Mackay]] played in the championship winning sides. More recently, the England goalkeeper Peter Shilton, Stefano Eranio and Igor Stimac all played for the Rams. Bobby Davison was also a favourite of Rams fans.  Recent famous players also include locally born Matthew Debyshire who has achieved some degree or recognition at [[Blackburn Rovers F.C.|Blackburn Rovers]] but has expressed desire to play a more successful clubs like Tottenham Hotspurs.

==Local rivals==

Derby County's main rivals are [[Nottingham Forest F.C.|Nottingham Forest]], who are based in [[Nottingham]], a city just a few miles north-east of Derby. [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]], also based in the East Midlands, come a close second.  Fans from the north of Derbyshire often dislike [[Sheffield Wednesday F.C.|Sheffield Wednesday]] or [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]].
