title: Vitamin C
text:
[[File:L-Ascorbic acid.svg|thumb|Ascorbic acid (vitamin C)]]
'''Vitamin C''' (also known as '''ascorbic acid''', '''hybrin''')<ref>{{Cite web|title=MeSH Browser|url=https://meshb.nlm.nih.gov/record/ui?ui=D001205|access-date=2026-04-01|website=meshb.nlm.nih.gov}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2017-10-23|title=Vitamins and minerals - Vitamin C|url=https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-c/|access-date=2026-04-09|website=nhs.uk|language=en}}</ref> is a [[vitamin]]. It is found in fresh [[fruit]]s, [[berry|berries]] and [[vegetable]]s. It is one of the [[water]]-soluble vitamins (like [[B vitamins|vitamin B]]). Vitamin C is important in wound healing.<ref name=":0" /> It helps the body keep the [[skin]], [[Blood vessel|blood vessels]], [[Bone|bones]] and [[Cartilage|bone cartilage]] healthy.<ref name=":0" /> 

Without enough vitamin C, a person can get a [[disease|sickness]] called [[scurvy]].<ref name=":0" /> Lack of vitamin C was a serious health problem on long ocean trips where supplies of fresh fruit were quickly used up. Many people died from scurvy on these trips before vitamin C was known as the cause. 

Vitamin C was first discovered in 1928. In 1932, it was proved to stop the sickness called scurvy. That fruit was a cure for scurvy was known long before vitamins were known to exist.

Humans cannot make vitamin C and have to get it from diet. Most [[animal]]s make their own vitamin C but some [[mammal]]s cannot. Those that cannot include the main suborder of [[primate]]s, the [[Haplorhini]]: these are the [[tarsier]]s, [[monkey]]s and [[ape]]s, including [[human]]s. Others are [[bat]]s, [[capybara]]s and [[guinea pig]]s.

[[File:Patates à l'eau.JPG|thumb|280px|Potato with peel contains 20 mg/100 g of vitamin C]]

== History ==
Through history the need for people to eat fresh plant food to help them get through long [[siege]]s or long sea trips was known by some wise people but was often forgotten.

The first attempt to prove this idea was by a ship's doctor in the [[Royal Navy]] called James Lind. At sea in May 1747 he gave some crew members [[lemon]] juice as well as their normal food, while others continued on normal food alone. The results showed that lemons prevented the disease. Lind wrote up his work and published it in 1753. Lind's work was slow to be noticed. In 1795 the British navy adopted lemon or [[lime]] juice as food for sailors. The men hated the sour taste, and had to be forced to take it. Limes, oranges; [[sauerkraut]], salted cabbage, malt, and soup were tried with various effects. [[James Cook]] relied on sauerkraut to prevent the disease on his long voyages of exploration.

It was originally thought that only humans got scurvy. However, in 1907 [[Alex Holst]] and [[Theodore Frohlich]], two [[Norway|Norwegian]] chemists found that [[guinea pig]]s could also get it if not given fresh food.

In 1928 the Arctic explorer [[Vilhjalmur Stefansson]] proved that [[Eskimo]]s ([[Inuit]]) are able to avoid scurvy with almost no plant food in their diet by eating raw meat.

In 1912 the [[Polish American]] scientist [[Casimir Funk]] first used the word [[vitamin]] for something present in food in small amounts that is essential to health. He named the unknown thing that prevented scurvy Vitamin C.

From 1928 to 1933, the [[Hungary|Hungarian]] research team of [[Joseph L Svirbely]] and [[Albert Szent-Gyorgyi]], and separately the [[United States|American]] [[Charles Glen King]], first took out vitamin C from food and showed it to be an [[acid]] they called [[ascorbic acid]].

In 1933/1934, the British chemists  [[Norman Haworth]] and  [[Edmund Hirst]], and separately the [[Poland|Polish]] [[Tadeus Reichstein]], successfully synthesized the vitamin.
It was the first man-made vitamin. This made it possible to make lots of vitamin C cheaply in factories. Haworth won the 1937 [[Nobel Prize for Chemistry]] for this work.

In 1959 the American [[J.J. Burns]] showed that the reason why some animals get scurvy is because their [[liver]] cannot make one chemical [[enzyme]] that other animals have.

== Function ==
In living organisms, ascorbate (vitamin C) is an [[antioxidant]], since it protects the body against [[oxidative stress]].<ref name=Padayatty>{{cite journal |first1=Sebastian J. |last1=Padayatty |first2=Arie |last2=Katz |first3=Yaohui |last3=Wang |first4=Peter |last4=Eck |first5=Oran |last5=Kwon |first6=Je-Hyuk |last6=Lee |first7=Shenglin |last7=Chen |first8=Christopher |last8=Corpe |first9=Anand |last9=Dutta |title=Vitamin C as an antioxidant: evaluation of its role in disease prevention. |pmid=12569111 |year=2003 |pages=18–35 |issue=1 |volume=22 |journal=Journal of the American College of Nutrition |doi=10.1080/07315724.2003.10719272 |s2cid=21196776 |url=http://www.jacn.org/cgi/content/full/22/1/18 |access-date=2011-03-18 |archive-date=2010-07-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100721110215/http://www.jacn.org/cgi/content/full/22/1/18 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is also a [[cofactor]] in at least eight [[enzyme|enzymatic]] reactions, including several [[collagen]] making (synthesis) reactions that cause the most severe symptoms of scurvy when they are dysfunctional.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.food.gov.uk/multimedia/pdfs/evm_c.pdf|title=UK Food Standards Agency|publisher=|access-date=2011-03-18|archive-date=2007-11-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071129082537/http://www.food.gov.uk/multimedia/pdfs/evm_c.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> In animals, these reactions are especially important in wound-healing and in preventing bleeding from capillaries.

* Vitamin C is needed for the production of [[collagen]] in the [[connective tissue]]. These fibres are in many places throughout the body; providing firm but flexible structure. Some [[biological tissue|tissues]] have a greater percentage of collagen, especially: [[skin]], [[mucous membrane]]s (like the gums) teeth, and [[bone]]s
* Vitamin C is required for making of [[dopamine]], [[noradrenaline]], and [[adrenaline]] in the [[nervous system]] or in the [[adrenal gland]]s
* Vitamin C is also needed to make [[carnitine]], important in the transfer of energy to the cell [[mitochondrion|mitochondria]]
* It is a strong [[antioxidant]]
* The [[tissue (biological)|tissues]] with greatest percentage of vitamin C—over 100 times the level in blood plasma—are the [[adrenal gland]]s, [[pituitary]], [[thymus]], [[corpus luteum]], and [[retina]]
* The [[brain]], [[spleen]], [[lung]], [[testicle]], [[lymph nodes]], [[liver]], [[thyroid]], [[small intestine|small intestinal]] [[mucous membrane|mucosa]], [[leukocytes]], [[pancreas]], [[kidney]], and [[salivary glands]] usually have 10 to 50 times the concentration present in plasma

=== Therapeutic use ===
Vitamin C is needed in the diet to prevent [[scurvy]]. It also has a reputation for being useful in the treatment of [[cold]]s and [[flu]], but results for this are mixed. The evidence to support this idea is ambiguous and the effect may depend on the dose size and dosing regime. 

==Daily requirement==
[[Vitamin|Vitamins]] are dosed in mg (milligrams), the total weight of the product (such as vitamin C) found in supplements or food. However, unlike [[vitamin D]] and other vitamins, where international units (UI) are used to convert the mg dose into other amounts needed for diet or supplements, and are based on how bioactive the vitamins are in the body, vitamin C does not do this.<ref>{{Cite web|title=What is Mcg in Vitamins? Guide to Vitamin Labels|url=https://www.naturemade.com/blogs/health-articles/what-is-mcg-in-vitamins|access-date=2026-04-19|website=Nature Made®|language=en}}</ref> The UI dose is usually not used in vitamin C and they normally use the mg dose. However, the UI dose of vitamin C is sometimes, or can be, 50mcg (micrograms, sometimes written as μg) equals 1 UI of vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Convert mcg to UI|url=https://www.thecalculatorsite.com/articles/units/convert-ui-to-mcg.php|website=TheCalculatorSite}}</ref>

A healthy person eating a balanced diet should be able to get all the vitamin C needed<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2017-10-23|title=Vitamins and minerals - Vitamin C|url=https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-c/|access-date=2026-04-09|website=nhs.uk|language=en}}</ref> to prevent the symptoms of scurvy from their daily diet. Vitamin C is not stored in the body which means it is needed every day.<ref name=":1" /> People who smoke, those under stress and [[Woman|women]] who are [[Pregnancy|pregnant]] have a slightly higher requirement.{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}} Because vitamin C cannot be made by the body on its own, it needs to come from diet<ref name=":1" /> or supplements. Taking less than 1,000 mg of vitamin C a day is not likely to cause harm.<ref name=":1" />

The amount of vitamin C needed to avoid deficiency symptoms and maintain health has been set by different national agencies as:
* 40 mg per day according to the [[UK Food Standards Agency]] and [[NHS]]<ref name=":1" />
* 60–95 mg per day [[US Food and Nutrition Board]] 2001 revision

Some researchers have calculated the amount needed for an adult human to achieve similar [[Serum (blood)|blood serum]] levels as Vitamin C synthesising mammals as follows:
* 200 mg per day - [[Linus Pauling Institute]] and [[National Institutes of Health|US National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) Recommendation
* 3000 mg per day - Vitamin C Foundation's recommendation
* 6000–12000 mg per day–Thomas Levy, Colorado Integrative Medical Centre recommendation
* 6000–18000 mg per day - [[Linus Pauling]]'s daily recommendation

High doses (thousands of mg) may result in [[diarrhea|diarrhoea]], which usually stops if the dose is reduced immediately.<ref name=":1" /> Alongside diarrhoea, high dose of vitamin C can cause gas ([[flatulence]]) and [[stomach pain]].<ref name=":1" /> Some researchers (Cathcart) claim the onset of diarrhoea to be an indication of where the body’s true vitamin C requirement lies.

The small size of the ascorbic acid molecule means the kidneys cannot retain it in the body. Quite a low level in the blood serum will cause traces to be present in the urine. All vitamin C synthesising mammals have traces in the urine at all times.

In April 1998 [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] reported alleged [[carcinogenic]] and [[teratogenic]] effects of excessive doses of vitamin C. This was given great prominence in the world's media. The effects were noted in [[test tube]] experiments and on only two of the 20 markers of free radical damage to DNA. They have not been supported by further evidence from living organisms. Almost all mammals manufacture their own vitamin C in amounts equivalent to human doses of thousands of milligrams per day. Large amounts of the vitamin are used in [[orthomolecular medicine]] and no harmful effects have been observed even in doses of 10,000 mg per day or more.

===Vitamin C deficiency===
Lack of ascorbic acid in the daily diet leads to a disease called scurvy, a form of [[avitaminosis]]. [[Symptom|Symptoms]] of scurvy include:<ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-10-25|title=Scurvy|url=https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/scurvy/|access-date=2026-04-09|website=nhs.uk|language=en}}</ref> 

* Swollen, bleeding [[gums]], sometimes loose [[Tooth|teeth]]
* [[Tiredness]], weakness in the body, and feeling sad

* Superficial bleeding, fragile [[blood vessel]]s
* Red or blue parts appearing on the skin (usually on the [[Leg|legs]] and [[Foot|feet]]) 
* Poor healing, bruising easily 
* Compromised [[immunity]]
* Mild [[anemia]]

==Sources of vitamin C==
===Plant sources===
Citrus fruits (such as [[lime]], [[Indian gooseberry]], [[lemon]], [[orange (fruit)|orange]], and [[grapefruit]]) are good sources of vitamin C.

Other foods that are good sources of vitamin C include [[papaya]], [[broccoli]], [[brussels sprout]]s, [[blackcurrant]]s, [[strawberry|strawberries]], [[cauliflower]], [[spinach]], [[cantaloupe]], sweet peppers, and [[kiwifruit]].

The following table is to give an idea of how much vitamin C is in different plant foods. Each individual fruit will vary.

The amount of vitamin C in foods of plant origin depends on the kind of plant, the kind of [[soil]] where it grew, how much rain and sun it got, the length of time since it was picked, and how it was stored since then.
Cooking food destroys vitamin C.

===Animal sources===
Most species of animals synthesise their own vitamin C. It is therefore not a vitamin for them. It is made by a series of [[enzyme]]-driven steps which convert [[glucose]] to [[ascorbic acid]]. This is done either in the [[kidney]]s ([[reptile]]s and some [[bird]]s), or the [[liver]] ([[mammal]]s and [[perching birds]]). The loss of an enzyme which is essential for [[ascorbic acid]] synthesis has occurred quite frequently in [[evolution]]. It has happened in most [[fish]], many [[bird]]s; some [[bats]], [[guinea pig]]s and most but not all [[primate]]s, including [[human]]s. The [[mutation]]s have not been lethal because ascorbic acid is so common in various food sources, especially fruit.

It was only realised in the 1920s that some cuts of meat and fish are also a source of vitamin C. However, the muscle and fat which make up the modern western diet are poor sources. As with fruit and vegetables cooking destroys the vitamin C content.

===Artificial chemical synthesis===
Vitamin C is produced from [[glucose]] by two main routes. The Reichstein process developed in the 1930s uses a single pre-fermentation followed by a purely chemical route. The more modern Two-Step fermentation process was originally developed in [[China]] in the 1960s, uses additional fermentation to replace part of the later chemical stages. Both processes yield approximately 60% vitamin C from the glucose feed.

In 1934, the Swiss pharmaceutical company [[Hoffmann-La Roche]] was the first to mass-produce synthetic vitamin C, under the brand name of Redoxon.
Main producers today are [[BASF]]/ [[Takeda]], [[Hoffmann-La Roche|Roche]], [[Merck]] and the China Pharmaceutical Group Ltd of the [[People's Republic of China]].

==Vitamin C advocacy==
[[Fred R. Klenner]], a doctor in [[Reidsville, North Carolina]] reported in 1949 that [[poliomyelitis]] yielded to repeated [[megadoses]] of [[intravenous]] vitamin C.

[[Nobel Prize]] winning chemist [[Linus Pauling]] began actively promoting vitamin C in the [[1960s]] as a means to greatly improve human health and resistance to disease.

Some medical and scientific opinion sees vitamin C as a low cost and safe way to treat infectious disease and to deal with a wide range of poisons.

A meta-study of the published research claimed that relatively high levels of vitamin C must be maintained in the body for it to function effectively as an [[antioxidant]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=New Developments and Novel Therapeutic Perspectives for Vitamin C|journal=The Journal of Nutrition|date=October 2007|year=2007|volume=137|issue=10|pages=2171–2184|url=http://jn.nutrition.org/content/137/10/2171.full|accessdate=22 February 2016|publisher=American Society for Nutrition|doi=10.1093/jn/137.10.2171|pmid=17884994|last1=Li|first1=Yi|last2=Schellhorn|first2=Herb E.}}</ref>

Some research shows that there are veterinary benefits of vitamin C as well.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Disease prevalence among dogs and cats in the United States and Australia and proportions of dogs and cats that receive therapeutic diets or dietary supplements|journal=Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association|date=August 2006|year=2006|volume=229|issue=4|pages=531–534|doi=10.2460/javma.229.4.531|pmid=16910851|url=http://avmajournals.avma.org/doi/abs/10.2460/javma.229.4.531|accessdate=22 February 2016|last1=Freeman|first1=Lisa M.|last2=Abood|first2=Sarah K.|last3=Fascetti|first3=Andrea J.|last4=Fleeman|first4=Linda M.|last5=Michel|first5=Kathryn E.|last6=Laflamme|first6=Dorothy P.|last7=Bauer|first7=Cassandra|last8=Kemp|first8=Brona L. E.|last9=Van Doren|first9=Janine R.|last10=Willoughby|first10=Kristina N.}}</ref> This is relevant to the question of whether cats and dogs can be healthily kept on non-meat diets.

One meta-study of the published research examined the effectiveness of ascorbic acid in the treatment of infectious disease and toxins. It was conducted in [[2002]] by Thomas Levy, medical director of the Colorado Integrative Medical Center in [[Denver, Colorado|Denver]]. It claimed that overwhelming scientific evidence exists for its therapeutic role.<ref>{{cite book|last=Levy|first=Thomas E.|title=Curing the Incurable: Vitamin C, Infectious Diseases, and Toxins|url=https://archive.org/details/curingincurablev0000levy|year=2002|publisher=Livon Books|isbn=1401069630}}</ref>

Some vitamin C advocates say that vitamin C is not used therapeutically because it cannot be patented. [[Pharmaceutical]] companies seek to generate [[revenue]] and [[profit]] their [[shareholder]]s. They may be reluctant to research or promote something that will make them little money.<ref>{{cite news|last=Sorkin|first=Andrew Ross|title=Do Drug Companies Make Drugs, or Money?|url=http://dealbook.nytimes.com/2014/06/02/do-drug-companies-make-drugs-or-money/?_php=true&_type=blogs&_r=1|accessdate=22 February 2016|newspaper=The New York Times|date=2 June 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=LaMattina|first=John|title='Do Drug Companies Make Drugs, or Money?' |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/johnlamattina/2014/07/29/do-drug-companies-make-drugs-or-money/#750db64f7fcf|work=Forbes.com|accessdate=22 February 2016}}</ref>

title: Dichlorphenolindophenol
text:
{{Orphan|date=March 2012}}
'''DCPIP''' (its full name is ''2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol'') is a [[blue]] [[chemical]] used as a [[dye]] because when it is [[oxidized]] it is blue.  Once DCPIP is [[reduction (chemistry)|reduced]] (by addition of [[electron]]s) it does not have a color anymore. This [[Chemical reaction|reaction]] can be reversed, and the [[Colorless|colourless]] DCPIP will turn blue again, when it is [[oxidation|oxidized]].

== Purpose ==
DCPIP is often used to measure the [[electron transport chain]] in [[plant]]s. It has a higher [[redox]] potential (electron affinity) than the [[Iron|Fe]]-[[Sulphur|S]] complex in [[Cytochrome|cytochrome b]] and will therefore "steal" electrons from it. This means that cytochrome c does not  receive them. The process cuts off the electron supply of  [[:Category:Photosynthesis|photosystem]] I. A common way to illustrate this change is by the addition of [[vitamin C]] [[solution]]. This reduces the 'jelly' by transforming it to a colourless mass. This experiment can be carried out to illustrate the effect of changing [[cell]] sizes on SA/V ([[Surface-area-to-volume ratio|surface area:volume ratio]]). This is known as [[Titration]].

== References ==

title: Healthy diet
text:
[[File:USDA Food Pyramid.gif|thumb|right|325px|{{Center|[[United States Department of Agriculture]] [[food pyramid]] (click to enlarge)}}]]
A '''healthy diet''' or '''balanced diet'''<ref>{{Cite web|title=MeSH Browser|url=https://meshb.nlm.nih.gov/record/ui?ui=D000072001|access-date=2026-04-05|website=meshb.nlm.nih.gov}}</ref>       is a [[diet (nutrition)|diet]] that contains the right amounts of all the [[food group]]s. It includes [[fruit|fruits]], [[vegetable]]s, [[grain]]s, [[dairy products]], and [[protein]]. It does not include too much or too little of any kind of food.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://gethealthy.eliv.info/cgi-bin/index.pl/diet.html |title=Natural, Organic Healthy Living & Diet |access-date=2007-12-11 |archive-date=2018-02-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180211145025/http://gethealthy.eliv.info/cgi-bin/index.pl/diet.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Eating wrong amounts of a food group, whether it be too much or too little, is called an 'unhealthy diet' or an 'imbalanced diet'. A healthy diet is one that includes more foods that come from [[plant]]s, animals and fewer [[convenience food]]s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.berkeleywellness.com/healthy-eating/food/slideshow/14-keys-healthy-diet |title=14 Keys to a Healthy Diet |author= |website=University of California Berkeley Wellness |publisher= |accessdate=25 April 2016}}</ref>

== Basic nutrition ==
What is known about [[nutrition]] and diet keeps changing as more is learned.<ref name=Mayo>{{cite web |url=http://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/nutrition-and-healthy-eating/basics/nutrition-basics/hlv-20049477 |title=Nutrition basics |author=Mayo Clinic staff |website= |publisher=Mayo Foundation for Medical Education and Research |accessdate=25 April 2016}}</ref> However, basic nutrition remains much the same.<ref name=Mayo/> The best advice is to talk to a [[Medical doctor|doctor]] or [[dietitian]] for personalized information based on an individual's [[lifestyle]], [[health]], and food likes and dislikes.<ref name=Mayo/>
* Basic nutrition begins with a diet based on the major food groups that includes [[vegetable]]s, [[whole grain]]s, and [[dairy product]]s.<ref name=Mayo/> It should also have lean [[protein]] such as [[bean]]s, legumes, [[nut (fruit)|nut]]s and [[seed]]s plus healthy fats.<ref name=Mayo/>
* A basic nutrition plan should include [[wikt:guideline|guideline]]s for how much food from each group to eat.<ref name=Mayo/>
* Foods should be those that can be found in local [[grocery store]]s instead of specialty and [[gourmet]] food stores.<ref name=Mayo/>
* A basic food plan should be based on an individual's [[budget]], lifestyle and (healthy) preferences.<ref name=Mayo/>
* Drink plenty of water.<ref name=PCFSN>{{cite web |url=http://www.fitness.gov/eat-healthy/how-to-eat-healthy/ |title=How to Eat Healthy |author= |website= |publisher=President's Council on Fitness, Sports & Nutrition |accessdate=25 April 2016}}</ref> Drink fewer [[Soft drink]]s, [[energy drink]]s and [[sports drink]]s which usually have [[sugar]].<ref name=PCFSN/>
* Read the [[Nutrition facts label|food labels]] to see what is in the foods.<ref name=PCFSN/> For [[example]], labels usually show what foods are lower in [[Table salt|sodium]] such as in [[soup]], [[bread]], and [[Frozen food|frozen meals]].<ref name=PCFSN/>
* A healthy diet should include [[seafood]]s (such as [[salmon]], [[tuna]], and [[trout]]) and [[shellfish]] (such as [[crab]], [[mussel]]s, and [[oyster]]s). Seafood has protein, [[mineral]]s, and [[omega-3 fatty acid]]s which are [[heart]]-healthy.<ref name=PCFSN/>
* Basic nutrition should contain balanced amounts of [[macronutrients]] for [[energy]].<ref name=EFIC>{{cite web |url=http://www.eufic.org/page/en/nutrition/carbohydrates/ |title=Carbohydrates |author= |website= |publisher=The European Food Information Council |accessdate=25 April 2016 |archive-date=14 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414202251/http://www.eufic.org/page/en/nutrition/carbohydrates/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Carbohydrates are one of the three macro-[[nutrient]]s in the human diet (fat and protein are the other two).<ref name=EFIC/>
* A healthy diet can replace [[dieting]] for weight loss.<ref name=zelmanWebMD>{{cite web |url=http://www.webmd.com/diet/dieting-is-out-healthy-eating-is-in |title=Dieting Is Out; Healthy Eating Is In |author=Kathleen M. Zelman |date=17 June 2010 |website= |publisher=WebMD, LLC |accessdate=25 April 2016}}</ref> Eating healthy, along with [[physical exercise]] and practicing moderation, can lead to better health in the long run.<ref name=zelmanWebMD/>

== Special diets ==
There are some diets made for people with some diseases. Here are some examples:

*[[DASH diet]] (Dietary Approaches to Stop [[Hypertension]])
* [[Gluten-free diet]] ([[Coeliac disease]])
* [[Ketogenic diet]] ([[Epilepsy]])

title: Dye
text:
{{cleanup|date=March 2026}}
'''Dye''' is a [[substance]] used to [[color]] materials. It is often used to color the [[fabric]] used to make [[clothing]]. It has low [[solubility]]. A [[pigment]] will not do this because it will not stick to the [[fiber]]s of the fabric and color them. A dye can be natural, usually made from plant material such as berries, or a dye can be artificial, meaning that it is made by humans from chemicals such as [[petrochemical]]s.

Most natural dyes are gotten from different parts of a [[plant]] like the [[Root|roots]], [[Fruit|fruits]], [[bark]], [[Leaf|leaves]], [[wood]], [[Fungus|fungi]] and [[Lichen|lichens]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Harvesting color : how to find plants and make natural dyes|url=https://archive.org/details/harvestingcolorh0000burg|last=Burgess, Rebecca, 1977-|date=2011|publisher=Artisan|others=Green, Paige|isbn=978-1-57965-425-2|location=New York|oclc=667210526}}</ref> Most dyes are synthetic and are made from petrochemicals.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_F4hAwAAQBAJ&dq=organic+dye+laser&pg=PA539|title=Laser Fundamentals|last=Silfvast|first=William T.|date=2008-07-21|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-85557-0|language=en}}</ref>

==Classification==
Dyes can be classified based on their [[solubility]] and chemical properties. 

* [[Acid dye]]s can dissolve in water.  They are used on [[fiber]]s such as [[silk]], [[wool]], [[nylon]].  Most [[food coloring]] that are made by man are acid dyes.  Examples of acid dye are Alizarine Pure Blue B, [[Acid red 88]], etc.
* Basic dyes can dissolve in water.  They are mainly used on [[acrylic]] fibers.  They may also be used on wool and silk.  Basic dyes are also used to make [[paper]] colourful.

title: Poetry
text:
'''Poetry''' is written, spoken or sung [[language]] that is used in stronger or more original ways than [[prose]] is used. Poetry uses the ''[[Meaning|meanings]]'' of words as prose does; but it also uses the ''[[Sound|sounds]]'' of words as if they were [[music]], especially [[Rhyme|rhymes]], other repeating sounds, and [[Rhythm|rhythms]] ([[Tempo|beats]] or [[Meter (poetry)|meters]]).<ref>"poetry". Oxford Dictionary of Literary Terms (4 ed.), OUP 2015. Online access via Wikipedia Library 2 January 2023.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Sherazi|first=HH|title=It is All About Poems|url=https://itisallaboutpoems.com/|access-date=2023-01-02|website=owl.purdue.edu|archive-date=2023-08-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230820041015/https://itisallaboutpoems.com/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Poetry arranges words and groups of words to make [[Repetition|repetitions]] and [[Parallelism (grammar)|parallelisms]]. Poetry uses [[Figure of speech|figures of speech]], [[Ellipsis|ellipses]] and [[delayed identifications|delayed identification]] to suggest that there is more meaning in the language.

Some people believe that poetry began when language began. They think it is probably "as old as [[history]] and older, present wherever [[religion]] is present."<ref>{{Cite web|title=poetry - Poetry as a mode of thought: the Protean encounter {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/art/poetry/Poetry-as-a-mode-of-thought-the-Protean-encounter|access-date=2023-01-02|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}}</ref>

The English words "poetry," "poet," and "poem" first appeared in English in the 14th century. They come from the [[Latin]] word ''poeta'', which itself probably comes from ''poiein'', a [[Greek language|Greek]] word that means "to make."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Poets|first=Academy of American|title=Poetry {{!}} Academy of American Poets|url=https://poets.org/glossary/poetry|access-date=2023-01-02|website=poets.org}}</ref><ref>"poetry". Oxford Dictionary of Literary Terms (4 ed.), OUP 2015. Online access via Wikipedia Library 2 January 2023.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=poetry {{!}} Search Online Etymology Dictionary|url=https://www.etymonline.com/search?q=poetry&ref=searchbar_searchhint|access-date=2023-01-02|website=www.etymonline.com}}</ref>

There are three major kinds of poetry: [[lyric]], [[narrative]], and [[dramatic]].<ref>"poetry". Oxford Dictionary of Literary Terms (4 ed.), OUP 2015. Online access via Wikipedia Library 2 January 2023.</ref>

* Lyric poetry tends to be brief and is often about [[Emotion|emotions]].
* Narrative poetry tells a story with a [[Plot (narrative)|plot]].
* Dramatic poetry can be [[Performance|performed]] as a [[Play (theatre)|play]].

A poem can be as short as a few words or as long as a book. A one-line poem is called a monostich.<ref>{{Cite web|last=briefpoems|date=2016-01-06|title=Slates – One-line poems (Monostich)|url=https://briefpoems.wordpress.com/2016/01/07/slates-one-line-poems-monostich/|access-date=2023-01-02|website=Brief Poems|language=en}}</ref> A poem that is as long as a book is an [[epic]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Epic {{!}} Definition, Characteristics, Examples, Development, & Facts {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/art/epic|access-date=2023-01-02|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}}</ref>

Poems are often printed on the page as lines and groups of lines called [[Stanza|stanzas]].

There are many different "poetic forms" or ways to shape a poem on the printed page or in the [[ear]] of the person who hears it. Some forms are: the [[sonnet]], [[haiku]], the [[ballad]], the [[stev]], the [[prose poem]], the [[ode]], [[free verse]], [[blank verse]], [[Limerick (poetry)|limerick]], and [[Nursery rhyme|nursery rhymes]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Brewer|first=Robert Lee|title=List of 168 Poetic Forms for Poets|url=https://www.writersdigest.com/write-better-poetry/list-of-50-poetic-forms-for-poets|access-date=2023-01-02|website=Writer's Digest|language=en}}</ref>

title: Literature
text:
[[File:Printing3 Walk of Ideas Berlin.JPG|thumb|Sculpture in [[Berlin]] depicting a stack of books on which are inscribed the names of great German writers.]]
[[Image:Old book bindings.jpg|thumb|240px|Old book bindings at a [[library]]]]
'''Literature''' is a group of works of [[art]] that are made of [[word]]s. Most are written, but some are shared by word of mouth. Literature usually means a work of [[poetry]], [[theatre]] or [[narrative]].<ref name="brit">{{Cite encyclopedia |url= http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/343579/literature |title=literature -- Britannica Online Encyclopedia |encyclopedia=britannica.com |accessdate=26 June 2010}}</ref> There are many different kinds of literature, such as [[poetry]], [[Drama|plays]], or [[novel]]s. They can also be put into groups by their [[language]], [[history|historical]] time, place of origin, [[literary genre|genre]], and subject.<ref name=brit/> The word "literature" comes from the [[Latin language|Latin]] word "literatura," which means "writing formed with letters."<ref>{{Cite web |url= http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?search=literature&searchmode=none |title=Online Etymology Dictionary|work=etymonline.com |accessdate=26 June 2010}}</ref>

Most of the earliest works were [[epic poem]]s. Epic poems are long stories or [[myth]]s about adventures, such as the [[Epic of Gilgamesh]] from ancient [[Mesopotamia]]. ''[[Ramayana]]'' and ''[[Mahabharata|Mahabharta]]'', two [[India|Indian]] epics, are still read today. The [[Iliad]] and ''[[Odyssey]]'' are two famous [[Greek language|Greek]] poems by [[Homer]]. They were shared over time through speaking and [[memory]] and were written down around the 9th or 8th century BCE.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Homer and the epic poems the Iliad and the Odyssey {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/summary/Homer-Greek-poet|access-date=2023-03-25|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}}</ref>

Literature can also mean [[imagination|imaginative]] or [[creative]] writing, which is read for its [[art]]istic value. Literature is also related to people and community. According to Sangidu (2004) as quoted by Arfani et.al (2023), "literature is a part of society, a fact that inspires authors to involve themselves in the life order of the community where they are and try to fight for the position of the social structure and the problems face in society". <ref>{{Cite journal|last=Arfani|first=Sri|year=2023-11-22|title=Humanity Aspect in Movie of The Captain: Directed by Andrew Lau|url=https://jurnal.ut.ac.id/index.php/ijelp/article/view/5150/1608|journal=International Journal of English Language and Pedagogy (IJELP)|volume=1|pages=151-163|via=Universitas Terbuka}}</ref>

title: Oesophagus
text:
{{no sources }}

[[File:Stomach diagram.gif|right|thumb|Oesophagus in the gastrointestinal system]]

The '''oesophagus''' (or '''esophagus''') is also called the '''gullet'''. It is the part of the [[gastrointestinal system]] between the mouth and the [[stomach]]. It connects the [[pharynx]] and the stomach. It is about {{convert|25|cm}} long.

The oesophagus is lined with [[muscle]], and is [[lubrication|lubricated]]. Its muscle pushes food down into the stomach. The oesophagus can contract or expand to allow for the passage of food. The muscular movement that pushes the food down the oesophagus is called [[peristalsis]]. At the entrance to the stomach there is a ring of muscle called a [[sphincter]]. This is usually closed, but relaxes as food approaches, allowing it to enter the stomach. In the stomach, the food is churned until it turns into a soupy mixture called [[chyme]].

== Fetal development ==
The airways and intestines form as the same tube in [[Embryo|embryonic]] development. It starts forming at the belly button (foregut).

title: Protease

A '''protease''' is a digestive  [[enzyme]]. It breaks down long chains of  [[protein]]s into shorter [[amino acids]]. Proteases have [[convergent evolution|evolved]] a number of times. title: Dental floss
text:
[[Image:Dental floss (whole).jpg|right|thumb|180px|Dental floss]]
'''Dental floss''' is a special type of [[thread]]. It is used for cleaning spaces between [[Tooth|teeth]] which cannot be reached by [[toothbrush]]es. It is important to floss before brushing teeth and to floss at least once a day.  Tooth brushing will not clean food that is packed between teeth. This 'food packing' can lead to unhealthy teeth and gums. [[Bacteria]] grow in this 'packed food' between teeth. These bacteria cause the surface of teeth (enamel) to break down. Then the teeth and gums and sometimes even the jaw can become seriously diseased. 

These bacteria that come from the food on the teeth and between the teeth are called "plaque" or "bacterial plaque" and also can cause the gums to become less healthy. "[[Gingivitis]]" which means gum disease is one type of disease that flossing helps to prevent. Very serious diseases can start on the teeth and move to the bone of the jaw, damaging the jaw badly. Flossing your teeth reduces the danger of these serious diseases of the jaw bone. These hard-to-cure jaw bone diseases are called "periodontal disease". 

Food that is trapped between the teeth can be uncomfortable and even cause pain. Some food is hard, for example meat, apple. Ground meat is soft and so is apple sauce. Chicken and turkey meat are hard and full of fibres and very often get trapped between the teeth. When hard food is trapped between the teeth it can cause discomfort and sometimes pain. When hard food is pressed by the teeth against the gum it can cause pain. Some people use [[toothpick]]s to try to remove trapped food from between the teeth and other people use dental floss to do this.

Dental floss can do most things that a toothpick can do but dental floss is much thinner than a toothpick and can thus get to places that most toothpicks cannot reach. So floss presumably does a better job at getting bits of food out from between the teeth, relieving discomfort and pain quicker.

When a person first starts flossing, bleeding can happen. This is normal and happens because teeth and gums that are not flossed are less healthy. It will stop as the teeth and gums get healthier with flossing.

title: Rickets
text:
{{Infobox disease
| Name           = Rickets
| pronounce      = {{IPAc-en|ˈ|r|ɪ|k|ɨ|t|s}}
| Image          = Valgus.jpg
| Caption        = [[X-ray]]s and pictures of a child with rickets, showing the leg bones curving inward
| Field         = [[Pediatrics]]
| ICD10          = {{ICD10|E|55| |e|50}}
| ICD9           = {{ICD9|268}}
| DiseasesDB     = 9351
| eMedicineSubj  = ped
| eMedicineTopic = 2014
| MedlinePlus    = 000344
| MeshName       = Rickets
| MeshNumber     = D012279}}

'''Rickets''' is a [[disease]] that happens in young children.  It happens in children who do not get enough [[vitamin D]] and [[calcium]].  It causes larger spaces inside [[bones]], and makes them dry, like [[Sponge (tool)|sponges]].  It can make the legs curve toward each other (so the [[knee]]s touch) or away from each other.

Rickets in adults is called '''osteomalacia'''.<ref name=wb>Cole Jr., Madison B. (2016).  "Rickets." ''World Book Advanced.'' World Book.  Retrieved February 22, 2016.</ref>

The word "rickets" comes from the [[Greek (language)|Greek]] word ''rhakhis'', which means "[[spine]]."

== Cause ==
People need both vitamin D and calcium to make their bones strong.

Vitamin D helps the bones absorb (take up) calcium.  Low vitamin D makes it hard to absorb calcium.<ref name=nof>{{cite web |url=http://nof.org/calcium |title=Calcium and Vitamin D: What You Need to Know |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |website=National Osteoporosis Foundation |publisher= |accessdate=March 5, 2016 |quote=}}</ref>

The [[human body]] makes vitamin D<sub>3</sub> in the [[skin]], from [[cholesterol]].  Then the [[liver]] changes vitamin D<sub>3</sub> into [[calcitriol]], which sends calcium from the [[blood]] into the bones.  The bones need calcium to stay strong.  However, the skin will not make vitamin D<sub>3</sub> unless enough [[ultraviolet]] light shines on it.  [[Sunlight]] contains ultraviolet light, so getting enough sun is one way of getting enough D<sub>3</sub>.<ref name=wb/><ref name=nof/>

People need calcium for [[calcification]]. Calcification uses calcium to help make bones bigger and stronger.  Low calcium makes bones delicate and easier to [[Bone fracture|break]].<ref>"Rickets." Nutrition and Well-being A-Z. Ed. Delores C.S. James. New York: MacMillan Reference USA, 2004. 2 vols.</ref>

== Prevention ==
Rickets can be prevented if a person gets plenty of calcium and vitamin D.<ref name=wb/>

The best way to do this is to get a lot of sunlight, and eat foods that have a lot of vitamin D and calcium in them.  However, people who cannot get enough vitamin D and calcium this way can take supplements (vitamin pills that have calcium and vitamin D in them).<ref name=nof/>

===Calcium===

Foods that have a lot of calcium in them include:<ref name=nof/>
* [[Milk]] and other [[dairy product]]s like [[cheese]]s
* Some green [[vegetable]]s, like [[broccoli]], [[spinach]], and [[kale]]
* Today, many products are "fortified" with vitamin D: the vitamin was added when the food was made.  These foods include some kinds of [[orange juice]], [[breakfast cereal]]s, [[bread]]s, and even bottled [[water]].  The food's label will say how much calcium it has in it.

Calcium is absorbed best by the bones when it is taken in amounts of 1000[[Milligram|mg]] or less.  Because of this, doctors suggest eating smaller amounts of foods with calcium in them, at different times in the day, instead of all at once.<ref name=nof/>

===Vitamin D===
[[File:Frog Pond at Boston Common.jpg|thumb|300px|These people's bodies are making vitamin D while they play in the sun]]
There are three ways to get vitamin D: sunlight, foods, or supplements (vitamin pills that have vitamin D in them).  However, many people cannot get enough vitamin D just from their [[diet]].<ref name=nof/>

There are only a few foods that have a lot of vitamin D in them.  They include:<ref name=nof/>
* "Fatty fish" that were caught in the wild, like [[mackerel]], [[salmon]], and [[tuna]]
* Cooked [[egg yolk]]
* Vitamin D is added to some foods, like some kinds of dairy products, cereals, and orange juices

[[Breastfeeding|Breast milk]] may not have enough vitamin D in it to prevent rickets.  Babies who are only breastfed, and not fed any other foods, may be given vitamin D drops to make sure they do not get rickets.<ref name=mayorisk/> However, this is not a significant risk if mothers and child have some exposure to sunlight. Children with dark skin are more likely to need additional vitamin D.

==Risk factors==
These things make a person more likely to get rickets:<ref name=mayorisk>{{cite web |url=http://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/rickets/basics/risk-factors/con-20027091 |title=Rickets: Risk Factors |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=June 1, 2013 |website=Mayo Clinic |publisher=Mayo Foundation for Education and Research |accessdate=March 5, 2016 |quote=}}</ref>
*They are between three and 36 months old.  Children this age are at the.      greatest risk for rickets because their bones are growing so quickly, and are supposed to get bigger and stronger during this time
* They were born [[premature birth|prematurely]] (earlier than normal)
* They live in the Northern parts of the world, where there is less sunshine
*They spend too little time outside
[[File:XrayRicketsLegssmall.jpg|thumb|200px|X-ray of a child with rickets, showing the legs curving outward]]
*They always wear [[sunscreen]] when going out
** Even mild sunscreen decreases the amount of vitamin D the body makes by 95% (by stopping the body from taking in vitamin D from sunlight)
** However, people should still wear sunscreen when they might get [[sunburn]]ed
*They do not eat enough food that has calcium or vitamin D in it, because of [[lactose intolerance]] or a strict [[vegan]] [[diet]]
*They cannot make or use vitamin D because of a [[disease|medical disorder]], like [[coeliac disease]], or because they take certain [[anticonvulsant|anti-seizure medications]]

==Symptoms==
[[Signs and symptoms]] of rickets include:<ref name=wb/>
* Brittle (easily broken) bones or [[teeth]]
* [[Bleeding]] more than normal
* Stunted growth (not growing like a healthy child would)
* [[Sweating]]
* Weakness (feeling tired all the time)
* Body [[pain]]

title: Bile
text:
'''Bile''' or '''gall''' is an [[Alkali|alkaline]], green-yellow [[fluid]]. It is secreted from the [[liver]] of most [[vertebrate]] animals, and is often stored in the [[gall bladder]]. Bile helps [[digestion|digest]] [[fat]].

The components of bile are, in descending order of composition, the following:
* [[Water]] 
* [[Cholesterol]]
* [[Bile pigment]]s
* [[Bile salt]]s

The name ''gall'' comes from the [[Greece|Greek]] word ''cholè'' meaning green or yellow. These colours come from the bile pigments. One of them is green and the other is yellow. When they are mixed together, they make feces brown. The term cholesterol and the illness [[cholera]] were named after gall.

Bile is also stored in bile ducts. Often after liver transplants, bile comes out of the body.

Bile increases fats' total [[Surface-area-to-volume ratio|surface area to volume ratio]] so their digestion is easier and faster. Hence, more fats and fat-soluble [[vitamin]]s like vitamins [[Vitamin A|A]], [[Vitamin D|D]], [[Vitamin E|E]] and [[Vitamin K|K]] can be absorbed. This keeps fat out of [[feces]] so they are brown instead of white, grey or greasy.

Protoplasm
text:
{{no sources|date=October 2021}}
[[File:Allium-Differenzierung05-DM100x HF ba1.jpg|thumb|right|Plant cells have strong [[Cell wall|walls]], and inside the wall is a [[cell membrane]], then a thin layer of cytoplasm with the [[nucleus]] and other [[organelle]]s in it. The cytoplasm is pressed against the cell wall by the very large [[vacuole]]. In this picture the cell nuclei are dark-coloured.]]

"'''Protoplasm'''" is an old term which means the living [[substance]] that makes up a [[cell]]. It is no longer much used. Biologists prefer to talk about the [[cytoplasm]] and the [[cell nucleus]].

In [[plant]] cells, it is surrounded by a [[cell wall]]. In [[animal]] cells, the whole cell is made of protoplasm, surrounded by a [[cell membrane]]. Protoplasm in living beings is made up of about 75{{ndash}}80% [[water]]. However, this is rather misleading because the cytoplasm is full of structures called [[organelles]], which do various tasks. The [[endoplasmic reticulum]] is the largest of these structures; there are many other organelles.  

The word "protoplasm" was first used in 1846 by Hugo von Mohl to describe the substance in plant cells, apart from the cell wall, the cell nucleus and the vacuole. After the invention of the [[electron microscope]] it was clear that a living cell is much more complicated than von Mohl knew.

title: Amylase
text:
'''Amylase''' is an [[enzyme]] which breaks down [[starch]] into [[sugars]] which the body can use.

More accurately, it is a family of similar enzymes which work in a wide range of animals, plants and [[fungi]]. There are two variants in humans: alpha-amylase, and gamma-amylase.<ref>[http://pdb101.rcsb.org/motm/74 PDB-101: Molecule of the month]</ref>

Alpha-amylase is a major [[digestion|digestive]] enzyme. Its optimum [[pH]] is 6.7–7.0. It is found in [[saliva]] and [[pancreas|pancreatic juice]]. It takes starch chains and breaks them into smaller pieces with two or three glucose units. It can break down [[starch]] into [[maltose]]. It works in the mouth and [[stomach]] during digestion.

The gamma-amylase has most acidic optimum pH of all amylases because it is most active around pH 3. Therefore, it works best in the [[stomach]], which does have an acidic pH.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.worthington-biochem.com/introbiochem/effectspH.html|title=Effects of pH (Introduction to Enzymes)|work=worthington-biochem.com|accessdate=17 May 2015}}</ref>

==Human evolution==
Apparently, early humans did not possess salivary amylase. The closest evolutionary relatives of humans, [[chimpanzees]] and [[bonobo]]s, have either one or no copies of the gene for producing salivary amylase.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Vuorisalo, Timo & Arjamaa, Olli 2010. |title=Gene-culture coevolution and human diet |journal=American Scientist |volume=98 |issue=2 |page=140 |url=http://www.americanscientist.org/issues/feature/2010/2/gene-culture-coevolution-and-human-diet |access-date=2016-05-14 |archive-date=2016-03-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304110626/http://www.americanscientist.org/issues/feature/2010/2/gene-culture-coevolution-and-human-diet |url-status=dead }}</ref>  A duplication event of the [[AMY1A|AMY1]] gene led to the production of amylase in the saliva. The same event occurred independently in [[rodents]]. This shows the importance of salivary amylase in organisms that eat relatively large amounts of starch.<ref name=Perry2007>{{cite journal|last1=Perry G.H. ''et al 2007'' |title=Diet and the evolution of human amylase gene copy number variation.|journal=Nature Genetics |year=2007|volume=39 |issue=10|pages=1256–60|doi=10.1038/ng2123|pmid=17828263|pmc=2377015}}</ref>

[[Carbohydrates]] are a food source rich in energy. After the [[agricultural revolution]], human diet began to rely more on plant and animal domestication in place of hunting and gathering. This shift marked the beginning of a diet composed of 49% carbohydrates as opposed to the previous 35% observed in [[Paleolithic]] humans. As such, starch became a staple of human diet. Humans that contained amylase in the saliva would benefit from increased ability to digest starch more efficiently and in higher quantities.

Not all humans have the same number of copies of the AMY1 gene. Populations which rely on carbohydrates have a higher number of AMY1 copies than populations that eat little starch. The number of AMY1 gene copies in humans can range from six copies in [[agricultural]] groups such as European-American and Japanese (two high starch populations) to only 2-3 copies in hunter-gatherer societies such as the [[Aka people|Biaka]], [[Datog]], and [[Yakuts]].

The [[correlation]] between starch consumption and number of AMY1 copies suggests that more AMY1 copies in high starch populations is caused by [[natural selection]]. It is a favorable [[phenotype]] for those individuals. Therefore, it is likely that having more copies of AMY1 in a high starch population increases [[fitness]] and produces healthier, fitter offspring. Geographically close populations with different eating habits possess a different number of copies of the AMY1 gene. This offers strong evidence that natural selection has acted on this gene.<ref name=Perry2007/>

title: Variegated leaf
text:
[[Image:Ficus aspera 2.jpg|thumb|220px|Variegated leaves of the ficus aspera]]

A '''variegated leaf''' is a type of leaf.

== Uses ==
A variegated leaf is useful in conducting experiments to show that [[chlorophyll]] is needed for photosynthesis to happen. They are also popular in [[horticulture]].

=== Experiments ===
The easiest of these experiments is to stain the places where [[starch]] is produced (starch is a more compact form of [[glucose]]).

Place the leaves in boiling water for six minutes to soften the cells, and then in [[ethanol]] (alcohol). When the leaves are drained of colour, spread them out on a flat surface. Soak the leaves in [[iodine]] and the green parts will turn blue/black and the non green parts will stay the yellowish brown colour of iodine liquid. The green parts contain starch, which makes [[iodine]] turn blue/black. The blue/black stain is what shows starch is present. You could take "before & after" photos to prove the black areas were green at the start.

title: Seam ripper
text:
A '''seam ripper''' is a cutting [[tool]]. It is used for removing stitches in [[sewing]] and cutting open buttonholes made on a [[sewing machine]]. Sometimes it is also called a thread ripper.

The tool usually has a handle, shaft, and head. The head has two points: one flattened to form a pointed [[blade]] and the other  forming a small point. 

To use a seam ripper to remove sewn threads, the blade is placed underneath the thread to be cut. The thread slips down between the two points, and the tool is then lifted upwards allowing the blade to cut through the thread. Then the loose thread ends can be removed.

title: Vitamin C
text:
[[File:L-Ascorbic acid.svg|thumb|Ascorbic acid (vitamin C)]]
'''Vitamin C''' (also known as '''ascorbic acid''', '''hybrin''')<ref>{{Cite web|title=MeSH Browser|url=https://meshb.nlm.nih.gov/record/ui?ui=D001205|access-date=2026-04-01|website=meshb.nlm.nih.gov}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2017-10-23|title=Vitamins and minerals - Vitamin C|url=https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-c/|access-date=2026-04-09|website=nhs.uk|language=en}}</ref> is a [[vitamin]]. It is found in fresh [[fruit]]s, [[berry|berries]] and [[vegetable]]s. It is one of the [[water]]-soluble vitamins (like [[B vitamins|vitamin B]]). Vitamin C is important in wound healing.<ref name=":0" /> It helps the body keep the [[skin]], [[Blood vessel|blood vessels]], [[Bone|bones]] and [[Cartilage|bone cartilage]] healthy.<ref name=":0" /> 

Without enough vitamin C, a person can get a [[disease|sickness]] called [[scurvy]].<ref name=":0" /> Lack of vitamin C was a serious health problem on long ocean trips where supplies of fresh fruit were quickly used up. Many people died from scurvy on these trips before vitamin C was known as the cause. 

Vitamin C was first discovered in 1928. In 1932, it was proved to stop the sickness called scurvy. That fruit was a cure for scurvy was known long before vitamins were known to exist.

Humans cannot make vitamin C and have to get it from diet. Most [[animal]]s make their own vitamin C but some [[mammal]]s cannot. Those that cannot include the main suborder of [[primate]]s, the [[Haplorhini]]: these are the [[tarsier]]s, [[monkey]]s and [[ape]]s, including [[human]]s. Others are [[bat]]s, [[capybara]]s and [[guinea pig]]s.

[[File:Patates à l'eau.JPG|thumb|280px|Potato with peel contains 20 mg/100 g of vitamin C]]

== History ==
Through history the need for people to eat fresh plant food to help them get through long [[siege]]s or long sea trips was known by some wise people but was often forgotten.

The first attempt to prove this idea was by a ship's doctor in the [[Royal Navy]] called James Lind. At sea in May 1747 he gave some crew members [[lemon]] juice as well as their normal food, while others continued on normal food alone. The results showed that lemons prevented the disease. Lind wrote up his work and published it in 1753. Lind's work was slow to be noticed. In 1795 the British navy adopted lemon or [[lime]] juice as food for sailors. The men hated the sour taste, and had to be forced to take it. Limes, oranges; [[sauerkraut]], salted cabbage, malt, and soup were tried with various effects. [[James Cook]] relied on sauerkraut to prevent the disease on his long voyages of exploration.

It was originally thought that only humans got scurvy. However, in 1907 [[Alex Holst]] and [[Theodore Frohlich]], two [[Norway|Norwegian]] chemists found that [[guinea pig]]s could also get it if not given fresh food.

In 1928 the Arctic explorer [[Vilhjalmur Stefansson]] proved that [[Eskimo]]s ([[Inuit]]) are able to avoid scurvy with almost no plant food in their diet by eating raw meat.

In 1912 the [[Polish American]] scientist [[Casimir Funk]] first used the word [[vitamin]] for something present in food in small amounts that is essential to health. He named the unknown thing that prevented scurvy Vitamin C.

From 1928 to 1933, the [[Hungary|Hungarian]] research team of [[Joseph L Svirbely]] and [[Albert Szent-Gyorgyi]], and separately the [[United States|American]] [[Charles Glen King]], first took out vitamin C from food and showed it to be an [[acid]] they called [[ascorbic acid]].

In 1933/1934, the British chemists  [[Norman Haworth]] and  [[Edmund Hirst]], and separately the [[Poland|Polish]] [[Tadeus Reichstein]], successfully synthesized the vitamin.
It was the first man-made vitamin. This made it possible to make lots of vitamin C cheaply in factories. Haworth won the 1937 [[Nobel Prize for Chemistry]] for this work.

In 1959 the American [[J.J. Burns]] showed that the reason why some animals get scurvy is because their [[liver]] cannot make one chemical [[enzyme]] that other animals have.

== Function ==
In living organisms, ascorbate (vitamin C) is an [[antioxidant]], since it protects the body against [[oxidative stress]].<ref name=Padayatty>{{cite journal |first1=Sebastian J. |last1=Padayatty |first2=Arie |last2=Katz |first3=Yaohui |last3=Wang |first4=Peter |last4=Eck |first5=Oran |last5=Kwon |first6=Je-Hyuk |last6=Lee |first7=Shenglin |last7=Chen |first8=Christopher |last8=Corpe |first9=Anand |last9=Dutta |title=Vitamin C as an antioxidant: evaluation of its role in disease prevention. |pmid=12569111 |year=2003 |pages=18–35 |issue=1 |volume=22 |journal=Journal of the American College of Nutrition |doi=10.1080/07315724.2003.10719272 |s2cid=21196776 |url=http://www.jacn.org/cgi/content/full/22/1/18 |access-date=2011-03-18 |archive-date=2010-07-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100721110215/http://www.jacn.org/cgi/content/full/22/1/18 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is also a [[cofactor]] in at least eight [[enzyme|enzymatic]] reactions, including several [[collagen]] making (synthesis) reactions that cause the most severe symptoms of scurvy when they are dysfunctional.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.food.gov.uk/multimedia/pdfs/evm_c.pdf|title=UK Food Standards Agency|publisher=|access-date=2011-03-18|archive-date=2007-11-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071129082537/http://www.food.gov.uk/multimedia/pdfs/evm_c.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> In animals, these reactions are especially important in wound-healing and in preventing bleeding from capillaries.

* Vitamin C is needed for the production of [[collagen]] in the [[connective tissue]]. These fibres are in many places throughout the body; providing firm but flexible structure. Some [[biological tissue|tissues]] have a greater percentage of collagen, especially: [[skin]], [[mucous membrane]]s (like the gums) teeth, and [[bone]]s
* Vitamin C is required for making of [[dopamine]], [[noradrenaline]], and [[adrenaline]] in the [[nervous system]] or in the [[adrenal gland]]s
* Vitamin C is also needed to make [[carnitine]], important in the transfer of energy to the cell [[mitochondrion|mitochondria]]
* It is a strong [[antioxidant]]
* The [[tissue (biological)|tissues]] with greatest percentage of vitamin C—over 100 times the level in blood plasma—are the [[adrenal gland]]s, [[pituitary]], [[thymus]], [[corpus luteum]], and [[retina]]
* The [[brain]], [[spleen]], [[lung]], [[testicle]], [[lymph nodes]], [[liver]], [[thyroid]], [[small intestine|small intestinal]] [[mucous membrane|mucosa]], [[leukocytes]], [[pancreas]], [[kidney]], and [[salivary glands]] usually have 10 to 50 times the concentration present in plasma

=== Therapeutic use ===
Vitamin C is needed in the diet to prevent [[scurvy]]. It also has a reputation for being useful in the treatment of [[cold]]s and [[flu]], but results for this are mixed. The evidence to support this idea is ambiguous and the effect may depend on the dose size and dosing regime. 

==Daily requirement==
[[Vitamin|Vitamins]] are dosed in mg (milligrams), the total weight of the product (such as vitamin C) found in supplements or food. However, unlike [[vitamin D]] and other vitamins, where international units (UI) are used to convert the mg dose into other amounts needed for diet or supplements, and are based on how bioactive the vitamins are in the body, vitamin C does not do this.<ref>{{Cite web|title=What is Mcg in Vitamins? Guide to Vitamin Labels|url=https://www.naturemade.com/blogs/health-articles/what-is-mcg-in-vitamins|access-date=2026-04-19|website=Nature Made®|language=en}}</ref> The UI dose is usually not used in vitamin C and they normally use the mg dose. However, the UI dose of vitamin C is sometimes, or can be, 50mcg (micrograms, sometimes written as μg) equals 1 UI of vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Convert mcg to UI|url=https://www.thecalculatorsite.com/articles/units/convert-ui-to-mcg.php|website=TheCalculatorSite}}</ref>

A healthy person eating a balanced diet should be able to get all the vitamin C needed<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2017-10-23|title=Vitamins and minerals - Vitamin C|url=https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/vitamins-and-minerals/vitamin-c/|access-date=2026-04-09|website=nhs.uk|language=en}}</ref> to prevent the symptoms of scurvy from their daily diet. Vitamin C is not stored in the body which means it is needed every day.<ref name=":1" /> People who smoke, those under stress and [[Woman|women]] who are [[Pregnancy|pregnant]] have a slightly higher requirement.{{Citation needed|date=April 2026}} Because vitamin C cannot be made by the body on its own, it needs to come from diet<ref name=":1" /> or supplements. Taking less than 1,000 mg of vitamin C a day is not likely to cause harm.<ref name=":1" />

The amount of vitamin C needed to avoid deficiency symptoms and maintain health has been set by different national agencies as:
* 40 mg per day according to the [[UK Food Standards Agency]] and [[NHS]]<ref name=":1" />
* 60–95 mg per day [[US Food and Nutrition Board]] 2001 revision

Some researchers have calculated the amount needed for an adult human to achieve similar [[Serum (blood)|blood serum]] levels as Vitamin C synthesising mammals as follows:
* 200 mg per day - [[Linus Pauling Institute]] and [[National Institutes of Health|US National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) Recommendation
* 3000 mg per day - Vitamin C Foundation's recommendation
* 6000–12000 mg per day–Thomas Levy, Colorado Integrative Medical Centre recommendation
* 6000–18000 mg per day - [[Linus Pauling]]'s daily recommendation

High doses (thousands of mg) may result in [[diarrhea|diarrhoea]], which usually stops if the dose is reduced immediately.<ref name=":1" /> Alongside diarrhoea, high dose of vitamin C can cause gas ([[flatulence]]) and [[stomach pain]].<ref name=":1" /> Some researchers (Cathcart) claim the onset of diarrhoea to be an indication of where the body’s true vitamin C requirement lies.

The small size of the ascorbic acid molecule means the kidneys cannot retain it in the body. Quite a low level in the blood serum will cause traces to be present in the urine. All vitamin C synthesising mammals have traces in the urine at all times.

In April 1998 [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] reported alleged [[carcinogenic]] and [[teratogenic]] effects of excessive doses of vitamin C. This was given great prominence in the world's media. The effects were noted in [[test tube]] experiments and on only two of the 20 markers of free radical damage to DNA. They have not been supported by further evidence from living organisms. Almost all mammals manufacture their own vitamin C in amounts equivalent to human doses of thousands of milligrams per day. Large amounts of the vitamin are used in [[orthomolecular medicine]] and no harmful effects have been observed even in doses of 10,000 mg per day or more.

===Vitamin C deficiency===
Lack of ascorbic acid in the daily diet leads to a disease called scurvy, a form of [[avitaminosis]]. [[Symptom|Symptoms]] of scurvy include:<ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-10-25|title=Scurvy|url=https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/scurvy/|access-date=2026-04-09|website=nhs.uk|language=en}}</ref> 

* Swollen, bleeding [[gums]], sometimes loose [[Tooth|teeth]]
* [[Tiredness]], weakness in the body, and feeling sad

* Superficial bleeding, fragile [[blood vessel]]s
* Red or blue parts appearing on the skin (usually on the [[Leg|legs]] and [[Foot|feet]]) 
* Poor healing, bruising easily 
* Compromised [[immunity]]
* Mild [[anemia]]

==Sources of vitamin C==
===Plant sources===
Citrus fruits (such as [[lime]], [[Indian gooseberry]], [[lemon]], [[orange (fruit)|orange]], and [[grapefruit]]) are good sources of vitamin C.

Other foods that are good sources of vitamin C include [[papaya]], [[broccoli]], [[brussels sprout]]s, [[blackcurrant]]s, [[strawberry|strawberries]], [[cauliflower]], [[spinach]], [[cantaloupe]], sweet peppers, and [[kiwifruit]].

The following table is to give an idea of how much vitamin C is in different plant foods. Each individual fruit will vary.

The amount of vitamin C in foods of plant origin depends on the kind of plant, the kind of [[soil]] where it grew, how much rain and sun it got, the length of time since it was picked, and how it was stored since then.
Cooking food destroys vitamin C.

===Animal sources===
Most species of animals synthesise their own vitamin C. It is therefore not a vitamin for them. It is made by a series of [[enzyme]]-driven steps which convert [[glucose]] to [[ascorbic acid]]. This is done either in the [[kidney]]s ([[reptile]]s and some [[bird]]s), or the [[liver]] ([[mammal]]s and [[perching birds]]). The loss of an enzyme which is essential for [[ascorbic acid]] synthesis has occurred quite frequently in [[evolution]]. It has happened in most [[fish]], many [[bird]]s; some [[bats]], [[guinea pig]]s and most but not all [[primate]]s, including [[human]]s. The [[mutation]]s have not been lethal because ascorbic acid is so common in various food sources, especially fruit.

It was only realised in the 1920s that some cuts of meat and fish are also a source of vitamin C. However, the muscle and fat which make up the modern western diet are poor sources. As with fruit and vegetables cooking destroys the vitamin C content.

===Artificial chemical synthesis===
Vitamin C is produced from [[glucose]] by two main routes. The Reichstein process developed in the 1930s uses a single pre-fermentation followed by a purely chemical route. The more modern Two-Step fermentation process was originally developed in [[China]] in the 1960s, uses additional fermentation to replace part of the later chemical stages. Both processes yield approximately 60% vitamin C from the glucose feed.

In 1934, the Swiss pharmaceutical company [[Hoffmann-La Roche]] was the first to mass-produce synthetic vitamin C, under the brand name of Redoxon.
Main producers today are [[BASF]]/ [[Takeda]], [[Hoffmann-La Roche|Roche]], [[Merck]] and the China Pharmaceutical Group Ltd of the [[People's Republic of China]].

==Vitamin C advocacy==
[[Fred R. Klenner]], a doctor in [[Reidsville, North Carolina]] reported in 1949 that [[poliomyelitis]] yielded to repeated [[megadoses]] of [[intravenous]] vitamin C.

[[Nobel Prize]] winning chemist [[Linus Pauling]] began actively promoting vitamin C in the [[1960s]] as a means to greatly improve human health and resistance to disease.

Some medical and scientific opinion sees vitamin C as a low cost and safe way to treat infectious disease and to deal with a wide range of poisons.

A meta-study of the published research claimed that relatively high levels of vitamin C must be maintained in the body for it to function effectively as an [[antioxidant]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=New Developments and Novel Therapeutic Perspectives for Vitamin C|journal=The Journal of Nutrition|date=October 2007|year=2007|volume=137|issue=10|pages=2171–2184|url=http://jn.nutrition.org/content/137/10/2171.full|accessdate=22 February 2016|publisher=American Society for Nutrition|doi=10.1093/jn/137.10.2171|pmid=17884994|last1=Li|first1=Yi|last2=Schellhorn|first2=Herb E.}}</ref>

Some research shows that there are veterinary benefits of vitamin C as well.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Disease prevalence among dogs and cats in the United States and Australia and proportions of dogs and cats that receive therapeutic diets or dietary supplements|journal=Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association|date=August 2006|year=2006|volume=229|issue=4|pages=531–534|doi=10.2460/javma.229.4.531|pmid=16910851|url=http://avmajournals.avma.org/doi/abs/10.2460/javma.229.4.531|accessdate=22 February 2016|last1=Freeman|first1=Lisa M.|last2=Abood|first2=Sarah K.|last3=Fascetti|first3=Andrea J.|last4=Fleeman|first4=Linda M.|last5=Michel|first5=Kathryn E.|last6=Laflamme|first6=Dorothy P.|last7=Bauer|first7=Cassandra|last8=Kemp|first8=Brona L. E.|last9=Van Doren|first9=Janine R.|last10=Willoughby|first10=Kristina N.}}</ref> This is relevant to the question of whether cats and dogs can be healthily kept on non-meat diets.

One meta-study of the published research examined the effectiveness of ascorbic acid in the treatment of infectious disease and toxins. It was conducted in [[2002]] by Thomas Levy, medical director of the Colorado Integrative Medical Center in [[Denver, Colorado|Denver]]. It claimed that overwhelming scientific evidence exists for its therapeutic role.<ref>{{cite book|last=Levy|first=Thomas E.|title=Curing the Incurable: Vitamin C, Infectious Diseases, and Toxins|url=https://archive.org/details/curingincurablev0000levy|year=2002|publisher=Livon Books|isbn=1401069630}}</ref>

Some vitamin C advocates say that vitamin C is not used therapeutically because it cannot be patented. [[Pharmaceutical]] companies seek to generate [[revenue]] and [[profit]] their [[shareholder]]s. They may be reluctant to research or promote something that will make them little money.<ref>{{cite news|last=Sorkin|first=Andrew Ross|title=Do Drug Companies Make Drugs, or Money?|url=http://dealbook.nytimes.com/2014/06/02/do-drug-companies-make-drugs-or-money/?_php=true&_type=blogs&_r=1|accessdate=22 February 2016|newspaper=The New York Times|date=2 June 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=LaMattina|first=John|title='Do Drug Companies Make Drugs, or Money?' |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/johnlamattina/2014/07/29/do-drug-companies-make-drugs-or-money/#750db64f7fcf|work=Forbes.com|accessdate=22 February 2016}}</ref>

title: Dichlorphenolindophenol
text:
{{Orphan|date=March 2012}}
'''DCPIP''' (its full name is ''2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol'') is a [[blue]] [[chemical]] used as a [[dye]] because when it is [[oxidized]] it is blue.  Once DCPIP is [[reduction (chemistry)|reduced]] (by addition of [[electron]]s) it does not have a color anymore. This [[Chemical reaction|reaction]] can be reversed, and the [[Colorless|colourless]] DCPIP will turn blue again, when it is [[oxidation|oxidized]].

== Purpose ==
DCPIP is often used to measure the [[electron transport chain]] in [[plant]]s. It has a higher [[redox]] potential (electron affinity) than the [[Iron|Fe]]-[[Sulphur|S]] complex in [[Cytochrome|cytochrome b]] and will therefore "steal" electrons from it. This means that cytochrome c does not  receive them. The process cuts off the electron supply of  [[:Category:Photosynthesis|photosystem]] I. A common way to illustrate this change is by the addition of [[vitamin C]] [[solution]]. This reduces the 'jelly' by transforming it to a colourless mass. This experiment can be carried out to illustrate the effect of changing [[cell]] sizes on SA/V ([[Surface-area-to-volume ratio|surface area:volume ratio]]). This is known as [[Titration]].

title: Healthy diet
text:
[[File:USDA Food Pyramid.gif|thumb|right|325px|{{Center|[[United States Department of Agriculture]] [[food pyramid]] (click to enlarge)}}]]
A '''healthy diet''' or '''balanced diet'''<ref>{{Cite web|title=MeSH Browser|url=https://meshb.nlm.nih.gov/record/ui?ui=D000072001|access-date=2026-04-05|website=meshb.nlm.nih.gov}}</ref>       is a [[diet (nutrition)|diet]] that contains the right amounts of all the [[food group]]s. It includes [[fruit|fruits]], [[vegetable]]s, [[grain]]s, [[dairy products]], and [[protein]]. It does not include too much or too little of any kind of food.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://gethealthy.eliv.info/cgi-bin/index.pl/diet.html |title=Natural, Organic Healthy Living & Diet |access-date=2007-12-11 |archive-date=2018-02-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180211145025/http://gethealthy.eliv.info/cgi-bin/index.pl/diet.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Eating wrong amounts of a food group, whether it be too much or too little, is called an 'unhealthy diet' or an 'imbalanced diet'. A healthy diet is one that includes more foods that come from [[plant]]s, animals and fewer [[convenience food]]s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.berkeleywellness.com/healthy-eating/food/slideshow/14-keys-healthy-diet |title=14 Keys to a Healthy Diet |author= |website=University of California Berkeley Wellness |publisher= |accessdate=25 April 2016}}</ref>

== Basic nutrition ==
What is known about [[nutrition]] and diet keeps changing as more is learned.<ref name=Mayo>{{cite web |url=http://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/nutrition-and-healthy-eating/basics/nutrition-basics/hlv-20049477 |title=Nutrition basics |author=Mayo Clinic staff |website= |publisher=Mayo Foundation for Medical Education and Research |accessdate=25 April 2016}}</ref> However, basic nutrition remains much the same.<ref name=Mayo/> The best advice is to talk to a [[Medical doctor|doctor]] or [[dietitian]] for personalized information based on an individual's [[lifestyle]], [[health]], and food likes and dislikes.<ref name=Mayo/>
* Basic nutrition begins with a diet based on the major food groups that includes [[vegetable]]s, [[whole grain]]s, and [[dairy product]]s.<ref name=Mayo/> It should also have lean [[protein]] such as [[bean]]s, legumes, [[nut (fruit)|nut]]s and [[seed]]s plus healthy fats.<ref name=Mayo/>
* A basic nutrition plan should include [[wikt:guideline|guideline]]s for how much food from each group to eat.<ref name=Mayo/>
* Foods should be those that can be found in local [[grocery store]]s instead of specialty and [[gourmet]] food stores.<ref name=Mayo/>
* A basic food plan should be based on an individual's [[budget]], lifestyle and (healthy) preferences.<ref name=Mayo/>
* Drink plenty of water.<ref name=PCFSN>{{cite web |url=http://www.fitness.gov/eat-healthy/how-to-eat-healthy/ |title=How to Eat Healthy |author= |website= |publisher=President's Council on Fitness, Sports & Nutrition |accessdate=25 April 2016}}</ref> Drink fewer [[Soft drink]]s, [[energy drink]]s and [[sports drink]]s which usually have [[sugar]].<ref name=PCFSN/>
* Read the [[Nutrition facts label|food labels]] to see what is in the foods.<ref name=PCFSN/> For [[example]], labels usually show what foods are lower in [[Table salt|sodium]] such as in [[soup]], [[bread]], and [[Frozen food|frozen meals]].<ref name=PCFSN/>
* A healthy diet should include [[seafood]]s (such as [[salmon]], [[tuna]], and [[trout]]) and [[shellfish]] (such as [[crab]], [[mussel]]s, and [[oyster]]s). Seafood has protein, [[mineral]]s, and [[omega-3 fatty acid]]s which are [[heart]]-healthy.<ref name=PCFSN/>
* Basic nutrition should contain balanced amounts of [[macronutrients]] for [[energy]].<ref name=EFIC>{{cite web |url=http://www.eufic.org/page/en/nutrition/carbohydrates/ |title=Carbohydrates |author= |website= |publisher=The European Food Information Council |accessdate=25 April 2016 |archive-date=14 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414202251/http://www.eufic.org/page/en/nutrition/carbohydrates/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Carbohydrates are one of the three macro-[[nutrient]]s in the human diet (fat and protein are the other two).<ref name=EFIC/>
* A healthy diet can replace [[dieting]] for weight loss.<ref name=zelmanWebMD>{{cite web |url=http://www.webmd.com/diet/dieting-is-out-healthy-eating-is-in |title=Dieting Is Out; Healthy Eating Is In |author=Kathleen M. Zelman |date=17 June 2010 |website= |publisher=WebMD, LLC |accessdate=25 April 2016}}</ref> Eating healthy, along with [[physical exercise]] and practicing moderation, can lead to better health in the long run.<ref name=zelmanWebMD/>

title: Dye
text:
{{cleanup|date=March 2026}}
'''Dye''' is a [[substance]] used to [[color]] materials. It is often used to color the [[fabric]] used to make [[clothing]]. It has low [[solubility]]. A [[pigment]] will not do this because it will not stick to the [[fiber]]s of the fabric and color them. A dye can be natural, usually made from plant material such as berries, or a dye can be artificial, meaning that it is made by humans from chemicals such as [[petrochemical]]s.

Most natural dyes are gotten from different parts of a [[plant]] like the [[Root|roots]], [[Fruit|fruits]], [[bark]], [[Leaf|leaves]], [[wood]], [[Fungus|fungi]] and [[Lichen|lichens]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Harvesting color : how to find plants and make natural dyes|url=https://archive.org/details/harvestingcolorh0000burg|last=Burgess, Rebecca, 1977-|date=2011|publisher=Artisan|others=Green, Paige|isbn=978-1-57965-425-2|location=New York|oclc=667210526}}</ref> Most dyes are synthetic and are made from petrochemicals.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_F4hAwAAQBAJ&dq=organic+dye+laser&pg=PA539|title=Laser Fundamentals|last=Silfvast|first=William T.|date=2008-07-21|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-85557-0|language=en}}</ref>

==Classification==
Dyes can be classified based on their [[solubility]] and chemical properties. 

* [[Acid dye]]s can dissolve in water.  They are used on [[fiber]]s such as [[silk]], [[wool]], [[nylon]].  Most [[food coloring]] that are made by man are acid dyes.  Examples of acid dye are Alizarine Pure Blue B, [[Acid red 88]], etc.
* Basic dyes can dissolve in water.  They are mainly used on [[acrylic]] fibers.  They may also be used on wool and silk.  Basic dyes are also used to make [[paper]] colourful.

title: Poetry
text:
'''Poetry''' is written, spoken or sung [[language]] that is used in stronger or more original ways than [[prose]] is used. Poetry uses the ''[[Meaning|meanings]]'' of words as prose does; but it also uses the ''[[Sound|sounds]]'' of words as if they were [[music]], especially [[Rhyme|rhymes]], other repeating sounds, and [[Rhythm|rhythms]] ([[Tempo|beats]] or [[Meter (poetry)|meters]]).<ref>"poetry". Oxford Dictionary of Literary Terms (4 ed.), OUP 2015. Online access via Wikipedia Library 2 January 2023.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Sherazi|first=HH|title=It is All About Poems|url=https://itisallaboutpoems.com/|access-date=2023-01-02|website=owl.purdue.edu|archive-date=2023-08-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230820041015/https://itisallaboutpoems.com/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Poetry arranges words and groups of words to make [[Repetition|repetitions]] and [[Parallelism (grammar)|parallelisms]]. Poetry uses [[Figure of speech|figures of speech]], [[Ellipsis|ellipses]] and [[delayed identifications|delayed identification]] to suggest that there is more meaning in the language.

Some people believe that poetry began when language began. They think it is probably "as old as [[history]] and older, present wherever [[religion]] is present."<ref>{{Cite web|title=poetry - Poetry as a mode of thought: the Protean encounter {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/art/poetry/Poetry-as-a-mode-of-thought-the-Protean-encounter|access-date=2023-01-02|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}}</ref>

The English words "poetry," "poet," and "poem" first appeared in English in the 14th century. They come from the [[Latin]] word ''poeta'', which itself probably comes from ''poiein'', a [[Greek language|Greek]] word that means "to make."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Poets|first=Academy of American|title=Poetry {{!}} Academy of American Poets|url=https://poets.org/glossary/poetry|access-date=2023-01-02|website=poets.org}}</ref><ref>"poetry". Oxford Dictionary of Literary Terms (4 ed.), OUP 2015. Online access via Wikipedia Library 2 January 2023.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=poetry {{!}} Search Online Etymology Dictionary|url=https://www.etymonline.com/search?q=poetry&ref=searchbar_searchhint|access-date=2023-01-02|website=www.etymonline.com}}</ref>

There are three major kinds of poetry: [[lyric]], [[narrative]], and [[dramatic]].<ref>"poetry". Oxford Dictionary of Literary Terms (4 ed.), OUP 2015. Online access via Wikipedia Library 2 January 2023.</ref>

* Lyric poetry tends to be brief and is often about [[Emotion|emotions]].
* Narrative poetry tells a story with a [[Plot (narrative)|plot]].
* Dramatic poetry can be [[Performance|performed]] as a [[Play (theatre)|play]].

A poem can be as short as a few words or as long as a book. A one-line poem is called a monostich.<ref>{{Cite web|last=briefpoems|date=2016-01-06|title=Slates – One-line poems (Monostich)|url=https://briefpoems.wordpress.com/2016/01/07/slates-one-line-poems-monostich/|access-date=2023-01-02|website=Brief Poems|language=en}}</ref> A poem that is as long as a book is an [[epic]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Epic {{!}} Definition, Characteristics, Examples, Development, & Facts {{!}} Britannica|url=https://www.britannica.com/art/epic|access-date=2023-01-02|website=www.britannica.com|language=en}}</ref>

Poems are often printed on the page as lines and groups of lines called [[Stanza|stanzas]].

There are many different "poetic forms" or ways to shape a poem on the printed page or in the [[ear]] of the person who hears it. Some forms are: the [[sonnet]], [[haiku]], the [[ballad]], the [[stev]], the [[prose poem]], the [[ode]], [[free verse]], [[blank verse]], [[Limerick (poetry)|limerick]], and [[Nursery rhyme|nursery rhymes]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Brewer|first=Robert Lee|title=List of 168 Poetic Forms for Poets|url=https://www.writersdigest.com/write-better-poetry/list-of-50-poetic-forms-for-poets|access-date=2023-01-02|website=Writer's Digest|language=en}}</ref>
